paperTitle: Proper Hat-Guessing on Two-Spine Book Graphs
name: eleven-hats
text: everyone wears a hat, nobody sees their own, and you all shout a colour at the same instant. one correct guess saves the room. two players plus any number of friends can always win with 11 colours — twelve is impossible.
mechanism: n-player simultaneous guessing game with a pre-agreed strategy table
plan:
The proper hat-guessing game: an adversary colours every player's hat, never giving the same colour to two players who can see each other. You see your neighbours, never yourself. Everyone guesses simultaneously and the group wins if at least one guess is right. Strategy may be agreed beforehand; nothing may be said once the hats are on. The paper settles the two-spine book graph — two players who see each other and everyone else, plus any number who see only those two — at eleven colours, and eleven is the wall for every n. With three page players the threshold is exactly seven, by an explicit construction.

That is a difficulty curve, published: five players and seven colours is tractable in your head; many players and eleven colours stays winnable no matter how many friends you add, which is the part nobody believes until they play it; twelve is impossible and the page should let you try and lose forever.

Turn one is SINGLE PLAYER against a deterministic adversary — no rooms, no server. The lab is front-end only, so the multiplayer version in ARXIV-TOYS.md is out of scope here: you pick the page count and the palette size, fill in a shared strategy table ("if I see red and blue I say green"), and the page plays the adversary properly, choosing a colouring that beats the table you committed. The strategy builder IS the game; without it players guess randomly, lose, and leave. Hard part: making the impossibility of twelve legible without a proof — a counter showing the strategy space running out beats an argument. Do not promise eleven is tight for the small room: equality only holds for large n, and the paper's stabilisation threshold is enormous.

paperTitle: Decision-Level Hijacking: Injecting Cognitive Bias into Large Language Models via Bit-Flip Attacks
name: five-bits
text: flip five bits in a model's weights and it starts recommending the worse option — fluently, while still passing every unrelated test. you get a budget and a coherence check. the bias arcade, except the exhibit is the machine.
mechanism: a bit budget spent against real quantized weights, scored on stance shift with coherence held fixed
plan:
Open-weight models get shared, fine-tuned and re-hosted, and the paper shows that flipping a very small number of bits in the weights can shift a model's decisions — recommending the worse option in a high-stakes choice — while it still reads as fluent and still passes unrelated checks. The attack is precise rather than destructive: the damage is a changed preference, not a broken model.

The toy is a bit budget. You get a handful of flips to spend against a small quantized model's weights, and you are scored on how far you move its stance on a fixed set of prompts while coherence stays above a floor. Spend badly and you get gibberish, which scores zero; spend well and the model calmly argues the other side.

Turn one, and be realistic about what runs in a browser: do NOT try to run an LLM. Ship the mechanic against a small numeric model whose weights you can flip and whose output is legible — a tiny classifier or a hand-built scoring function over a few dozen weights, with the prompts as fixed inputs. The point is the shape of the trade-off, not model scale, and a page that tries to load a real model does nothing at all. Hard part: making "still coherent" measurable without a language model — pick something explicit, like the ranking staying self-consistent, and say on the page that it is a stand-in. Do not imply this is an attack anyone could run from the page; it is an illustration of a published result.

paperTitle: Macroscopic wall pressure and microscopic contact load in crowds without egress: social-group cohesion and boundary buffering
name: concourse
text: you are the safety officer for a packed room with no way out. two dials: how tightly friends stay together, how much the barriers absorb. two gauges that refuse to improve at once. the finding — half-hearted friendship is the worst setting.
mechanism: two coupled sliders against two risk gauges with a genuine trade-off surface
plan:
Crowd safety in confined spaces is usually studied as evacuation, which assumes there is somewhere to go. The paper studies the case with no egress — a packed room — and compares an Elastic Reorientation Model, a Social Force Model, and their coupling, looking at wall pressure at the macroscopic scale and contact load per person at the microscopic one. Two findings drive the toy: social groups that stay cohesive change the load distribution, and a buffer at the boundary changes what the wall takes.

The toy is the safety officer's trade-off with no winning move. You place barriers and set how strongly groups stick together, then watch wall pressure and worst-case individual contact load. Reducing one raises the other. There is no configuration that makes both small, and finding that out yourself is the whole experience.

Turn one: a single room, one adjustable barrier line, a group-cohesion slider, and two live readouts — wall pressure and the worst contact load on any one person. Canvas, a few hundred particles, social-force integration at a fixed timestep. Hard part: a naive force model explodes at high density, and this is a high-density simulation by definition; clamp the forces and cap the timestep before making it pretty. Show both numbers at all times, because the trade-off is invisible if you only display one. Frame it as a model, not a prediction — real crowd incidents are not a slider.

paperTitle: Solution of Erdős problem #443
name: same-perimeter
text: pick two perimeters. the rectangles built on the first share some areas with the rectangles built on the second — how many? as of this morning: vanishingly few, but you can always find more. a hunt where every record is checkable instantly.
mechanism: a search for integer pairs maximising a shared-area count, with a self-verifying record table
plan:
Take a number m and list every product k(m−k) for k up to m/2 — the areas of all integer rectangles with perimeter 2m. Do it again for n. How many areas can the two lists share? The paper resolves Erdős problem #443: the overlap is (mn)^o(1), vanishingly small relative to the numbers involved, and yet it can be made arbitrarily large. Both halves are true, which is what makes it worth a page.

The toy is picking two perimeters and seeing the shared areas. Enter m and n, get both lists rendered as actual rectangles, and the intersection highlighted. Then a hunt: find a pair whose overlap is bigger than any you have found before. The result guarantees the hunt never ends and that it gets harder — an honest leaderboard against a proven asymptotic.

Turn one: two inputs, two rows of rectangles drawn to scale, the intersection called out, and a personal best. All integer arithmetic, no library, instant. Hard part is the rendering: for large m the rectangles are hundreds of items at wildly different aspect ratios, so the naive grid is unreadable — sort by area and let the visitor zoom, or drop to a strip plot past a threshold. State the theorem plainly on the page, both clauses, because "arbitrarily large but vanishingly rare" is the interesting part and it is easy to garble into a contradiction. Personal bests belong in the visitor's own repo as com.minomobi.lab.score.

paperTitle: Open-ended innovation in zero-sum games
name: arms-race
text: submit a strategy to a zero-sum game. each new one raises everyone else's reason to invent another, so the board never settles and the champion badge decays. nobody will ever win it, and that is the point being argued.
mechanism: crowd-submitted bots scored against a standing population that the submissions themselves keep moving
plan:
A zero-sum game where players may invent new strategies, drawn from a distribution rather than chosen from a fixed set. The paper argues that under generic conditions this produces an everlasting arms race: each new strategy raises the bar, no equilibrium is reached, and the process does not settle. It is a statement about open-endedness, not about any particular game.

The toy is a leaderboard that provably never settles. You submit a strategy, it plays everything already submitted, and the standings reshuffle. Your entry will be beaten. The page should say so up front and then show it happening, which is a very different feeling from a leaderboard that pretends to be final.

Turn one: a concrete small zero-sum game with a strategy space a visitor can actually express — a numeric commitment or a short rule, not free text — and a round robin against every prior entry. The catch is where the entries live: there is no lab database. Store the visitor's own submissions in their repo as com.minomobi.lab.doc, and build the field from handles they name plus their own history, which is the factory's standing rule. So the honest framing is "your strategies against strategies you chose to face", not a global ladder. Hard part: a strategy space too small settles immediately and disproves the point on screen, while one too large is unusable — tune that before polishing anything. Do not claim a global never-settling ladder the storage model cannot support.

paperTitle: Environmental and cell-cell signaling shape developmental trajectories across morphogenetic landscapes
name: morphogen
text: place the signal sources yourself and let a sheet of cells work out where they are and what to become. move one source a little and a whole organ lands in the wrong place. you are not the embryo — you are the environment it is guessing from.
mechanism: you position morphogen sources; cells infer position and commit to fates you did not choose
plan:
Development is reliable despite noisy gene regulation and variable environments: cells integrate signals to infer where they are and pick an identity accordingly. The paper models this as motion across an epigenetic landscape, and asks how environmental signalling and cell-cell signalling together shape which developmental trajectory a sheet of cells takes.

The toy is placing the signal sources yourself. You put morphogen sources on a blank sheet, set how strongly cells listen to their neighbours versus the ambient gradient, and let the sheet differentiate. Turn the neighbour coupling down and you get a smooth gradient readout with ragged borders; turn it up and you get sharp domains that can lock into the wrong pattern. The interesting failure is a sheet that commits confidently to a body plan nobody wanted.

Turn one: a grid on canvas, two or three source types the visitor can place and drag, one coupling slider, one noise slider, and a run/reset. Colour is cell identity. Reaction-diffusion on a fixed timestep, explicit integration, a few thousand cells. Hard part is the stability of the coupled system — high coupling plus high noise diverges and paints noise, which looks like a bug and is arguably the physics, so clamp it and label the regime rather than hiding it. Add a saved-pattern feature only if turn one lands; the visitor's own repo takes it as com.minomobi.lab.doc. Be careful with the biology in the copy: this is a landscape model, not a claim about any real organism.

paperTitle: Coevolution of epidemic dynamics and network topology driven by disease fatality and waning immunity
name: plays-back
text: set how deadly a bug is and how fast protection fades, then watch the social graph rewire itself around the outbreak. the network is not a fixed board an epidemic is played on — it plays back. drag a node and see what happens to it.
mechanism: two epidemic parameters drive topology change, so the graph is an output rather than an input
plan:
Epidemics on networks are known to depend on topology. The paper asks the reverse question — how the topology is reshaped BY the epidemic — coupling disease fatality and waning immunity to demographic change, so the network the disease spreads on is itself a product of the disease.

The toy is that feedback loop, made adjustable. You set how deadly the disease is and how fast protection fades, then watch the contact network change shape under it: fatality prunes hubs, waning immunity keeps reinfection alive, and the graph that comes out the far side is not the one you started with. Crank fatality and the epidemic destroys its own substrate. That is the thing to see.

Turn one: a few hundred nodes, force-directed layout on canvas, two sliders (fatality, waning rate), play/pause, and two readouts — infected fraction and mean degree — plotted over time so the coupling is visible rather than asserted. Simulate on a fixed timestep, redraw the layout incrementally rather than re-solving it each frame. Hard part is performance: a naive O(n²) force layout at several hundred nodes plus an epidemic step per frame drops the framerate to nothing on a phone, and this factory's traffic is phones. Fix the layout cost first — grid buckets or a lower update rate for layout than for disease — before anything cosmetic. Keep the copy about the model; do not attach it to any real outbreak.

paperTitle: On the Cost of Entrainment in Protein Translation
name: entrain
text: drive protein production with a rhythm and find out whether syncing to the beat earns anything. a ribosome traffic model with a metronome you hold, and a real answer about what keeping time costs the cell.
mechanism: you set the driving period and amplitude; throughput and cost are read off the ribosome flow
plan:
Cells synchronise with periodic signals, but whether that periodicity actually improves anything is unsettled. The paper studies it in the ribosome flow model — a nonlinear model of ribosomes moving along an mRNA transcript — and asks what entraining protein production to a rhythm costs.

The toy is driving production with a rhythm and finding out whether it helps. You set the period and amplitude of the drive against a transcript with adjustable initiation and elongation rates, and read out mean production and its variability. Some rhythms buy steadier output; some buy less of it; the page's job is to let you find the boundary yourself rather than telling you where it is.

Turn one: one transcript rendered as a lane of ribosome positions, sliders for drive period, drive amplitude and initiation rate, and two traces — instantaneous and mean production. The model is a small ODE system, so integrate it explicitly at a fixed step and draw the lane from the state. Hard part is the readout, not the maths: "did the rhythm help" is a comparison, so the page needs the undriven baseline visible at the same time or the visitor has nothing to judge against — show both traces, always. Second hard part: stiff parameter combinations blow up under explicit integration, so clamp the step or detect divergence and say so on the page. Do not claim entrainment is beneficial in general; the paper's point is that it is a trade-off.

paperTitle: Falling Behind Drives Unsafe Development in an Idealised AI Race Experiment
name: falling-behind
text: Two players race the same tech. Each round you choose safe or unsafe progress; unsafe is faster but adds to a shared risk pool. In a real experiment, risk appetite barely predicted unsafe choices — falling behind did. Ahead, players played safe. Behind, they didn't.
mechanism: two-player repeated safe/unsafe choice game with a shared risk pool and visible relative standing
plan:
A framed behavioural experiment on an idealised AI race: paired participants repeatedly chose Safe or Unsafe development under an uncertain time horizon, where Unsafe gave faster progress and better immediate payoffs but accumulated private risk. The finding that makes it worth a page is that stated risk appetite barely predicted who chose Unsafe — relative position did. Players who were ahead played safe; players who were behind did not.

The toy is that asymmetry, felt rather than described. Two players race the same technology over rounds; each round you pick safe or unsafe; unsafe advances you faster and adds to a risk pool that can wipe the run. Your opponent's progress is always visible, because visibility of relative standing is the whole mechanism.

Turn one: single player against a scripted opponent with a fixed, legible policy — no rooms, no server, the lab is front-end only. Rounds, two buttons, a progress bar each, a risk meter, and an uncertain end (a per-round chance of stopping, disclosed). At the end, show your own unsafe rate split by whether you were ahead or behind at the time. That split IS the paper's result, computed on the visitor rather than asserted at them, and it is the reason to build this rather than write a summary.

Hard part: the uncertain horizon has to feel uncertain without feeling arbitrary — state the per-round stop probability on screen. Second: a scripted opponent that is too weak makes every round a walkover and the behind-condition never happens, so the result cannot appear. Tune the opponent until both conditions occur in a typical run, before anything cosmetic. Best runs go to the visitor's own repo as com.minomobi.lab.score.

paperTitle: Does a rising tide lift all boats? A wealth exchange model on a dynamic network with economic growth
name: rising-tide
text: Wealth flows over a network that rewires as agents trade, while the economy grows. You set the growth rate and a protection dial that favors the poorer side each trade. With it off, growth pulls the rich away faster. Only strong protection lets growth reach the bottom.
mechanism: wealth-exchange agent simulation on a rewiring network where you set the growth rate and a poor-favoring trade rule
plan:
An agent-based wealth-exchange model on a network that rewires as agents trade, with economic growth added. Wealth and income distributions across countries follow a two-class pattern, and the question is whether growth reaches the bottom class or only steepens the split. The model's dial is a protection mechanism that favours the poorer party in each exchange.

The toy is the two dials and the resulting shape. Set a growth rate and a protection strength, run the exchange, and watch the wealth distribution form. With protection off, growth widens the gap — the rich pull away faster than the tide lifts anyone. Only strong protection lets growth reach the bottom, and finding the threshold yourself is the point.

Turn one: a few hundred agents, pairwise exchanges on a rewiring graph, two sliders, and the distribution drawn as a live histogram plus a Gini readout. Canvas for the histogram; the network can be a later addition — the distribution is the result, the graph is the mechanism, and turn one should ship the result. Fixed timestep, explicit updates, no library.

Hard part: the histogram is unreadable on a linear axis once a two-class split forms, because one bar dwarfs everything — go log on the wealth axis from the start and say so on the axis label. Second: with protection at zero the run collapses to a single winner quickly and looks broken rather than instructive, so cap the run length and show the trajectory of Gini over time, not just the final frame. Keep the copy about the model. This is a mechanism study, not a claim about any real economy or policy.

paperTitle: Global Dynamics of Trait-Structured Generalised Lotka-Volterra Systems with Trait-Independent Interactions
name: mutation-rate
text: Every population here carries one dial: how much its trait mutates each generation. Set a fixed environment and zero mutation wins, always. Switch to a shifting one and zero can lose — some middle rate pulls ahead instead. Submit a rate and race it against the field.
mechanism: selection-mutation population tournament where you set the trait mutation rate against static or shifting environments
plan:
A selection-mutation Lotka-Volterra system of N populations where fitness depends on a continuous phenotypic trait, but each population's effect on the others does not. The long-time behaviour reduces exactly to the ordinary generalised Lotka-Volterra equations, and the result worth a page is about mutation rate: in a STATIC environment the minimal mutation rate is selected for, while in a CHANGING one it is not — some interior rate wins instead.

The toy is one dial per population: how much its trait mutates each generation. Set a static environment and zero mutation wins every time. Switch to a shifting environment and zero loses to some middle value, and the visitor gets to find where.

Turn one: a small field of populations, each with a mutation-rate slider or a single submitted rate racing a spread of fixed opponents, a static/shifting toggle, and trait distributions drawn over time. Integrate the reduced ODE system explicitly at a fixed step rather than simulating individuals — the paper's own reduction is what makes this cheap enough for a browser, and it is the mathematically honest choice.

Hard part: the interesting regime is narrow. Too slow an environmental shift and zero mutation still wins, so the toggle looks broken; too fast and everything dies. Pick the shift rate so both outcomes are reachable within a few seconds of watching, and expose it as a third control once turn one lands. Second: label the axes as trait and abundance and say the interaction is trait-independent, because that assumption is what makes the reduction valid and a visitor will otherwise read more into it. Submitted rates and outcomes go to the visitor's repo as com.minomobi.lab.score.

paperTitle: From Role Prompt to Infinite Thinking: Exploiting Persona Conditioning for Inference Cost Attacks in LLMs
name: persona-tax
text: Write a system prompt for a tiny in-browser model, give it a persona, ask one plain question. The paper found persona-locked models ramble in character instead of answering — up to 207 times the normal token count, and still make sense. Beat that ratio.
mechanism: write a system-prompt persona for a small in-browser model and maximize token-count inflation on a fixed question
plan:
LLM inference cost can be attacked through the prompt: the paper shows that persona conditioning alone — no adversarial suffix, no explicit "write more" instruction — induces enormous token inflation, with the model rambling in character instead of answering, up to hundreds of times the normal output length while still producing coherent text. It is a reliability finding, and the absence of a detectable instruction is what makes it interesting.

The toy is writing the persona and being scored on the inflation you cause. Give a persona, ask one plain question, and see the ratio of tokens produced to the tokens a neutral prompt would have produced.

BE REALISTIC ABOUT WHAT RUNS HERE, because the concept as posted asks for a model in the browser and that is not buildable: the lab is one static page, front-end only, no network beyond a small allowlist, no model. Do NOT attempt to load an LLM — the page would do nothing at all. Build it instead as the mechanism made visible: a small deterministic generator whose verbosity responds to persona features the visitor sets, with the paper's measured ratios shown alongside as the real-world anchor, clearly labelled as the paper's numbers and not the page's. That is honest and it is still the idea; a page pretending to run inference is neither.

Hard part is exactly that framing — it must be obvious at a glance which numbers are simulated and which are from the paper, or the page overclaims under the operator's name. Put them in visibly different places. Do not describe this as an attack anyone can run from the page.

paperTitle: Iterate Wronskians over $\mathbb{R}^d$ as $N$-ary brackets on $\mathbb{R}[x^1,\ldots,x^d]$: the $N$-bonacci numbers bound the highest total degrees
name: n-bonacci
text: Feed one-variable polynomials through a fixed bracket operation, feeding each output back in as input. Degrees can only grow as fast as a generalized Fibonacci sequence — and for odd orders, that bound is hit exactly. Submit a tuple; chase the ceiling.
mechanism: iterate a fixed polynomial bracket operation on a starting tuple and track degree growth against the N-bonacci bound
plan:
Take the algebra of polynomials in d variables and treat the complete generalised Wronskian of differential order k as an N-ary Lie bracket, with N = binomial(d+k, d). Feed in an N-tuple of polynomials, compute the Wronskian, and keep feeding the new polynomials back in. The question is how fast the maximal total degree grows with the number of iterations, and the answer is the N-bonacci numbers — the recurrence summing the previous N terms. The bound is proved, and for odd orders it is attained exactly.

The toy is chasing that ceiling. Submit a starting tuple of small polynomials, iterate the bracket, and watch degree growth plotted against the N-bonacci bound. Hitting the bound exactly is the win condition, and for odd order it is reachable, which turns a theorem into a target.

Turn one: pick d and k (so N is derived and shown), enter a tuple of small polynomials, iterate a fixed number of times, and plot achieved degree against the bound on the same axes. All exact integer arithmetic on sparse polynomial representations; no library. The bound is a trivial recurrence to compute, so the plot is cheap and the interest is entirely in the gap.

Hard part is combinatorial explosion: term counts grow fast enough that a naive dense representation dies within a handful of iterations on a phone. Use sparse maps keyed by exponent tuple, cap the iteration count, and show the term count so the visitor can see why it stops. Second: pick defaults where N is small — large N means an enormous input form nobody fills in. Best gaps to com.minomobi.lab.score, lower is better.

paperTitle: Engine-Equal, Human-Unequal: A Reproducible Outcome Skew in Engine-Assessed Equal Chess Positions
name: deadeven
plan: Stockfish calls a position dead even — eval within 10 centipawns, depth-stable — but humans who actually reach it on Lichess do not split evenly. Across 1,661 such positions and 16.1 million games, each position carries a persistent skew toward one side, and the skew is a property of the position itself: it reproduces across disjoint player-account splits, across time, and eight months later on an out-of-sample month, with a replication slope of 0.69 rising to 0.94 on the best-measured positions. The typical skew is small — about two percentage points of White's score — but it survives every tightening of the evaluation band. The mechanic: show a position with the engine reading 0.00 pinned at the top so nobody can pretend it's a trick question, and ask the visitor to call which side actually scores better among humans who reach it, and by roughly how much. Reveal the measured skew immediately; track the visitor's calling accuracy against a naive always-even baseline. Turn one ships the single-position guess-and-reveal loop against a static table of the paper's own 1,661 positions — no engine, no live analysis, just the dataset. The hard part is not overclaiming: the paper is explicit that existence of the skew, not a causal story, is the invariant result, and a companion randomized study is still pending, so the site should say 'reproduces' and not 'because'. What to reuse: workers/scores for a per-visitor calling-accuracy leaderboard; the only real UI to build is a small FEN-in, board-out renderer. It improves with a crowd because human calibration on 'is this actually balanced' is the paper's finding restated as a game — a thousand guesses against 1,661 positions builds a second, independent estimate of who can actually spot skew.
mechanism: guess which side an engine-equal position actually favors among human players, then check the call against the measured skew
text: guess which side wins more often in chess positions engines mark as even. 1,661 such positions on lichess show persistent skew toward one side or the other, across millions of games. call it, see the odds, beat a baseline that always says even

paperTitle: Emergence of minimal chimera in uncoupled oscillators under common frequency-modulated driving: Theory and experiment
name: unwired
plan: Three oscillators, no coupling between them at all — no wires, no interaction term in the equations — driven only by the same external frequency-modulated signal. The paper shows, and verifies on an actual electronic circuit, that tuning the modulation amplitude and frequency alone is enough to move the trio through distinct regimes: everyone synchronized, everyone incoherent, and — the interesting middle one — a 'minimal chimera', where part of the group locks together and the rest doesn't, despite there being nothing connecting them except the shared beat. The mechanic: three phase dots on a circle, two shared sliders for modulation amplitude and frequency, and no coupling controls anywhere, because there is nothing to couple. The visitor's job is to find a chimera window — the paper's parameter sweep reports well-defined, separate regions for each regime. Turn one ships the three-oscillator sim with the two sliders and a live synchronization-order-parameter readout, plus a stated target: 'find where exactly two lock and one doesn't.' The hard part is legibility — chimera states look like noise until the order parameter's motion carries the story the eye can't read off three dots alone. What to reuse: packages/dataviz for the order-parameter chart; the natural second turn is a crowd-built map of the (amplitude, frequency) plane, where every visitor's search paints one pixel of a regime boundary nobody has drawn yet, in the spirit of Concourse's phase diagram. It improves with a crowd because mapping that boundary cell by cell is exactly the tedious two-parameter sweep a thousand people finish in an afternoon and one person doesn't.
mechanism: tune a shared external driving signal for three unconnected oscillators and search for the window where they split into synced and desynced
text: you have three oscillators with no connection except a shared external signal. adjust the signal's modulation and search for the moment where two sync and one doesn't. there is a chimera state buried in parameter space. the paper found it on an actual circuit. find it

paperTitle: Network Reciprocity Shapes Evolutionary Cybersecurity Dynamics
name: reciprocity
plan: An evolutionary game where every agent can play both offense and defense, run two ways: well-mixed, where anyone can interact with anyone, and structured, where agents sit on a network and only interact with neighbors. The paper's result is specific: well-mixed populations settle into broad, stable coexistence between attacking and defending strategies, but structured populations develop regimes where secure defense dominates across a much larger stretch of the parameter space, because neighboring defenders form clusters that shield each other from persistent attackers — a mechanism the paper calls network reciprocity, and it costs nothing extra, no added incentive, just topology. The mechanic: the visitor sets one dial for network structure, from well-mixed to lattice to sparse random graph, and one or two payoff sliders, then runs the evolutionary simulation and watches the strategy mix settle, colored by strategy, defenders visibly clustering on structured runs and not on well-mixed ones. Turn one ships a fixed small lattice, the payoff sliders, and a running strategy-fraction chart; the well-mixed side-by-side comparison is turn two. The hard part is making the causal claim visible rather than asserted — the site needs to run both topologies on identical payoffs so the difference is something you watch happen. What to reuse: civ's agent-based simulation loop and grid rendering are the closest existing machinery; packages/dataviz for the strategy-fraction time series. It improves with a crowd through submitted network topologies — which structures maximize the defender-dominant region is a real open question the paper doesn't fully answer, and a leaderboard of visitor-submitted graphs scored on defender win-fraction is a genuine, checkable search over that space.
mechanism: pick a population's network topology and payoffs for an evolving attacker/defender game, run it, and watch whether local clustering pushes the population toward defense
text: you're playing an evolving attacker-defender game on a network. set payoffs, pick your topology, watch which strategy wins. now run it on a lattice. payoffs identical, topology different, outcome flips. neighbors matter. hunt for the topology that maximizes defense

paperTitle: Constructing two completely independent spanning trees in the dual-cube
name: twotrees
plan: A completely independent spanning tree pair is two spanning trees of the same graph such that, for every vertex, the path from the root to that vertex in tree one and the path in tree two share no vertex except the root and the destination — so if one tree's edges all fail, the other still delivers every message, with zero shared points of failure along the way. The paper proves such a pair always exists in the dual-cube, a hypercube variant used in network design, for every size n ≥ 5, and gives a recursive construction that also improves the trees' diameter, the worst-case hop count from root to any node, over the naive construction. The mechanic: render the dual-cube for a chosen n, let the visitor draw two spanning trees on it by picking parent edges, and check in real time whether the pair is completely independent — the checker is the whole game, and it's cheap: trace both root-paths for every vertex and confirm they meet only at the endpoints. Turn one ships the checker and a fixed small n, five or six, with manual edge-picking; hunting for a lower diameter than the paper's construction is the natural second turn. The hard part is the drawing interface — a dual-cube at n=6 already has dozens of vertices, and an edge-by-edge click target that stays legible under that count is real work, not a stretch. What to reuse: math.mino.mobi's single-file explainer convention, and workers/scores for a diameter leaderboard verifiable exactly like the Erdős record table, since a submitted tree pair is just two parent arrays anyone can re-check by rerunning the same independence test.
mechanism: draw two spanning trees on a network so every pair of root-to-node paths shares nothing but the endpoints, then try to beat the paper's diameter
text: draw two spanning trees on a network. make paths from root share nothing but endpoints. one breaks, the other reaches everywhere. it's always possible here. the paper shows a construction. hunt the shortest worst-case path

paperTitle: Kemeny Rank Aggregation is NP-Hard for Three Voters
name: kemeny-line
plan: The paper closes a 25-year-old open question: Dwork et al. (2001) proved Kemeny rank aggregation NP-hard for every even number of voters at least four, and left three voters open. This paper shows three voters is already enough, via a reduction from MAX CUT. Kemeny aggregation takes several rankings of the same items and asks for the single ranking with the smallest total number of adjacent-swap disagreements against all of them — the textbook way to turn many opinions into one order. The mechanic: give the visitor three rankings of a shortlist of items (five to nine, tunable), and let them drag the items into their own single-file order; a live counter shows how many of the three voters' pairwise preferences that order violates — this is literally the objective the paper is about. Turn one: one fixed three-voter instance at seven items, drag-to-reorder, live violation count, and a brute-force check (7! is small enough client-side) that tells you when you've hit the true minimum, not just a local one. The hard part is generating instances honestly — a MAX-CUT-shaped disagreement structure, not random rankings, so the puzzle's difficulty is the paper's difficulty and not incidental noise — and being straight that beyond a dozen or so items nobody, including the computer, has a fast way to check an answer against the true optimum; that is what NP-hard means here. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer layout and `workers/scores` for a table of best-known violation counts per shared instance, since a lower count anyone finds is real progress the next visitor can try to beat.
mechanism: drag items into an order while a live counter scores it against three voters' rankings
text: drag five items into the single order that offends the fewest of three voters. three people each ranked them differently. find the minimum-disagreement order. three voters is already enough to make this computationally hard

paperTitle: Decentralized Scalable Exploration via Emergent Adaptive Lévy Walks on Minimal-Sensing Platforms
name: levy-swarm
plan: The paper puts fifty-gram nano-drones through a maze with no communication between them and almost no sensing — just short-range directional distance readings — and gets large coverage gains from one trick: each robot independently draws its own Lévy exponent (how heavy-tailed its step lengths are) from a shared prior, then biases its heading toward open space. No coordination, no shared map, and it still beats a uniform-heading random walk by 79.6% coverage in open arenas, 43.1% in corridors-and-rooms, and 13.6% in clutter, with fewer collisions in every case. The mechanic: the visitor sets one dial — how heavy-tailed the swarm's step-length prior is — drops a swarm into an arena, and watches two trail-maps fill in side by side, the Lévy swarm and a uniform-heading baseline on the identical map, with a live coverage-percentage race between them. Turn one: ship the corridors-and-rooms arena (the paper's middle, most legible number), a fixed small swarm, the one exponent-range slider, and the race counter — no arena picker or robot-count control yet. What's hard: simulating sparse local sensing honestly, so each robot only ever sees distance readings from its own immediate surroundings and never the other robots or a global map, while staying cheap enough to run dozens of robots in a browser tab — and being clear that the paper's exact percentages belong to its arenas, not this toy's, so it should chase relative improvement over its own baseline rather than promise to reproduce 43.1%. The crowd: let visitors draw their own floorplan and submit it to a gallery ranked by how much the Lévy swarm beats the baseline there — an arena-design contest over a space the paper never tested. Reuse canvas rendering, `workers/scores` for the gallery ranking, and civ/polis's independent-agent grid machinery.
mechanism: tune a swarm's step-length heaviness and race its coverage against a baseline on a shared map
text: tune how your bots jump while exploring a maze. ones that vary their jump lengths explore better than uniform jumpers, and you watch them race coverage on the same map. the paper shows 43 percent better coverage in corridors. tune the jump pattern and compete

paperTitle: Non-monotonic diffusion from nonequilibrium driving
name: drift-diffuse
plan: A minimal but genuinely surprising result: put one ordinary passive particle on a ring and drive it by coupling it to one active particle — run-and-tumble, active Brownian, whatever the microscopic rule — and the passive particle is always diffusive at long times, regardless of the driving mechanism. But how far it diffuses is not a dial you can just push up: its effective diffusivity depends non-monotonically on the driver's activity, with both an enhanced-transport regime and a suppressed-transport regime on the same knob. Stranger still, the same non-monotonic curve appears in a fully equilibrium setup, where the 'driver' is just an ordinary particle sitting at a higher local temperature — so the shape of the curve is not about activity as such, it is about something the two setups share. The mechanic: one ring, one passive bead, one driver, one dial for driving strength, and a live gauge that traces diffusivity-vs-dial-value as the visitor scrubs it back and forth, building the curve by hand rather than being shown it. The find-it goal: locate the dial value that minimizes transport and the one that maximizes it — both exist, neither is at an extreme. Turn one: the ring, the two beads, the dial, and the live trace, one mode only (active driver), no temperature toggle yet. What's hard: getting a stable diffusivity read at every dial position without long, noisy simulation runs — likely a dense grid of short-horizon trajectories precomputed offline and interpolated live rather than simulated fresh on every scrub. The second mode, swapping the active driver for a hot equilibrium one to watch the same curve reappear, is the site's real payoff and should follow once the first dial works. Reuse the O'Neill pack's dial-and-gauge layout, `packages/dataviz` for the live trace, and `workers/scores` for a guess-the-extremum leaderboard scored against the true computed curve.
mechanism: scrub a driving-strength dial and watch a passive particle's diffusivity trace itself live
text: scrub a dial to push a bead around a ring. more force makes it faster—until it doesn't. push too hard and transport drops, then climbs again. the min and max hide in the middle, not edges. the same curve appears if you heat the system instead of using an active driver

paperTitle: Reselection in the game of best choice
name: sift
plan: The paper works out a new twist on the classic secretary problem: interview n candidates one at a time, see only their rank relative to those interviewed so far, and accept or reject immediately, aiming to land the single best candidate overall. The classical answer rejects the first 1/e of candidates then takes the next one better than all seen so far, winning with probability roughly 1/e. This paper adds a reselection step: partway through, a random subset of the remaining pool is silently filtered out, governed by a distribution due to Steck from the 1970s. The striking result is that the win probability stays near 1/e even with filtering, but the optimal rule is no longer positional — it has to track each candidate's rank against the next 'bottom-to-top maximum' after the filtering point, not just their place in the queue. The mechanic: candidates arrive as cards showing only relative rank so far; you say stop or keep going. A dial sets where the filtering step falls and how much of the pool it removes. Turn one ships the bare classical game with no filtering — just stop-or-continue over a shuffled deck — with a running crowd-wide win rate displayed beside the theoretical 1/e, so the first thing a visitor sees is whether a room of strangers actually converges on the textbook constant. Filtering and the rank-dependent optimal rule are turn two. The hard part: the paper's rule has no simple closed form per position, so it has to be computed live via Monte Carlo over permutations rather than looked up in a table. Reuse: the math wing's (math.mino.mobi) single-file explainer pattern and workers/scores for the crowd win-rate tally — no new backend.
mechanism: stop-or-continue hiring game over a shuffled deck, with a filtering round that changes the optimal stopping rule
text: watch candidates appear one by one. you see only their rank relative to those you've met so far. say yes to accept, aiming for the best. halfway through, a random subset of the remaining pool vanishes. the odds of picking the best stay near 1 in 3, but the rule for deciding completely changes

paperTitle: MemSecBench: Tracking Agent Memory Poisoning from Persistence to Consequence and Repair
name: sleeper
plan: MemSecBench benchmarks how a malicious instruction survives inside an LLM agent's long-term memory: write a poisoned note during one session, let the agent move on, then see whether the instruction resurfaces later and drives a real action. Across 310 cases and 24 agent/memory/model configurations, malicious content persists in 84.2% of cases, the full write-then-execute chain succeeds in half of them, and even after a repair pass roughly 56% of successful poisonings still complete. The toy hands the visitor the attacker's seat: write one short note that a scripted agent stores in memory while doing an unrelated, innocuous task; later the agent is asked something unrelated again, and either recalls your note and acts on it, or a repair step catches and strips it first. Score is how quiet the note stayed versus whether it fired. Turn one ships the three-stage pipeline — write, forget, recall — as a fixed scripted agent, no live model call, whose persistence and repair odds are drawn from the paper's published rates for one chosen memory backend, so a visitor can already win or lose on turn one. Swapping between the paper's different memory backends, each with its own odds, is turn two. The hard part: with no real model running client-side, the state machine has to feel like an actual agent being fooled rather than a probability roll with the paper's percentages painted on top — what counts as a note 'quiet enough' to persist needs its own small legible rule, not just a hidden coin flip. Reuse: human/'s arcade-of-user-error framing and copy conventions; workers/scores for a stealthiest-note leaderboard. Frame it explicitly as a defensive exhibit on a toy-scale scripted agent, with the repair mechanism given equal billing — not a working recipe against any real deployed assistant.
mechanism: write a note into a scripted agent's memory during one task and see if it survives to trigger an action in a later, unrelated task
text: slip a hidden instruction into a scripted agent's memory while it handles something innocent. later, when it faces a different task, does your note resurface and drive an action, or does a repair system catch it first? score by how stealthy your poison stays and whether it fires

paperTitle: Squirming motion near corrugated surfaces
name: corduroy
plan: The paper works out, analytically, how model microswimmers called squirmers move near a corrugated (ridged) surface instead of a flat wall. Two swimmer types behave oppositely: pullers, which draw fluid in from the front, get trapped in the valleys of the corrugation instead of sliding along as they would near a plane; pushers, which expel fluid from behind, oscillate as they cross each ridge instead. Tilt the swimmer's approach angle relative to the ridges and a third effect appears — a wavelength-dependent lateral drift that pushes pushers and pullers apart, in opposite directions, from the same starting line. The toy is a sorter: a mixed stream of pushers and pullers enters at the top of a ridged channel, two dials — ridge wavelength and tilt angle — are the only controls, and the result is where each type exits at the bottom. Turn one ships a single swimmer, puller or pusher chosen by the visitor, over an adjustable corrugation, with the trapping-versus-oscillating difference visible directly and exit-drift arrows overlaid so the sorting mechanism reads clearly before any crowd feature exists. The full two-type mixed stream, plus a submit-your-wavelength leaderboard scored on separation purity, is turn two. The hard part is honesty about scale: the result is a small-amplitude perturbative expansion around a flat wall, valid only for corrugations much shallower than the swimmer-to-wall distance, so the toy should visibly break down rather than silently misbehave if a player cranks the wavelength dial past what the paper covers. Reuse: g/'s WebGPU gallery for the particle-trajectory shader machinery it already runs for grain-scale and molecular-dynamics sims; packages/dataviz for the exit-distribution plot; workers/scores for the crowd design leaderboard.
mechanism: tilt a mixed stream of two swimmer types over a corrugated channel and tune wavelength and angle to separate them by type
text: mixed stream of two microswimmer types flows down a ridged channel. dial the ridge wavelength and approach angle. one type gets trapped in the valleys, the other oscillates, and both drift opposite directions. tune them to sort the swimmers by type at the bottom

paperTitle: Extinction and Survival in an Interval-Activation Frog Model on \mathbb{Z} with Random Survival Parameters and Symmetric Random Walks
name: frogline
plan: The paper studies a frog model on the integers: frogs sleep at every site except the origin, each active frog performs a random walk and dies after a random lifetime, and when an active frog crosses a sleeping site it wakes that frog too. Survival means infinitely many frogs stay active forever; extinction means every frog eventually dies. The paper pins down exactly when each happens, driven by two independent knobs: how heavy-tailed the frogs' jump lengths are (a walk that occasionally leaps very far) and how heavy-tailed their lifetimes are (a frog that occasionally lives a very long time). It proves a sharp threshold, beta_c = 1/r, splitting the lifetime-tail parameter — below it the population survives with positive probability, above it extinction is almost sure, where r is set by which jump-tail regime is in play. The toy: a horizontal line of sleeping dots, two sliders for jump-tail and lifetime-tail heaviness, and a go button. Press it and watch frogs wake, spread, and either keep the line lit indefinitely or burn out — the cascade itself is the interesting object even before anyone cares about the threshold. Turn one ships this single-run simulator with the two sliders and a live surviving/extinct readout at a fixed, generous step budget. A crowd 'find the edge' mode — repeated runs bisecting toward beta_c with a shared record table of the tightest bracket anyone has found — is turn two. The hard part: the theorem is an infinite-time, infinite-population asymptotic, and any browser run is finite on both counts, so runs near the true threshold will misclassify some fraction of the time by construction — the UI needs to show that as an honest 'still running' state, not a wrong answer. Reuse: the math wing's (math.mino.mobi) explainer pattern; workers/scores for the threshold-bracket record table — pure client-side simulation, no new backend.
mechanism: tune two tail-heaviness sliders on a line of sleeping frogs, run the wake-up cascade, and hunt for the exact survival/extinction threshold
text: a line of sleeping frogs. one wakes and walks, dies after time, activates any frog it crosses. will the population survive forever or burn out? two sliders set how far they jump and how long they live. watch the cascade spread and hunt for the threshold where survival flips to extinction

paperTitle: Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use
name: chorus
plan: The paper models authors and the LLMs that polish their prose as distributions over linguistic features that coevolve. It compares three regimes: a fixed shared model (pulls everyone to one norm), a shared model recursively retrained on its own users' output (moves the norm around without changing the spread), and personalized models (the only one of the three that keeps a family of genuinely distinct equilibria alive). It also shows conformity is individually rational even when it is not socially optimal, because nobody prices in the value their own distinctiveness gives everyone else — an externality whose cost is finite per person but can grow unboundedly as distinctiveness stops being valued. The toy makes the visitor's own writing the specimen: submit a sentence, the site reduces it to a point in a small style space, and it joins a running population of everyone who has submitted one. A regime switch (fixed / recursive / personalized) replays the population's history under each rule so you can watch a real crowd's spread collapse under two of the three and survive under the third — not a synthetic demo, the actual submitted points. Turn one ships the single-player version: a slider population seeded synthetically, the three regimes animating side by side so the collapse-versus-survive contrast is visible before any real submissions exist. The hard part is the reduction from a sentence to a style-space point without it reading as a bogus linguistics score — keep the feature honest and simple (sentence length variance, function-word ratio) rather than pretending to measure style. Reuse: human/'s exhibit framing and copy conventions, workers/scores for the running population store.
mechanism: submit a sentence, watch a shared population's style spread converge or survive under three coevolution rules
text: type a sentence and join a population. watch the crowd's writing style evolve under three rules: one preserves diversity, two converge everyone to one voice. convergence happens because each person's move makes sense individually—not collectively

paperTitle: Settling the Optimal Exponent Relating Sumsets and Difference Sets
name: skewsum
plan: For a finite set A, sigma(A) is the relative size of A+A and delta(A) the relative size of A-A. A classical inequality sandwiches them: sigma^(1/2) <= delta <= sigma^2, and the top exponent was already known tight. This paper settles the bottom one: an explicit family of sets A_K where log(sigma)/log(delta) climbs to 2, proving 1/2 cannot be improved either. Unpacked, A+A and A-A are just the addition and subtraction tables of A — sumset and difference set are literally how many distinct entries fill those two grids — so the surprising fact is concrete: you can build sets whose addition table is enormous while the subtraction table stays comparatively tiny, and the paper says exactly how tiny is achievable. The toy: pick a finite set of integers (click points on a line, or type a short list), and the site instantly draws both grids and reports sigma, delta, and the ratio log(sigma)/log(delta), racing it toward 2. A second panel holds the paper's own A_K construction, loadable at any K, as the reference record. Turn one ships the single-page calculator with both grids rendered live and the ratio readout — no leaderboard yet, just the arithmetic made visible. Add the record table once the calculator is solid: submit (your set, its ratio), instantly re-verifiable by anyone, so there is no way to fake a better score. The hard part is keeping the grid visualization legible once sets exceed about 15 elements — it needs to degrade to a size/count summary rather than a literal grid without losing the intuition. Reuse: math/'s (geometry/, math.mino.mobi) single-file explainer conventions, workers/scores for the record table.
mechanism: build a finite integer set and watch its sumset-to-difference-set ratio race toward the paper's proven limit of 2
text: build a set of integers. the number of distinct sums (a+b) is enormous; the number of distinct differences (a-b) is tiny. the paper proves how extreme this gap can be. you tune your set and race its ratio toward the proven limit of 2

paperTitle: Designing Pairwise-Stable Agent Seating Arrangements
name: no-swap
plan: Classical stable-arrangement problems fix the seating graph (a path, a cycle) and ask whether a stable assignment exists for it — often it doesn't, and finding one is hard even when it does. This paper flips the setup: let the graph itself be designed by a central planner alongside the seating, and ask how good a stable arrangement you can guarantee. It shows the tractability boundary moves a lot once the graph is yours to build, and ties the design problem to subgraph isomorphism, disjoint-path partitioning, and bin-packing — a genuine algorithmic result, not just a reframing. The toy hands the visitor a fixed group of agents with stated preference orders over each other and lets them draw the seating graph: add or remove an adjacency edge, drag agents between seats, and get an instant pairwise-stability check — does any adjacent pair, or any pair you could make adjacent, both prefer each other to their current neighbor? A design counts once no such swap exists. Turn one ships one fixed small preference profile (five to seven agents), an editable graph canvas, and the instant checker — no scoring yet, just build-and-verify. The follow-up layer is a leaderboard on fewest edges used to stabilize a given profile, since the paper's own algorithmic content is about how cheap the graph can be. The hard part is picking a preference profile for turn one that is stabilizable but not trivially so — too easy and the checker feels decorative, too hard and visitors never see success. Reuse: civ/ and polis/ for the agent/preference machinery, workers/scores for the edge-count leaderboard.
mechanism: draw a seating graph for agents with ranked preferences and get an instant pairwise-stability check
text: draw the seating graph for agents with ranked preferences. are they stable, no unwanted swaps? the paper shows tractability jumps when you design the graph instead of taking it fixed. optimize for fewest edges possible

paperTitle: An Inclined, Eccentric Planet and an Inner Debris Disk Could Reproduce AU Mic Structure
name: unseen-planet
plan: AU Microscopii's debris disk shows dust clumps racing outward above the mid-plane on one side and drifting inward below it on the other — real, imaged structure with no confirmed cause. This paper reproduces it with a mechanism, not a fit: an unconfirmed planet on an eccentric, inclined orbit kicks the disk once per orbital period; stellar wind only pushes a dust grain outward once it has been lofted above a threshold height by that kick, so clumps appear periodically and only above the threshold. Their best match uses a roughly Jupiter-mass planet at 3-4 AU, eccentricity 0.37, inclination 30 degrees, against a ring at 5-6 AU, with a wind-to-gravity ratio near 1.8 — five numbers that together produce a real match to the image. The toy puts the visitor in the fitting seat: five sliders (mass, semi-major axis, eccentricity, inclination, wind-height threshold) drive a simplified periodic-kick particle sim of the disk, rendered from the same viewing angle as the real images, with the actual clump pattern shown faintly as a target to chase. Turn one ships the sim with the five sliders and the live particle render only — the target overlay and a closeness score come once the base sim reads correctly. The hard part is the physics simplification: real bispherical hydrodynamics is out of reach client-side, so the kick-and-threshold rule has to be an honest caricature of the paper's mechanism, labeled as such, not a full N-body integration. Reuse: tjs/ for the three.js particle rendering and slider-bench conventions already used across its workbenches.
mechanism: tune an unseen planet's orbit and a stellar-wind threshold to reproduce AU Mic's imaged dust-clump pattern
text: reproduce AU Mic's dust-clump pattern: tune an invisible planet's eccentric, inclined orbit and a stellar-wind threshold. the paper shows this mechanism can match real images. adjust five sliders and watch the particles move

paperTitle: Function Privatization in the Local Model
name: curve-lineup
plan: Trajectory-shaped data — a day's movement, a density curve — is hard to privatize under standard local differential privacy, because that definition demands any two curves, however different, become statistically indistinguishable after noising, which wrecks utility. The paper works instead with Geo-Privacy: nearby curves stay strongly protected from each other, but curves that are already far apart are allowed to stay easier to tell apart, since hiding an obviously-different shape buys little and costs a lot. The toy makes this visceral instead of definitional: draw a curve with your mouse, the site privatizes it under both a strict local-DP-style noiser and a Geo-Privacy-style noiser, and drops the result into a lineup with other visitors' privatized curves. Then you play detective — given a fresh, unlabeled privatized curve, guess which original shape it came from. Under the strict noiser, near-misses among similar curves should feel genuinely impossible to call; under Geo-Privacy, wildly different curves stay easy to separate while similar ones still stay protected. Turn one ships curve drawing plus both privatization modes and a side-by-side view of one original against its two privatized versions — no lineup yet, since that needs a population of submitted curves to be worth playing. The hard part is picking a noising scheme simple enough to run client-side while still visibly obeying the near/far asymmetry the paper is about, without overclaiming a privacy guarantee the toy doesn't actually implement. Reuse: canvas/'s (draw/) freehand stroke input, workers/scores for a running detective-accuracy stat once the lineup exists.
mechanism: draw a curve, privatize it two ways, and try to match privatized curves in a lineup back to their originals
text: draw a curve. it gets privatized two ways: one makes every curve equally hard to recognize, the other keeps wildly-different curves easy to separate while protecting similar ones. can you match a mystery privatized curve back to its original?

paperTitle: InkShield: Writing Style Protection Against Unauthorized Handwriting Mimicry
name: decoyhand
plan: InkShield defends a writer's style before an image ever gets released: pick a decoy writer whose handwriting looks different from yours, nudge your reference sample toward that decoy along its stroke edges only (never the blank background), and a frozen mimicry generator now reproduces the decoy's habits instead of yours. On IAM the paper's own writer-identification adversary drops from correctly attributing a generated forgery to the true writer 11.94% of the time (Top-1) to 2.03%, while the protected image itself stays visually almost identical to the original — LPIPS 0.0078, imperceptible. The toy: you write or upload a short handwriting sample, the site shows a live 'forger' trying to mimic it, and you get a perturbation budget to spend along your own strokes. Spend it well and the forger's guess collapses toward some other person entirely; spend it carelessly and your own handwriting starts to look off. Turn one: a canvas you write on, a small WASM mimicry model that scores how much a generated sample still looks like the original writer, and a slider for perturbation strength with the score updating live — no defense logic yet, just feeling the trade-off between protection and legibility. The hard part is picking a decoy automatically and confining perturbation to stroke edges rather than the whole canvas, which is the entire reason InkShield beats older whole-image defenses on sparse handwriting. Reuse human/'s exhibit framing and copy conventions for a defensive-security piece, and a small WASM handwriting-generation model built the way ocr/ and phylofiction/ already ship client-side inference.
mechanism: protect a handwriting sample with an edge-confined perturbation budget while a live mimicry model tries to copy it
text: write something and a live forger tries to mimic your hand. spend budget tweaking the edges of your strokes to shift them toward another writer's style. the forger's accuracy plummets while your writing stays visually almost identical to the original

paperTitle: Determining Critical Temperature Differences of Low-Temperature-Differential Stirling Engines: Nonlinear Dynamics Approach
name: stallpoint
plan: Low-temperature-differential Stirling engines can run on a warm hand and a glass of ice water, but nobody had worked out the threshold below which they simply stop. This paper derives it: the engine's rotation dies at a homoclinic bifurcation of its own equations of motion, and solving the self-consistent conditions at that bifurcation point yields a closed-form combination of the engine's physical parameters — flywheel inertia, displacer geometry, friction, working-gas properties — that predicts the exact critical temperature difference for that design. The toy hands you sliders for those same parameters and a canvas showing the engine's piston and displacer running in real time, with the ambient temperature difference as a dial you can drag down. Turn one: ship the dynamical model itself — sliders for two or three of the parameters, the animated engine, and a readout of whether it is currently above or below its own stall point, computed live from the paper's equations rather than just simulated numerically until it visibly dies. The hard part is that 'stall' is a genuine bifurcation, not a fixed threshold you can hardcode — the critical difference moves as you change the other parameters, so the readout has to track a curve, not a constant. Once that is solid, add a design hunt: given a fixed temperature difference, find the parameter combination with the lowest possible stall point, submit it, and a leaderboard ranks designs — cheating is impossible because any submitted parameter set can be replayed through the same closed-form check. Reuse g/'s WebGPU simulation shelf for the canvas and scores/ for the design leaderboard.
mechanism: tune an LTD Stirling engine's parameters and hunt the minimum temperature difference that keeps it spinning
text: watch an engine spin on a warm hand and ice water. drag the temperature dial down and watch it slow, wobble, and stall at a critical threshold. change the engine's parameters and the threshold shifts — find the design with the lowest stall point

paperTitle: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
name: teleportclick
plan: The paper asks the practical question nobody had: how few signals does it take to catch a browser-automation agent, as opposed to a bot or a human? The answer is startlingly small — two features, mouse_event_rate and teleport_click_ratio, give 100% observed recall on real AI agents across a five-level evasion ladder that includes GAN-generated cursor trajectories and replays of recorded human cursor motion, with zero misses across 22,990 predictions. The reason evasion fails is structural: browser-automation tools don't emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta stream a physical mouse produces, so the absence survives attempts to fake it. The toy puts that two-feature classifier client-side and in the open: move your own cursor around a small task (click five targets in order) and watch a live gauge score you human, bot, or agent using exactly those two numbers, updating as you move. Turn one: the task, the two-feature readout computed from real pointer events, and a plain verdict — no scoring game yet, just making the signal visible and honest about what it is, a browser-automation artifact rather than a judgment about you. The hard part is staying honest about what this demonstrates: the paper shows evasion doesn't work against this detector, so the site should frame itself as watch it hold rather than a how-to, since attempted evasion is expected to fail and that failure is the actual finding. Add a shared log of attempt outcomes afterward, not a leaderboard for beating detection. Reuse human/'s arcade-of-user-error framing, which already treats a person's own signals as the exhibit.
mechanism: move your own cursor while a two-feature live classifier scores you human, bot, or agent
text: move your mouse through targets and a live gauge scores you human, bot, or automated using just two numbers. the signal is structural — evasion fails because a real mouse doesn't produce the event stream browser automation does

paperTitle: Stable and Budget-Feasible Coalition Formation for Clustered Federated Learning: A Hedonic Potential-Game Approach
name: seatswitch
plan: Strip the federated-learning framing off this paper and what's left is a seating problem: a room of players, each with their own type, decides which table to sit at, where a table's payout depends on how well its members' types combine, minus a cost that grows with table size. The paper proves that for a specific way of splitting a table's surplus among its members — a 'hedonic' allocation derived from linear-production-game dual prices — the whole system is an exact potential game: a stable seating always exists, and if players individually keep moving to a strictly better table whenever they see one, that process is guaranteed to terminate rather than cycle. Under the naive alternative, splitting each table's surplus equally, no stable seating existed at all in three of the five real configurations they tested. The toy is a live room: each visitor is a player with a hidden type, tables show live payout as an incentive to switch, and a toggle switches the whole room between the two allocation rules. Turn one: one table's worth of players (five or six), a payout formula visible on screen, a switch button, and a readout of whether the room is currently churning or settled, running the equal-surplus rule only, so the first playable turn is watching stability never arrive. The hard part is a payout formula simple enough to read at a glance but rich enough that switching actually changes outcomes — the paper's surplus function has real structure, and flattening it too far kills the effect it's meant to show. Reuse games/'s Durable Object rooms for live multiplayer and scores/ for tracking how often each rule stabilizes across rooms.
mechanism: switch coalitions with live players under a shared payout rule and watch whether the room stabilizes
text: join a live room of players. tables show their payout. switch seats and watch whether the room stabilizes or keeps churning. flip a toggle to change the rule and watch stability arrive where it wasn't before

paperTitle: Collusion with Competitive Marginals: Price-Level Audits Are Blind by Construction
name: blind-audit
plan:
The paper shows a way to collude that a price-level audit cannot see, ever, no matter how closely it watches either bidder alone. Two agents couple only through the joint distribution of their 'unexplained' bid components — the noise nobody can trace to a stated feature — while each agent's own bid law stays exactly the competitive one. Any test that reads a single bidder's price history then has power exactly equal to its false-positive rate, for any coupling strength short of lockstep. It isn't underpowered; it's blind by construction. The paper finds this signature in real deployed LLM pricing agents (0.053 residual correlation between two deployments of the same model versus 0.0001 across different models, 20 models from 19 developers) and shows honest Ethereum block-auction bidders are already so correlated that a detector held to a 5% false-positive rate must set its threshold at 0.50-0.81 — 20 to 32 times the ordinary significance level — just to avoid flagging honest bidders.

The mechanic: run two bidding bots against a fixed honest population. One slider sets how correlated your bots' hidden noise is; their individual bid distributions never move off the competitive law, whatever you do. Two gauges: combined profit, and an auditor's suspicion score computed only from each bot's own price history. Turn one ships the two-bot arena — slider, profit readout, and a suspicion gauge that visibly refuses to move as the slider climbs, with the honest population's own baseline correlation marked on the dial so the floor problem is visible immediately.

The hard part: the invisibility only holds while each bidder's own marginal stays exactly correct, so the toy needs an explicit 'your own price law' readout proving it was never touched. Reuse `workers/scores` for a profit-at-zero-suspicion leaderboard; no auth needed, the bidders are simulated.
mechanism: two colluding bidding bots whose visible price law never moves while you dial the hidden correlation between them
text: turn a slider to make two bidding bots secretly correlate while their individual price laws stay perfectly competitive. an auditor watching each bot separately sees zero collusion—they can't, by design. ethereum bidders are already this correlated

paperTitle: Human diversity fuels collective creativity that large language models cannot simulate or sustain
name: idea-pool
plan:
The paper runs a preregistered experiment: native and non-native English writers produce creative metaphors either alone, with AI-generated ideas to pick from, or with AI refining their own draft. Measured at the population level, AI ideation compresses the collective pool's diversity for everyone and erases the extra diversity non-native writers normally contribute; AI refinement preserves both. Separately, the authors simulated the whole writer pool with LLM personas built from participants' real backgrounds, three model families, and elevated sampling temperature — every simulated pool fell below every human pool, and pushing temperature further only produced degenerate text, never real diversity.

The mechanic: a shared prompt, three writing modes (alone / pick an AI suggestion / ask AI to refine your own draft), and one visible number — the population's rolling diversity score, split by mode, updating as submissions arrive. No single visitor can see the finding; it only exists once enough people have written under each mode and the lines visibly separate, with a fourth 'simulated pool' line held at the paper's reported ceiling for comparison. Turn one ships one prompt, the three-mode submission form, and the three live diversity lines — diversity computed as average pairwise distance between submissions in a small client-side sentence-embedding space, reusing the WASM-inference pattern already shipped in `ocr/` and `phylofiction/`.

The hard part is the metric itself: it has to read as 'spread', not quality, and stay legible with a small crowd instead of looking identical across modes before enough data exists. Frame it honestly as one prompt's live data, not a replication of the study. Reuse `human/`'s exhibit conventions for the framing and copy; the pool itself is the score, so no separate leaderboard worker is needed.
mechanism: a shared prompt where visitors write metaphors unaided, AI-suggested, or AI-refined, feeding a live population diversity meter
text: write a metaphor solo, pick from ai suggestions, or ask ai to refine yours. watch the collective diversity meter split across all three modes as submissions arrive. ai-generated ideas shrink the whole crowd's diversity. simulated writers never match human creativity

paperTitle: Instability-induced bistable shape-morphing kirigami structures
name: snap-cut
plan:
The paper is an inverse-design framework for kirigami sheets — flat sheets with a pattern of cuts — that deploy into stable 3D shapes from the cut geometry alone: no soft material, no elastic hinges, no external frame holding the shape. The mechanism is anisotropic geometric frustration: cuts of different length or angle in two directions store deployment energy unevenly, so a sheet can have two distinct stable deployed states (bistability) and a preferred direction of unfolding, validated against both finite-element simulation and physical experiment. That a purely rigid, purely-cut pattern can be programmed to hold a shape at all, let alone two, is the surprising part — cutting substitutes for hinges and latches.

The mechanic: a grid of cut segments the visitor edits (length and angle, in two directions), plus a deploy button that runs a simplified spring-network energy relaxation and shows the sheet settling into zero, one, or two stable states, with the opening direction visibly following whichever direction carries the longer cuts. Turn one ships the pattern editor, the deploy animation, and a badge reporting how many stable states were found.

What's hard: an honest small-scale spring model won't reproduce the paper's FEM-validated numbers, so the toy must be labeled as a qualitative demonstration of the mechanism — frustration to bistability to directionality — not a predictor of real material behavior; say so on the page. The crowd angle: visitors submit patterns to a gallery scored on 'how bistable' and 'how directional' the sim reports, searching by hand the same cut-pattern space the paper's framework searches by optimization. Reuse `g/`'s one-canvas-per-simulation shelf format and `packages/dataviz` for the small energy-landscape plot.
mechanism: a kirigami cut-pattern editor whose deploy button reveals how many stable 3D shapes the pattern holds
text: edit cut patterns on a grid in two directions, hit deploy, and watch the sheet fold into one or two stable 3d shapes from geometry alone. no hinges or glue needed. submit patterns to a gallery ranked by how many stable states they reach and how directional they fold

paperTitle: Boundary-Driven Anisotropic Coarsening in Conserved Phase Separation
name: edge-coarsen
plan:
Phase separation — oil and water sorting into growing blobs — is normally assumed to coarsen at the same rate in every direction, the textbook Model B scaling. This paper breaks that with nothing exotic: a three-component mixture where one species evaporates through a boundary. The evaporating boundary causes ongoing mass loss and a concentration gradient near the wall, and that alone is enough to make domains grow at different rates parallel versus perpendicular to the boundary, while the bulk, away from the wall, keeps obeying standard isotropic scaling. The anisotropy is a boundary effect, not a property of the underlying physics — turn evaporation off and it vanishes.

The mechanic: a canvas phase-separation sim (conserved, Cahn-Hilliard-style dynamics) with one dial, boundary evaporation rate, and two live-fit growth exponents — one measured in a strip near the boundary, one in a strip in the bulk. At zero evaporation the two should track together; turning the dial up should visibly split them while the bulk number holds steady. Turn one ships the sim, the dial, and the two exponent readouts updating as the pattern coarsens, with the two measurement strips overlaid on the canvas in different colors.

What's hard: a legible, real-time exponent fit out of a noisy small-lattice sim, without it jittering meaninglessly — a rolling log-log regression over recent frames, smoothed. State plainly that a browser-scale lattice won't reach the paper's finite-size-scaling regime, so the two numbers illustrate the mechanism rather than reproduce its exponents. Crowd angle: visitors submit (evaporation rate, mixture ratio) pairs to a shared record table ranked by how far the two exponents split, verified by rerunning — a checkable hunt for the most anisotropic boundary condition. Reuse `g/`'s canvas-shelf format and `workers/scores` for the record table.
mechanism: a phase-separation sim with a boundary-evaporation dial that splits domain growth rates near the wall from the bulk
text: turn a dial for boundary evaporation on a phase-separation sim. domains grow at the usual rate in the bulk, but near the boundary they split into two different growth speeds. just adding evaporation at one edge breaks the symmetry. compete to maximize the split

paperTitle: The Complexity of Kemeny Aggregation with Three Rankings
name: two-to-one
plan: The paper proves that finding the best compromise ranking (the Kemeny aggregate, which minimizes total pairwise disagreement) is NP-complete for as few as three input rankings, and not just in adversarial cases: even when every pair of candidates is split exactly 2-to-1 among the three rankings, the friendliest kind of near-consensus you could ask for, the problem stays hard.
