The proof encodes a max-cut instance directly into the three rankings, so a hard instance is literally a graph in disguise, and solving it exactly recovers a maximum cut. The mechanic: the visitor sees three rankings of a small set of items (six to ten) and drags the items into their own proposed aggregate order. A live counter shows total Kendall-tau distance to the three inputs while dragging, and on release the site reveals the true minimum, computed exactly offline from the max-cut graph the puzzle was built from. Turn one ships exactly that loop: one generated instance, the drag-to-rank interface, the live disagreement counter, and the reveal, with no explanation of max-cut needed yet. The hard part is making the hardness legible without a graph-theory lecture: a puzzle's difficulty should visibly correlate with something the visitor can see, such as how tangled the three inputs look, rather than being asserted. A later turn can add a difficulty dial tied to the underlying graph's edge count. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions (as with erdos/) for the interface and workers/scores for a record table of fastest correct solves per difficulty tier, since checking a submitted aggregate against the true optimum is cheap and exact at this size.
mechanism: drag-sort a proposed compromise ranking against three fixed rankings and check it against the true minimum-disagreement aggregate
text: drag items to create a compromise between three rankings. live meter shows disagreement. release to see the best arrangement—which stays hard to find even when all three rankings nearly agree

paperTitle: Tampered Memory Elephant Random Walk on One-Dimensional Integer Lattice
name: half-memory
plan: The elephant random walk repeats, with fixed probability p, a uniformly-chosen step from its own past; above a threshold on p it turns superdiffusive. This paper asks how much of that memory can be corrupted before the effect disappears: split the timeline into a tampered set (steps replaced by fresh independent coin flips) and a retained set (ordinary elephant memory), and ask how large the retained fraction needs to be. The answer is a clean threshold at one half: if the retained fraction of steps stays above 1/2, the full diffusive/critical/superdiffusive phase transition in p survives; below 1/2, the walk is always merely diffusive no matter how strong p is; exactly 1/2 is its own boundary case. The mechanic: two sliders, memory strength p and retained fraction, and a canvas showing a walk (or a fan of several, for a cleaner signal) stepping in real time, plus a running estimate of its growth exponent from spread versus step count. Turn one ships the sliders, the animated walk, and the live exponent readout, with p defaulted into the superdiffusive range so dragging retained-fraction below one half is visibly a collapse back to plain diffusion. The hard part is getting a readable exponent out of a noisy finite simulation fast enough to feel responsive, likely by running several parallel walks and averaging mean-squared displacement rather than trusting one trajectory. The paper settles the deterministic-partition case and only conjectures the random one; a later turn can let visitors submit their own tampering patterns and the site tallies estimated exponents near the threshold as informal crowd evidence toward the open case. Reuse the math wing's explainer conventions and workers/scores for a submitted-pattern record table.
mechanism: dial a random walk's memory strength and how much of its memory survives tampering, then watch its growth exponent flip across a one-half threshold
text: dial a random walk's memory strength and corruption. watch it spread on a canvas. exactly at one half remaining, the spreading changes. below that threshold, stays the same regardless of memory strength

paperTitle: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
name: peek-or-poke
plan: People sometimes learn by watching someone else and sometimes by trying things themselves, and this paper models the choice as a cost-benefit calculation that requires theory of mind: an agent estimates how informative watching a specific other agent's next move would be, by reasoning about that agent's goal, and weighs it against the cost of learning directly. Validated on a game the authors built where players repeatedly choose to observe another agent or explore on their own, the 'Rational Mentalizing' model quantitatively matches real human choices. The mechanic reproduces that game: each round, the visitor sees a hidden-reward environment and a bot with a legible but not fully obvious goal, and chooses to peek (watch what the bot does next, learning something about the environment for free) or poke (spend the round exploring directly). Turn one ships one environment, one bot, the peek/poke choice, and a running tally of choices and outcomes, with no model comparison yet. A second turn overlays the Rational Mentalizing model's predicted peek/poke curve against the visitor's actual choices, so they can see where they over- or under-used social learning relative to the model. The hard part is tuning the bot's legibility: too obvious and peeking is free, trivializing the choice; too unreadable and peeking teaches nothing, and the mechanism the paper is about disappears. Reuse games/'s room machinery for pairing visitors with live or replayed bot runs, human/'s arcade-of-user-error framing for tone, and scores for personal history; since a thousand people playing this produces a live, larger-scale replication of the paper's own study, that aggregate is the crowd payoff, not a leaderboard.
mechanism: each round, choose to watch a bot's next move or explore the environment yourself, then compare your choices to a theory-of-mind utility model
text: each round peek (watch a bot's move) or poke (explore). the bot's trying to solve something partly visible. your pattern of choices should match how someone reasoning about the bot's goal would choose

paperTitle: Anonymous sharing is pairwise phase-blind
name: checkpoint-storm
plan: Checkpoint storms, synchronized bursts when many training jobs write to the same shared storage, are usually blamed on phase-locking, the same oscillator-coupling math that explains synchronized fireflies. This paper shows that blame is backwards for the ordinary case: model each job's write cycle as an oscillator coupled only through a shared resource that is anonymous, meaning the rate it hands an active job depends on how many jobs are active and not on which one, and the coupling vanishes exactly. For identical jobs the two-job phase-gap return map is the identity function, no attraction and no repulsion, and the firing order freezes forever, for any fleet size and any bandwidth cap; only a weak third-order effect survives, and it is a fixed point with more expanding directions than contracting ones, not something trajectories drift toward. Real synchrony only reappears once jobs stop being identical and interchangeable under a hard cap. The mechanic: a ring of animated jobs sharing one pipe, with two dials, anonymity (does the pipe treat jobs by identity or just by count) and heterogeneity (identical jobs or varied write/compute ratios), and a stated goal: make the write pulses lock into a storm. Turn one ships the ring, the two dials, and a live phase-gap-variance readout, with no scoring, just the challenge of watching it refuse to lock under full anonymity no matter how it is perturbed. The hard part is making a null result feel like a result: showing that different random starts drift apart rather than converge, unlike a firefly simulation, so the absence of synchrony reads as a finding rather than a bug. No existing surface's code applies directly; reuse packages/dataviz for the phase-gap chart.
mechanism: dial a shared resource's anonymity and a job fleet's heterogeneity, then try to force periodic write cycles into a synchronized storm
text: arrange jobs in a ring, all writing to a shared pipe. dial whether the pipe treats them anonymously and whether the jobs are identical. try to force their writes into a synchronized storm. but when the pipe is truly anonymous, it refuses to lock—no matter what

paperTitle: Quantum Chaos and Diffusive Transport from Geometric Randomness
name: corridor-width
plan: Quantum chaos usually needs either many interacting particles or disorder scattered into an otherwise regular lattice. This paper gets it from neither: non-interacting particles on a graph built from pure geometric randomness, layers of sites wired to the next layer with uniform-strength links but wired irregularly, go chaotic or not depending only on how wide the layers are. Wide layers push the system into full quantum chaos: energy levels show Wigner-Dyson repulsion and a particle placed on one site diffuses outward through the graph. Narrow, quasi-one-dimensional layers instead produce a spectrum where localized and delocalized states coexist, level repulsion is suppressed even as the delocalized states still carry a particle ballistically across the graph. No impurities were added anywhere; the wiring itself is the only randomness. The mechanic: a slider sets the corridor's layer width, regenerating a small randomly wired layered graph drawn as a branching maze; the visitor drops a particle on a node and watches it spread. Turn one ships the width slider, the graph generator, and the spreading animation using a simple discrete quantum-walk update, with no spectral statistics yet. A second turn adds a live level-spacing histogram beside the animation so the visitor can see repulsion versus clustering track the same slider that changes how the particle spreads. The hard part is doing real spectral statistics, diagonalizing the graph's Hamiltonian and binning the spacings, fast enough in-browser; capping the graph at a few hundred sites and precomputing a small library of graphs per width is more realistic than live diagonalization on every drag. Reuse packages/dataviz for the histogram; no existing surface's code applies directly, though the corridor-as-maze visual would sit comfortably beside the O'Neill pack's structural aesthetic if themed later.
mechanism: set a randomly wired graph's layer width and watch a quantum particle's spreading and its energy-level statistics flip between chaotic and localized
text: adjust a slider to build a wired corridor, then drop a quantum particle on it. watch whether it spreads or gets trapped as you adjust. the width alone decides—no impurities, no randomness, just geometry

paperTitle: Hash Chemistry: Minimal Models for Evolutionary Growth of Complexity
name: cardinality-leap
plan: Hash Chemistry scores entities of arbitrary size with a single deterministic hash function, which turns a modest rule into access to a combinatorially vast possibility space the paper calls a cardinality leap. The newest variant, Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry, adds spatial locality to how replicators compete, and run at large scale on a GPU the paper finds something specific: the size of the space itself acts as a control parameter. Below a threshold, populations stay compact and diverse; above it, growth tips into a runaway size-dominance regime where one lineage's descendants crowd out everything else, through a stochastic, nucleation-like transition. The mechanic: entities are short symbol strings, scored purely by hashing their contents, no training, no lookup table, so any child can invent a genuinely new structure. The visitor sets one dial, the size of the space, then runs generations of mutation and selection and watches whether the population stays compact or tips into one dominant giant. Turn one: a small non-spatial version — hash-scoring, mutation, selection, the size dial, and a live chart of entity-size distribution across generations, ending each run labelled compact or runaway. The hard part is that the transition is genuinely stochastic near the threshold: one run at a borderline size can go either way, so a single visitor watching once will see noise, not a phase transition. The fix is to aggregate: show a live histogram of how every visitor's run at each size setting resolved, so the actual phase boundary emerges from traffic rather than any one run. Reuse fluoddity's deterministic genome-scoring pattern, reef's crowd-aggregation habits, and packages/dataviz for the histogram.
mechanism: grid-size dial driving a hash-scored replicator population toward compact growth or runaway size-dominance
text: set how much space symbolic strings have and watch them either branch into diversity or crash into one dominant giant at a sharp threshold

paperTitle: Sumsets and generalized arithmetic progressions in multiplicative subgroups
name: sumcap
plan: The paper studies multiplicative subgroups A of a finite field's unit group and proves, among other things, that once A is not tiny and not nearly the whole group, no target value has an outsized number of representations as a sum of two elements of A — specifically, for index at least 3 and |A| at least 5, every nonzero c is hit by fewer than |A|/2 pairs. Restrict the toy to prime fields, where the subgroups are exactly the d-th power residues (quadratic residues, cubic residues, and so on), so a visitor's intuition about residues carries over cleanly. Pick a prime p and a divisor d of p−1; the app derives A automatically as the unique subgroup of that order, then computes r(c), the count of pairs (a,b) in A×A with a+b ≡ c mod p, for every c, and draws it as a bar around a ring of residues with the |A|/2 ceiling marked as a line. The hunt is for the c that comes closest to that ceiling — a claim anyone can check in one click by recomputing the pair (p, d, c). Turn one: a curated list of primes, a subgroup-order slider restricted to the theorem's valid regime, and the histogram with its ceiling line. The hard part is honesty at the edges: subgroups with |A| at most 4, or index below 3, sit outside the theorem's guarantee and can look deceptively similar on the same chart, so the UI must gray those settings out rather than silently plotting a bound that does not apply there. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer convention (erdos, kakeya, capset) and workers/scores for a recomputable record table of closest approaches to the ceiling.
mechanism: pick a prime and subgroup order, then hunt the sumset histogram for its closest approach to the paper's density ceiling
text: pick a prime and subgroup order, then hunt the ring of sums for the outlier that comes closest to the paper's density bound

paperTitle: Synchronization, Kinematic Waves and Spike-Phase-Separation in Feedback Ising Neural Networks on Heterogeneous Graphs
name: kinwave
plan: The paper models neurons as a kinetic Ising network with a homeostatic feedback loop between excitability and population firing rate, and shows analytically how heterogeneity in the network's connectivity controls what the population does collectively. At low heterogeneity, the population settles into a synchronized limit cycle, born from an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation, everyone pulsing together. Raise the heterogeneity and, before synchronization takes hold each cycle, a kinematic wave sweeps visibly from low-degree periphery neurons inward to the high-degree hubs. Push heterogeneity further still and the whole thing freezes into a phase-separated state via a pitchfork bifurcation: some neurons locked high, others locked low, the collective rhythm gone for good. The mechanic is one dial, network heterogeneity, turning a small node-link graph from breathing in unison, to rippling from edge to center, to frozen and split. Turn one: implement the mean-field homeostatic update on a small synthetic network whose degree spread is set by the one heterogeneity parameter, animate node colour by firing state, and plot the population firing rate live alongside it, so the sync-to-frozen transition reads as a trace collapsing, not just as nodes going still. The hard part is that the frozen state can look like the sim merely stalling unless the trace shows the specific signature the paper reports: the per-neuron rate and the per-synapse rate pulling apart from each other as heterogeneity rises, which needs its own small chart to be legible at all. Reuse neuro, the wing built for cognitive-science models reimplemented from their papers and shown against the published result, where the homeostasis piece already lives, and packages/dataviz for the rate traces.
mechanism: one heterogeneity dial driving a feedback neuron network between synchronized pulsing, a periphery-to-hub wave, and a frozen split
text: turn the heterogeneity dial: watch neurons pulse together, then ripple from edges inward, then lock into a frozen split

paperTitle: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
name: recourse-gap
plan: Algorithmic recourse tells a rejected applicant what to change to get approved, but the paper shows most such advice only cares about flipping the model's output, not whether the change reflects real improvement versus gaming the surface features. Its causal performative framework routes a recourse action through a small causal graph connecting observed features to the true, hidden qualification, and shows that policies ignoring that structure induce large behavioral responses that degrade once the model retrains on them, while causal-aware recourse settles into stable equilibria that resist gaming. The mechanic: a visitor plays a rejected applicant against a shared classifier and is offered two possible actions, one a cosmetic feature flip, one a change that actually runs through the hidden causal path to the true qualification, without being told which is which. They act, see the decision move, and can press a shared retrain button that folds the whole population's recent actions back into the classifier. The gaming action's success rate visibly decays after each retrain; the causal one keeps working, because it moved the thing the label actually depends on. Turn one: one small causal graph, two candidate actions, a single applicant's decision, and a retrain button whose effect on the two actions' success rates is shown as a running pair of numbers. The hard part is pacing: the lesson only lands if retrains are frequent enough that the decay of the gaming action reads as a pattern within a few clicks, not as one ambiguous random fluctuation. Reuse human, the arcade of user error, whose whole premise is a person mishandling a system, and workers/scores for population-level gaming-survives-N-retrains tracking.
mechanism: choose a recourse action against a shared classifier that periodically retrains on the crowd's behavior
text: play a rejected applicant choosing between cosmetic and causal recourse actions, then watch which one keeps working as the shared classifier retrains

paperTitle: Eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations of rational numbers via optimal control
name: sylvester
plan:
An Egyptian fraction writes a number as a sum of distinct unit fractions: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/11, say. The greedy algorithm builds one for any target by always subtracting the largest unit fraction that still fits underneath it. The paper answers a question going back to Erdos and Graham: is greedy eventually the best way to underapproximate — the k-term sum closest to the target from below — or can a smarter choice of denominators always beat it? For every positive rational, greedy wins forever after some finite number of terms, in both the version where denominators may repeat and the version where they must stay distinct. It also builds an irrational number where greedy is optimal and unique at every single step, with no catching-up needed.

The mechanic: pick a target rational, and watch two term-by-term expansions build underneath it on a number line — greedy on top, the true best k-term underapproximation (found by search) below. For most fractions the two rows agree almost immediately; the site marks the term index where they lock together for good. Turn one ships that single race for one hand-picked fraction with a visible crossover marker, no leaderboard yet.

The hard part: computing the true best k-term underapproximation is a search over which denominators to use, not a formula, and it gets expensive fast — the toy needs a term cap (maybe 6) and a fraction picker that stays inside what a browser can brute-force in the time a visitor will wait.

Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer pattern and the number-line device from the Erdos rectangle toy, and scores for a record table once a search-your-own-fraction hunt ships: crowd value is finding rationals where greedy takes unusually long to catch up, verifiable by anyone re-running the same two rows.
mechanism: race the greedy Egyptian-fraction algorithm against the true best underapproximation and find where they merge
text: watch two methods build fractions underneath your target and race to merge: one always grabs the biggest unit fraction that fits, the other searches for the true best. they always converge, but the gap between them before they lock is where the story lives

paperTitle: Convergence to the exact kinetics of the one-dimensional Riviera model
name: riviera
plan:
The Riviera model is random sequential deposition on a 1D lattice with one extra rule: you can build on an empty lot unless doing so would leave a single vacant lot pinned between two houses on both sides — that lot becomes permanently unbuildable, an isolated gap. Building continues at uniformly random empty lots until every remaining empty lot is one of these stranded singles: the street is jammed. No exact formula for the final fraction of lots built, the jamming density, is known; the paper derives an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations for the process and shows a systematic closure at increasing order converges very fast toward the true value, without ever writing that value down in closed form.

The toy: a street of lots, click (or auto-run) to attempt a build at a random empty lot; lots that fill turn built, lots that become permanently isolated turn red, and the run ends when nothing empty remains except stranded ones. Turn one ships one street, one run, and the final density displayed at the end — a single number, no history yet.

The mechanic gets its stakes from what nobody has: the exact jamming density. Because the paper never gives a closed form, the honest crowd move is aggregation — every visitor's run is one more independent sample, and the site keeps a running mean across every completed street, shown converging toward the paper's own high-order numerical estimate as runs accumulate. That's the hard part to get right: the running average has to read as approaching a number nobody can currently write down exactly, not as a personal high score, or the game is pointless after the first jam.

Reuse scores for the aggregate counter (sum of density times runs, not a personal leaderboard) and a plain canvas strip — no build, no worker changes beyond that.
mechanism: randomly build houses along a street under one rule and watch the block jam
text: click empty lots to randomly build houses until the street jams. the exact jamming density has no formula—the only way to pin it down is running a thousand simulations and averaging the results. each of your runs adds one more point to the crowd's estimate

paperTitle: Evolutionary adaptation through bet-hedging in finite populations under fluctuating environments
name: hedge
plan:
A minimal birth-death model: individuals inherit a phenotypic strategy — how spread-out their offspring's phenotypes are across a randomly switching environment. Pure bet-hedging survives crashes but grows slowly; pure specialism grows fast in one environment and can be wiped out when it switches. The paper's finding is that population size decides which strategy evolution actually converges to: large populations settle on the growth-maximizing strategy because they can absorb an occasional bad generation, while small populations evolve toward the more risk-averse, extinction-resistant strategy instead, facing the identical fluctuating environment. It gives a heuristic approximation for where that split falls.

The toy: two colonies, same environment-switching schedule, different starting sizes, run side by side across many generations. Each colony's evolved bet-hedging parameter is plotted live, and, periodically, the shared environment flips. The payoff moment is a flip that would wipe out a non-hedging population — the large colony has often drifted less cautious and takes a real hit, while the small one, having evolved more spread, rides it out. Turn one ships exactly that: two colonies, one slider for switching rate, a run button, and the two evolved-strategy traces.

What's hard: the model is stochastic and the interesting behavior, a visible near-extinction in the large colony, needs enough generations and the right switching rate to show up in a single run without a long wait — probably pre-tuned defaults rather than exposing every parameter from day one, or most runs will be visually uneventful.

The crowd angle: let visitors submit switching-rate and population-size pairs and log which colonies went extinct, building a shared map of the danger zone rather than each visitor discovering it alone. Reuse scores for that log; no other surface needed.
mechanism: run two populations of different size through the same random environment switches and see which strategy evolution favors
text: run two colonies through the same random environmental switches, one large and one small. evolution shapes each into a different strategy: the big one can afford specialists, the small one spreads its bets as insurance. watch them diverge as the world flips around them

paperTitle: Mpemba effect in a chemomechanical model of the Kinesin molecular motor
name: mpemba
plan:
The Mpemba effect is the famous claim that a system started farther from equilibrium can relax faster than one started closer, usually discussed for water and freezing. This paper finds it in a specific biological system: a six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin motor protein, the one that walks along microtubules by cycling through ATP-binding states. Two different starting distributions over those six states, one nominally closer to equilibrium, race toward it — and the paper shows the farther one can win, both when the motor sits at rest and when it is being chemically or mechanically driven, mapping which regions of a two-parameter phase diagram produce the inversion versus the boring, expected outcome. It also finds the effect shows up in something you could measure on a real motor: the relaxation of its stepping velocity, not just its internal state probabilities.

The toy: two colored tokens, each a different starting distribution over the six kinesin states, dropped onto a shared free-energy landscape and left to relax; a small readout tracks each one's distance from equilibrium over time. Most starting pairs behave as expected — closer wins. Turn one ships that single race for one pre-set pair, with the states and landscape drawn plainly enough to read as a real molecular machine, not an abstract Markov chain.

The hard part: finding a starting pair that actually inverts is a search over the paper's two-parameter phase diagram, so the toy needs that diagram as a background layer visitors can click into, not a blind random-pair generator that mostly produces uninteresting races.

Reuse scores once the phase diagram ships: a record for the largest confirmed inversion (biggest head start, still loses) found, verifiable by anyone rerunning that exact pair.
mechanism: pick two starting distances from equilibrium for a molecular motor and race them to see which settles first
text: drop two starting points for a molecular motor onto its energy map and watch them both relax toward equilibrium. the point closer to rest usually reaches it first, but sometimes the farther point gets there faster. that flip is what the paper proves can happen

paperTitle: A data-driven stage-structured host-parasitoid model for optimizing Trichogramma interventions against soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) outbreaks
name: trichogramma
plan:
A calibrated model of a real pest problem: the soybean pod borer, and the tiny parasitic wasp (Trichogramma) farmers release as its egg-killing predator. The model couples the pest's full life stages to the wasp's egg-parasitism and was fit to field data from Jilin province by MCMC. From it the paper derives an economic injury level — 0.0389 larvae per square meter, the density above which crop damage costs more than acting would — and finds two answers for how to intervene: a continuous release rate of 2.645 wasps per unit time holds the pest below that line without wasting parasitoids on an already-suppressed population, and if you release in batches instead, every 5 days is the balance between suppression and how often a farm can realistically act.

The toy hands you the release schedule instead of the paper's optimizer: pick a strategy — steady rate, or batches on an interval you choose — run a season against the coupled pest-wasp dynamics, and get scored on two numbers, days spent over the injury threshold and total wasps spent. The paper's own optimum, 2.645 continuous or every 5 days, is shown as a reference line on the scoreboard, not the answer key — visitors are free to try uneven schedules or front-loaded releases the paper's fixed-strategy analysis never tried.

Turn one: the coupled dynamics running for one fixed schedule (the paper's continuous rate) with the two gauges, injury-threshold line and wasp count, visible across a season, no schedule editor yet.

Hard part: the underlying model is stage-structured on both species — the toy needs to run that faithfully enough that beating 2.645 means something, not a cartoon simplification that makes every strategy look equally good.

Reuse scores for the two-gauge leaderboard once the schedule editor ships.
mechanism: schedule parasitic wasp releases against a pest outbreak and try to beat the paper's own optimum on cost and suppression
text: pick a wasp release schedule against a crop pest and run a season: steady rate, batches, or your own design. the paper found 2.645 per time unbeatable for cost and suppression, but you can try. score is days over damage threshold plus total wasps used

paperTitle: The evolution of cooperation under imperfect phenotypic recognition
name: close-cousins
plan: The paper generalizes the classic phenotype-matching model of cooperation: instead of helping only exact phenotypic twins, individuals help with a probability that fades with phenotypic distance. Under weak selection with mutation in both strategy and phenotype, the authors derive a threshold for cooperation to be favored and show two clean monotone facts: sharper discrimination always lowers the threshold (exact matching is the best case in this whole family, not just a convenient special case), and more phenotype dimensions help even when recognition stays blurry. Low phenotype mutation strangles cooperation; high phenotype mutation drives the threshold to its floor. The toy is a discrimination dial: the visitor sets how forgiving recognition is, from 'help anything vaguely similar' to 'help only near-identical,' plus how many independent traits the population tracks, and watches a population of colored dots either fill up with helpers or collapse to defection. Turn one ships one trait dimension, one sharpness slider, and a live gauge computed from a fast client-side population simulation (Moran-style, not the paper's closed-form transform, to avoid overclaiming a derivation nobody here reproduced) showing whether cooperation is currently favored. The hard part is resisting the urge to implement the actual Laplace-transform threshold formula from the paper without deriving it firsthand — a simulation that reproduces the two monotone results honestly is safer than a formula copied from an abstract. A later turn can turn this into a hunt: find the exact sharpness value where the population flips, submit it, anyone can rerun the simulation to check. No existing surface fits cleanly; this would be a new single-page site, dataviz package for the population plot.
mechanism: tune a discrimination-sharpness dial and phenotype dimension count, watch a simulated population tip into or out of cooperation
text: drag a dial tuning recognition sharpness and watch colored dots become helpers or defectors. sharper discrimination lowers the cooperation threshold, and more trait dimensions help—even blurry recognition works better

paperTitle: Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation
name: filter-dodge
plan: The paper black-box tests three commercial multimodal moderation APIs against seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations — no gradients, no surrogate model, no knowledge of the target. All three get bypassed. Even fixed, content-blind transforms like color inversion and grayscale conversion flip an unsafe verdict to safe while the image stays completely recognizable to a human. Robustness varies sharply by harm category, with self-harm and multimodal content the most fragile. The toy hands the visitor the attacker's seat: one image flagged 'unsafe' by a small toy-scale classifier we train and ship ourselves — not an attack on any real commercial API — and a row of transform buttons drawn from the paper's list (grayscale, invert, rotate, crop-and-pad, add noise). A live badge shows the classifier's verdict updating as transforms toggle on and off, next to a perceptual-similarity meter proving the content hasn't actually changed. Turn one ships exactly that: one image, four or five transform toggles, one instant verdict badge — no leaderboard yet. The hard part is the classifier itself: it has to be a real, honestly-trained toy model that fails the way the paper describes, not a strawman rigged to fall over, and it has to run as a small WASM artifact built in CI so there's no server and no inference bill. This is offensive-security material about a published attack on deployed systems, so the defense discussion belongs on the page next to the game, same as the site's other AI-safety exhibit that builds the thing it's about. A later turn adds a leaderboard on fewest transforms needed, via the shared scores worker, turning the crowd into a live search over the same transform space the paper enumerates.
mechanism: apply simple image transforms to flip a toy classifier's safe/unsafe verdict while a similarity meter proves the content is unchanged
text: toggle image transforms—grayscale, invert, rotate, noise—and flip a moderation verdict from unsafe to safe. the image stays visibly unchanged. simple transforms fool every classifier tested

paperTitle: Effect of biharmonic coupling in frequency-weighted Kuramoto oscillators
name: hysteresis-loop
plan: The paper maps the full two-parameter phase diagram of frequency-weighted Kuramoto oscillators with combined first- and second-harmonic coupling. Three collective states compete — incoherent, an antipodal multibranch state, and a symmetry-broken multibranch state — separated by three bistable regions and one narrow tristable region where all three are simultaneously stable attractors. The transitions into either ordered state are discontinuous and hysteretic: frequency weighting makes synchronization explosive, so the coupling strength where the population locks in going up is not the strength where it falls back apart coming down. The toy is two coupling dials over a visible ring of oscillator dots with an order-parameter gauge. The mechanic that sells it: drag the first-harmonic dial up past a threshold and the population snaps into sync; drag it back down and it stays synced well past where it locked in, only breaking apart at a noticeably lower value — a hysteresis loop the visitor traces with their own hand rather than reads about. Turn one ships one dial (first-harmonic strength, second-harmonic fixed near zero), a population of thirty to fifty oscillators with weighted frequencies drawn from a fixed distribution, direct numerical integration of the actual oscillator equations (not the paper's analytic reduction), and the order-parameter gauge showing the jump and the lag. The hard part is tuning population size and integration speed so the discontinuity is visible and fast enough for a browser slider, and, in a later turn, finding the tristable window, which the paper describes as narrow — a natural crowd hunt once both dials are live, checkable by anyone rerunning the same integration. Reuse the dataviz package for the order-parameter trace.
mechanism: drag two oscillator-coupling dials and watch a synchronization state jump at a different threshold going up than coming down
text: drag a coupling dial up and a ring of oscillators snaps into sync. drag back down and they stay locked far past where they first synchronized. the threshold to lock in and the threshold to break apart sit nowhere near each other

paperTitle: An improved range for the maximum critically $t$-intersecting hypergraphs
name: small-universe
plan: A k-uniform hypergraph is t-intersecting if every two edges share at least t elements, and critical if its smallest t-transversal has size exactly k. Frankl proved the maximum size of such a family is at most C(k+d, d), where d = k-t, once k is at least d to the fourth power, and conjectured the same bound holds far more broadly, for k greater than roughly c times d squared. This paper nails the conjecture for c = 30, pushing the guaranteed range down dramatically. The toy is a family-building game: pick k and t, watch d and the target wall C(k+d,d) appear, then click together a family of k-element subsets of a ground set while a live checker turns any pair sharing fewer than t elements red. The insight the visitor should stumble into by playing, not by reading: shrink the ground set to exactly k+d elements and take every single k-subset of it, and the pairwise overlap condition satisfies itself automatically, by simple inclusion-exclusion. The maximum isn't found by clever avoidance — it's the laziest possible construction, and the wall the paper proves is unbeatable is exactly its size. Turn one ships a small fixed case (k=4, t=2, ground set size adjustable up to eight or so), a compact subset picker instead of free-form clicking since C(10,4) is already 210 subsets, the red/green pairwise checker, and a progress bar racing family size against the wall. The hard part is keeping the picker legible at this combinatorial scale and the O(family squared) checker fast as the family grows. Reuse the extremal-geometry hub for framing and the shared scores worker for a speed leaderboard on reaching the known wall.
mechanism: build a family of k-element subsets under a live pairwise-overlap checker, racing to reach a binomial wall that cannot be beaten
text: click k-element subsets into a family and race a binomial wall—pairs have to overlap enough or they turn red. the wall is mathematically unbeatable. and the peak? just take every k-subset of k+d elements and stop

paperTitle: Delegated Fair Division
name: envy-relay
plan: The paper studies fair division where goods aren't split directly among people but delegated through a layer of centers: a center receives a bundle on behalf of its members and then redistributes internally. The catch is that fairness has to hold at both levels at once — centers must not envy each other's bundles, and each center's own members must not envy their centermates. The paper gives efficient algorithms for two versions, depending on whether members compare themselves against everyone in the world or only against their own center's roster, and proves envy-based guarantees hold at both levels simultaneously. The toy hands the visitor a small fixed instance — three centers, two members each, a handful of indivisible goods with a hidden valuation grid per member — and has them drag goods to centers, then to members, while a live checker flags envy at either level as it happens. Turn one ships one instance, one info-structure mode, and the checker; a mode toggle switching whether members can see outside their center comes later, since that's the paper's actual variable and changing what a player can see mid-game is the hard part to get right without it feeling arbitrary. The other hard part is showing eight valuation vectors without a wall of numbers — probably a small heatmap per agent instead of a table. Reuse the games surface for the room and drag interaction, scores for a fastest-to-zero-envy time on a shared instance bank so the crowd is racing the same puzzle, not separate copies of it.
mechanism: drag indivisible goods to centers then to members while a live checker enforces envy-freeness at both levels
text: drag goods between centers then within each center. both levels stay fair or you haven't won: centers with each other, members with their own

paperTitle: Characterizing the oxidation state of rocky exoplanets with the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE)
name: redox-read
plan: The paper simulates what LIFE, a proposed space mid-infrared interferometer, could actually measure about a rocky exoplanet's interior: not directly, but through the atmosphere its volcanism produces. Their retrievals show a clean trend across the mantle's oxidation state (measured in log units of oxygen fugacity relative to the iron-wüstite buffer, IW): oxidizing mantles vent CO2-dominated atmospheres, reducing mantles vent NH3-dominated ones, and intermediate mantles show up as CH4, each band spanning a few IW units, resolvable for an Earth-sized planet at 10 parsecs from a Sun-like star. The toy turns that trend into a guessing instrument: the visitor sees a bar chart of one hidden planet's relative CO2/CH4/NH3 abundances, generated from a randomly drawn oxidation state, and places a marker on an IW dial for where they think the mantle sits before revealing the true value and their error. Turn one ships one spectrum, one dial, one reveal — no history yet. The hard part is being honest about fidelity: the toy can't run ARCiS/LIFEsim, so spectra should be synthesized from the paper's own coarse dominance bands rather than a full radiative-transfer model, and the page needs to say plainly that this is the trend, not a reproduction of an actual retrieval. Once that's in place, the real payoff is collective: log every visitor's guess against the true value by IW bin, and the growing table becomes a live, checkable answer to which oxidation states are actually easy or hard to tell apart from spectra alone — the paper's distinguishability claim, replicated by a crowd instead of asserted.
mechanism: guess a hidden exoplanet's mantle oxidation state from a synthetic CO2/CH4/NH3 spectrum bar chart
text: guess an exoplanet's mantle oxidation from its atmospheric spectrum. oxidizing mantles vent CO2, reducing ones vent ammonia

paperTitle: Investigating Effective Uncertainty Visualizations for Ordinal Crowdsourced Data of Crowding Conditions
name: queue-call
plan: The paper runs a human-subjects study on how to visualize uncertainty in crowdsourced ordinal data — specifically, how crowded a train platform is, reported by commuters whose reports disagree. Comparing visualization styles, they find a real trade-off: cluster visualizations reduce cognitive load and raise people's confidence and trust in their read, while bubble treemaps make people more accurate at actually guessing the true crowd level, even though it feels harder to use. The toy doesn't illustrate that trade-off, it reruns it: a visitor is shown one of the two visualization styles, chosen at random, rendering a synthetic set of disagreeing crowding reports for a platform, and has to guess the true crowd level (empty, moderate, packed) and rate their own confidence before finding out if they were right. Every guess, correct or not, gets logged against which visualization it came from, so the site accumulates a live, growing version of the paper's own comparison — accuracy and confidence broken out by viz type — across however many people visit rather than the study's fixed lab sample. Turn one needs exactly one scenario generator with a known ground truth, the two visualization renderers, the guess-plus-confidence form, and a running aggregate table, seeded with the paper's own numbers as a placeholder until enough live guesses exist to speak for themselves. The hard part is generating enough distinct scenarios that repeat visitors can't just memorize answers, and being clear on the page that this is a replication in progress, not a finished result, especially while the sample is thin. Reuse dataviz's stats helpers for the running confidence intervals and scores for storing per-visualization tallies.
mechanism: guess a platform's true crowd level from one of two randomly-assigned uncertainty visualizations, feeding a live crowd-scale replication of the study
text: guess how crowded a train platform is from reports that disagree with each other. the way the disagreement is visualized changes what you get wrong

paperTitle: Rheology of dense suspensions of granular spherocylinders by particle-based simulation
name: rod-jam
plan: The paper builds a particle-based simulation of rod-shaped granular particles (spherocylinders) suspended in a fluid under shear, tracking friction and lubrication forces between rods up to an aspect ratio of 20. Two results make it a toy rather than a demo: shearing produces a viscosity spike right at start-up that then relaxes to a steady state, and that steady-state viscosity climbs with both packing density and rod aspect ratio, while the rods' alignment climbs too, but only up to a critical point that itself depends on aspect ratio. So there are two dials that both push the same two gauges in ways that interact. The toy hands the visitor those two dials — volume fraction and aspect ratio — over a canvas of rods, and a start-shear button; hitting it jostles the rods, the viscosity trace spikes then settles, and an alignment gauge climbs toward wherever its critical point sits for that aspect ratio. Turn one ships a fixed small population of rods, the two sliders, the shear button, and the two live traces — no leaderboard yet. The hard part is doing this cheaply: the paper's collision and lubrication forces are a real 3D physics model, and a 2D canvas running in a browser at interactive framerate has to be a stylized stand-in, not a reproduction — the page needs to say so, rather than implying the traces are the paper's actual numbers. Reuse the g gallery's 2D particle-canvas conventions and dataviz for the traces; once the sim is solid, a scores leaderboard for lowest peak viscosity at a fixed volume fraction turns it into a crowd search over aspect ratio, echoing the two-dial, two-gauge, no-winning-move shape that already worked for Concourse.
mechanism: tune packing density and rod aspect ratio, run a shear simulation, and watch viscosity and alignment gauges respond
text: adjust particle density and shape, then hit shear. watch viscosity spike then settle as the rods align. two dials, two gauges, both respond

paperTitle: Optimal Play in Hex on Finite and Infinite Boards
name: hex
plan: Hex is a classic connection game on a rhombic board where the first player is known to have a winning strategy, but almost nothing else about optimal play is understood — how short a forced win can be, and how few stones it takes. This paper pins two exact numbers down for the first time: on a 5-wide board, the shortest guaranteed winning path has length exactly 7 (λ(5)=7), confirming a 2004 conjecture of Campbell's; and on the infinite 5×∞ strip the same quantity drops to 5 — shorter than on the finite board, the counterintuitive part, since more room should help the defender, not the attacker. The mechanic: a real 5-wide Hex board, playable pass-and-play by two people sharing a screen, with a running counter tracking the length of any completed winning connection. The site doesn't announce the theoretical minimum up front — the first goal is discovering, by playing, that 7 is hard to beat, and that going wider makes it easier rather than harder. Turn one ships the board itself: hex-grid rendering, legal-move enforcement, win detection via connected-path search, and the path-length counter — no AI opponent, no scoring, just a board two people can actually finish a game on. The hard part, named honestly: an optimal Hex engine for 5-wide boards is a real solver, not a lookup table, and one that plays provably-shortest wins is a later-turn project, not a turn-one one; until it exists the counter is descriptive, not prescriptive. Reuse `games/` for the room and pass-and-play shell it already runs for board games, and `scores` for a leaderboard once a solver exists — lowest winning-path length achieved by a human, tracked separately for the finite and infinite-strip variants, since the paper says those numbers genuinely differ.
mechanism: two-player pass-and-play Hex on a 5-wide board with a live shortest-winning-path length counter
text: connect opposite sides before your opponent does. first player always wins — takes 7 moves on a 5-wide board, but only 5 on an infinite strip. more space shortens the win, not lengthens it

paperTitle: Intersections of Dragon Curves of the 18th Iteration
name: unfold
plan: The dragon curve is usually drawn by folding a strip of paper in half repeatedly and unfolding every crease to a right angle; the classic Heighway dragon comes from a 90° unfold and famously never crosses itself. This paper generalizes the fold angle and asks when the curve starts crossing itself, focusing on one specific generation: the 18th iteration. It finds that two particular edges of that curve first intersect once the unfolding angle passes 95.828° — a threshold established by directly examining those two edges, not a general theorem covering every angle or every iteration. The mechanic: an angle slider driving a live-rendered dragon curve at a fixed iteration depth, so dragging the slider past roughly 90° visibly deforms the familiar dragon into something that starts to overlap itself, with the two crossing edges from the paper highlighted the instant they touch. Turn one ships the renderer and slider alone, at a shallow iteration (6-10) where redraws stay smooth, plus a fixed checkpoint marking the paper's 95.828° for the 18th iteration specifically, labeled as a fact about that one generation rather than a universal law. The hard part: the 18th iteration is 2^18 segments, and finding self-intersections is naively an O(n^2) problem, so live slider-dragging at that depth needs either a shallower default with an explicit 18th-iteration 'verify' button that runs the expensive check once, or a spatial index. Worth being honest, too, that the paper hands you exactly one threshold at exactly one iteration, not a formula for the 19th — which is the opening for a crowd: let people search for the first crossing angle at deeper iterations than the paper reached, with any claimed record independently recomputable by anyone, the same cheat-proof shape as any arithmetic record hunt. Reuse `math` for hosting and its single-file explainer convention; the renderer needs no new backend.
mechanism: an angle slider that morphs a rendered dragon curve through its fold angle, revealing where it starts to self-intersect
text: drag an angle slider and morph a dragon curve. at 90° it stays crisp. past 95.828° it starts folding back on itself, touching for the first time. keep dragging to tangle it further

paperTitle: Driving up Inference Energy on SNNs: Per-Sample and Universal Sponge Attacks
name: sponge
plan: Spiking neural networks run on neuromorphic chips by communicating with sparse binary spikes instead of dense numbers, which is exactly why they get picked for always-on battery hardware: fewer spikes, less energy. This paper shows the same property is an attack surface. A 'sponge' input, crafted to maximize spike activity rather than to fool the classifier, inflates the network's per-inference operation count 1.5-2.6x while the predicted label stays correct on 98%+ of samples; the more alarming version is a single fixed binary perturbation, XORed onto any input with no per-sample tuning at all, that still inflates the operation count 1.09-1.24x across every dataset tested. Mapped onto real neuromorphic hardware, that is up to 13.24 mJ of extra energy per inference, quietly draining a battery that was supposed to last because of the spikes it wasn't using. The mechanic: a spike raster for one sample sits beside a live energy meter and a live predicted-label readout, both driven by a small real spiking classifier running client-side; the visitor gets a bit budget and flips individual spike bits, watching the meter climb and the label — hopefully — hold. Turn one ships that loop alone: raster, running operation-count meter, label readout, manual bit-flipping, no scoring yet, one small pre-trained model on one small dataset (NMNIST digits, not the paper's larger benchmarks). The hard part: the paper's real attack is gradient-guided, and that search can't be reproduced live in a browser from nothing, so the honest move is pre-computed universal perturbations from an offline reproduction, offered for people to apply and explore, labeled plainly as the guided version rather than staged as live discovery. This is offensive-security material about a published attack on real edge hardware, so it ships as an exhibit on a toy-scale model with the defense discussion attached, not as a working recipe against anyone's deployed device. Reuse `human/`'s exhibit framing for that honest-risk copy, the WASM-inference pattern already shipped elsewhere in the repo, and `scores` for a later leaderboard on most energy inflation per bit spent without breaking the label.
mechanism: flip individual spike bits in an event-based input to maximize a live energy meter while a client-side spiking classifier keeps its label
text: flip bits in a neural network to watch the energy meter climb. without changing what it predicts, drain a battery 1.5 to 2.6x faster. explore a hidden liability: those efficient spikes are also an attack surface

paperTitle: Measuring Alignment With Reader Highlights Net of Position and Length
name: underline
text: highlight sentences to keep on a tight budget. get scored against Luhn's 1958 word-count heuristic, Claude Opus 5, and human readers. watch where you land on the paper's spectrum. every new visitor's picks turn the crowd baseline from illustration into real data
plan: The paper solves a real methodology problem: if you want to know whether a compressor keeps the sentences readers actually cared about, the obvious metric is confounded twice over, because crowd-marked sentences are front-loaded and longer than average. Their fix is to compare each marked sentence only against unmarked sentences at the same relative depth and the same within-document length rank. Scored that way, a language-model importance ranking beats matched neighbours by +0.196, a single human reader by +0.182 (indistinguishable from GPT-5.4, below Claude Opus 5), Luhn's 1958 word-count heuristic by +0.088, and naive truncation by +0.003 — statistically null, as it should be, since it only reads position. That is a ranked scale a visitor can be placed on. Turn one: show a document, let the visitor click sentences to mark the ones they'd keep on a tight budget, then compute their enrichment against pre-built matched-neighbour baselines (same depth quartile, same length rank) for two or three seeded documents, and plot the visitor's score on the paper's spectrum next to Luhn, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 5, and the human average. The hard part is staying honest about power: one person's highlights on one document is not a replication of a 120-document, 12-reader study, and the page has to say so plainly rather than implying a real p-value. What's genuinely load-bearing is that every extra visitor who highlights the same seeded documents turns the toy's own placeholder baseline into real crowd-mark data, literally reproducing the paper's setup rather than just illustrating it. Reuse: `workers/scores` for a session-score record (`com.minomobi.lab.score`, higherIsBetter true); no auth needed for turn one.
mechanism: highlighting sentences in a document and scoring the picks against a matched depth/length baseline

paperTitle: Partial vision leads to an unexpected emergent collective behavior in active aligning particles
name: blindspot
text: watch a flock of particles shift between three phases by tuning how wide each one sees and which way it looks. narrow vision creates tight chasing packs. backward-facing vision does the opposite: a weirdly homogeneous flock
plan: Standard flocking models (Vicsek) give every particle a full circle of vision. This paper cuts that circle into two blind-spotted cones and finds the blind spots are not just noise — they change the phase of the flock. Narrowing lateral vision destabilizes global order and produces dense travelling bands that don't appear with full vision. Breaking front-back symmetry does something sharper: forward-biased vision drives 'follow the leader' clustering (tight, chasing packs), while backward-biased vision stabilizes an unusually homogeneous flock with suppressed density fluctuations — the opposite personality from the same aperture, just pointed the other way. The mechanic is two dials on a canvas of a few hundred self-propelled particles: aperture (how wide each cone is) and orientation bias (how much of that cone faces forward vs. backward). Turn one ships the sim itself — particles that align only with neighbours inside their cone, plus thermal noise, plus the two sliders — with a live order parameter so the three regimes (disordered gas, banded flow, homogeneous flock) are visually distinct without needing to explain the physics first. What's hard is performance: cone-restricted neighbour lookups for hundreds of particles need spatial binning to stay smooth in a browser, and the slider ranges need tuning so the phase changes actually land inside the range a visitor will try, not off at the edges. What to reuse: `packages/dataviz` for a live order-parameter trace; `workers/scores` to log crowd-submitted (aperture, bias) coordinates against measured order and band density, building a phase map nobody has published for this exact model — the same crowd-search move `docs/ARXIV-TOYS.md`'s Concourse entry made for a different phase diagram.
mechanism: tuning a flock's vision-cone width and front-back bias and watching which of three phases emerges

paperTitle: Partizan Subtraction with Full and Truncated Support
name: richman
text: play an asymmetric pebble game: you take 3, the bot takes 1, and loses almost everywhere except a band near zero. slide a dial to trim your moves and watch your winning odds flip. hit one strange point where the outcome starts alternating unpredictably
plan: A heap of pebbles; Left may take 1 through L on her turn, Right may take 1 through R on his, last to move wins. If L ≠ R, the paper shows the player with the bigger move-set (the richer mover) wins for every heap size except finitely many exceptions — the small-heap cases where the underdog can still pull it off. To restore fairness they trim the richer player's smallest moves out (Truncated Support): a shallow trim leaves the imbalance intact above some heap size; a deep trim flips who dominates instead; and at one specific middle depth, the win pattern stops being predictable at all and becomes genuinely periodic, with infinitely many wins on both sides. That's a real difficulty curve. Turn one: fix L=1, R=3, show the heap as a row of stones, let the visitor play Right against a perfect-play bot (a P/N table is trivial dynamic programming for these heap sizes) and watch the richer side win everywhere except a small labelled band of exceptions near zero. A trim slider then lets the visitor pull moves out of Right's set live, with the P/N table recomputing underneath so the fairness transition — and the strange balanced middle point where the winner starts alternating unpredictably — is something you watch happen, not something you're told about. The hard part is picking L, R and a trim range small enough to stay playable by eye while still crossing all three regimes. Reuse: `games/` for a Durable Object room so two visitors can play head-to-head at a chosen (L, R, trim) and the site tallies real win rates against the DP table's prediction; `workers/scores` for those tallies.
mechanism: playing an asymmetric pebble-subtraction game against a perfect-play bot, with a trim dial that pulls the richer player's moves back toward parity

paperTitle: Non-reciprocity drives a Brownian dimer out of equilibrium
name: dimer
text: two beads in an asymmetric spring spontaneously spin from pure thermal noise, no motor. tune the asymmetry slider and watch the measured rotation match the paper's formula, then hunt for new stable patterns in the unexplored regime
plan: Two beads, each jiggled by the same single thermal bath, connected by a spring — except the spring pulls bead A toward B harder than it pulls B toward A, breaking Newton's third law at the level of the coupling. No external drive, no temperature difference, just one broken symmetry in the spring, and the pair spontaneously starts to circulate: a persistent rotational current appears out of pure thermal noise, a free-running two-body engine. The paper solves this exactly in the zero-rest-length limit (a clean closed form for the steady current) and only explores the finite-rest-length case numerically — meaning that regime is still an open hunt. The mechanic: a canvas with two dots joined by a visible spring, an asymmetry slider (0 = reciprocal, no rotation; 1 = fully one-sided) and a live readout of the measured circulating current. Turn one ships the zero-rest-length case only, with the measured current plotted against the paper's exact formula in real time, so the visitor can watch the simulation earn trust before the toy extends into the unsolved finite-rest-length regime. What's hard is getting a numerically stable current estimate out of a noisy Euler-Maruyama integrator fast enough to feel live, and being upfront that the more visually interesting finite-rest-length regime is genuinely unresolved in the paper, not just simplified for the toy. Reuse: a client-side canvas force-model in the vein of Concourse's ERM/SFM sim; `workers/scores` for a 'highest circulation found' leaderboard (`com.minomobi.lab.score`, higherIsBetter true) over the finite-rest-length parameter space, checkable by anyone re-running the same integrator on the submitted parameters.
mechanism: tuning the non-reciprocity of a spring joining two Brownian beads and reading off the circulating current it produces

paperTitle: The semi-inducibility of the blue--blue--red path on four vertices
name: semipath
text: build a graph by hand or generate standard shapes, watch a live score show how dense a specific pattern gets, and compare against the proven-optimal clique-plus-regular construction at the same size
plan: Take any graph G. Look at every ordered quadruple of vertices (v1,v2,v3,v4) where v1v2 is a non-edge, v2v3 is a non-edge, and v3v4 is an edge — a 'blue-blue-red path' stamped onto G by which pairs are and aren't connected. The paper asks how dense you can make that pattern (as a fraction of n^4) and settles it: the maximum is achieved by a graph built from a clique disjoint from an asymptotically regular graph, closing an exceptional case left open by an earlier classification. That's a build-a-graph-to-beat-a-target problem, and it's exactly checkable: anyone can recount the pattern in whatever graph they build. The mechanic: a canvas where the visitor adds vertices and edges by hand (or generates cliques and regular graphs via a slider) up to a few dozen nodes, with a live counter showing the pattern's density in their graph, next to a reference slider that builds the paper's own clique-plus-regular-graph construction at the same n so the visitor can watch their freehand attempts fall short of the proven-optimal shape. Turn one ships exactly that: the graph canvas, the live O(n^2)-ish incremental density counter, and the reference construction slider — no numeric ceiling asserted, since the abstract states that a maximum exists and names the extremal construction but doesn't give the closed-form value, and the toy shouldn't invent one. The hard part is keeping the live count responsive as the graph grows past a few dozen vertices without recomputing all n^4 quadruples from scratch on every edit. Reuse: the math wing's single-file explainer conventions; `workers/scores` for a 'closest to the construction' record table, recomputable by anyone the way the Erdos toy's record pairs are.
mechanism: building a graph and maximizing the live count of a fixed non-edge/non-edge/edge pattern against a reference construction

paperTitle: Franklin's identity for $n$-color partitions and companion Beck-type identities
name: partition-twins
plan: An n-color partition of m is a partition where a part of size k can be dressed in any of k colors, so 3 and 3-in-red-vs-3-in-blue count as different parts. The paper proves that among all n-color partitions of m, the set with exactly j distinct parts whose size and color are both divisible by r is exactly the same size as the set with exactly j distinct parts that each repeat r or more times — for every j, not just in total. Two families defined by unrelated-looking rules, in lockstep. The toy: pick m and r, and the page enumerates every n-color partition of m (small m keeps this exhaustive and instant), sorts them into the two families bucketed by j, and renders both columns as stacks of colored blocks — block height is part size, shade is color index. Counts per row match live as m or r changes; that's the whole first turn, and it already delivers the surprise, since nothing about the definitions suggests equal counts. The hard part, deliberately deferred: the paper gives an explicit bijection between the two families, and a second turn should let a visitor click a partition in one column and have its actual partner highlight in the other, but that requires pulling the real construction out of the proof rather than guessing one — ship turn one without it and say so. Crowd angle: a race mode where visitors guess a partition's partner before the page reveals it, timed, with a leaderboard, and the partitions people most often guess wrong get pinned as the site's featured examples — crowd-sourced hard cases, not a static demo. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions and workers/scores for the guess-race leaderboard.
mechanism: enumerate and sort n-color partitions into two rule-defined families and watch counts match
text: partition numbers into colored parts, then sort them two ways. one rule checks divisibility by r, the other checks parts that repeat r times — completely different rules but they always count the same. watch the columns stay locked as you adjust

paperTitle: Graph Is the Verifier: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Interprocedural Vulnerability Detection
name: evidence-chain
plan: The paper's motivating number: on a sample of real CVEs, 71.7% of vulnerable functions cannot be correctly classified by looking at that function alone — the evidence is in a caller, a callee, or a dataflow edge somewhere else. Their fix trains an agent against a code property graph and only rewards a verdict when the agent cites graph nodes that actually contain the evidence, checked by exact node-ID match rather than text similarity — so guessing the right answer without doing the legwork scores zero. The toy translates that scoring rule directly: a visitor is shown one function flagged suspicious, rendered as the center of a small graph of callers, callees, and dataflow edges. Nothing is visible except the target function's own code until you click a neighboring node, which reveals its snippet. You submit a verdict (vulnerable or not) plus which nodes you actually opened and used — and you're scored against a precomputed real evidence set for that case, exact match, the same rule the paper's reward uses. Turn one ships a single hand-built case (a bug whose root cause is a missing check three hops away) with this click-reveal-cite loop and a score. The hard part: authoring cases that are honestly interprocedural, not solvable from the target function alone, without shipping anything that scans a visitor's own code — this stays a fixed set of prepared cases, never a live scanner, to keep it a puzzle and not a tool. Crowd angle: a leaderboard on fewest nodes opened before a correct, evidence-backed verdict, and a way for solvers to submit their own small case once they've solved enough, growing the set.
mechanism: click through a code graph gathering evidence nodes, then a verdict scored only if the cited nodes match the real evidence
text: a function is flagged buggy, but the bug isn't there. click through the code graph gathering evidence: a missing null check somewhere, a cast three hops up the call chain. submit your verdict and which nodes you opened. you're scored by exact match with the real evidence that matters

paperTitle: Microscopic study of topological phase transitions: Percolation point of view
name: decoherence-map
plan: A topological qubit (the paper studies the color code and the toric code) survives noise until decoherence percolates across the lattice — enough corrupted sites connect into one spanning cluster and the protected information is gone. The paper's twist is explosive percolation: instead of corrupting sites at random, bias the process to avoid merging large clusters as long as possible, delaying the spanning transition. Plain decoherence, the color code and toric code track each other closely. Under the explosive, biased version, they diverge — the same noise process breaks the two codes differently, which the paper flags as evidence there's no universal microscopic story even between close cousins. The toy: a lattice grid, a decoherence-rate slider, and an explosiveness slider (0 = ordinary random percolation, higher = biased against forming a giant cluster). Corrupted sites paint themselves onto the grid live; a single gauge reports whether the logical qubit still survives (spanning cluster present or not). Turn one ships one code (the color code, the paper's primary case), both sliders, and that survive/fail gauge — using cluster-spanning as a stand-in for the paper's quasi-local entanglement-negativity measure, stated plainly as a simplification, not a reproduction. A second turn adds the toric code side by side so the divergence under explosive bias is visible directly. Crowd angle: every visitor's (rate, bias, survived?) trial plots onto a shared phase diagram that sharpens as trials accumulate — a real, cheap way to trace a boundary that's expensive to compute exactly. Reuse packages/dataviz for the phase-diagram chart and the same canvas-sim, no-server pattern as Concourse.
mechanism: set a decoherence rate and an explosive-percolation bias, watch a lattice corrode, and read off whether the logical qubit survives
text: watch quantum noise spread across a lattice. your logical qubit dies when the noise connects all the way across. but change the spreading pattern to avoid forming large clusters and delay decoherence. watch the threshold move as you shift between ordinary and explosive spreading

paperTitle: Effects of a disk structure on stellar motion at the Galactic Center
name: spin-or-disk
plan: Stellar orbits near Sagittarius A* are the tool used to measure the black hole's spin, via a specific relativistic effect: Lense-Thirring precession, frame-dragging from the spin itself. This paper's result is a spoiler for that measurement: if the mass around SgrA* isn't spherical but sits in a flattened disk (density falling as a power law in radius), the disk induces its own extra precession — a secular shift, an in-plane component, and an out-of-plane component — derived analytically. For one particular star, S301, the disk-induced out-of-plane precession can be large enough to compete directly with the frame-dragging signal. Meaning: the same observed wobble could be spin, or could be disk, or some of both, and current data can't fully tell them apart. The toy hands the visitor that degeneracy directly. Pick a star (turn one ships S301, the case where it matters), set a disk mass, a density power-law index, and an orientation relative to the orbital plane, and watch the orbit's ellipse precess using the paper's closed-form rate expressions. Two readouts sit side by side: the precession this disk configuration produces, and the precession the black hole's own spin would need to produce the same wobble alone — nudging one dial should visibly trade off against the other. The hard part, named honestly: the actual acceleration and precession formulas have to come from the paper's equations, not be approximated from the abstract; if that derivation isn't available when this gets built, turn one ships the qualitative two-dial, two-gauge tradeoff with illustrative rather than GR-exact numbers, clearly labeled as such. Crowd angle: visitors submit disk configurations that reproduce S301's actual observed precession within its error bars, and those accumulate into a shared cloud showing the full family of disk-versus-spin solutions the data can't currently distinguish — a real visualization of an open degeneracy, not a single guess.
mechanism: trade disk mass and shape against black-hole spin while both are forced to reproduce the same observed orbital precession
text: match a star's observed orbit around a black hole: is it the black hole's spin, a disk of gas, or both? they both produce the same orbit precession and trade off against each other. adjust one and the other shifts to keep the observed orbit matched

paperTitle: Recover, Decode, Reguard: Guard-Agnostic Defense Amplification against Encoded VLM Jailbreaks
name: decode-gap
plan: Safety classifiers that screen requests to vision-language models judge surface form, not meaning: a harmful request re-encoded as set theory, a rare language, or an image of text slips past a guard that would catch it in plain language. The paper builds the obvious fix, a recover-and-decode amplifier that transcribes and restates the request into plain text before the guard sees it, and evaluates it honestly against an eleven-attack ensemble: undefended, the ensemble breaks 89-91% of behaviours; guard plus amplifier still leaves 63-65% broken; a stricter reguard layer closes much of that gap but pushes benign over-refusal to 81-92%. No configuration in the paper reaches both low attack success and low over-refusal at once. The toy is a single strictness dial and two gauges: attack-success-rate and over-refusal-rate, wired to the paper's own numbers so the two gauges visibly fight as you drag the dial, with the amplifier as a second toggle that shifts the curve without breaking the tradeoff. Turn one: ship the dial, the two gauges, and a fixed frontier plotted from the paper's five guard/two-target data points, no live inference. The hard part is being honest that the frontier is precomputed from the paper's reported numbers, not a live classifier the visitor is fooling, and saying so on the page without deflating the point, which is that the tradeoff is real and load-bearing. Reuse: `human/`'s exhibit framing and honest-risk copy convention, `packages/dataviz/` for the two-gauge readout. A crowd layer can come later — inviting visitors to place a hypothetical guard config and checking it against the same frontier — but turn one is the dial and the two gauges alone.
mechanism: single strictness dial driving two opposed gauges (attack success vs over-refusal) plotted against a fixed empirical frontier
text: jailbreaks against vision models hide as rare languages, set-theory notation, text hidden in images. drag a dial to harden the guard. watch two gauges climb opposite ways: attacks stopped, benign requests blocked. there is no dial setting that wins both

paperTitle: Asymptotic bias of the plug-in Shannon entropy estimator under a regularly varying occupancy model
name: tail-lag
plan: This is the unseen-species problem given a precise clock. If you estimate the diversity (Shannon entropy) of a population by just counting what you've sampled so far — the plug-in estimator — you're always wrong, because you haven't seen the rare stuff yet. The paper proves how wrong, for populations whose rarity follows a power law with tail index alpha in (0,1): the bias shrinks as n^(alpha-1) times a slowly-varying correction, with an explicit constant. Small alpha means a long, thin tail of rare types and a bias that barely shrinks as you sample more; alpha near 1 means it clears up fast. The toy: load a corpus — word frequencies from a Bluesky firehose sample, k-mers from a genome, whatever's lying around — and sample it word by word or read by read. Two lines climb together: the running plug-in entropy estimate, and the true entropy computed on the full corpus. The gap between them is the bias, and turn one just needs that gap drawn live as the sample grows, with the corpus's fitted alpha displayed as a number that predicts how stubborn the gap will be. The hard part is fitting alpha honestly from a finite sample without pretending the asymptotic formula is exact at small n — show the fit as a fit, with a residual, not as ground truth. What makes it a crowd toy rather than a demo: visitors submit their own corpus and the site keeps a table of submitted alphas, ranked by how slow their gap closes — the person who finds the most stubbornly long-tailed real-world dataset holds the record, and the record is recomputable by anyone who resamples it. Reuse: `math.mino.mobi`'s extremal-geometry hub conventions for a new entry, `packages/dataviz/` for the paired curves, `workers/scores` for the alpha leaderboard.
mechanism: live plug-in-entropy-vs-truth convergence race on a user-submitted corpus, scored by fitted tail index
text: feed a corpus: word frequencies, genome reads, Bluesky posts. the entropy estimate climbs as you sample more—it's wrong at first because rare things haven't appeared. some corpora converge fast, some stubbornly slow. find the slowest: that's the longest-tailed dataset

paperTitle: Contrastive ESA: Human Evaluation of Multiple Translations at Once
name: spanrace
plan: Standard machine-translation evaluation shows a rater one translation at a time, which is noisy and slow because every rater invents their own scale from scratch. This paper's fix, cESA, shows a rater several translations of the same sentence side by side, has them mark major and minor error spans across all of them at once, then assign one absolute 0-100% score with the others as visible context — and validated across twelve English-to-Japanese models, this shared-context protocol cuts both annotation time and inter-rater noise versus the one-at-a-time baseline, while still producing a clean non-parametric model ranking with no post-hoc correction needed.
