The toy hands a visitor exactly that task: one source sentence, four translations stacked underneath, drag to paint error spans on any of them, then move one slider to score the set. Turn one is that single round, plus a reveal comparing your spans and score against the pooled crowd's. The mechanic is legible instantly because it's the same thing a language learner already does instinctively — noticing that one version sounds off next to the others — the paper just shows that doing it side-by-side instead of alone is measurably better science. The hard part is sourcing translation sets that have a real quality spread without a firm reference answer to grade against, so score against pooled-annotator consensus rather than a fake ground truth, and say so. What improves with a crowd: the paper's actual claim is that shared context reduces variance across raters, so a live per-sentence agreement score that visibly tightens as more people rate it is the toy demonstrating its own premise. Reuse: `games/` for round structure and identity, `workers/scores` for per-sentence-pair aggregate stats.
mechanism: side-by-side multi-translation error-span marking plus one absolute score, aggregated live against pooled rater consensus
text: mark error spans on four translations stacked. give one score. then see your judgment against the crowd's. you're already doing this when one version sounds off next to the others—the paper just validates this shared-context method

paperTitle: Mixed metric dimension of $2$-connected graphs
name: few-beacons
plan:
The paper proves that in any 2-connected graph other than a cycle, you can always uniquely identify every vertex and every edge using at most 2c(G) landmarks, where c(G) is the cyclomatic number — the number of independent cycles, i.e. edges minus vertices plus one. A landmark identifies something by its shortest-path distance to it (for an edge, the smaller of the distances to its two endpoints); a set of landmarks 'resolves' the graph if no two vertices or edges share the same distance vector. This is the mixed metric dimension, and the paper settles it in terms of a number you can read off a graph in seconds by counting edges beyond a spanning tree.

The mechanic: hand the visitor a 2-connected graph with a few cycles and a supply of landmark tokens. Dropping a token recomputes every vertex's and edge's distance vector live and highlights, in red, any pair still sharing one — done when red disappears. Score is the token count; the paper's 2c(G) is shown as a ceiling you should never need, and beating it is the actual game.

Turn one: render one fixed 2-connected graph with 2-4 independent cycles, implement BFS-based distance vectors and the ambiguous-pair highlighter, and let placing/removing tokens update live — no scoring or gallery yet, just the resolve-and-see-red loop on one graph.

The hard part is the edge case: two edges sharing all landmark distances even when their endpoints don't, which is why mixed metric dimension needs its own checker, not the ordinary vertex-only one. Reuse the math wing's single-page conventions and `workers/scores` for a per-graph best-token leaderboard.
mechanism: place minimum landmark tokens on a graph so every vertex and edge gets a unique distance fingerprint
text: drop tokens on a graph and watch every vertex and edge get distances to each. if two match their vector, they turn red. place tokens until red vanishes, using as few as you can. there's a tight ceiling based only on edges minus vertices plus one.

paperTitle: An Optimal Bound for Ramsey Goodness of Cycles
name: ramsey-loop
plan:
The paper closes a conjecture highlighted in Montgomery's 2026 ICM survey: for a cycle C_n and any graph H, once N is at least a constant times |H|, the Ramsey number R(C_n,H) hits its lower-bound formula exactly — (χ(H)-1)(n-1) + σ(H), where χ(H) is H's chromatic number and σ(H) is the smallest colour class in an optimal colouring of H. Below that threshold the exact value can run higher; past it, cycles are 'good' for every H with no slack at all, and the bound needed to guarantee it is linear in |H| — the best shape such a bound could take.

The mechanic: the visitor builds a red/blue colouring of the edges of a growing complete graph K_N. Red edges must never complete a red n-cycle; blue edges must never complete a copy of a chosen small H (triangle, path, star, offered as a gallery). A counter shows the theoretical wall, (χ(H)-1)(n-1)+σ(H), and the visitor's job is to survive one vertex short of it, then watch every colouring break once N reaches the wall — checked live, not merely asserted.

Turn one: fix H to a triangle and a small n, render K_N with clickable edges toggling red/blue, and a live checker flagging the first red n-cycle or blue triangle formed — no wall counter or gallery yet, just colour-and-get-caught for one case.

The hard part is the live subgraph detector: catching a closed red n-cycle, specifically, and a blue copy of an arbitrary small H, efficiently enough to run on every click. Reuse `erdos/`'s single-page math conventions and `workers/scores` for best-N-survived per choice of H.
mechanism: two-colour a growing complete graph's edges to dodge a red cycle and a blue subgraph, racing the exact wall where every colouring must fail
text: color edges of a complete graph as it grows, red or blue. red can't form a red n-cycle, blue can't form a blue copy of your chosen small graph. survive as long as you can — there's an exact threshold where every coloring fails.

paperTitle: SkillGate: Cost Efficient Runtime Malicious Skill File Detection in Coding Agents
name: trust-window
plan:
SkillGate is a deployed defense against a real supply-chain problem: coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot) now install 'skill' markdown files from public registries with one command and no security screening, and some of those files carry hidden instructions to exfiltrate credentials or redirect the agent. The paper's system doesn't read every file in full — a regex prefilter waves through obviously-safe files, and flagged files only have their matched snippet windows sent to an LLM judge rather than the whole document, cutting input tokens by 77% while hitting F1=0.817 and a 1.13% false-positive rate on a 1,650-file benchmark.

The toy hands the visitor that same constraint instead of the model: a skill file appears, mostly legitimate boilerplate, with a shrinking budget of characters the visitor may actually read (mirroring the snippet-window idea) before calling it safe or malicious. The injected instruction hides in a comment, a code fence, or an innocuous-sounding line near the end — exactly where a regex prefilter would or wouldn't look. Score is accuracy against a fixed, declawed corpus, with the visitor's own hit rate posted next to SkillGate's F1 for comparison, as calibration rather than competition.

Turn one: one hand-written pair of files (one clean, one with an obvious-in-hindsight backdoor line), a fixed 200-character reading budget spent by clicking lines to reveal them, ending in a safe/malicious button and a right/wrong reveal — no corpus, budget tuning, or scoreboard yet.

The hard part is writing malicious examples that are genuinely subtle rather than cartoonish, so the game teaches the actual failure mode instead of trivia. Reuse `human/`'s exhibit framing and `workers/scores` for the leaderboard.
mechanism: read a suspicious skill file under a shrinking character budget and call it safe or malicious before the budget runs out
text: open a suspicious skill file mostly hidden. reveal lines as your budget shrinks, spot something wrong, call it safe or malicious. your score gets compared to the algorithm's score — a measure of how much you can trust a quick scan.

paperTitle: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
name: runway
plan:
The paper models a startup as a single number — funding, momentum, whatever you like — doing a random walk between a lower boundary (failure) and an upper one (success), where the founder picks, at every instant, which 'activity' drives the walk. Each activity sits at a point in a plane of drift-to-volatility (riskiness) against drift-to-cost (efficiency). The paper's result is structural: the optimal policy never uses an activity that's dominated on both axes — it only ever switches between activities on the efficient frontier of that plane, and which activities make the frontier, and therefore the whole shape of the optimal strategy, changes with the numbers, which the paper classifies completely.

The toy: the visitor sees five or six candidate activities plotted on the risk/efficiency plane (a marketing push, a pivot, a fundraise, a grind), picks one per tick, watches the walk move, and can switch anytime before hitting a boundary. A shadow line shows what the frontier-optimal player would have done from the same position — not to beat the visitor, but to make visible, after a run, whether a detour off the frontier is what cost the game.

Turn one: one fixed set of four activities, a canvas random walk with an adjustable current activity, and the two boundaries — win/lose only, no shadow line or frontier classification yet.

The hard part is the frontier logic itself: computing which activities are actually undominated for the current parameters, and keeping that consistent as the visitor's choices change nothing about the frontier but everything about which point on it matters. Reuse `civ/`'s simulation-loop conventions and `workers/scores` for fastest-to-success or most-turns-survived.
mechanism: pick which risk/cost activity drives a startup's random walk each tick, using only frontier-efficient choices to reach the success boundary
text: guide a random walk with your choice of activity each turn — marketing, pivot, fundraise, grind. each trades risk for cost. reach success before hitting failure. there's an efficiency frontier of activities, and the best path stays on it.

paperTitle: "Dragon Slayer Becomes the Dragon": How Players Perceive and Respond to Inequality in the Game World of Whiteout Survival
name: turncoat
plan: The paper interviews and think-aloud-observes players of the mobile game Whiteout Survival and finds a consistent pattern: people near the bottom of the resource/rank ladder criticize the game's unequal distribution, but the same players, once they climb by accumulating resources or social capital, start defending the very structures they used to call unfair. Fairness judgments track rank, not principle. The toy is a stripped-down incremental ladder — click to gather resources, spend them to climb a visible rank ladder that funnels rewards steeply upward — with periodic checkpoints that ask a single question: 'is this distribution fair?' yes or no. Turn one ships the ladder itself plus the checkpoint prompt, storing each answer alongside the player's rank at the time, no aggregation yet. The interesting artifact appears once many people have played: a chart of fairness-yes-rate against rank at time of answer, which either reproduces the paper's flip or doesn't, live, in front of the visitor. The hard part is making the ladder's inequality feel real rather than obviously rigged — the reward curve has to be steep enough that climbing changes what you'd defend, but earned enough that a low-rank player doesn't just call it a bad game and quit before the flip has a chance to show up. Reuse workers/scores to store (answer, rank, timestamp) tuples keyed by a new game slug — it's already a generic table behind auth.mino.mobi identity, so no new backend is needed. No 3D, no WASM: a canvas or DOM ladder and a modal are enough for turn one.
mechanism: an incremental resource ladder that polls your opinion on its own fairness as your rank changes, then aggregates the flip across everyone who played
text: climb a resource ladder and rate if it's fair as you rank up. everyone finds the bottom unfair and the top generous. same math, different opinions

paperTitle: Improved bounds on the inradius and inverse inradius process of the convex hull of planar Brownian motion
name: inradius
plan: The paper studies the convex hull of a planar Brownian path and two numbers attached to it: the inradius (the biggest circle that fits inside the hull) and its reciprocal, the inverse inradius. Along the way it proves closed-form expressions for the expected range of two independent 1-D Brownian motions, and uses an exit-time computation on what it calls the 'hourglass domain' to nearly quintuple the previous upper bound on the expected inverse inradius. The toy: run a planar random walk live on canvas, draw its convex hull as it grows, and continuously report the two numbers, normalized so hulls of different lengths are comparable. Turn one ships exactly that — walk, hull, live inradius and inverse-inradius readout, nothing else. A second turn adds the hunt: fix the step count, let the visitor reroll the walk as many times as they like, and keep a public record table of the roundest hull found (inradius near the bounding circle) and the most needle-like (inverse inradius blown up) at each step count — a record anyone can verify instantly by rerolling with the same seed, so cheating isn't possible. The hard part is honesty about what the record table means: rerolling isn't discovering new mathematics, it's sampling a known distribution for its tail, and the page should say so plainly rather than implying anyone is pushing on the paper's actual bound. Reuse the math/geometry hub's single-page explainer conventions and workers/scores for the record table, with no new backend beyond that.
mechanism: repeated planar random walks whose convex hull you inspect, hunting for the roundest and most needle-like hulls at a fixed step count
text: spin random walks and watch their outlines take shape. hunt for the roundest or sharpest outline at a fixed step count. everyone's best finds go public

paperTitle: Discrete power-law decay of subsystem distance after a quantum quench
name: quench
plan: The paper quenches the quantum transverse-field Ising chain — flips the field strength at t=0 and watches an entangled subsystem relax back toward its eventual stationary ensemble — and finds that the late-time decay of a rigorous distance measure between the two (the Bures distance) follows a power law whose exponent is not continuous. It only ever takes one of a short list of values: 1, 5/4, 3/2, 7/4, 2, 5/2, and potentially further ones, depending on which piece of a specific function tied to the pre-quench Hamiltonian's excitation structure is active. The previously known t^-3/2 decay for a ground-state quench turns out to be one entry on this list, not a special case outside it. The toy: two sliders, pre-quench field and post-quench field, and a live log-log plot of the decay curve with a fitted exponent readout that snaps to the nearest rung of the ladder as you drag. Turn one ships the sliders and plot against a precomputed grid rather than a live derivation — the exact classification depends on boundary and continuity properties of that excitation function that are easy to get subtly wrong on the fly, so the honest build solves the free-fermion quench on a coarse (pre-field, post-field) grid offline in a script, checks the result in as static JSON, and the browser only interpolates and displays which rung each point lands on. The pitch is that you cannot slide the exponent smoothly no matter how you turn the dials — the visible snapping is the physics, not a rendering artifact. Reuse packages/dataviz for the log-log chart and its axis conventions.
mechanism: two field-strength dials driving a live decay curve whose fitted exponent snaps between a fixed short list of values and never lands in between
text: dial two field strengths and the decay rate snaps between fixed speeds. it never transitions smoothly no matter how you twist the dials

paperTitle: General position sets in strong products with paths and cycles
name: no-through-line
plan: A general position set is a set of vertices in a graph where no vertex sits on a shortest path between two others — the graph analogue of 'no three points collinear'. The paper studies these sets in strong products: stack s copies of a graph H into a path-shaped bundle, and the largest general position set you can fit is exactly twice the size of H's own best set, gp(H) — for every s from 2 upward, whether the bundle is three copies deep or a thousand. It also gives exact values when the stacking graph is a small cycle instead of a path, and finds explicit counterexamples to the natural guess that gp multiplies across products of two cycles. The mechanic: render the product grid, let the visitor click vertices to build a set, and highlight live any triple where one point lies on a shortest path between the other two — that's the violation, not a straight line in the usual sense, since 'shortest path' bends around the grid's wraparound if a cycle is involved. Turn one ships a small fixed case (say P_3 boxed with C_5) with a counter showing progress toward 2·gp(H), and a slider for s that visibly does nothing to the ceiling, which is the paper's actual surprise. The hard part is the geodesic-violation checker — it needs real shortest-path computation on the product graph, not a geometric collinearity test, and it has to run instantly on every click. What to reuse: the record-table pattern from the Erdős perimeter concept — a leaderboard of (graph pair, set found) is cheating-proof since anyone can recheck it in milliseconds — plus workers/scores for the table.
mechanism: click-to-place vertices on a product graph, live geodesic-violation checker, race to match or beat the paper's bound
text: click vertices to build a set where none lies on a shortest path between any two others. stack copies of your graph and grow the set as big as you can. the bound never changes — always exactly twice the original, however deep you stack

paperTitle: Automorphism Groups in Extremal Families of Polyhedral Graphs
name: lopsided
plan: Take the smallest possible 3-connected planar graph (a polyhedron's skeleton) that has at least one vertex of every degree from 3 up to n. The paper proves that once n reaches 14, every such minimum graph has a trivial automorphism group — no rotation, reflection, or relabeling maps it to itself except the identity. Build it as small as you can and it comes out lopsided every time, and the proof works by showing the high-degree vertices always end up in a configuration nothing can preserve. The toy: a graph editor constrained to stay planar and 3-connected, where the visitor adds vertices and edges chasing the degree checklist (a running list of which degrees 3..n are still missing), while a live automorphism-group calculator reports what symmetry survives after each edit. Turn one ships small n (say up to 8, where symmetric examples still exist) so the visitor can actually find a symmetric one and feel the win, with the counter creeping toward 14 visibly out of reach. The hard part, named directly: computing automorphism groups of arbitrary graphs is expensive in general, but these graphs are small and planar, so a brute-force permutation search bounded by the degree sequence should stay fast enough for a browser — that bound needs proving out before committing to the UI. What to reuse: the erdos-style record table pattern (a construction is a graph, and anyone can recheck its automorphism group instantly, so no leaderboard cheating is possible) and workers/scores for tracking the largest symmetric example found per n.
mechanism: constrained planar-graph editor with a live degree checklist and automorphism-group calculator
text: build a planar graph hitting every degree from 3 to n, as small as possible, while a live counter watches for symmetry — rotations, reflections, permutations that map it to itself. chase the degree checklist. at degree 14, the symmetries vanish. every minimal graph breaks perfectly lopsided

paperTitle: Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment: A Decision-Support Framework Towards Governed Supply Chain Systems
name: chain-of-command
plan: The paper builds a framework for scoring how autonomous an AI agent is — along delegation, consultation, and collaboration — and tests it by running the classic beer distribution game (four tiers: factory, distributor, wholesaler, retailer, each reordering stock under delay and demand noise) with each tier's ordering agent set to a different autonomy score. The finding: autonomy isn't free capability, it's positional. Turning it up helps the tiers closer to the factory and actively hurts the tiers closer to the retailer, even though nothing about the retailer's own agent changed — a same-cause, opposite-effect result depending only on where you sit in the chain. The toy: the visitor runs the four-tier beer game with one slider per tier controlling that tier's autonomy score, watches weekly orders and inventory swing across all four tiers, and gets a per-tier cost breakdown at the end. Turn one ships single-player, all four sliders under one visitor's control, with the cost table making the upstream-gain/downstream-harm split visible after one run. The hard part is tuning the underlying beer-game simulation so the positional effect actually shows up at toy scale and isn't drowned by noise — that needs calibrating against something like the paper's own parameters before the sliders mean anything. What to reuse: games/'s Durable Object rooms, so a stretch turn seats four humans each on one tier competing to minimize total chain cost while only controlling their own dial; workers/scores for a leaderboard of best total-cost configurations by tier assignment.
mechanism: four-tier supply-chain simulation with a per-tier autonomy dial, run and read the cost split
text: run a four-stage supply chain: factory, distributor, wholesaler, retailer. each gets its own autonomy dial. watch orders and inventory move as you tune them. the finding: raise autonomy upstream and chain costs fall. raise it downstream and they spike. same dial, opposite effects by position

paperTitle: Cyclic Neighborhoods in Digraphs
name: cycloop
plan: The paper studies digraphs where every vertex's in-neighborhood and out-neighborhood, taken as its own little sub-digraph, is never acyclic — every neighborhood you look at must already contain a directed cycle among itself. It proves that satisfying this everywhere forces density: a strongly connected such digraph needs at least 7n/3 edges, a strongly 2-connected one needs 8n/3, and both ratios are tight. The toy is a construction puzzle: a canvas of n dots, click two to draw a directed edge, click again to remove it. Each vertex glows red until both its neighborhoods contain a cycle, green once they do. A live counter shows current edges against the 7n/3 floor for the vertex count you're using, so you're always racing a number you can see. Turn one ships the editor and the live check for a small fixed n (six to nine dots) — arrow-drawing, cycle detection on each induced neighborhood, red/green vertices, and the edge-count-versus-floor readout. No strong-connectivity enforcement yet; that's a later pass. The hard part is making 'this cluster of dots loops back on itself' legible without saying 'induced subdigraph' — the red/green glow per vertex has to carry that alone. It's also easy to get the cycle-detection direction wrong (in-neighborhood vs out-neighborhood point different ways) and only notice on a case that should fail. Reuse geometry/'s single-file explainer conventions and erdos/'s framing; workers/scores for a record table of the sparsest verified construction at each n, which nobody can fake since the edge list recomputes the check instantly.
mechanism: click-to-draw directed graph editor with live per-vertex cycle detection, minimizing edges against a proven density floor
text: draw arrows between dots. each vertex glows green when its neighborhood contains a cycle. the sparsest strongly connected graph satisfying this needs exactly 7n/3 edges—a density bound the paper proves is tight. race it on screen

paperTitle: Fuglede's Conjecture on Cyclic Groups of Square-Free Order: The Case of Rapidly Growing Prime Factors
name: fuglede
plan: Fuglede's Conjecture asks whether a set tiles space by translation exactly when it admits an orthogonal Fourier basis — tile and spectral, two completely different-looking properties, conjectured to always coincide. This paper settles both directions for cyclic groups of square-free order whose prime factors grow fast enough, and the closing line is the hook: until now no cyclic group with an arbitrary number of distinct prime factors was known to satisfy the conjecture at all, and this gives an infinite family that does. The toy puts Z_n on a clock face. You place beads to mark a candidate tile T, then place a second color to mark a translate set S; the clock live-checks whether T+S covers every hour exactly once — that's tiling, and it's the whole first turn: bead placement, mod-n arithmetic, a green ring when the cover is exact and red ticks on whatever's missed or doubled. A later turn adds the spectral half — pick a frequency set for T and the site renders the Gram matrix of the resulting characters as a small heatmap, orthogonal reading as a diagonal-only grid — and lets you watch tile and spectral line up for the paper's family. The hard part, named plainly: 'spectral set' has no clock-face intuition the way tiling does, so that half needs its own honest framing (a search assist, not a manual construction) or it will just confuse. Reuse geometry/'s explainer format and erdos/'s conventions; workers/scores for a ledger of confirmed (n, T) pairs, verifiable by anyone re-running the same check.
mechanism: bead-placement clock editor that live-checks whether a chosen subset tiles Z_n by translation, extended to a spectral orthogonality check
text: mark a set on a clock. use translates to tile each hour exactly once. this same set also satisfies a completely separate mathematical condition. the paper is the first to prove both always work together for an infinite family of cyclic groups

paperTitle: Erdős-Pósa property of rooted tree minors
name: posa
plan: The classic Erdős–Pósa duality says: for any fixed tree T, a graph either contains k vertex-disjoint copies of a T-minor, or a small set of at most ck vertices kills every T-minor — packing and covering, always one or the other, with a linear constant. This paper shows the same duality survives when you additionally demand every copy be rooted in a chosen vertex set S, at no extra cost to the constant, improving an earlier quadratic bound on the rooted case to linear. The special case T = K2 is exactly Gallai's classical theorem on disjoint S-paths, i.e. Menger's theorem restricted to a subset of endpoints — which is the unpacking that makes this legible: it's the familiar 'many disjoint paths or a small cut' game, generalized from paths to trees. The toy is a two-role duel: mark a root set S on a graph, then either pack in disjoint rooted copies of a small pattern (starting with T = K2, a path between two S-vertices) or, once stuck, nominate a small vertex set that kills every remaining copy. The site verifies disjointness and kill-completeness. Turn one ships only the K2/Menger case — a path-finding and min-cut check, both easy to verify correctly — with general small trees (stars, spiders) as later work, since minor-model verification for an arbitrary T is real implementation risk and getting it wrong silently would be worse than not shipping it yet. Reuse geometry/'s conventions; consider games/ for a live packer-versus-breaker duel mode once the core check is solid.
mechanism: packer-vs-breaker duel: find disjoint rooted tree copies or a small vertex set that kills them all
text: pack disjoint rooted trees into a graph or find a small set of vertices that blocks them all. one always works. the paper proves that adding the root requirement keeps the bound linear—no quadratic penalty, just as tight as the classical theorem

paperTitle: Reciprocal theorem for ion-releasing colloidal particles
name: ionswim
plan: The paper extends the reciprocal theorem to colloidal particles that release ions into an electrolyte, and finds that the cloud of released ions left hanging around the particle behaves like an excess charge Q. That charge couples to any electric field present and adds a whole extra term to the particle's propulsion speed, proportional to Q times the field. The sign of Q comes from something almost embarrassingly simple: whichever released ion species diffuses away faster leaves the other behind, so the sign is just the diffusivity difference between the two species you're releasing. Push that difference through zero with a field switched on and the extra thrust term flips sign — the paper states this plainly, that the correction 'may dramatically change its magnitude, and even sign.' The toy hands you two sliders: ion diffusivity asymmetry (which species leaves faster, and by how much) and external field strength and direction. A propulsion arrow on the particle updates live from the paper's closed-form speed expression, and crossing zero on the asymmetry slider while the field is on visibly flips the arrow. Turn one ships exactly that: two sliders, one arrow, one speed readout, computed directly from the formula on an idealized particle — no fluid simulation. The hard part is keeping the formula honest: simplify enough to run in a browser without quietly claiming to solve the full coupled electrokinetic problem the paper does. Reuse packages/dataviz for a speed-versus-field chart; a fastest-reversal leaderboard is checkable instantly since it's just recomputing the closed form.
mechanism: two-slider microswimmer designer where ion-diffusivity asymmetry and field strength set propulsion speed and can flip its direction
text: slide ion diffusivity asymmetry and external field strength. a propulsion arrow on the particle updates live from the formula. cross zero on the asymmetry slider and the arrow flips—which ion species escapes fastest can reverse the entire direction of motion

paperTitle: Improved Bounds for Distinct Multiples in Intervals
name: distinct-multiples
plan:
F(n) is the smallest window length such that any F consecutive integers contain, for every m from 1 to n, a multiple of m — and all n of those multiples distinct from each other. The paper improves both ends of this: the lower bound climbs to n·exp((1/50)·log n/log log n), beating three previous records and disproving a standing conjecture that F(n) stayed close to n log n; the upper bound drops to roughly n^1.4031, a specific algebraic root. The gap between those two curves is enormous and nobody knows which is closer to the truth.

The toy is the search itself. Pick n, then look for the shortest run of consecutive integers where you can assign each of 1..n a distinct multiple inside the run — a matching problem you solve by hand on a number line. Multiples of each m glow along the strip; you drag-assign one to each m, and the site instantly tells you whether the run works and whether it beats the current record for that n. Turn one: a number-line widget for one fixed small n, showing candidate multiples, letting the visitor manually assign them, and validating distinctness — no solver, no hints, just verification. Records post to a table keyed by n; anyone can recheck a claimed F(n) in milliseconds because a valid assignment is the whole proof.

The hard part is scaling past tiny n: manual assignment gets tedious once dozens of numbers compete for the same multiples, and eventually you want an assist (partial auto-matching, or a hint revealing one assignment) without letting the assist quietly solve the puzzle for the visitor. Reuse the math hub's single-file explainer pattern and a lightweight record table like the existing Erdős-rectangle page; no auth needed since every record is self-verifying.
mechanism: hunt for the shortest run of consecutive integers holding a distinct multiple of every number up to n
text: pick n, then find the shortest run of consecutive integers where each of 1..n appears as one distinct multiple inside. drag them onto a number line and verify. the bounds on how short are absurdly far apart—nobody knows which is closer

paperTitle: Straightedge-and-Compass Constructibility of the Reciprocal-$k$-th-Power Law
name: reciprocal-k
plan:
Given two lengths a and b, the paper asks when a single fixed sequence of compass-and-straightedge moves can build the length c solving 1/c^k = 1/a^k + 1/b^k for every a, b — one recipe that works for any input, not a construction tailored to specific numbers. The answer is exact: only when k is a power of two. For k=1 this is the everyday parallel-resistance / thin-lens law, buildable with a folklore similar-triangles trick; for k=4 the paper gives an explicit recipe built from third, fourth and mean proportionals, and doubling it reaches k=8, 16, and so on. For k=3, 5, 6, 7 — no such construction exists, ever, by an algebraic-degree obstruction on the number 2^(1/k).

The toy is a compass-and-straightedge canvas: draw two segments a and b, pick k, and try to land on c. Turn one ships k=1 only, with the classical construction available to attempt freely (draw parallel segments of length a and b, connect the diagonals, read c off the crossing height) plus a checker measuring how close the constructed point sits to the true c. Later turns add k=2 and k=4 with the paper's recursive method, and a wall mode where the visitor watches the impossible k values fail to close no matter how they build.

The hard part is making the impossibility feel earned rather than asserted: a degree ladder showing that every compass-straightedge step only ever takes a square root, so reachable lengths sit on rungs at degree 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — and 2^(1/k) lands exactly on a rung only when k already is one. Reuse the math hub's geometry conventions and any existing construction-canvas code there; add a fewest-steps leaderboard once k=4 ships, since a construction is just a replayable list of moves anyone can check.
mechanism: compass-and-straightedge construction of the generalized parallel-law length, for k that are powers of two
text: draw two line lengths with compass and straightedge, pick a number k, then construct the third length solving 1/c^k = 1/a^k + 1/b^k. works only when k is a power of two. try k=3 or k=5? algebra forbids them, every time

paperTitle: Neoplatonic solids
name: neoplatonic
plan:
A 6-net is a triangulated sphere where no vertex touches more than six triangles. The paper's finding: every such net (checked exhaustively up to 50 vertices, over ten million of them) folds into a unique solid built entirely from unit equilateral triangles — no stretching, no gaps — and a separate unique ideal polyhedron in hyperbolic space. Two combinatorial choices, two rigid geometric objects, and no other choice is possible once the mesh is fixed. The paper's own name for the Euclidean output, 'neoplatonic solid,' is earned because it can be as irregular and non-convex as you like, unlike its five ancient cousins, and still be the one and only shape that mesh can become.

The toy is a mesh editor: start from a seed triangle and keep attaching triangles to grow a closed sphere, with the tool refusing any move that would push a vertex past degree six — you feel the constraint rather than reading about it. Finish (or load a preset net) and the site renders the resulting neoplatonic solid in three.js, rotatable, with unit-length edges visibly enforced.

Turn one: ship the degree-capped mesh editor plus a small gallery of precomputed nets and their solids to establish the payoff before attempting live solving, since the paper's actual realization method is a numerical homotopy continuation from a hyperbolic starting point — not something to improvise client-side in one turn. State plainly that solving an arbitrary visitor-built net is a stretch goal, not a turn-one promise.

The crowd angle: every finished net a visitor builds joins a growing shape gallery, so the site accumulates a zoo of solids nobody would have drawn on purpose. Reuse three.js from tjs/packages and the math hub's explainer conventions.
mechanism: build a max-degree-six triangulated mesh and get back the unique equilateral-triangle solid it folds into
text: grow a spherical mesh by attaching triangle to triangle, each triangle sharing edges with the last. stop when you've closed it. no vertex can touch more than six triangles. now fold the net into 3d—you get exactly one equilateral-triangle solid, always

paperTitle: On t-colorable k-plane drawings
name: kplane
plan:
Take a graph drawn with crossing edges, colored with t colors, and demand that no edge be crossed more than k times by edges sharing its own color — crossings with other colors are free. The paper pins down exactly how dense such a drawing can get for small t and k, and shows that even checking whether an existing drawing satisfies the rule is NP-complete once t is 2 or more: the rule is easy to state and hard to verify in general, an unusual pairing.

The toy turns the density bound into a target: given n points on a canvas, draw and color edges by hand, trying to pack in as many as possible before some edge collects more than k same-colored crossings. A live counter flags the first edge that busts its budget; a second line shows the paper's proven ceiling for that t, k, n so the visitor knows exactly how far from optimal they are.

Turn one ships the smallest interesting case, t=2 and k=1: place points, click-drag to draw an edge, pick one of two colors, and get instant crossing feedback per edge — no solver, no hints, just the counter and the ceiling line. The hard part is the live crossing check: every new edge has to be tested against every existing edge of its own color, cheap at small n but needing real incremental bookkeeping once a visitor is packing dozens of edges onto a canvas full of near-misses.

The crowd angle: a drawing is just coordinates and colors, so any claimed edge count is instantly replayable and checkable, which makes a fewest-vertices-to-hit-the-bound or most-edges-under-budget leaderboard free to build. Reuse the draw/canvas surface's interaction conventions and workers/scores for the leaderboard.
mechanism: draw and color a graph's edges to maximize density while capping same-color crossings per edge
text: place points on a canvas. draw edges between them, color each edge red or blue, and pack them dense. but no edge can be crossed by more than one edge of its own color. how many edges fit? the paper sets an exact limit for any board

paperTitle: Nordhaus-Gaddum Inequalities for Dominating-Set Counts in Bipartite Graphs
name: domdual
text: build a bipartite graph by toggling edges between two columns. two numbers below: dominating sets in your graph, dominating sets in the opposite, their sum. the paper sets a bound on that sum. can you make it equal exactly? some bipartite graphs do
plan:
A dominating set of a graph is a vertex subset that touches every vertex, in it or adjacent to it. Nordhaus-Gaddum results bound a graph invariant on G and its complement together. This paper is about counting: how large can the number of dominating sets in G plus the number in G's complement get? For bipartite G with parts A and B, it proves the sum is at most 2(2^|A|-1)(2^|B|-1)+2, and characterizes exactly which bipartite graphs hit that bound with equality — a partial resolution of a standing conjecture of Keough and Shane.

The mechanic: an editor for a small bipartite graph, two columns of vertices with edges toggled between them (capped around 8-by-8 so brute-force subset counting stays instant), with two live numbers underneath: the dominating-set count in G, the count in the complement, their sum, and the bound line. The visitor's job is to push the sum as close to the bound as the theorem allows, ideally hit exact equality — the paper says equality has a specific structural signature, which the visitor gets to discover by trial rather than being told up front. A record slot takes the part sizes and edge list; anyone can recompute both counts and the sum from that submission in milliseconds, so no record can be faked.

Turn one ships the bipartite editor, live dominating-set counts recomputed on every edit for both G and its complement, the bound line, and a single best-so-far record — no shared leaderboard plumbing yet. What's hard is correctness under editing: toggling one edge changes G and its complement simultaneously, and both counts must be recomputed together or the displayed sum lies. Reuse workers/scores for a shared leaderboard once the counting is verified correct, and the math geometry-pack scaffold for the page itself.
mechanism: edit a small bipartite graph and chase the Nordhaus-Gaddum bound on dominating-set counts in G and its complement

paperTitle: An Exact Obstruction to Uniform Average Mixing on $P_{11}$
name: nomix
text: quantum walk on an 11-vertex path bounces forever. pick any way to average its motion over time: point samples, a uniform window, exponential decay. no matter what you choose, it never becomes uniform. watch a certificate prove it cannot
plan:
A continuous-time quantum walk on a graph has a transition matrix M(t) that oscillates forever. Average mixing asks whether, for some way of averaging M(t) over time — some probability distribution on t — the long-run average becomes the uniform matrix J/n, every vertex equally likely to be found anywhere. This paper proves the 11-vertex path P11 can never do this, for any distribution whatsoever, and the proof is a single explicit witness: a rational symmetric matrix Y with the inner product ⟨Y, M(t)⟩ equal to 1 for every t — so it stays 1 no matter how you average — while ⟨Y, J/11⟩ is 12/11. That 1/11 gap is fixed and permanent.

The mechanic: the visitor picks a distribution over sample times from a small preset menu — a few point masses, a uniform window, an exponential decay — and the site computes the corresponding time-average of M(t) for the walk on P11 and shows it as an 11-by-11 heatmap beside the uniform target heatmap. Every choice produces a visibly different average matrix, but a live readout of ⟨Y, average⟩ underneath refuses to move: it always reads 1, next to the uniform target's 12/11. The visitor is trying to close a gap they cannot close, and sees the exact certificate the paper uses to explain why, not just a failed attempt.

Turn one fixes the graph to P11, offers four or five preset time-distributions rather than free-form dragging, and renders the two heatmaps plus the ⟨Y,·⟩ readout. What's hard is computing M(t) = |e^{iAt}|^2 entrywise and averaging it precisely enough that the 1-vs-12/11 gap reads as exact rather than noisy — use the path's exact eigendecomposition, not numerical time integration. Reuse the math geometry-pack scaffold; all client-side 11-by-11 linear algebra, no server.
mechanism: pick a time-sampling distribution for a quantum walk on an 11-vertex path and watch a fixed certificate prove the average can never equalize

paperTitle: House-monotone multi-level apportionment has logarithmic quota discrepancy
name: comb-quota
plan: The paper answers an open question about apportioning seats through a hierarchy: as a legislature grows one seat at a time, can every nested group always hold a seat count between its rounded-down and rounded-up fair share (quota), while no group ever loses a seat it already has (house-monotone, the property that prevents the classic Alabama paradox)? For a 'comb' hierarchy — a spine of D equally-sized leaf groups nested one inside the next — the answer is no once D is large: any monotone seat-adding sequence is forced to violate quota somewhere, and the unavoidable error grows like log D, not a constant. A van der Corput seat-order gets within a constant of that bound, which is also given. The toy is a seat-by-seat replay: render the comb as nested bars, one per leaf group, and a counter that adds one new seat at a time to the whole structure, assigning it via the van der Corput rule. Each group's current seats are shown against its live quota window (its fair share rounded both ways); a violation lights the bar red. A toggle lets the visitor try to keep every group inside quota by hand instead, which forces seats to jump backward — breaking monotonicity live, so the trade-off is felt, not stated. Turn one ships the static replay for a fixed D (say 16) with the automatic van der Corput rule and the quota-violation counter running to the end of the sequence; the hand-driven toggle and variable D are the next turn. The hard part is keeping the visualization legible once D is more than a handful of bars — the comb needs to read as a spine with nested groups, not a flat bar chart, or the log-growth in violations has nothing to anchor to. Reuse: the math wing's single-file explainer convention and `workers/scores` for a leaderboard of lowest total quota-violations achieved by hand at a given D, checkable by replay.
mechanism: step a hierarchical seat count forward one seat at a time under a monotonicity-vs-quota trade-off
text: add seats one at a time to nested groups, keeping each between its fair share rounded down and up. errors grow like log(depth) no matter what you do. try it by hand and watch monotonicity break

paperTitle: Robust Scale-Free Auctions
name: give-it-away
plan: An auction designer who knows only that bidders' values are independent, identically distributed, and drawn from a 'regular' distribution — not the distribution itself, not even its scale — wants a mechanism that does well against the worst distribution meeting that description, compared to what a designer who knew the true distribution could extract. For two such bidders, the paper solves this exactly: the best 'standard' auction (one that always gives the item to whoever bid higher) mixes the second-price auction with a relative-markup auction and guarantees a worst-case ratio of about 0.524413 to the fully-informed optimum. Then it shows standardness itself is costly — a mechanism that sometimes hands the item to the *lower* bidder does better, reaching about 0.524829. The toy hands the visitor the designer's seat: two sliders set a simple mechanism — a base rule (second price) plus a 'sometimes give it to the lower bidder' probability, applied when the two bids are close. An adversary panel, computed live from the paper's characterization of worst-case regular distributions, reports the resulting worst-case ratio against the true optimum. The 0.524413 standard ceiling is marked on the meter as a line the visitor starts below and tries to cross by leaning on the lower-bidder rule, chasing the proven 0.524829 record. Turn one ships the meter and the fixed second-price baseline only — showing 0.524413 computed live and marked, no lower-bidder slider yet — so the adversary computation is validated against the paper's own number before the harder nonstandard case is added. The hard part, named plainly: computing the adversary's worst-case ratio for an arbitrary user-chosen mechanism in-browser is the actual research problem the paper solves for two specific mechanism families, not a general solver, so turn one must only expose the mechanisms the paper gives closed forms for, not free-form designs. Reuse: `workers/scores` for a record table of ratios found, `erdos/`-style single static page.
mechanism: tune an auction rule against a live-computed worst-case adversary and watch your revenue guarantee move relative to two proven ceilings
text: tune an auction rule with sliders: lean on a 'give it to the lower bidder' penalty and watch your worst-case revenue guarantee climb. sometimes losing is winning

paperTitle: Intention Inference Under Execution Noise: Separating Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty in Social Dilemmas
name: slip-of-the-hand
plan: In the iterated prisoner's dilemma, standard models treat what an opponent did as what they meant — so a defection reads as hostility even when it was really your partner's intended cooperation, corrupted in transit. This paper adds execution noise on top of intent: what you observe is a noisy readout of a hidden intention, and it shows that agents which explicitly reason about that gap (was this a betrayal or a slip?) sustain cooperation up to a derivable critical noise level, above which cooperation collapses regardless of strategy — and that the benefit of bothering to infer intent at all is contextual, not universal: it helps against opponents who are conditionally cooperative, but under high noise, two intent-inferring agents can spiral into a correlated collapse of mutual suspicion. The toy is a two-player noisy prisoner's dilemma room: each round, both players choose an intended move, but the room flips it to its opposite with probability ε before the other player sees it — so a shown defection might be a slip. Players don't get to see ε directly; they have to feel it out over rounds, same as the paper's agents. A shared dial (visible after the round, not during) reveals the noise level was set close to, above, or below the room's derived critical threshold, and a running histogram across every room played shows the crowd's aggregate cooperation rate as a function of ε — the site's own empirical version of the paper's threshold, built from real games rather than simulation. Turn one ships the two-player room itself, fixed at one mid-range ε, with the flip mechanic and a per-round outcome log — no aggregate histogram yet, since that needs volume across many played rooms first. The hard part is making a flipped move legible without giving away that it was flipped; the game only works if a defection is genuinely ambiguous in the moment. Reuse: `games/` for the DO room and matchmaking, `workers/scores` for the aggregate cooperation-vs-noise histogram once enough rooms have been played.
mechanism: play iterated prisoner's dilemma where your and your opponent's moves are silently flipped with a hidden probability
text: play iterated prisoner's dilemma where each move flips to its opposite with a hidden probability. find the critical noise level where cooperation always collapses, no strategy survives

paperTitle: Caustics and Superenergy in the Quantum Bouncer
name: over-the-limit
plan: A quantum ball dropped onto a hard floor under gravity has exact solutions (Airy-function eigenstates, same family as the semiclassical rainbow), and a Gaussian wavepacket built from a superposition of them develops caustics — the same bright fold lines you get in a rainbow or in light through a cup, but here in probability density. The paper's actual finding is stranger than the caustic itself: in some regions near a caustic, the *local energy* of the wavepacket exceeds the largest energy eigenvalue among the states that make it up — 'superenergy,' a region where the whole is locally hotter than any of its parts, and the paper quantifies exactly how much and traces it with the Bohm trajectory picture as well as the standard one. The toy: the visitor sets an initial wavepacket for the quantum bouncer — drop height, width — and watches it evolve as a density plot, with a second overlay heatmap that lights up wherever local energy exceeds the input's own maximum eigenvalue, so 'superenergy' is a thing you can see appear and vanish as the packet bounces. The hunt is to find launch parameters that maximize the peak superenergy fraction reached during a bounce, a number anyone can recompute exactly from the same closed-form solution, so a record is always checkable. Turn one ships the wavepacket evolution and density plot alone, correct against the known Airy-eigenstate solution for a couple of fixed parameter sets, with the superenergy overlay following once the baseline evolution is verified against the paper's own figures. The hard part is the eigenvalue truncation: superenergy is only well-defined relative to which eigenstates you decide are 'in' the wavepacket, and an under- or over-truncated basis will manufacture or hide superenergy that isn't physically there — this needs a stated, fixed truncation rule, not a knob. Reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the heatmap rendering; `workers/scores` for the peak-superenergy record table.
mechanism: shape a quantum wavepacket's launch and watch a live overlay mark where its local energy exceeds any of its constituent eigenstates
text: drop a quantum wavepacket on a hard floor and watch it bounce. heat marks where the local energy exceeds the highest energy in the packet—superenergy, hotter than its parts. hunt for the peak

paperTitle: A simplified min-max formula for the inverse arborescence problem
name: bribery
plan: The paper solves the inverse arborescence problem: given a digraph, a cost on every edge, and a target spanning arborescence you'd like to be cheapest, what is the smallest total change to the costs (measured edge by edge, summed as absolute value) that makes your target the single cheapest arborescence in the whole graph? It gives an exact min-max formula — a minimizer on the cost side and a matching dual certificate — computable in polynomial time. The toy: you're handed a small rooted network with fixed starting costs, you pick any spanning tree as your favorite, and the tool tells you the minimum total edit needed to make it win, edge by edge, thicker lines for bigger changes. Turn one ships one small fixed graph (six or seven nodes), a click-to-select target tree, and an exact solve by brute force at that size, showing before/after costs and the total spent. The hard part is making the dual side legible: the formula also produces an object certifying you can't do better, and a raw dual variable means nothing to a visitor — better to render it as the rival tree (or set of rivals) whose cost your edits are racing against, so 'why did it cost that much' has a visible answer instead of a trust-me number. Reuse the math hub's single-page explainer conventions and workers/scores for a record table of the graphs that turn out hardest to bribe, since any claimed record is exactly re-checkable by re-running the same small solver.
mechanism: edit edge costs by the smallest total amount needed to make a chosen spanning tree the cheapest one
text: pick a spanning tree as your favorite in a weighted network. what's the minimum total cost adjustment to make it beat all rivals? the tool computes it exactly and shows you which tree you're racing against

paperTitle: Second-Order Potentials for Finite Games: Existence, Characterisation, and Game Decomposition
name: split
plan: Monderer and Shapley showed a game is an exact potential game exactly when every pair of players' incentives agree on cross-differences — a strict symmetry condition most real payoff tables fail. This paper builds a second-order potential (the MS-potential) from those same cross-differences when the symmetry breaks, shows it's unique up to each player's own separable terms, and then uses a least-squares construction to extend it to every finite game, no exceptions: any payoff table splits into a common-interest potential game (a version where everyone secretly agrees on what's good) plus an individualistic residual that absorbs the rest. The toy is a payoff-matrix editor for a small two-player game — say two actions each to start — where dragging any payoff live-updates two synced heatmaps that sum back to the original: the shared-interest half and the leftover conflict half, with a single number reporting what fraction of the game is 'team' versus 'rivalry.' Turn one ships that editor plus a gallery of textbook games (prisoner's dilemma, chicken, pure coordination) so a visitor can check the split against games they already have intuition for before trusting it on their own. What's hard is keeping the arithmetic invisible — the paper's construction is a least-squares projection, and showing the matrix algebra would kill the toy; the heatmaps and the one ratio number have to carry the whole idea. Reuse workers/scores for a submitted-games gallery ranked by how close to pure-team or pure-rivalry a submission lands, since any submission is instantly re-decomposable by anyone who doubts it.
mechanism: edit a payoff table and watch it split live into a shared-interest part and a rivalry part that sum back to the original
text: drag any payoff in a game and watch it split into a cooperative part and a conflict part that sum back to the original. every game decomposes this way

paperTitle: Beyond the PPAD hardness of Auto-bidding Auctions
name: diffuse
plan: Computing an autobidding equilibrium is PPAD-complete in the worst case, yet real advertisers running simple pacing strategies converge quickly every day — this paper resolves the gap by showing the hardness needs atomicity (a handful of bidders whose individual moves matter) and vanishes once bidder values are drawn from a nonatomic distribution, which is the realistic case with a large population. Under that 'diffuse' framing the equilibrium becomes a separately monotone generalized Nash equilibrium, and the paper supplies the first solver with last-iterate linear convergence: not just convergence, but a guaranteed geometric rate. The toy hands the visitor a repeated single-good auction with a simple multiplicative budget-pacing rule and one dial — population size, from two or three bidders up past a thousand. Run it at the low end and the distance-to-equilibrium plot can stall or cycle; slide the population up and the same rule snaps into a straight line on a log-scale plot, the visual signature of linear convergence. Turn one ships a fixed simple auction, the population slider, a run button, and that live convergence plot with an explicit 'still moving' versus 'locked in' readout. The hard part, named honestly: the paper's actual solver targets a monotone GNE with real convergence guarantees, and turn one instead ships a standard ad-tech multiplicative pacing heuristic that only echoes the phenomenon — say so on the page rather than implying the guarantee transfers. Reuse packages/dataviz for the convergence plot and workers/scores for fastest-to-lock submitted configurations.
mechanism: slide the number of bidders in a shared pacing auction and watch convergence go from chaotic to a straight line
text: run a repeated auction where each bidder follows a simple budget rule. slide the population from a few to thousands and watch the system's convergence go from chaotic to a perfect straight line

paperTitle: Divisive Normalization Shapes Low-Rank Slow Manifolds for Continuous Working Memory
name: shatter
plan: Continuous attractor networks can hold a smooth, continuous memory — an angle, a hue — but are notoriously fragile to fine-tuning, and standard recurrent nets like GRUs and LSTMs typically fail the same task a different way: instead of holding a smooth manifold of possible values, they carve the state space into a handful of discrete point attractors and snap any remembered value to the nearest one. The paper's fix is divisive normalization — dividing a unit's activity by a pooled signal rather than subtracting it, a mechanism long observed in real cortex — and it shows this single change is what lets a network converge to a robust, high-fidelity continuous manifold instead of shattering, especially once the input is time-varying rather than a single static cue. The toy: hold a value in memory by setting a slider (an angle on a dial), inject a noisy, time-varying nudge, and watch a small recurrent network's recalled value over time — under divisive normalization it drifts and recovers smoothly along a visible curve; switch to subtractive-only inhibition and it snaps between a visible handful of dots instead. Turn one ships exactly that: a hand-built small ring-style recurrent network (a caricature built to the paper's governing idea, not a trained reproduction of the RDNN, since only the abstract is available) with a normalization-type toggle, a value slider, a noise slider, and the live recalled-vs-true plot. The hard part is being honest about that gap on the page. Reuse the neuro surface, whose whole premise is cognitive-science mechanisms rebuilt from their papers and shown against the published result.
mechanism: toggle a recurrent network's inhibition type and watch a held memory drift smoothly or snap to discrete points under noise
text: hold a value in a small recurrent network's memory by sliding a dial. add noise, then toggle how neurons inhibit each other. watch memory either drift smoothly or snap between discrete points

paperTitle: Conjugation invariants determine the metacommutation permutation only up to relabelling
name: metacommute
plan:
Hurwitz quaternion primes of norm p correspond to p+1 points, and multiplying by a prime Q of a different norm q induces a permutation π_Q of those points — metacommutation. Earlier work computed π_Q's sign and fixed-point count, even its full cycle structure, from data that only depends on Q up to conjugation: its norm q and its trace. This paper proves that's the ceiling — no conjugation-invariant quantity of Q can recover π_Q as an actual labelled permutation, or even predict where one named point goes. The witness is small and fully explicit: at p=3, q=5, the four quaternions 2+i, 2+j, 2+k, 2−i are all conjugate to each other, so every invariant agrees on all four — yet they induce four different 4-cycles on the same four points.

The mechanic: four points, labeled, on screen. The visitor picks one of the four quaternions — all announced as the same, by every invariant you're allowed to compute — and watches it permute the four points its own way; picking a different one of the four gives a different shuffle of the identical points, with the shared invariants (sign, fixed points) displayed and staying put while the actual mapping changes underneath them.

Turn one renders exactly the paper's own (p,q)=(3,5) table — the sixteen refactorizations are printed in its appendix — rather than computing quaternion arithmetic live, which is honest since the paper hands over the exact numbers. A later turn could open a hunt for other small (p,q) witnesses once real metacommutation arithmetic exists, echoing the record-style hunts elsewhere on the math wing, but that needs the arithmetic built first, not promised now.

Reuse: math wing conventions and layout; no auth, no backend, no new arithmetic beyond the hardcoded witness for turn one.
mechanism: picking among quaternions that share every invariant and watching each permute the same four labeled points differently
text: four objects that match on every count — identical, indistinguishable — yet each shuffles four labeled points in its own way. pick one and watch it shuffle

paperTitle: Gap distributions between successive personal bests in cricket: Data and Models
name: recordgap
plan:
Classical record theory says the gap between successive personal-bests in an i.i.d. sequence follows a universal law. Real cricket careers aren't i.i.d. — players learn, age, and go through form — so the paper fits real gap distributions (from ESPN Cricinfo Test/ODI/T20 careers) to a truncated power law P(g) ∝ g^-α e^-λg, finding α between 0.799 and 0.843. Bootstrap-shuffle each player's own innings — same scores, same career length, order destroyed — and the fitted exponent jumps to α≈0.939–0.979, much closer to the memoryless baseline. The exponent is a fingerprint of whether a career was lived in order or scrambled.

The mechanic: the visitor picks a real player's innings-by-innings scores from a small built-in set, watches personal-best moments get marked and their gaps plotted, and reads off the fitted α live. A shuffle button bootstrap-reorders that player's own innings and refits — the exponent visibly climbs. Turn one ships exactly that: one career, marked records, gap histogram, α before and after a shuffle, side by side.

The crowd layer: a blind round — two gap histograms from the same scores, one real order and one shuffled, guess which is real. Track collective accuracy across rounds and players — a real number nobody currently has, how detectable career-shaping actually is from gap statistics alone.

What's hard: fitting a truncated power law to a few dozen noisy gaps per career is fragile — show a bootstrap confidence band on α rather than a single confident number, and say plainly that the paper's exponent range is aggregated across many careers, not a guarantee for any one shuffle a visitor tries.

Reuse: packages/dataviz for the histogram and the power-law estimator; workers/scores for the blind-round leaderboard.
mechanism: shuffling a cricket career's innings order and watching the personal-best gap exponent shift
text: pick a cricket career. shuffle its innings in random order and watch the gaps between personal bests shift — real careers hold a shape that scrambled innings lose

paperTitle: Reaction Delays Boost, Rectify, and Reverse Motility in Activity Landscapes
name: backlash
plan:
The paper studies self-propelled particles whose speed doesn't track their local environment instantly — there's a lag, 'delayed motility.' Drop such a particle into a spatially periodic activity landscape (patches that are naturally faster or slower) and that lag alone is enough to break the balance that normally forbids net drift: an asymmetric landscape starts pumping particles in one direction, a symmetric one still gets a diffusion boost, and the sharp part is that a single delay-time dial can flip the direction of transport — a genuine current reversal, with no walls, gradients, or extra dimensions required. It holds for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and inertial particles alike.

The toy: a periodic 1D strip where the visitor drags a few control points to shape an activity profile (default an asymmetric sawtooth), picks a particle model, and moves one delay slider. A swarm of dots crawls the strip while a live current readout tracks net drift; slide delay past the reversal point and the whole swarm's direction flips as the readout crosses zero. Turn one ships exactly that: the fixed sawtooth, one particle model, the delay slider, the swarm, and the current readout with a highlight the instant the sign flips.

The hard part is the simulation itself: an actual delayed-response equation of motion, not a scripted flip, that reproduces a real reversal for an asymmetric profile while only boosting diffusion for a symmetric one — entirely client-side, fast enough for hundreds of particles at 60fps. Getting that qualitative distinction wrong would misrepresent the result.

Reuse the WebGPU particle-sim shelf at g.mino.mobi (bearings, sand) for the swarm renderer, packages/dataviz for the current-versus-delay chart, and workers/scores later for a leaderboard on landscape shapes that reverse current fastest per unit delay.
mechanism: drag an activity-landscape shape and a delay slider, watch a particle swarm's net drift flip sign
text: drag a wavy landscape to set how fast it is at each point. adjust the delay in how particles respond to it. watch a swarm crawl along it. push the delay slider and the entire swarm reverses direction — the response lag alone is enough to pump particles one way or the other

paperTitle: Asymptotically attaining the Moore bound
name: mooreward
plan:
For a graph with maximum degree d and diameter at most k, there's a trivial ceiling on how many vertices it can have — roughly d^k, the Moore bound. The paper proves that as d grows, for any fixed k, the best achievable order gets arbitrarily close to that ceiling: the ratio n_k(d)/d^k tends to 1, resolving a conjecture of Bollobás. The construction is an explicit family of regular graphs built from partial flags over finite fields.

The toy fixes k=2, the smallest interesting case, where the exact Moore bound is d^2+1 and is met only by a handful of famous graphs (the Petersen graph at d=3 is one; d=57 is a still-open case). The visitor gets a canvas, a degree slider (d from 3 to 8), and builds a graph by hand — click to add a vertex, drag to add an edge, blocked once any vertex would exceed degree d. A live BFS checks diameter and a score bar shows order achieved against d^2+1. Turn one ships that loop: canvas, degree slider, live degree/diameter checking, and the score bar — no attempt yet at the paper's general finite-geometry construction.

The hard part, named honestly: exact Moore graphs at diameter 2 barely exist, so most players will hit a ceiling well short of d^2+1 no matter how they build, and the site has to make that a fact worth learning rather than a broken game — near-Moore is itself a real research question, not a skill issue. Diameter computed live on a graph mid-edit needs to stay cheap, which is easy at these sizes (all-pairs BFS on a few dozen vertices).

Reuse the math.mino.mobi extremal-geometry hub for a slot, and workers/scores for a record table keyed by (d, k) — a genuine record-chasing structure, since a submitted graph is trivially checkable by anyone.
mechanism: hand-build a degree-capped graph and chase how close its order gets to the Moore bound
text: build a graph by hand. drag to add vertices, click to connect edges. cap each vertex at degree d. make every pair of vertices reachable in 2 hops or less. a score tracks your count versus the moore bound: the theoretical max for these constraints. it's barely achievable even at small d

paperTitle: Population Structures with Positive Feedback and Asymmetric Division
name: budclock
plan:
Budding yeast divide asymmetrically — a mother cell buds off a smaller daughter, and the mother can divide again sooner than that daughter can. The paper shows that this asymmetry, combined with positive feedback on division timing, is enough on its own to make a population of cells self-organize from random starting phases into stable temporal clustering: p distinct clusters of mother cells and q clusters of daughters (p ≤ q), locking into a periodic p:q arrangement with no external pacemaker. Simulations show these structures form spontaneously from randomized populations and are stable once formed.

The toy is a circular phase wheel — one dot per cell, position on the circle is where it sits in its division cycle. The visitor sets two sliders, division asymmetry and feedback strength, hits randomize to scatter every cell's phase uniformly, and presses run. Dots that started scattered pull into tight clumps live on screen; a readout counts clumps and reports the p:q split as it locks in. Turn one ships that whole loop — wheel, two sliders, randomize, run, and the live p:q readout — with no leaderboard yet.

The hard part is faithfulness: the division-and-feedback rule has to be close enough to the paper's model that p:q genuinely tracks the two sliders rather than being a canned animation, and the site needs a real criterion for 'locked' so the readout doesn't flicker between counts while clumps are still settling. There's no existing surface here to lean on — this is a new one-page sim, not a repurposed engine, and packages/dataviz is only useful for the wheel rendering, not the model itself.

A later crowd layer is plausible — a gallery of screenshotted (asymmetry, feedback) pairs and the p:q ratio they produce, built by visitors hunting for interesting ratios — but turn one is single-player and that is honestly a page, not yet a site.
mechanism: tune division asymmetry and feedback strength, randomize a cell population, and watch it snap into p:q clusters
text: set sliders for division asymmetry and feedback strength. randomize a population of cell phases around a circle. press run and watch them snap into clusters — mothers and daughters self-organize into a repeating p:q rhythm with no external pacemaker. the population syncs itself

paperTitle: Improved Euclidean Shallow Light Trees
name: canopy
plan:
A shallow-light tree connects a set of points to a root under two competing constraints: root-stretch (how much longer than the straight line your path to the root is allowed to be, expressed as 1+ε) and lightness (how much heavier than the minimum spanning tree the whole structure is allowed to be). A 1993 result fixed the tradeoff at lightness roughly 2/ε and showed it was tight for general graphs, leaving open whether the Euclidean plane could do better. This paper answers yes, twice: one construction gets lightness down to about 1.67/ε, a second gets to about 0.987/ε, more than halving the old leading constant and landing close to the proven floor of about 0.862/ε.

The toy: a canvas of roughly twenty points with one marked root and an ε slider drawn as a translucent stretch circle around each point. The visitor builds a tree by hand, clicking to lay edges from point to point back to the root; any edge that would push a vertex's path length past its stretch circle is flagged red and rejected. A running score shows the tree's total weight divided by the point set's MST weight — your lightness — plotted against a reference line for the old 2/ε bound. Turn one ships that: fixed point set, ε slider, hand-drawn tree with live stretch checking, and the lightness score against the 2/ε line.

The hard part, to say plainly on the page: the paper's 0.987/ε figure is a limit as ε shrinks toward zero, not a number a twenty-point canvas at ε=0.3 can literally hit, so the reference lines are targets to chase in the limit, not a pass/fail check on any one drawing.

Reuse math.mino.mobi for a slot in the extremal-geometry hub, and workers/scores for a leaderboard on lowest lightness achieved for a shared point set at a fixed stretch.
mechanism: hand-draw a spanning tree under a stretch cap and chase the lowest weight-versus-MST ratio
text: place nodes on a canvas with one marked root. adjust an epsilon slider to set how much longer each node's path to root can be. hand-draw edges connecting all nodes to root without breaking any stretch cap. your score: tree weight divided by minimum spanning tree weight. chase the lowest ratio

paperTitle: EFX Allocation In (Multi)Hypergraphs
name: fair-split
plan: The paper works in fair division: EFX (envy-free-up-to-any-good) allocations are famously not known to always exist for indivisible goods, even for additive valuations - a major open problem. This paper narrows the gap for a graph model where agents and goods are vertices and edges of a (multi-)hypergraph: only the agents at a good's endpoints can value it. Its result: whenever the hypergraph has girth at least 4 (no short cycles among who-wants-what), an EFX allocation always exists and a poly-time algorithm finds it, for arbitrary monotone valuations, not just additive ones. The toy is a hypergraph builder: place a handful of agent nodes, click pairs or triples of agents to add a good that only they value, and assign it a value per agent. A split button runs the paper's construction and shows the resulting allocation plus an envy check per pair. Turn one should be small and honest: three or four fixed agents, click-to-connect goods, a live girth readout that flags any triangle or 4-cycle among goods, and a split that only runs once girth clears 4, explaining why it declines otherwise. The interesting later move is deliberately building a girth-3 hypergraph, a triangle of overlapping demand, to see whether the guarantee actually breaks - and the toy must not oversell that: the paper proves existence above girth 4, not non-existence below it, so a successful split on a triangle is not a counterexample. What's hard is keeping that distinction visible on the page rather than implying the demo proves impossibility. Reuse: nothing shared for turn one - a pure client-side graph editor and allocation routine; a later leaderboard of hardest-to-split hypergraphs found by visitors would be checkable by anyone re-running the same envy check.
mechanism: build an agent-goods hypergraph and run the paper's fair-allocation algorithm, gated by a live girth readout
text: draw a graph of who wants which goods and hit split; the algorithm allocates everything fairly, but only when your graph avoids short cycles

paperTitle: Chaos suppression via adaptive feedback control of intermittency: From exactly solvable ergodic maps to interacting microbubble clusters
name: tame
plan: Intermittency is a classic route to chaos: a system alternates long calm stretches with sudden chaotic bursts, governed by one parameter. The usual fix is active control - watch the trajectory, detect an incipient burst, nudge it back. This paper does something more elegant: it promotes the control parameter itself to a second dynamical variable that evolves under its own map, drawn from the same family as the system it steers, with no orbit detection, linearization, or triggered perturbations. For a class of exactly solvable one-dimensional maps it derives, in closed form, the invariant measure of the coupled system and a generalized Lyapunov spectrum before and after control switches on; the spectrum's positive region collapses once the parameter self-adjusts. It then shows the same trick taming real chaotic oscillations in a simulated cluster of ultrasound-driven microbubbles. The toy is a single intermittent map rendered as a live time series next to a running histogram of local Lyapunov exponents. One slider sets the base parameter and produces the expected bursty chaos; a toggle switches on the self-adjusting parameter and the bursts visibly die out as the histogram's positive lobe shrinks toward zero. Turn one ships exactly that - one map, one slider, one toggle, one accumulating histogram - and nothing more. The hard part is trustworthy visuals: a Lyapunov estimate needs many iterations to stop being noisy, so the histogram must accumulate across frames rather than reset, and the toggle transition should show the spectrum shrinking rather than jump-cutting to calm. What improves with a crowd: let visitors submit their own map from a small parametrized family and compete on how few iterations the self-adjusting controller needs to collapse the positive spectrum, a public and instantly-recomputable record of hardest chaos tamed. Reuse: no existing surface fits directly; build as a standalone canvas page, closest in spirit to g/'s shelf of single simulations.
mechanism: toggle a self-adjusting control parameter and watch a chaotic map's bursts collapse on a live Lyapunov histogram
text: slide into chaos, toggle control on, and watch the bursts collapse as the parameter self-adjusts in real time

paperTitle: Delay Attacks on the German Smart Metering Infrastructure: A Security Analysis of CLS Channel Timing Constraints
name: loadshed
plan: The paper analyzes a real weakness in Germany's smart-metering rollout: control signals for flexible loads such as heat pumps and EV chargers travel over a channel called CLS, and an attacker on the wide-area network path can delay those signals without forging or dropping them, just by holding packets back. Depending on the deployed configuration, the theoretical delay ceiling is roughly 48 hours before anything downstream notices. The number worth building around is the paper's own extrapolation: scaled from one device to the several hundred thousand CLS devices being deployed, a coordinated delay attack could shift enough flexible load at once to move grid frequency measurably, potentially triggering load shedding. The paper also proposes a fix, a TLS 1.3 extension that timestamps and bounds how stale an accepted command can be.
