The toy puts the visitor on the grid-operator side of a simplified frequency model: two sliders, delay duration capped at 48 hours and the fraction of the device fleet affected, and one gauge, simulated grid frequency deviation from 50Hz styled after real deviation bands. A later toggle turns on the paper's proposed timestamp bound and visibly clamps how far the gauge can move regardless of the other sliders - the point is watching the fix cap the hazard, not demonstrating an attack. Turn one ships the two sliders and the gauge only; the mitigation toggle is a later turn. What's hard: the frequency model must be a defensible toy physics, proportional load-shift to frequency response with no invented precision, and the page must read as grid-safety education rather than a working recipe - no protocol detail, no device addressing, an explicit note that this is a physics cartoon of the paper's extrapolation, not a simulator of any deployed system. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the gauge; no auth or backend needed for turn one.
mechanism: dial delay time and affected device fraction and watch a simulated grid-frequency gauge respond, then clamp it with a mitigation toggle
text: dial a delay up to 48 hours and the fraction of devices affected; watch grid frequency shift; toggle the paper's mitigation and see it clamp the hazard

paperTitle: Geometry-Controlled Motility of Microswimmers in elementary microfluidic confinements
name: dwell
plan: The paper tracks real Chlamydomonas algae cells swimming through PDMS microfluidic chips of increasing geometric complexity - straight channels, circular cavities, dumbbell-shaped double chambers - to separate two causes of confined motility: steric wall contact versus hydrodynamic wall coupling. The results split cleanly by geometry. In straight channels, cells hug the walls, align with the channel axis, and pick up a genuine hydrodynamic speed boost from the nearby wall. In circular cavities smaller than the cell's own persistence length, about 350 microns, cells switch from free exploration to wall-following orbits. In dumbbell chambers, two rooms joined by a narrow neck, how long a cell dwells in each room before crossing matches a purely geometric prediction, with no measurable hydrodynamic contribution even under strong confinement. That's the surprising line: the effect you would expect to matter most under tight confinement turns out not to matter at all once the geometry is right. The toy is a maze editor - a canvas where the visitor places circular rooms and connecting channels, drops a simulated swimmer built as a run-and-tumble active Brownian particle with the paper's fitted parameters, and watches it explore. Turn one ships one fixed geometry, a straight channel, showing the wall-hugging, axis-aligned behavior and its measured speed boost, so the first thing a visitor sees is the paper's simplest finding actually happening. The dumbbell dwell-time claim follows once room placement exists. The hard part isn't the physics - steric active-Brownian simulation is standard - it's making a null result legible: a hydrodynamic-coupling readout needs to visibly do nothing in the dumbbell case, so absence of an effect reads as a finding rather than a bug. What improves with a crowd: submit a room layout and get scored on how long the cell stays trapped in one compartment relative to the geometric prediction, a number anyone can re-verify by rerunning the same simulation. Reuse: packages/dataviz for readouts; closest existing sibling is g/'s shelf of simulations, though this can start on canvas2D.
mechanism: place rooms and channels for a simulated swimming cell and watch its confined trajectory follow the paper's geometry-only rules
text: place rooms of any size and watch a simulated cell explore. when the rooms are small enough, the shape alone determines how long it dwells; physics doesn't matter

paperTitle: From b-Coloring to $b^*$-Coloring: Large Girth and Parameterized Complexity
name: b-star
text: color a graph by hand. each color group must have a 'b-vertex' — someone whose neighbors cover every other color. then you need a witness *of* that witness. how many colors can you pack?
plan:
The paper studies b*-coloring, a stronger cousin of the b-coloring games colorists already know: a proper coloring where every color class has a b-vertex — a vertex whose neighbors between them wear every other color, so it can't be folded into a smaller palette — and b*-coloring additionally demands a vertex that itself sees a b-vertex of every color among its neighbors, a witness of witnesses. The b*-chromatic number is the most colors you can push through under that double certificate. The paper proves graphs of girth at least 7 are 'b*-monotonic' (deleting vertices never raises it) and exhibits d-regular, girth-5 graphs that hit exactly d+1, the ceiling.

The mechanic: a fixed small graph, a color palette, and a live checker. Click a vertex, assign it a color; the checker highlights which vertices are currently b-vertices and which color classes still lack a witness (and whether the witness-of-witnesses condition holds). Push the palette as far as it goes before a class breaks. Turn one: one graph (say, the Petersen graph or an 8-vertex ring-plus-chords), a color picker, and the three-part validity check running live after every click — no scoring yet, just: can you find a coloring the checker accepts, and how many colors did you reach?

The hard part is the definition itself — three nested conditions (proper, b-vertex per class, witness-of-witnesses) are easy to implement backwards, and the UI has to make the failure visible (which vertex, which condition) or it reads as an arbitrary rejection. Once the checker is trustworthy, add a leaderboard per graph: highest valid k found, verifiable instantly by anyone re-running the same three checks — cheating is checking, same trick as a computable record. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions and workers/scores for the per-graph record table.
mechanism: properly color a fixed graph by hand to maximize the palette while a live checker enforces the b*-coloring certificate

paperTitle: Predicting the occurrence of Braess paradox in the synchronization threshold of coupled oscillator systems
name: badwire
text: you have a network of oscillators trying to sync. click to wire two together. but adding a connection can make them *harder* to synchronize — that's Braess's paradox. can you spot the trap edges?
plan:
Braess's paradox says adding a road can make traffic worse; this paper proves the same happens to synchronization. In a network of coupled oscillators, adding an edge can raise — not lower — the coupling strength K_c needed for the whole network to lock into phase. The paper derives a first-order formula for how K_c shifts when a thin edge is added, and a clean criterion: the new edge is locally 'Braess' exactly when the two oscillators it connects are ordered oppositely to how they sit in the critical eigenvector at the synchronization threshold — the mode that first goes unstable.

The mechanic: a small fixed network of oscillators, each with its own natural frequency, sitting near its critical coupling. The visitor picks any two currently-unconnected nodes and proposes wiring them together; the sim recomputes K_c by bisection over simulated runs and reports before/after, with a verdict — this edge helped, or this edge is a trap. Turn one ships exactly that: one network, click-to-connect, recomputed threshold, no scoring required to be satisfying on its own.

The hard part is that K_c isn't closed-form to compute live — it has to come from an actual bisection search over simulated order-parameter runs, slower than the instant algebra of the other math toys here, so the UI needs a visible 'searching...' step rather than pretending it's instant. Once that's solid, add a shared library of networks and a table of the worst (most threshold-raising) edges found on each — verifiable by anyone re-running the same bisection, so it behaves like the other checkable leaderboards on this site. Reuse packages/dataviz for the network and eigenvector rendering, and g/'s pattern of one dial-driven canvas sim per page.
mechanism: click to wire two oscillators together and watch whether the synchronization threshold rises or falls

paperTitle: Synthetic paracrine signaling of colloids drives self-assembly limit cycles
name: breathe
text: tune three dials — signal production, decay rate, diffusion range — and watch a cloud of particles breathe: assemble, scatter, assemble again. no external clock, just chemistry making its own rhythm
plan:
The paper builds a minimal model of 'paracrine' colloids: particles that emit a diffusing signal molecule, and the local concentration of that signal turns neighboring particles' attraction up or down. That simple loop is enough to break time-reversal symmetry and produce a genuinely autonomous oscillation — clusters of particles assemble, the signal they've built up switches their own attraction off, they disperse, the signal decays, and they assemble again — a limit cycle with no external clock, driven only by the interplay of production rate, decay rate, and how far the signal diffuses before it fades.

The mechanic: a 2D field of colloids on a canvas, each secreting a signal into a coarse diffusing grid that locally raises or lowers pairwise attraction. Three sliders: production, decay, diffusion range. Turn one ships a fixed small population (a few hundred particles is plenty), the three sliders, and nothing else — watch the population breathe: cluster, scatter, cluster again, and notice the rhythm is emergent, not scripted.

The hard part is landing inside the actual oscillatory regime the paper identifies rather than producing either static clumping or undifferentiated noise — the window is real but narrow, and it needs tuning against the paper's own parameter sweep rather than guessing. Once the rhythm is visible and controllable, the natural second turn is a crowd-mapped phase diagram: visitors submit a (production, decay, range) point, the sim classifies it (steady / oscillating / no assembly) and drops it onto a shared map, the same checkable-by-recomputing pattern as the other search toys here. Reuse g/'s shelf-of-simulations pattern — it already hosts 'self-assembling bearings' — and packages/dataviz for the phase map.
mechanism: tune signal production, decay, and diffusion range and watch colloidal clusters assemble and disperse on their own, forever

paperTitle: Analysis of inverse stochastic resonance: Effects of neural excitability and timescale separation
name: noisedip
text: drag a slider to add noise to a neuron. its firing rate dips at a sweet noise level, then rises as you silence it. noise can suppress spiking more than silence
plan:
Inverse stochastic resonance is the counterintuitive finding that adding noise to a neuron can suppress its firing more than removing the noise entirely. This paper works it out for a bistable FitzHugh-Nagumo neuron poised in a narrow regime where a quiet resting state and an active spiking limit cycle coexist, separated by an unstable orbit. It proves the long-run firing statistics don't depend on where the neuron started (the system is ergodic, so there's one true answer, not an artifact of initial conditions), and derives a formula for the noise amplitude that minimizes firing, plus a sign criterion for when a genuine ISR dip exists at all rather than a monotonic effect.

The mechanic: one FitzHugh-Nagumo neuron simulated live in the browser, a voltage trace, and a single noise-amplitude slider. A rolling spike-rate counter updates as the visitor drags the slider. The reveal is the shape of the curve: firing rate doesn't fall monotonically as noise drops to zero — it dips at some noise level in the middle and rises on both sides, which is the whole paradox, visible rather than argued.

Turn one is exactly that: neuron, trace, slider, live spike counter, and parameters preset into the paper's bistable window. The hard part is that the window is narrow and codimension-two — get the excitability or timescale-separation parameters slightly wrong and the dip vanishes or the neuron never settles into bistability at all, so the presets need to come straight from the paper's own analysis, not eyeballing. Once the dip is reliably visible, add a predict-then-reveal round — guess the noise level that minimizes firing before the curve is drawn, score by distance, com.minomobi.lab.score with lower-is-better. Reuse neuro/'s pattern of models rebuilt from their papers and shown against the published result they replicate.
mechanism: drag a noise-amplitude slider on a simulated neuron and watch its firing rate dip at a nonzero noise level

paperTitle: Cardinal Grid Slime Trail is PSPACE-Complete
name: slime-trail
plan: Slime Trail is a real, playable two-player game: players alternate sliding a shared token to an orthogonally adjacent square, the vacated square is permanently removed, and whoever reaches the goal node wins — get cornered with no legal move and you lose instead. Ferland and Burke showed the game is PSPACE-complete on arbitrary planar graphs in 2017 and asked about the grid version people actually play; this paper closes that, building grid-legal gadgets (respecting the degree-4 bound and lattice parity) for a QBF reduction, and shows the eight-directional variant follows from a 45-degree rotation of the same construction. The mechanic is simply the game itself, board and all — no invented rules, the paper's subject is the artifact. Turn one: a grid, local two-player pass-and-play, legal-move highlighting, the vacated-square removal animation, and a win/loss banner. That alone is a shippable, playable page. The hard part is everything after: a bot opponent needs a real evaluation function, since the PSPACE-completeness proof is a hardness reduction, not a strategy — it tells you the game is hard to solve in general, not how to play it well, so don't ship a bot that can't actually threaten a decent human. The eight-directional mode is a natural second turn once four-directional works, sharing the removal/goal logic. Reuse `games/` wholesale: its Durable Object room pattern for live opponents, matchmaking, and `workers/scores` for win rates by board size — the natural crowd number is how board size and Reynolds-like density of removed squares affects first-player advantage, which nobody has measured.
mechanism: two-player token-and-erase pursuit game on a grid, played live
text: slide a token on a grid to an empty square — it vanishes behind you. your opponent moves next. get cornered and lose. two players, turn-based, simple rules. the paper closes a decades-old question: this game is mathematically one of the hardest puzzles there is

paperTitle: Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents
name: free-rider
text: write a rule for when to give based on someone's past. watch it compete across generations. the winners always copy generosity—pure history-tracking beats every complex strategy
plan: The paper runs an indirect-reciprocity donation game where LLM agents watch each other's giving history and decide how much to donate; their strategies evolve across generations by cultural transmission. Across four model backends, resistance to free-rider invasion varies by more than an order of magnitude, and the strongest predictor isn't sophisticated norm compliance (the Leading-Eight L1 norm doesn't predict robustness at all) but a simple trait: how strongly a strategy scales its giving to the recipient's own giving record, i.e. old-fashioned image scoring, plus how strictly it excludes known defectors from receiving anything. The mechanic: visitors write a short giving rule as a threshold on a visible reputation number ("give if their score is above X, scaled by how generous they've been to others"), not free-text parsed by a model — that's the honest simplification of the paper's natural-language strategies, and the plan should say so on the page. Turn one: play your rule for several rounds against a small fixed roster (an always-cooperator, an always-defector, an image-scoring rule) and get back your payoff plus a computed endowment-sensitivity number for your own rule, the same statistic the paper found load-bearing. Later turns pool submitted rules into one population and simulate generations, watching whether a free-rider introduced later can invade. The hard part is keeping the rule language expressive enough to matter while staying a threshold, not a prompt. Reuse games' Durable Object rooms for the population pool and scores for tracking generational invasion resistance per rule.
mechanism: authoring a threshold giving-rule and testing its resistance to free-rider invasion in an evolving population

paperTitle: Cluster-Cluster model in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
name: blowup
text: set a speed slider for how fast clusters move, watch them either stay separate forever or merge into one blob. some settings guarantee a winner, others depend on your starting configuration
plan: The paper's process: start with scattered finite clusters on a lattice; each cluster does a random walk at rate |C|^{-alpha}, so bigger clusters move slower when alpha is positive; when one bumps into another they merge. The result is a clean dichotomy: for alpha >= 0, no infinite cluster ever forms spontaneously in finite time, almost surely; for alpha <= -1-2/d (small clusters wildly fast, so mass snowballs), finite-time blowup happens almost surely; in between, in the band alpha in (-1,0), the outcome depends sensitively on the starting configuration, and the paper works out the exact phase diagram for that band in one dimension. The toy is a line of specks with an alpha slider: run the merge process, watch a live largest-cluster counter, and see whether the line settles into permanent fragments or eats itself into one blob. Turn one ships exactly that for d=1, with two marked safe zones (alpha >= 0, alpha <= -3) where the outcome is guaranteed by the paper and one live zone (-1, 0) where it depends on the seed you started from. The hard part is being honest that a browser run is a finite-size, finite-time sample of an almost-sure asymptotic statement — a run in the guaranteed-safe zone that blows up anyway just means the run wasn't long enough, and the copy needs to say that rather than let a slider feel like it disproves the theorem. Because the process is a deterministic function of alpha, dimension, and a random seed, a submitted (alpha, seed, survival-time) record can always be replayed and checked, so the crowd race for longest survival in the live zone is cheat-proof the same way a recomputable record is. Reuse packages/dataviz for the phase-diagram overlay and scores for the record table.
mechanism: setting a size-dependent movement rate for merging clusters and watching whether the system blows up into one blob

paperTitle: A Counterexample to Fourier Alignment in Single-Neuron Modular Addition
name: flatline
text: pick starting weights and watch a neuron train. from some points it locks onto one frequency; from others it stops cold with the signal spread flat everywhere. find the mysterious boundary
plan: Training a single ReLU neuron on modular addition is a standard toy problem in the grokking literature, and the folk expectation is that it converges by aligning to a single dominant frequency. This paper gives a genuine counterexample: from an open set of initial conditions (so a real, positive-probability slice of Gaussian init, not a knife-edge), the neuron instead goes completely inactive in finite time and freezes with its Fourier energy spread equally across every nonzero frequency class — dead, not aligned, and the appendix extends the same failure to several other training conventions. The toy: a 2D grid of initial conditions (phase and amplitude of the starting weight), pick a point, run the tiny gradient descent live in the browser, and get back a labelled outcome — aligned or dead — with a bar chart of the frozen Fourier spectrum. Turn one is exactly that single lookup: pick a point, watch training, read the spectrum. The hard part is fidelity, not scale: the death only shows up if the training loop matches the paper's exact setup (ReLU'(0)=0, the right modular-addition loss, fixed-step full-batch descent), and a slightly different convention will just show alignment everywhere and quietly hide the result, so the implementation needs to be checked against the paper's construction, not against intuition. Because training from a given seed is deterministic, a claimed dead point is instantly replayable and checkable, so the natural second turn is crowd-sourced: submissions accumulate into a shared heatmap of the open set on the initial-condition grid, mapping the boundary the paper proves exists but doesn't draw.
mechanism: picking a neuron's starting weights and watching whether gradient descent kills it or aligns it, then mapping the boundary between the two outcomes

paperTitle: From Cake-Cutting and Necklace-Splitting to Fair Division of Indivisible Items
name: faircut
text: drag cut points to divide items fairly among agents. an envy meter shows how many items each person envies. the math guarantees you can keep it to just one or two
plan: The paper takes continuous fair-division results (cake-cutting, necklace-splitting) and transfers them to indivisible items laid out on a path, producing connected allocations — bundles made of contiguous items, like cutting a string of beads at a few points — that are envy-free up to a small, bounded number of extra goods and chores. For identical valuations, or for arbitrary valuations when the number of agents is a prime power, the transfer gets envy-freeness up to one good and one chore; combined with necklace-splitting it extends to consensus guarantees for non-additive valuations, the first result of that kind. The toy: a line of items, each with a value shown per agent (goods are positive, chores negative, and you can toggle whose eyes you're viewing the line through), and the visitor drags cut points to split it into contiguous bundles for n agents. A live envy meter reports, for every pair, how many items they'd have to remove from a rival's bundle before the envy disappears — the EF-k number the paper bounds. Turn one is a fixed small instance, four agents (a prime power) and a dozen items, target EF1. The honest framing matters here: the visitor isn't discovering new math by dragging cuts, they're hunting for a construction the paper guarantees exists, so the page should offer a reveal ("here's a cut achieving the guarantee") rather than implying an open search. The hard part is getting the connected-allocation bookkeeping right, especially the chore side, where naïve intuition from cake-cutting misleads. Crowd angle: submit adversarial valuation profiles and race others to find the guaranteed cut in the fewest drags, tracked as solved-instance records.
mechanism: dragging cut points along a line of items to split it among agents while an envy meter tracks how close the split is to fair

paperTitle: When Truth Is Distributed: Misinformation Derails Collective Fact Recovery in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
name: one-liar
plan: The paper runs a five-agent object-movement task where each agent sees only part of the picture and the group must vote its way to a shared true answer. With every agent honest, the group recovers the truth 72.5% of the time. Plant one agent that lies about what it saw, and recovery collapses to 14.17% — a single false testimony gets adopted more readily than a true one, spreads to agents who never heard it firsthand, and keeps circulating even after the liar leaves the conversation. The toy replaces the LLM agents with a room of real people playing the same game: each player is privately shown one clue about a hidden layout, players exchange testimony over a few rounds (text, not voice, so testimony is a discrete claim you can trace), then the room votes on the shared answer. One round in ten silently makes one player's clue false and instructs them to lie convincingly. Turn one ships the honest version only: deal partial clues, run the testimony rounds, tally the vote, show whether the room got it right — no liar yet, just the substrate the deception mode plugs into next. What's hard is the tracing: to show the finding rather than just the outcome, the site needs to log which claims each vote actually cites, so a false claim's spread through the room becomes visible as a small directed graph, not just a lower score. Reuse the games surface for rooms and turn order, workers/scores for the running honest-vs-planted-liar recovery rate — the real payoff, since a thousand human rounds is a live replication of the paper's headline number with people instead of LLMs.
mechanism: n-player partial-information deduction game where testimony visibly propagates and one planted liar is tracked through the vote
text: see one clue about a hidden layout. others see different clues. text what you observed and vote on the truth. group's accurate 72% of the time. one liar in the room drops it to 14%. false testimony spreads further and sticks longer

paperTitle: Regional Chaos Synchronization towards controlling high-dimensional open environmental systems
name: regional-sync
plan: Global chaos synchronization forces an entire system to track a target trajectory everywhere; this paper asks what happens if you only try to control a small region of a much bigger chaotic field — a weather-control-scale problem, since you can't put actuators over the whole atmosphere. The finding: regional control is much harder than global control in a specific, counterintuitive way. Errors leak in from the untouched exterior and degrade the region even when the actuators are unchanged, and — unlike global sync, where any correct target trajectory works equally well — the choice of target trajectory now matters: one that matches the system's natural, uncontrolled path everywhere outside your region but diverges only inside it lets you actually hold the region, while an arbitrary target gets swamped by exterior noise. The toy puts the visitor in the seat of the controller: a 2D chaotic field (a coupled-map lattice is enough) renders live, the visitor draws a box (their 'target region') and picks or free-draws a target pattern for it, and actuators confined to that box try to force the field inside it to match. A live error gauge shows the fight between the actuator and the leaking exterior. Turn one ships the field running freely with no control, plus the region-drawing tool, so the base sandbox is real before synchronization logic lands. The hard part is making the leak legible without a wall of numbers — probably a second gauge showing error specifically crossing the region's boundary, separate from error inside it. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the gauges, the O'Neill pack's simulation-sandbox conventions, workers/scores for a leaderboard on best target-trajectory design at fixed region size and actuator budget — the paper's actual design problem, turned into something a crowd can search over.
mechanism: draw a control region on a live chaotic field and design a target trajectory that resists error leaking in from outside it
text: draw a region on a live chaotic field and design a pattern you want inside it. actuators confined to your region try to hold that pattern. but error leaks in from the wild exterior. some patterns resist the leak. others crumble. your design choice matters

paperTitle: The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees
name: onion-peel
plan: A random recursive tree grows by adding nodes one at a time, each attaching to a uniformly random existing node. The paper studies two different notions of 'how deep' a node sits: rank, the distance to the nearest leaf, and layer, the number of rounds it takes to reach that node if you repeatedly strip off every current leaf at once — like peeling an onion, or like k-core peeling but for trees. Both distributions have exact recursive formulas now, and the shapes are strikingly different: rank decays factorially, so almost every node sits within a couple of steps of some leaf no matter how big the tree gets, while layer decays only geometrically, so the onion has meaningfully fat outer-to-inner structure. Both are also self-averaging — grow many trees at the same size and the count of nodes at a given rank or layer barely fluctuates between them. The toy: grow a tree by clicking 'add node' (each new node visibly attaches to a random existing one), then hit 'peel' to strip leaves round by round, coloring every node by the layer it dies in like tree rings, while hovering any node shows its rank. Turn one ships exactly that — grow, peel, ring-color, hover-rank — as a single-tree, single-page demo with no aggregation yet. The hard part is not the mechanic but making the rank/layer distinction feel like two different measurements of the same object rather than one: probably a toggle that recolors the same static tree by rank instead of by layer, so the visitor sees the same skeleton produce two different pictures. Reuse packages/dataviz for the two histograms (predicted factorial and geometric curves overlaid on what the visitor's own trees produced), and workers/scores to accumulate a running histogram across everyone's generated trees, which is the site's actual crowd contribution: a live check of self-averaging at a scale no browser tab could grow alone.
mechanism: grow a random recursive tree, strip its leaves round by round, and compare the resulting rank vs. layer coloring of the same tree
text: grow a tree by clicking. each new node attaches to a random existing node. then peel: strip every current leaf round by round, like peeling an onion. almost every node sits near a leaf, but somehow the tree's outer layers are fat and deep

paperTitle: Responsibility in Multi-Agent Sequential Decision-Making: Comparing Human Judgments to Formal Models of Causal Attribution
name: blame-round
plan: The paper runs a modified Goofspiel — a bidding card game played over several rounds by multiple agents with only partial information about each other — engineers specific failures into it, and surveys people on who they blame, then checks that against several formal 'actual causality' definitions of responsibility. None of the formal methods consistently matches human judgment; what does move human blame is which agent had more information at the time and agent-specific bias, not the counterfactual math the formal methods use. The toy is the same game with the same question attached: play a short Goofspiel round with two or three co-players (bots at first), where cards are bid blind and a low-information player's guess sometimes sinks the group's score. When the round ends badly, every player privately allocates a fixed 100 points of blame across the players, sees the group's blame distribution, and sees how it compares to one explicit formal score — a counterfactual measure of 'how different would the outcome have been if this player had bid differently' — computed live from the actual hands played. Turn one ships the bare game: deal, bid, reveal, score, no blame phase yet, since the sequential bidding mechanic has to be right before anything gets stacked on it. What's hard is choosing one formal responsibility measure simple enough to compute and explain in a sentence without overstating what the paper found — the paper tests several and none wins outright, so the site should present its one baseline as 'a' formal answer, not 'the' formal answer, and let the visible gap between it and the crowd's votes be the point. Reuse games' DO rooms and turn order, workers/scores for the running human-vs-formal agreement rate — a literal, ongoing rerun of the paper's own survey with real playtesters instead of a one-time panel.
mechanism: multiplayer sequential bidding game where a bad outcome triggers a blame vote, scored against a live counterfactual responsibility formula
text: play goofspiel with others. bid blind each round. you only see part of their hands. round ends badly. now blame someone. your vote gets compared against a formal formula: if that player had bid differently, how much would the outcome change?

paperTitle: A proof of Andersen's rainbow path conjecture for large $n$
name: rainbow-path
plan: The paper proves that every properly edge-coloured complete graph on n vertices (large n) contains a rainbow path through n-1 of its vertices - a path using every colour at most once and missing at most one vertex. It settles Andersen's 1989 conjecture and beats the prior best of n minus about root-n-log-n. A companion result: every large Latin square has a cycle-free transversal of order n-2. The mechanic: the visitor is handed a properly edge-coloured K_n (small n at first, rendered as a circle of vertices with coloured chords) and builds a path by clicking edges one at a time; the interface rejects any edge that repeats a colour already used or revisits a vertex, and a live counter shows vertices covered against the n-1 target. Turn one ships a single fixed n (6 or 7), a hand-clickable path builder, and the counter - that alone lets someone feel the constraint and either hit n-1 or get stuck and see why. The hard part is the colouring generator: it must be a genuinely proper edge colouring (no vertex sees a repeated colour) or the puzzle is trivial or unsolvable by construction, and generating interesting-but-fair colourings for small n needs care. What's honest to flag: the theorem is asymptotic ("sufficiently large n"), so small-n instances are a puzzle inspired by the result, not an instance of it - the site should say that plainly. Reuse: the math wing's (`math`) single-file explainer conventions and layout; `scores` for a record table of best-found paths on adversarially hard colourings, since any claimed path is instantly checkable by anyone recomputing it, so cheating is arithmetically impossible the same way the Erdos toy's leaderboard is.
mechanism: click-to-build a rainbow path in a properly edge-coloured complete graph, racing the n-1 bound
text: click edges in a graph where each has a color, building a path using each color once. no matter how the graph is colored, there's always a path visiting n-1 vertices

paperTitle: Errorless Irrationality: A unified computational account of the inverse base-rate effect across predictive, observational, and unsupervised procedures
name: silent-bias
plan: The inverse base-rate effect: when one category is common and shows one symptom pattern, and a rarer category shows a rarer, more distinctive pattern, people irrationally over-attribute an ambiguous case (with cues from both) to the rare category - backwards from the base rates. The standard explanation is prediction-error learning. This paper strips the predictive setup down, first to observational learning (labels shown, no guess required) and then to fully unsupervised learning (no labels at all), and the bias survives both, at similar strength - meaning it does not need an error signal, contrary to the dominant theory. Their new model, OSCAR, explains all three regimes plus eye-tracking data nobody else's model reproduces. The mechanic: the visitor runs their own miniature version of the experiment on themselves - a sequence of cue cards sorted into a common category and a rare category, first with feedback after each guess, ending on the ambiguous probe card, and their own lean (common vs rare) is the data point. Turn one ships just the predictive-with-feedback phase plus the probe, since that alone reproduces the classic effect on the visitor personally, with a plain readout of which way they leaned and why it's numerically backwards. The hard part, saved for later turns, is the observational and unsupervised phases - staging a task that has no guessing and no labels but still measurably nudges the same bias, without it reading as "just watch and remember." What's hard about turn one alone is picking base rates and cue overlap that reliably produce the pull without feeling rigged. Reuse: `human`'s arcade-of-user-error framing and copy voice, this is exactly its kind of exhibit; `scores` for a running histogram of how visitors split on the probe, since a thousand data points is itself evidence the effect is real and not an artifact of one page's design.
mechanism: sort cue cards into categories, then face an ambiguous card and watch your own choice reveal the bias
text: sort cards into common and rare groups. then guess whether an ambiguous card belongs to common or rare. you'll lean one way consistently, even when nobody tells you if you're wrong

paperTitle: Simple evolution drives direct reciprocity to maximum payoff in social dilemmas
name: reciprocity-engine
plan: The paper shows that a simple evolutionary process - mutation near the boundary of strategy space, plus pairwise comparison at some intensity of selection - reliably drives populations of repeated-game strategies to the maximum possible payoff in all four classic social dilemmas: Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony. This needs large populations, intermediate-to-high mutation, and intermediate-to-strong selection. The catch: it only works in every game if strategies can use memory-2 (recall both players' last two moves). Memory-1 strategies solve three of the four games but in Snowdrift get consistently beaten by a specific counter-strategy the authors call the "Hold-trap." The mechanic: the visitor sets population size, mutation rate, and selection strength with sliders, picks a dilemma, and hits run - the population evolves generation by generation on screen while a chart tracks average payoff against the game's theoretical maximum, converging or not in real time. Turn one ships exactly this for Prisoner's Dilemma with memory-1 strategies only: three sliders, a run button, and the payoff-vs-max chart converging, which alone demonstrates the paper's headline claim. A second turn adds Snowdrift and a memory-1/memory-2 toggle so the visitor can watch the Hold-trap stall a memory-1 population and then watch memory-2 escape it. The hard part is speed: the simulation has to visibly respond to slider changes within a few seconds, which caps how large a population and how many generations can run per turn without the animation stalling - that tuning is the real design work. Reuse: `fluoddity`'s breed-and-mutate loop as the closest existing pattern for a live-evolving population; `scores` for a discovery board of parameter settings that reach max payoff fastest, or that reproduce the Hold-trap failure.
mechanism: tune mutation and selection sliders, run generations, and watch a strategy population converge on (or miss) the maximum payoff
text: tune population size, mutation rate, and selection strength. run generations of strategies playing prisoner's dilemma. watch average payoff climb steadily toward the theoretical maximum

paperTitle: Veiled in Starlight: Impacts of Stellar Contamination on Retrievals of TRAPPIST-1f's Atmospheric Composition
name: trappist-veil
plan: TRAPPIST-1f is a habitable-zone planet around an ultra-cool star, and the paper asks how well JWST could actually detect its atmosphere once you account for stellar contamination - the spectral fingerprint of unocculted starspots on the host, which the paper shows can imprint features stronger than any plausible planetary signal. Modeling a CO2-rich atmosphere against a worst-case contamination spectrum, they find about 10 transits gives strong evidence (Bayes factor over 150) for CO2, about 50 transits gives only weak evidence (over 3) for CH4, and even 100 transits fail to turn up H2O at all - contamination doesn't just add noise proportional to more transits, it can put a molecule permanently out of reach. The mechanic: the visitor is the mission scientist with a transit budget - pick a target molecule, drag a transit-count slider, and toggle contamination on or off, watching a Bayes-factor evidence bar respond. With contamination off, more transits always help; with it on, H2O's bar visibly plateaus instead of climbing, however many transits are spent. Turn one ships CO2 only, transits from 1 to 20, the on/off toggle, and the evidence bar diverging visibly around the paper's roughly-10-transit threshold. The hard part is honesty: there's no live retrieval running client-side, so the evidence curve has to be a lookup interpolated from the paper's own reported numbers, and the page must say so plainly rather than implying a real Bayesian fit is happening live. This is closer to a demo than a game - the crowd angle is thin, limited to a shared tally of who "found" each molecule under which settings - and that should be stated rather than oversold.
mechanism: pick a molecule, spend a transit budget, toggle stellar contamination, and watch the detection-evidence bar respond or plateau
text: pick a molecule to detect around trappist-1f and spend transits. toggle stellar contamination. CO2 emerges at ten transits, but H2O stays hidden no matter how many transits you spend

paperTitle: Circular sorting in the alternating group
name: triswap
plan: Prior work pinned exactly how many adjacent swaps it takes to sort n points on a circle into a power of the full rotation, for the symmetric group. This paper asks the same question for the alternating group, where the moves are 3-cycles instead of transpositions: starting from any even permutation of n circle-points, what is the worst-case number of 3-cycle moves needed to reach a state that is just the circle rotated by some amount? They pin the answer exactly for even n and for n congruent to 1 mod 4. For n congruent to 3 mod 4 the true worst case is one of exactly two numbers, and they exhibit constructions showing the larger of the two happens for infinitely many such n, without settling, for a given n in that family, which one it actually is. The mechanic: n points arranged on a circle, each move lets the visitor pick three points and cyclically rotate their labels one step; given an adversarially shuffled permutation, sort it into a rotation-power state within a move budget. Turn one ships the guaranteed-solvable case only, an even n or n congruent to 1 mod 4 with the paper's exact worst-case number as the target, so every claim on the page is a fact from the paper rather than aspirational. A second mode for n congruent to 3 mod 4, where visitors brute-force small cases and a leaderboard tracks which of the two values has actually been observed for which n, is the natural follow-up once turn one is solid, in the same spirit as the Erdos rectangle hunt. What is hard: the build agent needs the paper's actual formula and a worked example, not just the abstract, before it can put a real number on the target. Reuse: the math/geometry wing's single-file explainer conventions; workers/scores for the n congruent to 3 mod 4 record table.
mechanism: sort a shuffled ring of points into a rotation using 3-cycle moves within a move budget
text: n points shuffled on a circle. your move: pick three and cyclically rotate their positions. sort the whole circle within a move budget. for certain sizes, the paper proves the worst case is one of exactly two numbers—but not which

paperTitle: Thermodynamic statistics of given names in USA and France
name: condensate
plan: Using government name-registration data from the US and France spanning over a century, the paper shows given-name popularity distributions are stable in a specific way: plotted as Lorenz and Pareto curves, the same tools used for wealth inequality, the Gini coefficient sits in a narrow 0.85 to 0.95 band for the entire period. It then shows those distributions are well described by Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization, the same statistical-mechanics process behind Bose-Einstein condensation: two conserved quantities, analogous to energy and particle number, set a temperature, and below a threshold, population condenses onto the single most popular state, here the single most popular name. Time correlations between names were stable until roughly mid-century, then changed. The mechanic: two dials, a temperature and a second, chemical-potential-like parameter, generating a synthetic name-popularity curve from the Rayleigh-Jeans formula live; a toggle overlays a real curve for one bundled year and country. The visitor's job is to find the two-dial setting that reproduces the real curve's Gini coefficient and condensate fraction, the top name's share of all births, which the paper's own claim says should be possible with startling simplicity. Turn one ships the generator, the two dials, one real snapshot, and a live readout comparing simulated to real Gini and condensate fraction. What is hard: making the analogy to Bose-Einstein condensation land as delight rather than jargon, and being honest that a one-year fit is illustrative, since the paper's claim rests on the full hundred-year series holding stable, not any single snapshot. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the Lorenz curve and Gini computation; a guess-the-decade daily challenge from curve shape alone is a natural crowd layer once the core dial works.
mechanism: tune two thermal dials to fit a generated name-popularity curve to a real historical one
text: tune two thermal dials to model baby-name frequencies. match your curve to real century-old census data. name popularity follows Bose-Einstein condensation—the same thermodynamic physics that describes wealth inequality

paperTitle: Sharp Tail Bounds Beyond Twice the Mean
name: jackpot
plan: The paper proves a clean tail bound for sums of independent, non-negative random variables each with mean at most 1: the chance their sum reaches or exceeds a threshold t is at most 1-(1-1/t)^n, for any t at least 2n+1, deliberately the regime beyond twice the mean, where cruder bounds go slack. The bound is tight: equality holds exactly for n independent lottery tickets, each paying out either 0, with probability 1-1/t, or the full threshold t, with probability 1/t, the riskiest possible way to keep an expected value of 1. The mechanic: sliders for n, the number of players, and t, the jackpot line, auto-clamped to stay at least 2n+1, a distribution picker starting with the exact lottery-ticket case, and a running simulation plotting the empirical chance of hitting the jackpot as points against the smooth theoretical ceiling curve. The visitor's goal is to push the empirical curve as close to the ceiling as they can by choosing payout distributions, and the game is rigged so that no choice can ever cross it, which is the actual content of the proof. Turn one ships the two sliders, the lottery-ticket distribution live-simulating against the ceiling curve, and a numeric readout of how close the run got. What is hard: simulation noise at small trial counts will make the empirical curve wobble in a way that looks like crossing when it is not, which argues for computing the true probability with the paper's own dynamic-programming recursion instead of only sampling it. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the curve plot; workers/scores for a leaderboard of which distribution mixtures get closest to the ceiling across chosen (n, t) pairs, a genuinely re-checkable record.
mechanism: pick payout distributions for n players and watch the sum's tail probability chase a fixed theoretical ceiling
text: choose payout distributions for n players betting on a size-t jackpot. run simulations and watch the win probability trace toward a hard ceiling. the paper proves no distribution escapes it. the lottery on the ceiling is maximally risky

paperTitle: Collective search-and-capture under competing assignment policies
name: manhunt
plan:
The paper runs persistent random walkers on a lattice, each reorienting at rate alpha, hunting stationary targets they can only claim within a finite range R, and times how long the group takes to catch everything, T_c. The finding: T_c(alpha) is not monotonic. There is a sweet spot of persistence, walkers that turn neither too often nor too rarely, that clears the field fastest, and that sweet spot flattens as R grows. More striking: which walker claims a target when two reach it matters more than how walkers move. Simple greedy claiming and a slightly smarter cascading reassignment behave the same at small R, but true maximum-cardinality matching between walkers and reachable targets cuts completion time by several times at moderate R and by an order of magnitude at large R, a scheduling choice beating a motion strategy.

The toy: a lattice of dots, walkers hunting stationary targets. Two sliders, reorientation rate alpha and search radius R, and a switch between greedy and cascading assignment. Press go, watch walkers wander and claim targets, read off T_c, and drop that point onto a live T_c(alpha) curve that fills in as you try more values, so the dip becomes visible by your own hand instead of asserted. Turn one ships exactly that: the lattice, the two sliders, the two simple policies, the accumulating curve.

The hard part, deliberately deferred: real maximum-cardinality matching needs a bipartite-matching solver, not a turn-one build, and until it lands the page must not claim the order-of-magnitude number, only show greedy versus cascading. Reuse `g`'s canvas-sim shelf conventions for the lattice renderer and `workers/scores` later for crowd-submitted assignment policies ranked by T_c across shared seeds.
mechanism: walkers on a lattice hunting targets under a chosen claim-assignment policy, timed
text: drop random walkers on a grid hunting targets. adjust how often they reorient and which assignment rule they use. a live curve shows: one policy beats all movement strategies by orders of magnitude

paperTitle: Interaction size and dissent tolerance in majority-rule dynamics with collective reversal
name: faultline
plan:
The paper is majority-rule opinion dynamics with a twist: a group of n people flips together not only on strict unanimity but on near-unanimity, reversal fires with up to d dissenters tolerated. That one parameter changes the whole phase picture. Under strict unanimity a real order-disorder transition exists only for group sizes 3 and 4; every other n is stuck. Allow dissent and transitions reopen at larger n, tracing an accessibility boundary in the (n,d) plane instead of a fixed threshold. Widen the activation window enough and directional asymmetry can erase one of the two stable consensus states entirely through a saddle-node bifurcation, leaving a population that can only ever settle one way. The punchline: loose-but-not-broken alignment, some dissent tolerated, is the configuration most likely to flip a whole population, more than strict unanimity or outright disorder.

The toy: a grid of agents in two colors. Two dials, group size n and dissent tolerance d. Repeatedly the site pulls a random group of n agents and reverses their shared opinion if at most d of them disagree, then lets that ripple through repeated draws. Turn one ships that loop on a fixed small population, with a running count of full-population reversals and a two-axis grid below it that lights a cell green when your (n,d) choice produced a reversal in the run and gray when it locked in place, a phase map the visitor fills in one attempt at a time.

The hard part: the paper's transitions are mean-field results on an idealized population, so a small on-screen grid will show noisier boundaries than the paper's, and the page has to present its map as visitor-built rather than a claimed reproduction. Reuse `human`'s exhibit framing for the panel copy.
mechanism: a two-opinion population you tip via a group-size and dissent-tolerance rule, watching for a full reversal
text: color a population and watch groups vote to flip them. adjust group size and dissent tolerance. the phase map shows which values trigger full population reversals. modest dissent tolerance beats both strict unanimity and outright chaos

paperTitle: Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis
name: quorum-clock
plan:
The paper studies orchestrated LLM debates, agents that argue and vote, and asks whether anything can be certified about a debate before it finishes. It treats the exchange as one dynamical system on a communication graph and reads its future off the spectrum of a Koopman operator, a linear stand-in for the nonlinear back-and-forth fit from a short window of observed interaction. The sub-dominant eigenvalue fixes the debate's timescale and yields a convergence deadline computable before the debate is over, tracking observed convergence with log-log correlation 0.93 on their test model and bounding it correctly in 96% of 24 configurations. That eigenvalue's eigenvector separately names which agents are voting together, the debate's factions, before the debate settles.

The toy: draw a small graph of agents, a ring, a star, a couple of clusters, give each a starting opinion, and watch the first several rounds of a simple opinion-averaging process play out. At that point the site fits a linear operator to just those early rounds and, before letting the simulation continue, shows its call: a predicted round for consensus, and a coloring of agents into predicted factions. Press continue, watch the rest play out, and see how close the early call landed. Turn one ships exactly that: build a graph, watch early rounds, get a call, reveal the answer, see the miss distance.

The hard part is fitting a linear operator from noisy early data in-browser without it going numerically unstable on tiny graphs; start with regular topologies where the fit behaves, and only open custom graphs once that is handled. This uses a plain agent-averaging model, not real LLMs, and the page should say so, since the paper's headline numbers come from LLM debates and this reproduces the mechanism, not the benchmark.
mechanism: predicting a multi-agent debate's convergence round and factions from its early rounds, then checking the call
text: draw a network, seed opinions, watch several rounds of averaging. the system predicts which round they converge and which agents align. press play and see if the forecast lands

paperTitle: On uniform eventowns
name: eventown
plan: The classic eventown puzzle: build a town where every two clubs share an even number of members. This paper proves the uniform version — clubs are exactly k people (k=2t) out of n=2m townsfolk — tops out at C(m,t) clubs, and once n is bigger than about 10k^7 every maximum family has an 'atomic' structure: it is built from indivisible blocks, not an ad-hoc arrangement. Previously that bound was only known once n was exponential in k; this pins it to a polynomial threshold, a big practical tightening. The toy: a grid of n townsfolk, click to found a k-person club, and the site rejects any club whose overlap with an existing one is odd. A running counter shows your family size against C(m,t) as a target line. Turn one ships the town, the club-builder, the even-overlap checker, and the counter — that alone is a playable constraint puzzle with an immediate 'you broke the rule' moment. The hard part is not the founding UI but the checker: overlap parity must be computed and enforced live as clubs accumulate, and the target C(m,t) has to be computed for whatever m, t the visitor picks, including editable town size. The payoff turn is a 'reveal the atom' hint, unlocked after enough failed attempts, that shows one way to hit C(m,t) exactly by pairing up the town and building clubs only from whole pairs — the unpacking that makes 'atomic structure' concrete instead of a phrase from the abstract. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer convention (erdos/) and workers/scores for a per-(m,t) record table, since any claimed family size is instantly checkable by recomputing the overlaps.
mechanism: click-to-found k-person clubs on a townsfolk grid under a live even-overlap constraint, racing a computed target C(m,t)
text: start a town and click to found k-person clubs. any two must share an even number of members. the site blocks odd overlaps live. every valid family has a mathematical ceiling — can you reach it?

paperTitle: Maximizing directed cycles in tournaments
name: carousel
plan: A tournament here means every pair of n players has played once, so every edge points from winner to loser. The paper closes the last open case of a conjecture about which tournament shape contains the most directed cycles of a given length: for cycle lengths divisible by 4, it is not the random tournament (which wins for every other length) but a specific construction called the carousel tournament — players seated in a circle, each beating the next roughly half the circle clockwise. That is a genuine surprise: one clean, structured tournament beats pure randomness at its own game, and only for that one family of lengths. The toy: a circle of n dots, click any pair to set the arrow direction, and a live counter tallies directed 4-cycles (four players who beat each other in a loop) as you edit. Turn one ships exactly that — n small enough to reason about by eye (8-12 players), the click-to-flip edges, and the live cycle counter, plus two preset buttons, 'random' and 'carousel', so the visitor can see the gap the paper proves exists before trying to beat it themselves. What's hard: counting directed 4-cycles has to be fast enough to recompute on every edge flip for a complete graph, and the presets need the actual carousel construction, not an approximation, or the demonstration is a lie. Later turns let n grow and add a leaderboard of the highest 4-cycle count found for a given n, which is honest competition since carousel is only asymptotically optimal — small n leaves room to search. Reuse games/ or workers/scores for the per-n record table; no new backend needed since a submitted tournament is just an edge-orientation list, checkable by recomputation.
mechanism: click edges to orient a round-robin tournament, watch a live directed-4-cycle counter, and try to beat the carousel preset
text: click to flip edges and orient a tournament. a live counter tallies directed 4-cycles — four players who beat each other in a loop. the carousel seating beats randomness at this game. can you?

paperTitle: NP-Hardness of Non-Crossing Hamiltonian Path and Cycle in Non-Planar Graphs
name: crossless
plan: A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once. The extra rule this paper studies is drawing it without letting any two of its edges cross, given fixed vertex positions. Earlier hardness proofs only worked on planar graphs, where nothing ever crosses anyway, so they never actually isolated whether the no-crossing rule itself is what makes the puzzle hard. This paper reduces directly from 3-SAT to non-planar graphs, proving the crossing constraint alone is NP-hard, independent of planarity. The toy is the puzzle those graphs generate: a fixed layout of dots with some edges pre-drawn crossing each other, and the visitor drags a single path from dot to dot, vertex by vertex, with the site refusing any move whose new segment crosses a previously drawn one. Turn one ships one hand-built small instance (10-15 vertices) with the drag-to-extend path builder and live crossing rejection — genuinely playable and immediately legible as a puzzle, no proof required. The hard part, for later turns, is generating fresh instances at will: real difficulty needs graphs shaped like the paper's 3-SAT gadgets, not arbitrary random non-planar graphs, since ad-hoc crossings are usually easy to route around. Without gadget-shaped instances the puzzle is just fiddly, not provably hard, and that is the whole point of the paper. The crowd angle is a daily generated instance with a leaderboard of who solved it and how fast, plus an admitted-defeat counter for instances nobody solves that day, making the wall visible the way the twelve-colour case does in eleven-hats. Reuse the math wing's single-file layout (erdos/, math/) and workers/scores for daily records.
mechanism: drag out a Hamiltonian path on a fixed dot layout, one vertex at a time, with the site blocking any move that crosses a prior segment
text: drag out a path that visits every dot exactly once, vertex by vertex. the site blocks any move that crosses a prior segment. a mathematical proof says you can't always win.

paperTitle: A Note on the Influence of a Zero Length Nonce on GCM and GMAC
name: zero-nonce
plan: GCM authenticates a message with a tag built from a per-message nonce and a secret hash key. The ISO/IEC version of the standard allows an empty nonce; the NIST version explicitly forbids it, requiring at least one bit. This note shows that an empty nonce is enough for an attacker who sees one authenticated ciphertext to recover the hash key outright, after which they can forge a valid tag for any ciphertext they like — full authentication bypass, from a single message, from a standards footnote. The toy puts the visitor on the attacker's side of a toy-scale GCM-like scheme (small field, not real AES-128, so the arithmetic is legible and the whole thing runs in a browser tab): they're handed one authenticated message encrypted under a zero-length nonce, walked through recovering the hash key from it, and then get to forge a second ciphertext of their choosing and see it accepted. Turn one ships the smallest complete slice: a single fixed toy message and key, the recovery step shown as a worked calculation the visitor steps through (not typed math, actual intermediate values updating), and one forge-and-verify action at the end. The hard part is keeping the toy field small enough to be legible while still faithfully mirroring the real algebraic structure GHASH uses — simplify the arithmetic, not the vulnerability. A second card runs the identical scenario under a one-bit nonce, per the NIST rule, and the forge step fails, making the fix visible as the same UI failing safely. This is offensive-security material about a real, published, still-live standards gap: frame it plainly as a footnote in an ISO document, not a recipe, keep it toy-scale throughout, and don't wire it to any real GCM library. Reuse human/'s exhibit framing and WASM-in-browser conventions already shipped in ocr/ and aub/.
mechanism: recover a toy MAC's hash key from one zero-nonce message, then forge and verify a second ciphertext
text: you're handed one encrypted message under a zero-length nonce. recover the hidden key from it, then forge and verify a second message of your choice. the same game fails safely with a one-bit nonce.

paperTitle: Two base rates, two weights: base-rate neglect has a second axis
name: two-weights
plan: Base-rate neglect is usually treated as one failure: people under-weight how common an outcome is. This paper argues there is a second, separate failure hiding in the same judgments: people also under- or over-weight how common the cue itself is, and the two are independently manipulable — an experimenter can move one without moving the other, a double dissociation that a single-parameter theory of base-rate neglect cannot produce. The paper writes both as two weights in one Bayesian equation and shows the cue-frequency weight only shows up in graded ratings, not two-choice tests, because a forced choice cancels it out. The toy hands the visitor a stream of trials — a cue either appears or doesn't, an outcome either follows or doesn't, at rates the site controls — and after each trial asks for a graded rating (0-100, not yes/no) of how likely the outcome is. Turn one ships one block: 20-30 trials at a fixed cue rate and outcome rate, the rating slider, and a reveal at the end showing the visitor's own two weights plotted as a point, against the two axes literally labeled 'prior neglect' and 'cue neglect'. What's hard: computing a stable per-visitor weight estimate from a short trial block without it being noise, and choosing trial rates that actually separate the two effects rather than confounding them, which is the paper's whole methodological point. The real payoff, for a later turn, is a second block at different cue/outcome rates so the visitor sees their own point move on one axis but not the other — the double dissociation happening to them, not just described. Crowd angle: aggregate the two-weight scatter across all visitors, which is closer to the rating experiment the paper says hasn't been run yet than a canned demo would be. Reuse human/'s exhibit framing and rating-trial machinery.
mechanism: rate graded likelihood after each cue-outcome trial; the site fits your two neglect weights from your ratings and plots them
text: after each trial of cue and outcome, rate how likely the outcome is on a sliding scale. the site plots your two neglect weights — before and after seeing the cue. see the double failure happen.

paperTitle: The Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile: Euler Calculus and Stability for Topological Interaction of Ball Unions
name: ballunion
plan: The paper defines a single integer that measures how several point clouds overlap: grow a ball of radius t_i around each colored point cloud, take the union within each color, intersect the unions across colors, and report the Euler characteristic of that intersection — a count of components minus loops minus voids, generalized. It is rigid-motion invariant, stable under small perturbations, and for n points computable by one sorted alpha-complex sweep with no persistence machinery, worst-case optimal in even dimensions. The toy: two colored point clouds on a canvas, one radius slider that grows circles around every point simultaneously, the ball unions rendered live, and a running integer readout of the intersection's Euler characteristic that jumps as blobs merge, holes close, or components split off. Turn one ships two fixed small point sets (the visitor can drop more points later), the grow-and-render loop, and the live integer computed by rasterized connected-component/hole counting on the intersection region as radius increases — a legible, playable version of the invariant even before the exact alpha-complex algorithm is added. The hard part, named plainly: a rasterized approximation is not the paper's exact algorithm, and the two can disagree right at a topology change; the page should say which method it's using and not claim the exactness the paper proves unless the alpha-complex sweep actually ships. Reuse the math wing's (math.mino.mobi) single-file explainer convention and packages/dataviz for the growing-circle rendering; no server, no build.
mechanism: grow balls around two colored point clouds with one slider and watch an integer track the topology of their overlap
text: two colored point clouds: one slider grows circles around all points, watch an integer track their overlap's topology as holes close and blobs merge, the count jumps

paperTitle: Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erdős--Rényi Graphs: Gaussian Winner Selection and Pace to Unanimity
name: unanimity
plan: Two opinions, blue and red, sit on N voters. Each round the interaction graph is freshly resampled from a sparse Erdős–Rényi model, and every voter adopts whichever opinion is the majority among that round's neighbors, keeping their own on a tie. The paper pins down exactly how the initial lead Δ0 (blue count minus red count) determines the outcome: a big enough lead forces blue unanimity within two rounds; a narrower lead gives explicit bounds on how many rounds it takes; and in the critical window, where the lead scales like the square root of the edge probability, the win probability is exactly the Gaussian CDF Φ(√(2/π)·Δ0·√p), with unanimity reached in about log N / log log N rounds. That closed form is the hook — it's a fair-coin-with-a-known-bias hiding inside a graph process. The toy: set N and a starting lead, run the resample-and-vote loop, and watch the round-by-round vote count converge (or occasionally not, in blue's favor). Turn one ships one graph size, a lead slider, and a single animated run with a round counter and final winner. The hard part: tuning N and the edge probability so the critical window — where the lead is genuinely a coin-flip's worth of advantage — sits inside a range a slider can reach, rather than requiring N in the millions to see anything but a landslide. Reuse packages/dataviz/stats.js for the Gaussian overlay once repeated trials are added, and the math wing's page conventions; workers/scores could later log crowd trial counts against the predicted probability.
mechanism: set a population size and an initial vote lead, run repeated resampled-majority rounds, and watch it converge to unanimity
text: two opinions: set a population and initial lead, voters each round adopt neighbors' majority view on a reshuffling graph. in the critical window, a tiny lead becomes a coin flip before someone sweeps to unanimity

paperTitle: 3-Neighbor bootstrap percolation on two-dimensional grids
name: percolate
plan: In 3-neighbor bootstrap percolation, a grid cell gets permanently infected once at least three of its neighbors are infected, and a starting set of infected cells "percolates" if that rule eventually infects the whole grid. The paper nails down, for every remaining open case of rectangular grids, the exact minimum number of cells you need to seed to percolate the whole thing — closing out a line of work — and for grids wrapped into a torus, gives upper and lower bounds that sit within one of each other, exact in many divisibility cases. The toy is a search puzzle: click cells on a small grid to seed infection, run the spread and watch it propagate step by step, and see whether you percolated the whole grid with fewer clicks than you thought possible. A readout compares your seed count to the paper's proven minimum for that grid size. Turn one ships rectangular grids only, up to roughly 10x10, click-to-seed, a stepped animation of the 3-neighbor spread, and a pass/fail plus seed-count-vs-optimal readout, since rectangular grids are where the paper gives an exact number to check against. The hard part: toroidal grids only have bounds within one of the truth in many cases, not an exact target, so any torus mode must be labeled "closest known" rather than "optimal," and a visitor who beats the paper's upper bound on a torus is reporting something genuinely unresolved, not just losing at a puzzle. Reuse the math wing's conventions and workers/scores for a per-grid-size minimum-seed leaderboard — cheating is structurally hard since any claimed seed set can be re-run and recounted.
mechanism: click cells to seed a grid, run the 3-neighbor infection rule, and try to percolate the whole grid in fewer seeds than the paper's proven minimum
text: click cells to start infection: if three neighbors catch it, they spread it. puzzle: percolate the grid in fewer clicks than the paper's proven minimum. you probably can't beat it

paperTitle: Morphology of frozen labyrinths from irreversible threshold dynamics
name: frozen-labyrinths
plan:
Majority threshold dynamics is the standard smoothing rule: every cell looks at a Gaussian-weighted neighborhood and adopts whichever color is locally dominant, over and over, until the field relaxes to one solid color or clean stripes -- this is the reversible Merriman-Bence-Osher process, exactly solvable, and it always erases disorder. The paper's twist is one word: irreversible. Let each cell defect from its local minority at most once, then it is locked forever, right or wrong. Run that rule from a random near-50/50 start and something the reversible version never produces shows up: a frozen labyrinth, a maze of both colors stuck in a genuine minority state nobody chose to leave. It only happens in a narrow band of starting composition around balance, and that band narrows as the neighborhood gets wider.

The toy: a grid, a slider for starting composition (30%-70%) and a slider for neighborhood width. Hit run and watch cells flip out of their local minority one by one, each marked the instant it locks; when nothing can flip anymore, the grid is either uniform, striped, or a frozen labyrinth, and cells still sitting against their own local field glow -- that frustration signature is unique to the irreversible rule and appears nowhere in the smooth version. Turn one ships that grid, both sliders, and the freeze detector; no multiplayer needed yet.

The hard part is the neighborhood sum itself -- a real Gaussian-kernel convolution over the lattice, not a cheap Moore-neighborhood stand-in, or the window will not show up where the paper says it does. Reuse `g/`'s canvas-shelf convention for the sim; once the window is real, a `com.minomobi.lab.score` hunt for 'widest surviving window at a given neighborhood width' is a genuine, rerunnable record.
mechanism: a two-color cellular automaton where each cell may defect from its neighborhood's local majority exactly once, then freezes
text: run a grid where each cell flips to its local majority once then locks forever. at balance-point starting ratios, something emerges the smooth version never makes: a frozen labyrinth, a maze of both colors stuck against their own neighborhoods

paperTitle: A floor and a ceiling for the advancing contact angle
name: contact-band
plan:
Push a droplet's edge forward and the angle it makes with the surface -- the advancing contact angle -- should depend on how hard you push and what the surface is. Reported maxima scatter wildly across studies, 87 degrees to 147 degrees, which looks like a mess of chemistry. The paper's claim is that most of that mess is one piece of geometry: near a moving contact line, the free surface undergoes a hinged rotation, and that local wedge motion has two singular angles built in -- 90 degrees, where the hinge produces no wall shear and rotation is free, and 128.73 degrees (where tan2a = 2a), where a resonance arrests the rotation. Between them sits a band the angle cannot leave while the contact line stays quasi-steady, and a compilation of 68 real liquid-solid systems lands inside it, 87 to 119 degrees, unless the surface chemistry starts above the band or the flow gets fast enough to leave quasi-steady behind.

The toy hands you the contact line directly: drag a wedge across a surface, watch a protractor readout chase your drag speed and slam into an invisible ceiling near 128.73 degrees and a floor near 90 no matter how hard you push. Two dials let you actually break it, honestly: raise the surface's static-angle chemistry past the band, or crank drive speed into the non-quasi-steady regime -- both are the paper's real exits, not just 'push harder'. Turn one ships the wedge, the drag, and the two reference lines; the exits can be the second pass.

The hard part is not solving Navier-Stokes but reproducing the paper's closed-form local wedge kinematics honestly enough that the band holds under dragging rather than being hardcoded. Reuse `g/`'s single-canvas sim convention; the crowd can extend the paper's own 68-system table by submitting real static/advancing angle pairs for materials they have measured, live-checked against the band.
mechanism: dragging a wedge of liquid across a surface while its contact angle gets physically pinned inside a fixed band
text: drag a wedge across a surface and watch its contact angle slam into an invisible ceiling near 128.73 degrees no matter how hard you push. pure geometry: every liquid-solid system lands inside the same band, pinned between two singular angles

paperTitle: Schreier Sets of Intervals, Super-Schreier Sets, and Catalan Numbers
name: schreier-hunt
plan:
A Schreier set is a finite set of positive integers where the smallest element is at least as big as the set's size -- in effect a rule against crowding near zero: the more numbers you mark, the further out the first one has to start. The paper counts a specific shape of Schreier set: unions of exactly k 'separated' intervals, bars on the number line with real gaps between them, not touching. It proves the count of these, for bars capped at n, obeys a linear recurrence whose characteristic polynomial is (x-1)^(2k+1)(x+1)^k -- an oddly clean object for such a simple picture -- and then defines a second, 'super-Schreier' hierarchy whose counts instead obey a Fibonacci-type recurrence with a polynomial correction term. The title promises Catalan numbers turn up somewhere in the same territory; the toy does not need to reach that to be worth building.

The mechanic: a number line, and the visitor drags k separate bars onto it. Every drag gets instant feedback, a green check if the leftmost bar starts at or past the total bar-length (Schreier) and the bars do not touch (separated), red otherwise. Turn one is exactly that: single interval first, k=1, so the rule is legible with one bar, then k=2 to see 'separated' start to bite. A running tally shows, for the current cap n, how many valid configurations have been found by hand, building toward the paper's sequence before revealing it is linear-recurrent with roots at 1 and -1 -- plottable and checkable by anyone with a calculator.

The hard part is the visual metaphor carrying the whole inequality -- get the bar-and-gap picture wrong and it reads as an abstract number condition rather than a thing you can see. Reuse the `math` wing's single-file explainer convention and its record-table habit, since a claimed count here, like the Erdos rectangle toy, is trivially rerunnable by anyone.
mechanism: dragging interval bars onto a number line and getting an instant pass/fail on the Schreier condition, building toward the paper's counting sequence
text: place bars on a number line where the leftmost bar must start past the total width and bars cannot touch. each placement gets instant pass-fail feedback. build a count of valid arrangements and discover the paper's Schreier sequence -- a simple linear recurrence hiding in a visual rule

paperTitle: Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks
name: blind-boundary
plan:
Model extraction normally assumes you get more than a label back -- confidences, logits, something to gradient-climb on. The hard-label setting is meaner: query the network, get exactly one bit, nothing else, and the state of the art (Carlini et al., EUROCRYPT 2025) still recovers exact weights from that alone, in polynomial time -- it is just slow, because its dual-point clustering step runs a singular value decomposition costing O(n^2 d^3). This paper's fix is the fact worth building the toy around: in high dimensions, two random directions are already almost perpendicular to each other, essentially always -- a fact that sounds like a trick but is just what 'high-dimensional' means. Because of it, the paper swaps the expensive SVD clustering for plain inner products, making the same extraction an order of magnitude faster, and extends it from fully-connected networks to convolutional ones with max-pooling.

The toy is two rooms. Room one is pure intuition: spin up random vectors in increasing dimension and watch a live histogram of the angles between them collapse onto 90 degrees -- nobody has to trust the claim, they can watch it happen at d=2, d=20, d=200. Room two is the attack itself, toy-scale only: a black box returns one bit per query, which side of its decision boundary, on a limited budget, and you are trying to pin the boundary down well enough to match a held-out test set, scored against the budget spent.
