Turn one ships room one alone -- self-contained, no trained model needed, and it is the paper's actual mechanism, not just a hook.

The hard part, named honestly: the real ASV clustering needs a trained multi-layer net and enough queries to matter, which is a second turn's build. Reuse `human/`'s arcade-of-user-error framing for the honest-risk posture; this is offensive-security material about a published attack, so keep it toy-scale and ship the defense discussion alongside it.
mechanism: querying a black-box neural net with only yes/no answers to reconstruct its decision boundary
text: query a black box that only returns one bit -- which side of the decision boundary. pin it down well enough to beat a test set on your budget. high-dimensional vectors are nearly perpendicular, so the expensive clustering step becomes a few inner products

paperTitle: ABC: Numerical Data Collection under Local Differential Privacy without Prior Knowledge
name: domain-golf
plan:
Local differential privacy lets you learn an aggregate, an average say, from numbers nobody ever hands you in the clear: each person perturbs their own value before it leaves their device. Every standard mechanism for that needs one thing decided in advance -- the domain, the range the values could fall in. Guess too narrow and everything outside it gets clipped, silently biasing the result; guess too wide and the noise needed to cover that whole range swamps the signal. The paper's fix, ABC, has each user send their perturbed value plus one extra privatized bit -- was I clipped by the current guessed domain -- and the collector uses the aggregate of that bit-stream to widen or narrow its domain guess round by round, with a proof the estimate converges to the true range without ever having been told it.

The toy makes the visitor the collector and the crowd the dataset: ask one real question, how many browser tabs do you have open right now or similar, no login, and everyone who lands on the page contributes one privately-perturbed number. The page shows the running domain estimate physically narrowing toward the true range round by round, alongside the aggregate's error dropping, plus two ghost lines showing what a too-narrow and a too-wide fixed guess would have reported instead, wrong in opposite directions. Turn one ships the collector view against a synthetic pre-seeded crowd, a stored distribution standing in for real visitors, with the three-way comparison already live; wiring it to real submissions is the second turn.

The hard part is implementing the actual local perturbation mechanism, not a fake noise generator, so the privacy claim on the page is real, and explaining without a lecture why the collector is not allowed to just look. Reuse `scores`' worker pattern -- crowd data flowing into one small stateless endpoint, no PDS writes -- as the closest existing shape to imitate.
mechanism: collecting a private numeric statistic from a crowd whose value range you are never told in advance
text: collect private answers to a real question from a crowd -- each person sends a perturbed value, their data stays hidden. your domain guess tightens round by round as you watch the clipping pattern, converging to the true range without being told it

paperTitle: Erdős--Ko--Rado and Hilton--Milner Theorems in the Partition Lattice
name: seatmates
plan:
The paper proves an Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem for flats of the graphic matroid of K_{n+1}, which is really a theorem about partitions: take n+1 people and split them into groups (a seating chart). A rank-k flat is a chart with exactly n+1-k tables. Two charts intersect if some pair of people ends up at the same table on both charts. The paper shows that once n+1 is at least 8k, the largest possible family of pairwise-intersecting charts is the obvious one — everyone who seats a fixed pair together — a big step toward the long-conjectured n+1≥2k threshold, plus an exact answer for which two-table exception beats the star once n+1 is close to that boundary.

The mechanic: the visitor sets a headcount and a table count, then builds seating charts by dragging people into groups, adding each finished chart to a shared family. The site checks every new chart against every chart already in the family for a shared pair, and rejects it if it does not share one with all of them. The running tally sits next to the star bound so the visitor can watch how close they get.

Turn one: a single-chart builder plus the pairwise-check gauge for just two charts, before there is a running family at all — get the 'do these two share a seatmate' mechanic solid and legible first.

What's hard: presenting matroid rank as an ordinary seating chart without losing the constraint's teeth, and being honest that above the star, the general threshold is still open.

Reuse: the `math` wing's single-file conventions, `workers/scores` for the family-size record table.
mechanism: build seating charts and check them against a growing family for a shared seatmate pair
text: build seating charts where each new one must share at least one seatmate pair with all the old ones. how large a family can you grow? the paper proves once you hit a threshold, seating one specific pair together beats all other arrangements.

paperTitle: Edge-defect matrices and stability of the Kirchhoff index for complete graphs with deleted edges
name: kirchhoff
plan:
The paper gives a fast way to compute effective resistance in a complete graph with some wires cut: put every pair of n nodes on a 1-ohm wire, snip a set F of p wires, and instead of inverting the full n×n Laplacian, a p×p 'edge-defect matrix' built only from the cut wires gives exact answers for resistance between any two nodes, the total Kirchhoff index (sum of all pairwise resistances), and the spanning-tree count. It then settles the extremal question: among all ways to cut p wires, resistance is minimized and spanning trees maximized when the cut wires form a matching — no two sharing an endpoint — and it identifies the unique second-best shape too, one connected pair of cuts plus a matching on the rest.

The mechanic: a fully-wired network of n nodes on screen; the visitor clicks up to p wires to snip. The Kirchhoff index and spanning-tree count update live, computed off the small defect matrix so it stays instant as n grows. A 'beat the matching' prompt: cut any p wires, watch the numbers move, then compare against a matching of the same size — which nobody can beat.

Turn one: the wired network, the snip interaction, and the two live numbers — no scoring yet, just the sandbox that makes the invariant tangible.

What's hard: the minimum is settled, so a leaderboard chasing the best score is empty theatre. The honest crowd hook is the maximum instead — the paper never characterizes the worst p-cut, so a 'most fragile network' leaderboard is a genuine hunt rather than a race to a known answer.

Reuse: `math` wing conventions, `packages/dataviz` for the network render, `workers/scores` for the fragility leaderboard.
mechanism: snip wires from a fully-connected network and watch total resistance and spanning-tree count update live
text: wire every node to every other. snap edges and watch total resistance and tree count drop live. the paper proves one pattern of cuts beats all others. find the weirdest arrangement that gets close.

paperTitle: Residual Saturation under Pressure-Controlled Drainage
name: drainage
plan:
The paper reframes pressure-controlled drainage — squeezing the non-wetting fluid out of a porous rock — as bond percolation with trapping: raise the pressure, invade pore throats in order of increasing resistance, and some of the defending fluid gets surrounded and stuck (residual saturation) rather than pushed out. The result: residual saturation approaches a nonzero limiting value as the network grows, but it gets there slowly and predictably — the gap from the limit shrinks as a power law in system size, with exponent about 0.25 in a two-dimensional pore network and about 0.75 in three dimensions. Small 3D samples land much closer to their true answer than small 2D ones do.

The mechanic: a grid of pores and a pressure slider. Raising pressure invades pores in increasing-pressure order; some pockets of defending fluid get walled in as the front passes and stay stuck at full drainage. The visitor reads off the trapped fraction at breakthrough for their chosen grid size.

Turn one: a single fixed-size 2D grid, the slider, the invasion animation, and the trapped-fraction readout at full drainage — one run, one number.

What's hard, and where the crowd comes in: one grid is one noisy sample of the residual saturation for that size. The paper's exponent is a statement about many samples across many sizes. A later turn should let every visitor's run feed a shared scatter plot of trapped fraction against grid size, so the crowd runs the finite-size scaling study live instead of each person seeing one isolated number — a small but real Monte Carlo experiment rather than a demo.

Reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the scaling plot; canvas grid rendering, no server required for a single run.
mechanism: raise drainage pressure on a pore grid, invade it, and read off the trapped fraction at breakthrough
text: push pressure through a grid of pores and watch defending fluid get trapped in pockets as the front moves through. keep raising the slider and read how much is still trapped at full drainage.

paperTitle: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
name: driftwatch
plan:
The paper's target is a specific failure mode in AI agents: a runtime guardrail that only checks whether the current action looks safe can be walked past one small, individually reasonable step at a time, ending somewhere hazardous with no single action that ever looked wrong. Its fix, DreamGuard, keeps a running model of where the trajectory is headed and scores both the immediate action and the accumulated 'prefix risk' of everything so far, catching the drift before the last, irreversible step — at about 25 milliseconds per call, cheap enough to run on everything.

The mechanic: the visitor plays the agent, picking a short sequence of actions in a small fixed scenario — a handful of tools, one hazardous end state — trying to reach the bad outcome without ever making a single move that would, alone, be an obvious red flag. Two guardrails watch: a reactive one that only ever checks the latest action, and a prefix-aware one that tracks running trajectory risk. The visitor sees exactly where each guardrail intervenes — often the reactive guardrail lets the whole sequence through while the prefix-aware one stops it two moves from the end.

Turn one: the fixed scenario, the action picker, and the two guardrail readouts side by side — no scoring yet, just making the reactive-versus-proactive gap visible on one sequence.

What's hard: the site must not claim to reproduce DreamGuard's actual trained world model. It needs a small, honestly-labeled illustrative risk scorer built for the toy scenario, with the paper cited for the mechanism, not for the numbers on screen.

Reuse: `games`' room and scoring conventions for a 'shortest path past the proactive guard' leaderboard; `workers/scores`.
mechanism: walk a sequence of actions past a reactive guardrail and a prefix-aware one and see where each catches on
text: play an ai agent choosing moves in a scenario. each move alone seems safe, but the sequence drifts toward disaster. a guardrail checking only your latest action misses it. one tracking your full path catches the drift first.

paperTitle: Improved Upper Bound for Lindström's Unique-Sum Problem
name: unique-sum
plan: In 1969 Lindström bounded how big two subsets X and Y of the n-dimensional binary cube can be while staying a unique-sum pair: every x+y with x in X, y in Y must be recoverable back to the exact (x,y) that made it, no collisions allowed. He proved the exponential growth rate is between about 1.293 and 1.5 per dimension; nobody had moved the upper end since. This paper gets it down to about 1.4884, the first strict improvement in over fifty years, via a coordinate-projection trick that builds a smaller unique-sum system from a larger one. The toy is a builder: fix n, then let the visitor add binary vectors to X and Y one at a time. Every addition is checked live against every existing pair — a live sum table — and the moment two different (x,y) pairs would produce the same sum, that vector is rejected with the colliding pair highlighted. The score is |X|*|Y|; the visitor is trying to beat 1.4884^n, or more realistically, beat the current record submitted for that n. Turn one: render the checker for small n (say n=6, 64 vectors), let a visitor build a pair by clicking vectors into X or Y, show the running product and reject collisions. What's hard: making the collision check feel instant and legible at larger n (it's O(|X||Y|) naively, needs a hash-set of sums, not a re-scan) and picking a default n small enough to be winnable by hand but large enough that beating the record isn't trivial. Reuse: the math wing's (math.mino.mobi) single-file explainer conventions, workers/scores for a per-n record table — verification is free, since anyone can recompute a claimed pair's sums in microseconds, so cheating is structurally impossible, same shape as the Erdős rectangle-area leaderboard.
mechanism: build two binary-vector sets by hand while a live sum-collision checker rejects anything that breaks uniqueness, chasing a per-n record
text: click binary vectors into two sets while a live checker rejects collisions. your score is the product of their sizes. lindström bounded how big this can grow, and nobody improved the upper bound for fifty years — until this paper.

paperTitle: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
name: trust-promotion
plan: Self-evolving agent systems distill their own past trajectories into reusable 'skills' that later get trusted as instructions — untrusted experience quietly becoming trusted policy. This paper's attack, PoisonedEvolution, shows that a black-box contributor who can only submit ordinary-looking trajectory evidence (no access to the private pool, no edit rights) can still get a target behavior promoted into the trusted skill bank, because promotion checks for causal usefulness, recurrence, and generalizability rather than provenance. At 10% attacker support across six evolvers, 546 of 600 trials succeeded; three consistent records in a 30-record batch were enough, where one record alone was far weaker. The toy hands the visitor the attacker's exact constraint: a fixed submission budget (say 5 records out of a 30-record batch you don't otherwise control) to plant one target behavior into a simulated skill bank, where a promotion checker scores each candidate skill on recurrence, causal framing, and domain alignment — visible as three meters the visitor is implicitly optimizing against without being told the weights. Turn one: ship the promotion checker as a static scoring function, a batch of 25 decoy records already in place, and a form to author your 5 records; show whether the skill got promoted and which meter carried it. What's hard: making the scoring function faithful to the paper's three named factors (recurrence, causal framing, domain-aligned encoding) without turning it into an opaque black box — the visitor should be able to learn the mechanism by probing it, which means the meters need to react legibly to specific wording choices, not just totals. Reuse: human/'s arcade-of-user-error framing and its posture on building the exhibit as the thing it critiques; workers/scores for a leaderboard on fewest records needed to force promotion, which is a real search over the same space PoisonedEvolution's attacker occupies.
mechanism: spend a small budget of crafted evidence records trying to get a target behavior promoted past a recurrence/causality/alignment scorer into a trusted skill bank
text: author five false records out of thirty, trying to get a malicious behavior promoted. the checker scores on recurrence, causal framing, and alignment — you see the three meters but not their weights. at 10% support, 91% of attacks succeeded.

paperTitle: A Formation-Stage Bottleneck for Exomoons around Close-in Rocky Planets
name: moonbottleneck
plan: Giant impacts between rocky planets are how big moons are thought to form — debris flung into orbit settles into a disk that clumps into a moon. This paper simulates those impacts for planets close to their star (orbital periods 1-300 days) and finds the star itself is the problem: tidal and Coriolis forces from being close-in strip the circumplanetary disk before it can consolidate. Ultra-short-period impacts leave essentially no surviving disk at all; even at 10 days the disk that survives is radially truncated and badly depleted; high impact velocity (which close-in planets get almost for free) makes it worse; retrograde impacts claw back a little disk mass but not much. So there's a real, quantified bottleneck: moons should get rarer as planets sit closer to their star, for formation-stage reasons that have nothing to do with a moon surviving once formed. The toy is a mission-planner: the visitor sets orbital period and impact geometry (impact velocity within the paper's range, prograde vs retrograde) for a hypothetical giant impact, and a simplified surrogate model (fit to the paper's reported trend, not the real N-body code) reports whether a disk survives and how depleted it is, visualized as a thin ring shrinking or vanishing around the planet. Turn one: the slider-and-ring page alone, with the surrogate model and a clear label that it's a fit to the paper's qualitative trend, not a re-run of the simulation. What's hard: being honest about that gap — there's no closed-form disk-mass formula in the abstract, so the surrogate has to be built and clearly flagged as approximate, or the toy quietly claims precision the paper doesn't offer. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the period-vs-disk-mass chart; workers/scores for a record table of visitor-found configurations that beat the bottleneck (most disk mass retained at a given period), verifiable because the surrogate is deterministic.
mechanism: set orbital period and impact geometry for a giant impact and watch a surrogate model show whether a moon-forming disk survives the star's tidal stripping
text: set orbital period and impact geometry for a giant impact and watch the circumplanetary disk survive or vanish in the star's tidal grip. the model is a trend-fitted surrogate, not a full simulation. can you find the sweet spot where moons form?

paperTitle: Sun-Facing Diffractive Sail H-Reversal Trajectory: Theoretical Feasibility, Design Strategies, and Applications
name: sail-reversal
plan: Kinetic asteroid deflection needs the impactor moving fast and the mission launched quickly. A solar sail can build up speed for free using sunlight, but the classic maneuver for reversing its angular momentum toward a head-on hit (H-reversal) forces a reflective sail into high cone angles where it barely catches any sunlight. This paper swaps in a diffractive sail — one that bends light rather than bouncing it — and shows that facing it toward the sun the whole time avoids that penalty. Against an Apophis-style impact scenario, a one-stage diffraction-angle strategy beats a reflective sail by 21% more impact velocity and 35% less mission duration; a two-stage strategy (switching the diffraction angle partway through) adds another 9 km/s on top of that. The toy hands the visitor the mission designer's actual choice: pick one-stage or two-stage, then tune the diffraction angle(s) within the paper's feasible range (mapped by their hodograph method), and watch a simplified trajectory reach a target asteroid, reporting impact velocity and mission duration against the reflective-sail baseline. Turn one: the one-stage case only — a single angle slider, a 2D trajectory arc from Earth-orbit to intercept, and the two output numbers next to the RS baseline so the 21%/35% gap is visible immediately. What's hard: the real feasibility region comes from a hodograph analysis this toy can't reproduce exactly, so the client-side trajectory model has to be a deliberately simplified two-body approximation with the paper's specific numbers used as calibration/anchor points, not a live orbital solver — flag that plainly rather than implying full physical fidelity. Reuse: tjs/'s three.js conventions for the trajectory arc, packages/dataviz for the velocity/duration comparison chart, workers/scores for a leaderboard ranking visitor-found angle combinations on the joint impact-velocity/duration trade-off.
mechanism: tune a diffractive sail's diffraction-angle strategy and watch a simplified trajectory sim report impact velocity and mission duration against a reflective-sail baseline
text: tune a diffractive sail's angle strategy and watch it intercept an asteroid. the model is a simplified two-body approximation anchored to the paper, not a full orbital sim. can you beat the reflective sail's impact velocity and mission time?

paperTitle: On traces of randomly rolling polytopes
name: tumble
text: roll a 3d polytope across a plane and watch its vertices trace a path. if the trace ever loops back on itself, it will eventually cover the entire space with no gaps. play on a shared grid and watch the crowd complete what no single roll could
plan:
The paper studies a convex 3D polytope resting on a face on a plane; at each step it tips over a random edge of its current face until the next face lands flat. The trace is every point ever touched by a vertex as this repeats. The result: if that trace ever revisits a bounded region (has a convergent subsequence) then, with probability one, it eventually becomes dense in the plane — no partial coverage, no permanent gaps, just full or unbounded. It settles a conjecture of Hegyvari.

The mechanic: pick a polytope (a regular tetrahedron for turn one, since every face is the same triangle and the roll is unambiguous), set it flat on a plane view, and roll it — one edge-tip per click or auto-roll. Every vertex contact leaves a mark. Turn one ships a single visitor's tetrahedron rolling on their own canvas, with a coarse grid overlay counting new versus revisited cells, so you can watch the frontier either escape outward or start doubling back on itself.

The hard part is the kinematics: correctly tracking the polytope's 3D orientation and the plane-position of its footprint as it tips over an edge (a standard but fiddly unfolding computation), and choosing polytopes where the paper's hypothesis is plausible to witness live rather than ones whose trace visibly runs off to infinity for the whole session.

Where it earns a crowd: a shared Durable Object canvas per polytope, where every visitor's rolls land on the same grid. The dense-filling theorem becomes something the crowd visibly completes together — the more people roll the same shape, the fewer empty cells remain, until the last stubborn holes get filled by whoever happens to roll through them.

Reuse: games/'s Durable Object room pattern for the shared canvas, tjs for the 3D polytope render, workers/scores if a cells-filled record is worth keeping.
mechanism: roll a 3D polytope edge-over-edge and accumulate its vertex trace on a shared grid

paperTitle: A superlogarithmic saving for Oddtown modulo composite numbers
name: oddtown
text: build a family of sets under a constraint on their sizes and pairwise intersections. you can never beat n sets, the math says. yet with different divisibility rules you can reach 2n. the textbook ceiling cracks
plan:
Oddtown is a classic: build a family of subsets of {1,...,n} where every set has odd size but every pair intersects in an even number of elements, and you can never beat n sets — a one-line linear-algebra bound. This paper looks at what happens when odd/even is replaced by divisible-by-ell for composite ell, and the classic bound of n turns out to be beatable: with ell having two distinct prime factors (say ell=6), you can get close to 2n sets — no member's size divisible by 6, but every pairwise intersection is. The paper's new result trims the best known ceiling on how close to 2n you can get by a small amount, on the order of log n times log log n, and the trim leans on the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture, a major additive-combinatorics theorem proved only in 2023.

The mechanic: fix ell=6 and a small n (20-30). A grid of toggle cells, elements across the top, one row per set you're building. As you add a set, the page instantly flags every prior pair whose intersection size isn't divisible by 6 — a live constraint-violation highlighter, not a submit-and-fail form. Your score is how many valid sets you're holding at once; reference lines at n and at 2n show where you stand.

Turn one ships exactly that for ell=6: the grid, the live pairwise checker, and the two reference lines. Other ell values and a visible how-close-did-you-get gap are later work.

The hard part is making the constraint-checking read as a puzzle to solve rather than a spreadsheet to debug — the highlighter has to make a conflict feel local and fixable, not like a rejected form.

Reuse: the math wing's single-file conventions for the page itself; workers/scores for the record table, since a valid family is trivially re-checkable and cheating is arithmetically impossible.
mechanism: build a family of subsets under a divisibility constraint on sizes and pairwise intersections, racing a known ceiling

paperTitle: PromptShield Home: Ambient Multimodal Prompt Injection Defense for Smart-Home Agents
name: overhear
text: five smart-home scenarios: a tv shouting commands, a false alarm, a real voice in noise. for each pick which gatekeeper to trust—block everything, ask an ai, or trust the crowd vote. one always refuses (including real commands), the other trusts everything (including fakes). which wins this round
plan:
The paper benchmarks smart-home agents against ambient impostor commands — a TV that says unlock the door, a health monitor's false alarm, a real command lost in a noisy room — and scores three kinds of gatekeeper: plain detectors, a single vision-plus-audio AI, and multi-agent voting panels. The headline number is a trap: always blocking scores 82% accuracy, because true commands are rare in the test set, so raw accuracy is meaningless. The real finding is that detectors and AI models fail in opposite, non-overlapping ways — detectors act on everything, including impostors; AI models over-refuse, including real emergencies — and an oracle that always picked whichever layer was right for that scenario would hit 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single fixed layer. Nobody gets to be that oracle; that 17.6-point gap is the cost of committing to one architecture.

The mechanic: you're handed a short scenario transcript — TV audio, a mixed-occupancy household, a monitor chirp — and you pick which gatekeeper persona to trust for it: block-everything, cautious AI, or crowd vote. Turn one ships a fixed battery of five hand-written scenarios, one per benchmark category, with immediate reveal of the ground truth and a running tally against the 82% trap, the 76.5% single-layer line, and the 94.1% oracle ceiling as fixed reference marks.

The hard part is writing scenarios that embody each failure mode honestly without pretending to reproduce the paper's real dataset or per-item numbers — the reference lines are the paper's aggregates, not verdicts on these five scenarios.

Where the crowd matters: replace the crowd-vote persona with real visitor votes per scenario, literally instantiating the paper's own multi-agent-voting layer and measuring the room's collective accuracy against the same ceiling.

Reuse: human/'s exhibit framing and copy conventions; games/ for a voting room; workers/scores for the room's running accuracy.
mechanism: pick which gatekeeper (or crowd vote) to trust per ambient smart-home scenario, scored against an oracle ceiling

paperTitle: Control of collective activity to crystallize an oscillator gas
name: buzz
text: tune particle density and collision kick. particles that sit and buzz in place solo suddenly swarm into an active gas when crowded together. the motion comes entirely from their collisions alone, with no particle self-propelled. push harder and they crystallize
plan:
Motility-induced phase separation is the usual active-matter story: crowding suppresses movement, so activity and density are negatively coupled and the system splits into a dense static clump and a dilute active gas. This paper flips the sign: individually non-motile self-sustained oscillators, driven by contact-charge electrophoresis rather than self-propulsion, spontaneously form an active gas purely because their collisions are super-elastic — a collision injects more kinetic energy than it removes — so more crowding means more collisions means more injected activity, a positive feedback loop, with no motility in any single particle. Tuning that same feedback the other way lets the crowd crystallize instead.

The mechanic: a 2D canvas of dots that individually just sit and buzz in place, no self-propulsion. Two dials: particle count (density) and a collision-kick strength (the super-elastic factor). Below a threshold density, nothing happens — dots stay quiet. Cross it and the collisions start feeding each other, and the whole canvas turns into a jittering gas with no single particle doing anything but bouncing off its neighbours. Push the kick strength down instead and the same crowd locks into a lattice.

Turn one ships the two dials and the canvas with the binary quiet-versus-buzzing transition visible in real time; crystallization is a stretch goal once the gas phase is convincing.

The hard part is tuning the collision rule so the transition is a genuine emergent threshold and not just more-density-means-more-motion by construction — the paper's whole point is that no particle is self-propelled, so the buzzing has to come entirely from the collision rule.

Reuse: g/'s WebGPU particle-simulation shelf for the canvas and physics loop; workers/scores for a recipe leaderboard — density and kick-strength pairs that crystallize fastest, checkable by re-running the same seeded simulation.
mechanism: tune particle density and collision-kick strength and watch non-motile particles turn into a buzzing gas or a crystal

paperTitle: "Allow" to Achieve, Over-Privileged Inadvertently: The Unintended Cost of Task-Completion-Driven Pop-up Decisions in Mobile GUI Agents
name: over-privileged
plan: The paper injects Android permission popups into real mobile GUI-agent tasks and measures whether four frontier multimodal LLMs grant only what the task needs. The standout number: under the same Calendar task, changing nothing but the requesting app's name from Calendar to PiMusic drops grants from 26/32 to 0/32 — an 'App-Trust Bias' the paper separates from a second effect, 'Task-Prior Override', where holding the popup fixed and changing the task context also swings the decision. The toy puts the visitor in the agent's seat: a short mobile task (book a ride, add an event) runs as a strip of screenshots, and partway through a permission popup interrupts with a requester name, an icon, and a permission ask. Grant or deny, then move on. Turn one ships a single scenario with a single popup and an immediate reveal — was this permission needed for the stated task, per the paper's four-level relevance/risk framework — plus one repeat of the identical popup under a swapped requester name, so the visitor watches their own answer flip without noticing why until it's shown. The hard part is doing this honestly: the swap has to be the *only* variable, staged like the paper's controlled intervention, or the reveal is cheap theater instead of the paper's actual finding. Score as a 'permission literacy' rate and publish it alongside the four evaluated models' rates, so a human baseline exists where the paper has none. Reuse `human/`'s exhibit framing (this is exactly its shape: rig a game with the visitor's own trust heuristics), `workers/scores` for the leaderboard, and simple screenshot-strip UI — no agent model needed client-side, the task flow can be scripted.
mechanism: grant/deny decisions on staged permission popups, scored against a paper-derived relevance rubric
text: you grant permission popups in short mobile tasks. the same permission, same task, but change the requesting app's name and you flip your answer without noticing. watch yourself fall for app-trust bias

paperTitle: A Gap in the 42-Queue Layout Algorithm for Planar Graphs
name: queue-gap
plan: A queue layout fixes a left-to-right order of a graph's vertices and sorts its edges into 'queues' such that no two edges in the same queue nest (one edge's interval strictly containing another's, read along that order) — the nesting-forbidden counterpart to a book embedding's crossing-forbidden pages. The queue number is the fewest queues any order can achieve. For planar graphs the standing proof gives at most 49; a 2023 paper claimed a cleverer vertex-reordering trick pushes that down to 42. This note finds a gap in that argument — one step assumes a choice exists that isn't guaranteed to — so the proven bound for planar graphs, as of this week, is back to 49, with the true number still open. The toy is the puzzle underneath the dispute: hand the visitor a small planar graph, let them drag vertices into an order and drag edges into colored queues, and flag any nesting violation live. Turn one ships one fixed small graph (a maximal planar triangulation with ~8-10 vertices is enough to make queue choice non-trivial), the order-and-color interaction, live nesting checks, and a queue count. The hard part is the UI for 'nesting' — edges have to render as arcs above the vertex line so a nest is visually obvious, or the rule feels arbitrary. The crowd angle is real and unusual: because the algorithmic route to 42 just broke, the actual minimum queue number of even small planar graphs is publicly unsettled, so a leaderboard of best (fewest-queue) layouts found per graph, with instant verification of any submitted layout, is a genuine record table rather than a decorative one. Reuse `erdos/`'s and the math wing's single-file explainer conventions and `workers/scores` for the record table.
mechanism: drag vertices into an order and edges into queues, minimizing queues with no two edges in a queue nesting
text: place graph vertices on a line, drag edges into colored queues with no nesting allowed in each. a 2023 proof claimed 42 queues always work for planar graphs. last week someone found a gap in the proof

paperTitle: Hydrodynamic description of proliferating active matter
name: brownian-bugs
plan: The paper derives a continuum theory for particles that are born, compete locally, and die — no rule to steer toward neighbors, no alignment force at all — and applies it to the 'Active Brownian Bug' model. The surprising result: flocking-like coherent motion still emerges, produced entirely by the interaction of birth, death, and nonlocal competition. Linear stability analysis finds two distinct routes to structure — a Turing instability giving stationary periodic clusters, and a Hopf instability giving a coherently propagating flock — with thresholds the paper checks against simulation. The toy is a birth-death particle field the visitor tunes with two dials: proliferation rate and the range/strength of local competition (crowding pressure that kills nearby kin). No alignment code exists anywhere in the simulation, which is the point. Turn one ships the particle field itself — spawn, compete, die, on a canvas, dense enough to see texture — with the two dials and a live visual: uniform haze, frozen polka-dot clusters, or a moving swarm, so the regime is legible without reading a number. A later turn adds the phase map, plotting where the visitor's runs land relative to the paper's analytic Turing/Hopf boundaries, shown as reference lines rather than a claimed reproduction (a browser sim runs a far smaller population than the paper's stability analysis assumes). The hard part is tuning the competition kernel so all three regimes are actually reachable inside a comfortable slider range — too narrow a window and the toy is just noise or just a blob. Crowd angle: visitors bookmark parameter settings that produced a striking regime into a shared gallery, and gallery points overlaid on the phase map turn into a crowd-built empirical boundary, `fluoddity/`-style. Reuse `polis/`/`civ/` agent-simulation machinery, `packages/dataviz/` for the phase diagram, and `workers/scores` or a lightweight gallery store for submissions.
mechanism: tune proliferation and competition dials on a birth-death particle field and watch flocking emerge with no alignment rule
text: tune proliferation and competition pressure on particles with zero steering rules. flocking emerges and moves coherently. no alignment code anywhere — swarms self-organize from just birth, death, and crowding

paperTitle: Checked-In Secret Detection: Strings Are All You Need
name: barestrings
plan: The paper builds Secretron, a detector that finds hardcoded secrets in committed source code by looking almost entirely at the string literal itself rather than the surrounding code — narrowing context to 33.2% of what prior context-aware tools use still preserves over 80% of the semantic signal, and the resulting tool hit 98.74% F1 and found 48 previously unknown live secrets across 26 real applications. The counterintuitive result is that the string alone, stripped of the code around it, already carries most of the tell. The toy strips even further: the visitor sees only a bare string — no filename, no variable name, no surrounding line — and calls it secret or not. A running scoreboard compares the visitor's accuracy to Secretron's reported F1 on the same task, and to a naive regex baseline. Turn one ships one static page: a curated deck of safe example strings (synthetic look-alikes and disclosed, defanged samples — never a real credential), a yes/no control, and a running accuracy tally against the two reference numbers. What's hard: sourcing a deck that's honest about the paper's task without shipping anything that is itself a working secret, and picking near-miss distractors (API-key-shaped UUIDs, base64 config blobs) so the game isn't trivially easy — easy strings would misrepresent the paper's difficulty. What to reuse: human/'s bias-arcade framing for a game about a person's own intuition being tested, workers/scores for a crowd accuracy distribution (how good are people at this, actually?), and a note on the page that this is a detection aid, not a substitute for secret-scanning in CI.
mechanism: classify a bare string as secret-or-not with zero surrounding code context, scored against the paper's model
text: call bare strings as secret or not, no variable names or context — strings alone carry 80% of what context-aware detectors use to find secrets — guess against a model that hit 98.7% accuracy

paperTitle: Performance of radio-based detection to operational monitoring M5+ class solar flares
name: flarewatch
plan: Soft X-ray flux is the standard way to catch a major (M5+) solar flare early, but the sensor has to be in space. This paper asks whether ground radio alone can substitute, training a simple regularized logistic model on two years of GOES-16 and Radio Solar Telescope Network data. At 8800 MHz it works, but only partially: 53% precision and 65% recall, meaning roughly a third of major flares are missed, with true positives appearing 3-4 minutes before the X-ray threshold is crossed. That's a real, unglamorous operating point — better than nothing, not a solved problem — and it's the whole toy. The visitor is a ground-station operator watching a scrolling 8800 MHz flux trace (drawn from real archived GOES/RSTN windows around known flare and non-flare periods) and has one button: call it. Calling early and right scores a win with the paper's lead time; calling on a rise that fizzles is a false alarm; missing a real one is a miss. Turn one ships one fixed trace, the call button, and a scoreboard reporting the visitor's own precision/recall next to the paper's 53%/65% for direct comparison. What's hard: picking and trimming real archived windows (or clearly-labeled synthetic stand-ins built to match the paper's reported signal shape) so the task is genuinely as ambiguous as 53%/65% implies, not trivially obvious or trivially noise. What to reuse: workers/scores for an aggregate crowd precision/recall that can be tracked against the model's over time, and a plain honest-risk note that this is a monitoring aid for radar/radio disruption, not a flare-prediction claim beyond what the paper measured.
mechanism: call flare-or-not on a scrolling radio flux trace, scored for precision/recall/lead time against the paper's model
text: watch a radio flux trace scroll past and call when a solar flare arrives — ground-only radio gets 53% precision, 65% recall — better than nothing, far from solved — watch how hard this job actually is

paperTitle: On the dimensions of correlated equilibrium polytopes of generic games
name: collude
plan: A correlated equilibrium is a joint probability distribution over outcomes that a referee could recommend to two players — one per player, privately — such that neither wants to deviate once they see their own recommendation. For any fixed game, the set of all such distributions is a polytope sitting inside the simplex of joint outcome probabilities, and for a 2x2 game with four outcomes that polytope lives in a tetrahedron you can actually draw. The paper's result: under a genericity condition, whenever that polytope fails to fill the whole simplex, there's always some subgame — drop a strategy, restrict to fewer options — whose correlated equilibrium polytope is an exact affine copy of the original, settling a 2024 conjecture. The toy: the visitor sets the four payoffs of a 2x2 bimatrix game with sliders, and watches the correlated equilibrium polytope render live as a solid inside the outcome tetrahedron, along with its computed dimension. The hunt is to find payoffs where the polytope degenerates below full dimension, then find the smaller subgame the paper promises will match it exactly — checkable instantly by rendering that subgame's own polytope alongside. Turn one ships the four sliders, the live polytope render in the tetrahedron, and the dimension readout; the subgame-matching hunt is the next turn. What's hard: computing the polytope's vertices from payoffs correctly (linear programming over correlated-equilibrium incentive constraints) and rendering a possibly-degenerate 3D solid without it looking like a rendering bug rather than a real result. What to reuse: math.mino.mobi's (geometry/) single-file explainer conventions and existing polytope/simplex rendering approach if one exists there, workers/scores for a record of found-degenerate payoff configurations.
mechanism: tune a 2x2 game's payoffs and watch its correlated-equilibrium polytope render and change dimension live
text: tune payoffs on a 2x2 game and watch its correlated-equilibrium polytope shift and change dimension — degenerate polytopes always have a matching subgame — hunt for the subgame pairs yourself

paperTitle: Revisiting Channel Effectiveness: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation with Primitive Visual Stimuli
name: pop-out
plan:
The paper runs crowdsourced trials on seven chart-encoding channels — position, length, tilt, area, curvature, luminance, saturation — across four separate perceptual tasks: magnitude-estimation accuracy, discriminability, separability, and preattentive pop-out detection. The finding worth building around is a dissociation: length has top-tier magnitude accuracy but only moderate pop-out detection, while area has poor magnitude accuracy yet the highest pop-out detection rate of any channel tested. Accurate and fast are not the same skill, and which channel wins depends entirely on which one you need.

The mechanic: the visitor takes the two tests themselves. A pop-out test — a grid of marks, one item different on some channel, click it as fast as possible — and a magnitude test — two marks, click the bigger one, timed and scored for accuracy. Turn one ships both tests but restricted to exactly the two channels the paper's dissociation is about, length and area: run the pop-out grid for each, run the magnitude comparison for each, then show the visitor their own four numbers side by side so they feel the mismatch the paper found in aggregate, on their own reflexes, before any explanation of why.

The hard part is generating fair 'primitive' stimuli per channel — matched sizes, positions, and value ranges with no chart scaffolding to lean on — and in-browser reaction-time measurement is noisy, so it needs enough trials per channel to mean anything, with an honest note that a laptop test isn't the paper's controlled rig.

Reuse: `human/`'s exhibit framing and perceptual-test conventions; `workers/scores` for a per-channel, per-task leaderboard, so the crowd's pooled trials become a live version of the paper's ranking chart — and enough data to notice if a channel behaves differently from what the paper reports.
mechanism: timed click-the-odd-one-out and click-the-bigger-one trials, scored per visual channel
text: spot the different mark in a grid as fast as you can. judge which shape is bigger. one visual channel makes you fast, another accurate. they're different skills

paperTitle: A new look at some aspects of one-dimensional random sequential adsorption and its continuum limit
name: row-jam
plan:
Random sequential adsorption, one-dimensional version: a row of n molecules, and at each step you bond a uniformly random available adjacent k-tuple, removing it from play, until no k-tuple fits anywhere — a jammed row. This paper's new contribution is the two-species version of that process: run it with two tuple sizes k1 < k2 competing for the same row at once, each step drawing uniformly among every currently-available k1-tuple and k2-tuple position regardless of species, and derives explicit formulas for what share of the row each size claims, including the limiting behaviour as k2 grows with k1 fixed. A second result shows that the gaps left between bonded blocks, once rescaled by k, converge as k grows to the exact gap distribution already known for the continuous analogue of this process — cars parking at random along a line.

The mechanic: set k1 and k2, hit run, and watch a row of cells fill live — k1-tuples one colour, k2-tuples another — bonding at random until jammed, with two running counters tracking each species' claimed share.

Turn one: one canvas, two sliders (2–8), a run button that animates the process to completion, and on finish a stacked bar of the final split plus a histogram of the gap sizes between blocks. No server, no auth, entirely client-side.

What's hard: the sampling has to be genuinely uniform over every available tuple of either size at each step, not alternating turns between species by convention — get that wrong and the animation stops being the process the paper actually defines.

Reuse: `g/`'s canvas-simulation-per-page gallery convention; `workers/scores` not as a competition but as a shared running tally — every finished run adds its gap sizes to a public histogram, so pooled visitor runs sharpen toward the paper's limiting gap curve faster than any single browser tab could alone.
mechanism: two competing tuple sizes bond a shared row via random sequential adsorption until jammed
text: watch two tuple sizes fill a row by bonding at random. when they jam, their split is deterministic—one always claims more than the other

paperTitle: A Two-Player Zero Forcing Game
name: zeroforce
text: two players plant seeds and force color spreads on a graph, using as few as possible. whoever colors the whole graph with fewer seeds wins. paths and cycles are solved exactly. you never need more than twice the single-player minimum
plan: The paper turns zero forcing — the rule that a coloured vertex with exactly one white neighbour forces that neighbour to take its colour — into a competitive game. Alice and Bob alternate turns, each either planting a new seed of their own colour on a white vertex or firing a legal force, and each is trying to finish the graph having used as few seeds of their own colour as possible. A force-preservation rule stops a player wasting a turn purely to spitefully block a force the opponent had already locked in. The paper pins the resulting number Z_g(G) down exactly for paths, cycles, stars, complete and complete bipartite graphs, characterizes when it equals 2, and — by brute force through order nine — finds Z_g(G) never exceeds twice the ordinary zero forcing number, with no proof that this holds beyond nine vertices. The mechanic: two players share a graph, click white vertices to seed or coloured ones to force, and watch colour spread until the graph is full; final score is each player's own seed count, lower wins. Turn one ships human-vs-human pass-and-play on a path or cycle (both solved exactly in the paper), correct legality including force-preservation, and a scoreboard comparing seeds used to the paper's known Z_g value for that shape. What's hard: the paper's optimal play is a set-valued backward induction, not a simple bot, so turn one deliberately skips an AI opponent. The honest crowd hook is real: whether the ≤2·Z(G) bound survives past order nine is unverified, so let players submit any graph, play it out, and log seed totals against the bound — a live, growing test bank the paper's own computation stopped short of. Reuse: `games` for rooms and pass-and-play, `scores` for per-graph seed leaderboards.
mechanism: alternating seed-or-force turns on a graph, each player minimizing their own colour's seed count

paperTitle: Arranging convex bodies for maximum intersection volume: the sharp efficiency of centroid alignment
name: centroid
text: drag convex shapes to maximize their overlap. the game shows your score, the lazy centroid-align baseline, and the true optimal. centroid-align always captures at least 4/9 of optimal—a decades-old question now closed. the bound is tight and unattained
plan: Given several convex shapes, you want to slide them (translate only, no rotating or resizing) to maximize the area their overlap shares. The lazy solution is to just centre every shape's centroid at the origin and stop — no search at all. The paper proves this lazy strategy is never worse than a fixed fraction of the true best overlap: it always captures strictly more than (2/(n+1))^n of optimal, and that constant is sharp, approached but never attained by a family of cones over disks arranged around a sphere. For two convex shapes in the plane this pins the constant at exactly 4/9, closing a question open since 1996 (the old bounds were 9/25 as a guarantee and 4/9 as the worst known example — this paper proves 4/9 is the true floor). The mechanic: the visitor gets two draggable convex polygons and a live readout of three numbers — overlap achieved by hand, overlap the lazy centroid-align would have gotten for free, and the true optimum — turning the drag into a race against a strategy that requires no thought at all. A second mode hands over the paper's actual worst-case cone-over-disk family with its parameters exposed as sliders, and challenges the visitor to push the centroid-aligned overlap fraction down toward 4/9, watching it approach the floor without ever touching it — the infimum is proven unattained, which is the strangest part of the result and worth making visible rather than stated. Turn one ships the two-shape drag game with live polygon-overlap computation and the centroid/optimal benchmarks on screen; the infimum-chasing mode is the natural next turn. What's hard: computing the true optimum fast enough for live feedback, which turn one handles by keeping vertex counts small. Reuse: the `math` wing's single-file conventions, `scores` for closest-approach-to-4/9 records.
mechanism: drag convex shapes to maximize shared overlap, scored against the centroid-aligned baseline and the true optimum

paperTitle: Information and Locality in Cayley Graphs
name: window
text: you're dropped on a vertex, see colors in your local window, and click to guess your position. how many colors guarantee any vertex is uniquely pinned. same graph needs 2 colors for any shape, 4 when windows must stay connected
plan: A de Bruijn sequence is a cyclic string where every window of k symbols appears exactly once, so reading any window tells you precisely where you are in the cycle. This paper generalizes that idea from cycles to Cayley graphs of arbitrary groups: colour every generator with one of q colours, and ask how few colours guarantee that the pattern of colours in some local window around you always identifies your exact vertex, never leaving two spots looking alike. Three variants differ only in how much you're allowed to see — sep_q lets the window be any shape, csep_q requires it to be a connected patch that includes you, and chi_1 fixes the window to just your immediate neighbours and asks only for the colour count. Concrete numbers from the paper: a family of dihedral-type groups needs exactly d+1 colours under the unrestricted rule; a specific 14-vertex dihedral example needs only 2 colours if the window can be any shape but jumps to 4 once it must be connected — the same graph, two different honest answers; the 60-element icosahedral group A5 can be pinpointed from 3 immediate neighbours using 3 colours, and the 168-element PSL_2(F_7) (symmetry group of the Klein quartic) needs 4, both hitting the theoretical minimum for their size. The mechanic: the visitor is dropped at a random vertex of a shown graph, sees only the colours within their allowed window, and clicks where on the full map they think they're standing; a toggle switches between the any-shape and connected-window rules on the same graph to make the sep/csep gap visible directly. Turn one renders the 14-vertex example with a correct colouring from the paper, both window rules, and a right/wrong scored guess. What's hard: colourings for groups beyond the paper's examples are genuinely uncomputed, so the crowd hook is real — let visitors submit a colouring for a new group and verify uniqueness instantly, building a public record table past what the paper covers. Reuse: `math` wing conventions, `scores` for the record table.
mechanism: identify your exact position on a symmetric graph from only the colours visible in your local window

paperTitle: Iterated Distinct Absolute Differences of Integer Compositions
name: diffdepth
plan:
The paper: take a composition of n (an ordered sequence of positive integers summing to n), replace it with the sequence of consecutive absolute differences, and continue only if every difference is nonzero and all differences are distinct — you may then permute them in any order before repeating. The 'depth' is the longest chain of survivable rounds. The paper finds a(n), the smallest integer admitting a depth-n composition: a(n) = n+1+ceil(n(n+1)/4)+floor(n/2), shows every larger integer also reaches depth n, and counts (via four formulas mod 4) exactly how many minimal compositions achieve it.

The mechanic: the visitor is handed a target sum and builds a composition by typing or dragging blocks that must add to it. The site takes consecutive differences, ends the run if anything repeats or hits zero, and otherwise hands the surviving differences back as tiles the visitor reorders before the next round runs — that permutation choice is the actual game, since different orderings of the same multiset survive different numbers of rounds.

Turn one: fix a modest target sum, ship the composition builder, one round of difference-taking with a visible arrow diagram, the permutation-tile step, and a depth counter that compares your result against a(n) for the smallest n your sum could theoretically reach.

The hard part: proving the permutation choice matters requires letting people replay the same differences in a different order and watch the outcome diverge — a static walkthrough would make it feel arbitrary rather than chosen.

Reuse: the `math` wing's single-page, no-build convention; `scores` for a best-depth-per-target-sum table.
mechanism: build an integer composition, then choose how to permute its consecutive differences each round, to survive as many rounds as possible
text: build a sequence that adds to a target. work out the differences between each pair. now shuffle them and do it again. when a difference repeats or zeros, you stop. how many times can you survive? the order you pick changes everything

paperTitle: The maximum volume polytope with nine vertices inscribed in the sphere
name: maxvol
plan:
The paper resolves N=9 in a decades-old family of problems: of all convex polyhedra with nine vertices on the unit sphere, which has the greatest volume? Answer, settled here: 3*sqrt(2*sqrt(3)-3), achieved uniquely up to rotation by a triaugmented triangular prism of a specific determined shape — reached by narrowing 2,606 combinatorial vertex-arrangements to 50 simplicial ones, then to 5, by showing a maximizer can have no degree-3 vertex.

The mechanic: nine draggable points live on a rendered sphere; the site computes the convex hull of wherever they currently sit and reports its volume live, alongside a percentage of the way to the settled record. Getting within rounding of the record by hand, without being told the shape, is the game — and the site can confirm you found it, up to rotation, rather than just landed close.

Turn one: a three.js sphere with nine draggable handles, a live convex-hull volume readout, and the record value shown next to it so the gap is visible from the first drag. No leaderboard yet — that follows once dragging and hull volume actually work.

The hard part: robust convex-hull volume for a live-dragged point set, including near-degenerate and coplanar configurations mid-drag, computed client-side without a heavy geometry library.

Reuse: three.js, already used in `tjs/` and `g/`; the `math` wing's page conventions for the write-up; `scores` for a per-N leaderboard once N moves past nine into the open cases, where 'best volume anyone's found' is a real, currently unknown number.
mechanism: drag vertices around a sphere and watch the convex hull's volume update live against the settled record
text: drag nine points around a sphere to build a solid. watch its volume update against the record — the biggest any nine-point shape on a sphere can be. only one shape achieves it. how close can you get without being told what it is

paperTitle: Cross-cultural evaluation of taste-sound correspondences in AI-generated music
name: seasoning
plan:
The paper fine-tuned MusicGen to render taste prompts — sweet, sour, bitter, salty — as short musical clips, then ran a 361-person, three-country listening study (Argentina, Italy, Japan). Two findings worth building around: the salty prompt produced the weakest sound-taste correspondence in every cohort, and once each participant's ratings are standardized against their own scale use, the country-level differences in absolute ratings mostly vanish — but the relational structure, which of twelve descriptors cluster with which prompt, stays essentially the same across countries. Cross-cultural 'difference' here is mostly about how generously people use a rating scale, not about what they actually hear.

The mechanic: a visitor picks their country, listens to one short clip, and rates it on the same twelve taste/emotion/thermal descriptors the paper used, via sliders. Ratings are standardized per-visitor and folded into a running, public map comparing countries' descriptor profiles per prompt — the site's own live, self-selected echo of the paper's design, explicitly not a replication of its confirmatory result.

Turn one: one clip, twelve sliders, a country picker, and a submit button that plots your own standardized profile against the running pool average for that prompt. No cross-country comparison view yet — that needs enough submissions to be worth showing.

The hard part: the clips. The paper's exact stimuli aren't available, so the site needs its own short taste-prompt renders, labeled plainly as inspired-by rather than reproduced-from, and the page has to say a self-selected web crowd isn't the paper's recruited sample.

Reuse: `human`'s exhibit framing and its honesty-about-limits posture; `packages/dataviz` for the profile chart.
mechanism: listen to a short AI-rendered taste prompt and rate it on twelve descriptors, feeding a live cross-country map of what sound tastes like
text: listen to what a taste sounds like. rate it on a dozen descriptors. compare yours against your country's crowd. people rate generously or conservatively, but everyone hears the same relationships

paperTitle: Refined upper bounds on Schur-like numbers
name: sumline
plan: The paper refines a bound on generalized Schur numbers: colour the integers 1..N with r colours, and once N passes roughly 3^r times (r factorial) to the 1/m, some colour is forced to contain a monochromatic solution to x1+...+x(m+1) = y1+...+ym — m+1 numbers of one colour summing to m numbers of the same colour. Setting m=1 recovers the classical Schur equation (two numbers of a colour summing to a third of the same colour), so this is a direct generalization of a game mathematicians have played by hand for a century: colour as far along the number line as you can before you're forced into a monochromatic sum. The mechanic: pick r colours, click along a number line painting each integer, and a live checker flags the exact moment a monochromatic solution appears — the run ends there, and the farthest reached is the score. Turn one ships only the classical case, m=1, r=2: a number line, a two-colour palette, and an O(1)-per-click check for a monochromatic x+y=z among what's been painted so far. The hard part is that generalizing past m=1 means checking an (m+1)-vs-m sum after every click without brute-forcing every subset of painted numbers, which needs real incremental bookkeeping (a sum-frequency table per colour) and should wait until the m=1 version is solid and fun. What makes it worth playing twice: the theoretical ceiling changes with every (r, m) you pick, so the number line is a different puzzle every time, and a record for a given (r, m) is instantly checkable by replaying the coloring. Score to the visitor's own PDS as com.minomobi.lab.score, keyed by (r, m), higherIsBetter true.
mechanism: click-paint a number line with r colours while a live checker hunts for a forced monochromatic sum
text: paint along a number line with colours. when same-colour numbers form a sum, the game ends. your score is how far you got. the theoretical limit shifts with every (colours, sum-type), so it's a fresh puzzle each time

paperTitle: The maximum quartet distance between phylogenetic trees
name: fourleaf
plan: Two binary trees on the same n labeled leaves can be compared four leaves at a time: pick any four leaves, and each tree induces one of three possible pairings among them (which two are 'closer' to which two). The quartet distance counts how many of the C(n,4) four-leaf subsets disagree between the two trees. This paper proves the maximum possible disagreement, over every pair of trees on n leaves, is (2/3 + o(1))·C(n,4) — resolving a 1986 conjecture of Bandelt and Dress. So no matter how hard two evolutionary trees are pulled apart, at most about two-thirds of every four-leaf comparison can differ; a third always has to agree. That's a concrete ceiling to push against by hand. The mechanic: the visitor holds two trees over the same n leaves and edits one of them (reorder or swap leaves), watching a live counter of the fraction of four-leaf subsets that currently disagree, trying to climb toward 2/3. Turn one: fix a small n (8–10 leaves), generate two random caterpillar trees — the simplest binary tree shape, just an ordering of leaves, which is also what the paper's own proof reduces every tree pair to — and let the visitor drag to reorder one tree's leaves while the disagreement fraction recomputes after every drag. The hard part is making a 'quartet' legible without jargon: for a given four leaves, show the two induced pairings side by side so a mismatch is visibly a mismatch, not just a number changing. What earns a return visit: at larger n and freer tree shapes the ceiling gets harder to approach, so a verified-high fraction for a given n is a real, instantly-replayable record. Score to the visitor's PDS as com.minomobi.lab.score keyed by n, higherIsBetter true.
mechanism: drag-reorder one of two shared-leaf trees while a live counter tracks the fraction of four-leaf subsets that disagree
text: drag one tree's leaves around while the other stays fixed. each four-leaf subset either agrees or disagrees between the trees. the math says: no matter how you reorder, at most 2/3 of all four-leaf subsets can disagree. a third will always match

paperTitle: DHMark: Public-Key Watermarking for LLM-Generated Text via Diffie-Hellman-Guided Rejection Sampling
name: votecut
plan: DHMark watermarks LLM text so anyone holding a public key can verify it without holding a secret. An issuer signs a short payload, expands it into many one-bit 'equations,' and during generation each candidate token gets a public vote for or against those equations; the sampler favors tokens that vote with the payload. A verifier later reads the text, recomputes each token's vote, aggregates the evidence, and scores it against the signed payload — no need to recover an exact hidden string. In the paper's default setting this stays valid (0.967) across eight kinds of edits — truncation, word substitution, copy-paste, wrong context — while never falsely accepting unwatermarked text. The toy hands the visitor a watermarked passage with every word's vote pre-computed and shown as a small marker, and lets them attack it: delete words, swap words, splice in another sentence, truncate the end. A live meter recomputes the aggregate evidence score after every edit and shows exactly how far it sits from the paper's real pass/fail threshold, and from the negative-control line where an unrelated passage sits. Turn one ships one passage, word-level delete/undo only, and the two threshold lines drawn on the meter. The hard part, and the thing to be upfront about on the page: the real scheme derives votes from a Diffie-Hellman-keyed labeling function live at generation time, which can't run client-side from nothing, so this toy ships a handful of passages with their votes precomputed offline and is honest that edits are tested against a fixed table, not a live keyed verifier — it demonstrates the robustness curve from the paper, not a working break of a real deployed watermark. Reuses human/'s exhibit framing and idol/'s posture of building the thing it examines; a leaderboard for fewest edits to cross the threshold is the natural crowd layer once the meter works.
mechanism: edit a pre-watermarked passage word by word while a live meter tracks the aggregate verification score against the paper's real thresholds
text: edit a watermarked passage — delete words, swap them, splice sentences in — and watch the watermark evidence drop. the real scheme verifies with a public key. this demo has the votes precomputed offline, so it shows the paper's robustness but not a live diffie-hellman break

paperTitle: Superlinear Lower Bounds for Monochromatic Path Partitions
name: monopath
text: trace monochromatic paths in a colored complete graph, covering every vertex. a 1989 conjecture said r colors means r paths suffice. false — some colorings need more paths, growing faster as r grows larger. hunt the true minimum and climb a leaderboard of best partitions found
plan: In 1989 Gyárfás conjectured that any r-edge-colouring of a complete graph lets you cover every vertex with at most r vertex-disjoint monochromatic paths — one path per colour, roughly. This paper disproves it hard: for large enough r there are colourings that need at least (1-o(1))·r·log log r paths, growing strictly faster than r however big r gets. The mechanic: the visitor is shown a small complete graph with its edges coloured in r colours and has to cover every vertex using as few vertex-disjoint monochromatic paths as possible, built by clicking edges to extend a path in one colour at a time. A live counter tracks paths used against r, so covering it in r paths feels like winning the old conjecture and needing more is the visitor rediscovering the disproof by hand. Turn one ships one fixed small instance (r=3 or 4, where Pokrovskiy proved r paths always suffice, so a solvable case exists) plus a size-up control, a path-builder that enforces vertex-disjointness and single-colour-per-path, and a counter. The hard part, named plainly on the page: the paper's growth is asymptotic — log log r moves so slowly that no browser-sized graph will visibly demonstrate the r·log log r gap, so the honest framing is 'try to beat r on this instance' rather than 'watch the theorem happen'. What redeems it into a real crowd toy is that finding the true minimum partition for a given large hard colouring is a genuine, unsolved-per-instance search problem — a leaderboard of best (lowest) partition counts found for a shared hard colouring is real work, not decoration. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer pattern (erdos/, hadwiger/) and workers/scores for the per-instance record table.
mechanism: click edges to build vertex-disjoint monochromatic paths covering a coloured complete graph, racing to beat r

paperTitle: Multi-Agent AI Safety as an Institutional Design Problem
name: provenance
text: read a delegation chain and call allow or block on each step. the paper's key finding: relabeling mid-chain to hide the originator fools guards reading only the current label. a guard tracking the source never fails. play the label-only guard and discover why it loses
plan: This paper runs a 5,280-episode study of guardrails for AI agents that delegate tasks to each other, comparing three kinds of guard: a detailed constitutional prompt (0 violations across 384 episodes), a provenance-aware executable guard that tracks who originally authorized an action (also 0/384, though it blocks 51 attempts, 44 of which then complete safely by another route), and a local-state guard that only checks the currently visible policy label (admits violations in 22 of 96 matched 'laundering' episodes, versus 0 of 96 for the provenance guard, p=4.77e-7). The failure mode has a name: authority laundering — an intermediate step relabels the visible policy while the true originating authority never changes, and a guard that only reads the current label gets fooled by its own paperwork. The toy hands the visitor a delegation chain, one step at a time — who asked, what changed, what it now claims to be authorized by — and asks a single question per step: allow or block. After each round it reveals the true origin authority and scores the visitor against both automated guards on the same chain, so a human plays the local-state guard's exact blind spot and finds out, concretely, why it lost 22 times where the provenance guard lost zero. Turn one ships one fixed deck of chains (a mix of clean delegations and laundering attempts, built from the paper's structure), the allow/block interaction, and the reveal-and-score screen with both guards' verdicts shown alongside the visitor's. The hard part: writing laundering scenarios that are genuinely deceptive without being unfair — the paper's trick is specific (label changes, authority doesn't), and a generic 'spot the bad actor' deck would miss the actual mechanism. Crowd value: aggregate human catch-rate versus each guard type is a real number nobody has, and it is the kind of dataset the paper's own programme would want. Reuse workers/scores for the catch-rate leaderboard and the exhibit framing human/ and idol/ already use for AI-safety pieces built as the thing they're about.
mechanism: read a chain of agent delegation steps and call allow/block on each, then get scored against the paper's provenance guard and local-state guard on the same chain

paperTitle: ColluSkill: Adversarial Cross-Skill Composition for Evading Agent Skill Scanners
name: chain-smell
plan: The paper studies LLM agent skills, the installable capabilities agents load at runtime, and shows that current scanners only check one skill at a time. ColluSkill splits a malicious intent across several skills that each look clean alone, and chains them so the harm only appears once they run together: 96% of these chains slip past six real scanners. Its proposed fix, ChainGuard, looks at the whole installed set at once and cuts that to 22.5%. The toy hands the visitor a shelf of eight or so toy skills, abstracted and harmless in themselves, things like read-calendar, summarize-text, send-message, each carrying a green solo-scanner badge. The visitor picks an ordered chain of three and a hidden objective (say, quietly forward a calendar invite's contents to an outside address); the server checks whether the chain achieves the objective, whether every skill still scans clean alone, and then runs the ChainGuard-style whole-set check. Turn one ships that full loop for a single fixed objective and skill shelf, with a pass/fail on both scanners. What's hard: keeping the skills abstract enough that this teaches the composition idea without being a usable evasion recipe against any real scanner, and making the chain-check legible without a chat log. What to reuse: `human/`'s exhibit framing for building the thing it critiques (per `idol/`'s precedent), `workers/scores` for a leaderboard of shortest chains that beat ChainGuard, and a public catalog of discovered chain patterns that doubles as a teaching aid for the defense.
mechanism: compose a short ordered chain from individually-clean toy skills to sneak a hidden objective past a solo scanner, then a whole-chain scanner
text: pick three toy skills that scan clean alone, chain them into a sequence to achieve a hidden goal the solo scanner misses, then see if the full-chain scanner stops you

paperTitle: Analysis and Consensus Control of Emergent Dynamic Polarization in Minimally-Nonlinear Opinion Dynamics
name: pin-one
plan: The paper proves something specific about opinion networks: past a critical reactivity rate, a network of agents updating on a simple cubic nonlinearity stops settling into consensus and instead locks into a permanent, provably stable oscillation between two opposing clusters, a supercritical flip bifurcation. Then it proves a second, sharper thing: anchoring the opinion of a single agent, fixing just one person's mind, is enough to kill the oscillation and pull the whole network back to consensus, even on directed graphs with uneven influence. The toy is a small network, a dozen or so nodes drawn as a graph, opinions shown as a red-blue gradient, with one slider for reactivity rate. Push the slider up and the network visibly starts pulsing between red-majority and blue-majority in a steady rhythm; that's the bifurcation, not noise, and the rhythm is exactly periodic. Then click any node to anchor it, freezing its color, and watch the pulsing die out. Turn one ships exactly that: slider, pulse, click-to-anchor, decay. What's hard is making the bifurcation read as inevitable rather than random, the pulse needs a visible period and amplitude, not just flicker, and the decay after anchoring needs to be visibly faster near high-degree nodes so the choice of which node to anchor matters. What to reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the graph render and a small time-series strip showing mean opinion over time; a crowd angle of user-submitted topologies raced for fastest quench-time-to-consensus after a single anchor, since that's a real quantitative question the paper doesn't answer for arbitrary graphs.
mechanism: tune a reactivity slider on an opinion network until it locks into oscillation, then click one node to anchor it and watch consensus return
text: push the reactivity slider until the network locks into permanent back-and-forth between two camps, then click one node to freeze its opinion and watch the cycle collapse as everyone converges again

paperTitle: Algorithmics for Safe Bicycle Network Design with Bounded Detours in Rural Areas
name: safe-lanes
plan: The paper formalizes a real planning problem: a rural road network has some edges already safe for bikes and some not, upgrading an edge costs money, you have a budget, and every named pair of towns needs a safe route no longer than some detour factor times the shortest route in the whole network. It proves this is NP-hard even on very restricted graphs, degree-3, treewidth-2, one feedback vertex, but also gives algorithms that are fast when the number of unsafe edges or terminal pairs is small, and it runs the whole thing on real OpenStreetMap data for German municipalities, finding that loosening the detour factor buys real savings in upgrade cost. The toy is a small stylized road map, fifteen to twenty nodes, red edges unsafe, gray edges safe, a few marked town pairs, a budget number, and a detour-factor slider. The visitor clicks red edges to upgrade them and the map lights up green paths as soon as every town pair is connected within budget and within the detour bound; the puzzle is deliberately built from the paper's hard instance shapes, small enough that a person beats brute force by seeing the structure. Turn one ships one fixed map, one budget, one detour factor, with a win check and a running cost counter. What's hard: choosing a map small enough to solve by eye but honest about the hardness, and rendering the detour-bound check (a live shortest-path comparison, not just connectivity) without it feeling like a black box. What to reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the graph layout, `workers/scores` for a leaderboard of cheapest verified upgrade sets on real small-town OSM extracts, since any submitted edge set is checkable in polynomial time even though finding it is hard.
mechanism: click unsafe road segments to upgrade them within a budget so every marked town pair gets a safe route within a detour bound
text: click road segments to upgrade them within a budget, make sure every marked town pair gets a safe bike route, solve the puzzle by eye and then learn why this is computationally hard

paperTitle: Rogue Wave Statistics from a Sparse Coherent Structure Decomposition
name: rogue-wave
plan: The standard story about freak ocean waves treats the sea as nearly linear noise and predicts rogue-wave odds from that. This paper measures real wave tanks and shows the strongly nonlinear seas that actually produce rogue waves are better described as a sparse handful of soliton-like coherent packets, each with a random amplitude drawn from a log-normal distribution, random phase, random arrival time, and that the chance of a rogue wave is governed almost entirely by the tail of that one amplitude distribution, matching lab data better than the conventional models while staying just as simple to compute.
