The toy hands the visitor two dials: how many coherent packets are seeded per run, and the spread (tail heaviness) of their log-normal amplitudes. Press run and a synthetic sea surface animates as those packets overlap and interfere; any resulting crest more than twice the significant wave height is flagged as a rogue wave. Every run adds one point to a shared histogram of observed rogue-wave rate versus the two dial settings, next to a reference line showing what the old linear model would have predicted for the same dial settings, so the gap between them is the paper's actual finding, visible as a gap between two curves rather than asserted. Turn one ships a single run with the animation, the flag, and the running histogram, no reference line yet. What's hard: making packet interference look like a real sea rather than a decorative animation, and keeping the histogram meaningful with the small run counts a browser can produce before it needs many contributed runs to resolve the tail, which is exactly why this wants a crowd. What to reuse: `g/`'s WebGPU shelf conventions for the surface render, `workers/scores` repurposed as a shared-histogram store keyed by dial settings.
mechanism: set packet count and amplitude-tail spread, run a synthetic sea, and watch a shared histogram of rogue-wave rate build up against the old model's prediction
text: tune how many wave packets and how extreme their sizes get, run a synthetic sea, spot the freak waves, and add your run to a shared graph showing why the simple model outperforms the old one

paperTitle: Breaking the 4-Approximation Barrier in Strategyproof Two-Facility Location
name: global-pair
plan: A mechanism has to place two facilities to serve a set of agents on a line (or any Ptolemaic metric space), and each agent's cost is their distance to the nearer facility. A mechanism is strategyproof if lying about your location never lowers your cost. The best known strategyproof mechanism for a decade and a half was 'Proportional', with a worst-case cost 4x optimal; the paper breaks that barrier by randomizing between Proportional and a new mechanism, Global Pair, which draws a random pair of agents weighted by their distance apart and opens facilities exactly there — the mix achieves 11/3, about 3.667x. The two mechanisms turn out to be bad on complementary instances, which is why blending them works. Turn one: the visitor places agents as dots on a line, hits run, and watches the mechanism place two facilities (color-coded by which sub-mechanism fired that round) with each agent's cost drawn as a line to its nearer facility and the total shown against the true optimal placement. Second interaction, the one that makes it a game and not a demo: the visitor controls one agent and can misreport its position before the mechanism runs, trying to lower that agent's own cost by lying — and strategyproofness means it structurally can't work, which the visitor gets to verify empirically, round after round, on a mechanism that is not yet proven safe against every strategy an adversarial crowd might try (only against single-agent deviations, which is what the theorem covers). The crowd angle: a leaderboard of worst-found instances by cost ratio, checkable by anyone re-running the placement. What's hard: explaining a Ptolemaic metric space without the term — restrict turn one to the line, where every metric here is trivially Ptolemaic, and only mention the wider class as a footnote. Reuse workers/scores for the instance leaderboard; no auth needed since nothing is saved to a PDS.
mechanism: place agents on a line, watch a randomized mechanism site two facilities, then try to lie about your own position to beat a mechanism that's proven you can't
text: place agents on a line. a mechanism opens two facilities to minimize distance to the nearest one. now lie about your own position before each round and try to improve your cost. strategyproofness proves it won't work. test it anyway and see

paperTitle: Activation Probes Surface Code-Security Signals that the Model's Output Misses
name: read-the-weights
plan: Take a function and its security-patched version. Ask an open-weight model, in plain language, which one is vulnerable — most of the time it gives the same answer to both, because asking for a verdict collapses the distinction. But a single linear probe fit on the model's internal activations, never retrained on the specific bug type being tested, scores the vulnerable function above its fix 61-67% of the time across five different reviewer models — beating both chance and the model's own prompted yes/no answer, every time, on every model tested. The gap is the whole point: the information is present in the model and absent from what it says. Turn one is a three-way comparison round: the visitor is shown a real vulnerable/fixed pair (unlabeled, order randomized) and picks which is vulnerable, purely by reading the code — then the reveal shows what the same model's prompted answer said and what a precomputed probe score says, scored against the paper's real numbers so every round is a three-way bet: human, prompt, activations. Running a full reviewer model plus probe live in-browser for every round is heavier than this needs, so ship a fixed set of precomputed pairs with precomputed probe scores from an offline reproduction on one of the paper's open-weight models, and say plainly that the probe number is precomputed, not live. The crowd angle: aggregate human accuracy across thousands of rounds becomes a real, previously-unmeasured number to set against the paper's 61-67% and the model's near-50%, and it's the natural three-way leaderboard. What's hard: choosing pairs where the vulnerability is genuinely legible from the code (not a subtle CVE requiring deep framework knowledge) without cherry-picking easy wins that flatter the human score. Reuse workers/scores for the running human-accuracy tally; no model runs client-side, so no WASM inference cost.
mechanism: read a vulnerable/fixed code pair and guess which is which, then see how you scored against the model's own verdict and against a probe reading its activations
text: read two code versions—one vulnerable, one fixed. guess which is which. then see how you scored against the model's verdict and against a linear probe reading its weights. the probe catches the bug when the model's output misses it

paperTitle: Blocking codimension-one simplices on the moment curve
name: stab-the-triangles
plan: Take n points in the plane, no three collinear. Every triple spans a triangle; there are C(n,3) of them. The Blocking Conjecture asks: how few extra points does it take so that every one of those triangles has at least one extra point strictly inside it? The paper improves the best known lower bound on that count to roughly 41/13 of n (about 3.15n), meaning any blocking set, however cleverly placed, needs at least that many points once n is large — an open problem nudged, not closed. Turn one: the visitor gets a small point set (n around 6-10, kept small enough that C(n,3) triangles are checkable instantly) and places blocker points one at a time; the site highlights, live, which of the triangles are still unstabbed, and the round ends when none are left, reporting the blocker count used against n. That count-versus-n ratio is the game: can the visitor beat 3.15n on this instance, and can anyone find a configuration where they provably can't get close? Second interaction: let the visitor design the original n points, not just the blockers, since a bad point layout (near-convex position, say) changes how hard blocking is — this is the actual open question the paper is chipping at, so a good configuration paired with its best-found blocking count is a real, small, honest data point toward the conjecture, not just a game score. What's hard: verifying 'strictly inside' correctly and fast for every triangle as blockers are added, and keeping n small enough that the visitor can hold C(n,3) triangles in their head while still being large enough that the ratio means something. Reuse the math wing's explainer conventions and workers/scores for a record table of (points, blockers) pairs, recomputable by anyone since checking containment is arithmetic.
mechanism: place points to stab every triangle spanned by a point set, trying to use fewer than 3.15 per original point — a real lower bound from an open conjecture
text: place extra points to stab every triangle in a point set. you need at least 3.15 points per original one to block them all—or so the conjecture says. beat that bound here or design your own points and challenge others to block them efficiently

paperTitle: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fairness and Pareto Optimality
name: fair-lottery
plan: The paper is about fair division of indivisible items among agents with different values for each item, where instead of one allocation you construct a lottery over allocations. It proves that for two agents you can always build a lottery whose expected outcome is envy-free, while every single allocation the lottery might actually produce is envy-free up to one item and Pareto optimal — no coin-flip regret. It goes further: a lottery hitting the stronger EFX guarantee (envy vanishes even after removing any one item) exists too, and for integer valuations it is computable in pseudo-polynomial time. Then it breaks: for three agents splitting four items, there is a specific valuation profile where no lottery can be simultaneously envy-free-in-expectation and EFX-and-Pareto-optimal in every realization. The toy: two players enter how much they value a handful of items, the site computes and spins the guaranteed lottery, and shows the realized split satisfies both properties — every time, because two agents always work. Turn one ships exactly that two-player version, with a spin animation and the property checks lit up as they're verified. The follow-up turn is the trap: the fixed three-agent, four-item instance from the paper where the guarantee is impossible, letting a visitor watch the algorithm fail honestly instead of just being told it can. What's hard: the lottery construction is a real algorithm, not an approximation, so turn one needs the actual pseudo-polynomial construction working on real input, not a fake spinner. Reuse games' Durable Object rooms so three real people can bring their own valuations to the impossible case, and workers/scores to log how many submitted three-agent profiles turn out impossible versus fine, mapping the boundary the paper only proves exists at one point.
mechanism: split items between players via a computed lottery, then hunt the exact case where the guarantee provably cannot be built
text: two players value items, an algorithm builds a lottery split that's fair and efficient in every outcome. now try the three-player setup where both properties can't both hold

paperTitle: How People Evaluate AI-, Expert-, and Peer-Style Financial Advice
name: mislabeled
plan: The paper ran a controlled experiment: the same financial advice — same facts, same numbers, same recommendation — presented as coming from an AI assistant, a certified financial planner, or an online-forum peer, with the attribution either labeled correctly, left off, or mislabeled outright. Content held constant, only the story about who said it changed. Result: the human expert was rated better on 9 of 10 measures even with no label attached, but mislabeling — showing AI-written advice under an expert's name, or the reverse — moved the AI's own scores up by about half a standard deviation on situational fit and overall quality, and shrank the expert's advantage in situational fit by a similar amount. The label does real work independent of the words underneath it. The toy: a visitor reads one piece of financial advice, is told (accurately, not at all, or falsely) who wrote it, and rates it on the axes the paper used. Turn one ships one advice item, three attribution conditions assigned at random, and a rating form — no persistence needed yet, just the interaction. The payoff is the next turn: an aggregate panel showing the live crowd's ratings by condition next to the paper's reported effect sizes as reference lines, so a thousand visitors becomes a live replication rather than a one-off vignette. What's hard: writing advice content that is genuinely identical in substance across framings the way the original study controlled for, and resisting the temptation to make the AI-labeled version subtly worse-written, which would fake the finding rather than reproduce it. Reuse human's arcade framing and copy conventions, and workers/scores to store per-condition rating aggregates.
mechanism: rate the same advice under a randomly assigned, sometimes false, attribution label
text: read some financial advice. you're told (truthfully or falsely) whether it came from an ai or a human expert. same words, different author label—watch how much it changes your rating

paperTitle: A Content-Aware Pure Permutation with Intrinsic Avalanche Effect: Breaking the Diffusion-Permutation Dichotomy
name: pixel-avalanche
plan: The received wisdom in image scrambling is that pure permutation — moving pixels around without changing their values — can't have an avalanche effect: change one input pixel and you've only relocated that one pixel in the output, nothing else moves. This paper breaks that by making the permutation depend on image content: it runs Canny edge detection, triangulates the edges and corners with Delaunay triangulation, and uses that triangulation to define where every pixel goes. Change one pixel and you change the edge map, which changes the triangulation, which changes the whole permutation — measured at 97.10% NPCR (near-total pixel change) across 50 test images, against near-zero for ordinary permutation, converging in an average of 14.81 re-triangulation passes that ranges from about 6 to 31 depending on how busy the image is. The toy: a canvas showing a fixed demo image and its live Delaunay triangulation overlay. Click one pixel, watch the edge map flicker, the triangulation redraw, and the image reshuffle into what reads as static — then hit undo to see it wasn't random, it's deterministic and reversible. Turn one ships exactly that: one demo image, click-to-flip, a triangulation overlay toggle, and the before/after NPCR number computed live. What's hard: running Canny plus Delaunay at interactive speed in the browser without a visible stall, and picking a demo image where the effect reads as dramatic rather than as noise on noise. The crowd angle for a later turn: let visitors submit their own images and log iteration counts against a rough complexity score, building the same content-dependence curve the paper reports (6.4 to 30.7) from real submitted images instead of the paper's fixed 50.
mechanism: flip one pixel and watch a content-driven triangulation rescramble the whole image
text: click one pixel. its edges redraw, the triangulation recalculates, and the whole image scrambles—avalanche effect from pure permutation, which shouldn't be possible

paperTitle: Scaling Laws for Majority-based Opinion Dynamics in the Presence of Stubborn Agents
name: holdout
text: slide two dials setting stubborn opinion fractions and watch the network flip toward consensus. but where they balance, convergence turns exponential—small networks dither forever. the asymptotic curve shows the phase boundary where bigger networks might not settle
plan:
The paper studies a network where opinions are 0 or 1 and most agents update by the 2k-choices rule: sample 2k neighbours at random, count opinions among them plus your own, adopt whichever holds the majority. A fixed fraction of agents on each side never update — gamma_0 stubborn for 0, gamma_1 stubborn for 1. The obvious result holds: whichever side has more stubborn holdouts eventually wins the network. The interesting result is how long that takes. When gamma_0 and gamma_1 are both small and close together, convergence time is exponential in network size — the network can dither for what is, at any playable size, effectively forever. When either fraction is large, convergence collapses to logarithmic time, almost immediate. The boundary between the two regimes is sharp, not gradual.

The toy: two sliders, gamma_0 and gamma_1, over a fixed small network of a few hundred nodes. Hit run and watch the network flip node by node toward consensus while a step counter climbs. Turn one ships exactly that — sliders, a randomised graph, the 2k-choices update running visibly, a counter, nothing else. The honest problem is that a real exponential blowup will not show up at browser-friendly network sizes, since the paper's split is asymptotic. So alongside the live run, plot the paper's asymptotic step-count curve across network size with the current slider position marked on it — the browser shows a network settling, the curve shows why a bigger one might never finish settling. Reuse `civ`'s agent-simulation step loop for the network update and `scores` for a shared log of every run's (gamma_0, gamma_1, steps) triple, so the phase boundary emerges from everyone's slider choices rather than being drawn in advance.
mechanism: two stubborn-fraction sliders drive a 2k-choices opinion network across a sharp exponential/logarithmic convergence-time boundary

paperTitle: Eclipses by Artificial Satellites to Measure the Angular Sizes of Stars
name: flicker
text: a satellite eclipse dims a star; diffraction fringes in the light curve encode its width. slide to match the pattern and read the star's angular diameter. many independent fits stack sharper than any single guess, like the paper stacks real events
plan:
The paper proposes measuring stellar angular diameters — a quantity every telescope's diffraction limit blocks from direct measurement — from the light curve of a star being eclipsed by a satellite. As the satellite's edge sweeps across the star, the dimming is not a clean step: light diffracts around the edge into Fresnel fringes, and the spacing and decay of those fringes encode the star's angular size, provided the detector can timestamp photons on the microsecond scale (the instrument cited, SPINA, has demonstrated 8 nanosecond resolution). Their Bayesian analysis of simulated observations finds this delivers sub-2-milliarcsecond resolution for around ten thousand stars a year, with the sharpest hundred pinned below half a milliarcsecond.

The mechanic: you are handed a synthetic light curve, the real diffraction pattern of one occultation, rendered as photon counts against microsecond time. A slider sets your assumed stellar angular diameter and redraws a candidate fringe pattern over the true one; drag until they lock and a residual score reports how close you got. Turn one ships one fixed star, one fixed occultation geometry, the actual Fresnel diffraction integral computed client-side (a Cornu-spiral calculation, not a cosmetic curve), and the slider-and-overlay fit — nothing else. The hard part is that integral: get the diffraction physics wrong and the toy teaches nothing true about the paper. Reuse `tjs`'s canvas rendering for the light curve and `scores` for a fit-precision leaderboard. The crowd case is real, not decorative: average many independent visitors' fits of the same occultation and the mean converges tighter than any single guess, the way the paper's actual survey stacks thousands of events into a catalogue.
mechanism: slider-driven curve fit against a client-side Fresnel-diffraction light curve to recover a star's angular diameter

paperTitle: On the Sensitivity to Errors in Homomorphic Computing: Single Transient Bit-flip Client-side Error Characterization
name: amplify
text: assemble a circuit of encrypted adds and multiplies, choose one bit to flip, decrypt and compare. addition corruption surfaces as noise. multiplication corruption hides silently—the decrypted result looks plausible and wrong, bypassing the checks that would catch it
plan:
The paper injects single transient bit-flips into a CKKS homomorphic-encryption pipeline, the scheme behind computing on encrypted data without decrypting it, and finds the operations are not equally fragile. A flip during homomorphic addition perturbs the result by roughly the size of the flip. A flip during homomorphic multiplication does not behave that way: because CKKS is an approximate scheme by design, a corrupted product decrypts to a plausible-looking wrong number, with nothing thrown and no obvious tell. The paper frames this as a silent-corruption risk — the fault evades exactly the checks that would normally catch it, because the ciphertext itself carries no signal that anything happened.

The toy: a fixed-point number is obscured (not real CKKS — the point is the arithmetic behaviour, not the cryptosystem) and pushed through a small circuit of add and multiply steps you assemble. You get one bit to flip, and you choose where in the circuit and which bit position. After decryption you see the true answer beside the corrupted one, plus whether the corruption 'triggered' a plausibility check standing in for whatever monitoring a real deployment would run. Turn one: a drag-together circuit of add and multiply blocks, the flip picker, and the true-versus-corrupted compare view — no scoring yet. The hard part is resisting turning this into a bypass game; frame it as a fault-injection robustness exhibit with the defensive read stated on the page, the same posture `human/` already takes toward its arcade of user error, applied here to an arcade of hardware error. Reuse `human/`'s exhibit framing and copy conventions, and `scores` later for a quietest-corruption leaderboard once the mechanic is proven out.
mechanism: single bit-flip fault injected into a client-assembled encrypted add/multiply circuit, exposing which operation silently corrupts the result

paperTitle: Kohayakawa's conjecture and clique coverings of complements of paths and cycles
name: kohayakawa
plan: The paper proves a 1991 conjecture of Kohayakawa about induced paths in Kneser graphs, and uses it to settle a 1985 conjecture of de Caen, Gregory and Pullman: the minimum number of cliques needed to cover the complement of a path or cycle on n vertices is exactly log2(n) + Theta(log2 log2(n)). Unpacked, a clique in the complement of a path is just a set of numbers from 1..n with no two consecutive members, so the result says: you can always cover every number from 1 to n using about log2(n) such sets, and you provably cannot do much better. Turn one: the visitor gets a number line of length n and a 'new set' button; clicking assigns the current colour to a number, refused if it lands next to an already-placed same-colour number, with a live counter of sets used against the log2(n)+~2.5log2log2(n) target line so progress toward the bound is visible. This is unavoidably a hands-on packing puzzle, not a passive read. What's hard: making the 'why log2' legible — the natural construction assigns each set a bit-pattern from the binary expansion of the position, offset so consecutive numbers always disagree somewhere; showing that bit grid beside the final colouring is what turns a coincidence into an insight, rather than just showing the winning cover. What to reuse: the geometry/math wing's single-file conventions and the instant-recompute leaderboard pattern from an existing record-hunt page there — a claimed cover is a list of (number, set) pairs anyone can verify in one scan, so a shared scores table can hold true records for specific n where humans beat the naive binary construction.
mechanism: number-line packing puzzle: cover 1..n with sets that avoid adjacent numbers, racing a log2(n) bound
text: pack 1 to n into colour sets, with no two adjacent numbers the same colour. beat the paper's log₂(n) bound, or just watch how close you can get to the hard limit.

paperTitle: High-temperature photovoltaics for solar-electric Oberth maneuvers: ton-class payload feasibility for interstellar-precursor missions
name: oberth
plan: The paper asks whether a cheap, expendable rocket (Falcon Heavy) could send a ton of payload to 200 AU — deep enough for real interstellar-precursor science — within 25 years, using ordinary chemical launch plus a solar-electric Oberth maneuver: diving the probe to a 0.3 AU perihelion and firing electric thrusters hard while deep in the Sun's gravity well, where the same delta-v buys roughly three times the orbital energy it would at 1 AU. The catch is that solar panels get very hot that close in; the paper's answer rests on new high-intensity, high-temperature (HIHT) cells that keep working near 400 degrees C. Its finding: with a Jupiter gravity assist en route, panels only 10% more capable (by specific power) than today's best get you there in 25 years; without the assist, on a direct dive, you need roughly double today's specific power. Turn one: two dials — an HIHT specific-power multiplier and a Jupiter-assist on/off toggle — feed a simplified two-burn energy budget (perihelion Oberth gain plus a fixed assist bonus) that outputs an arrival-time estimate at 200 AU, colour-coded pass/fail against the 25-year bar, with the mission profile drawn as a spiral dive and kick. What's hard: the paper used real evolutionary trajectory optimisation; a browser toy needs an honest surrogate — closed-form Oberth energy gain plus a fixed assist bonus — labelled clearly as an approximation, so the two named thresholds (10% and 2x) stay the actual anchors rather than whatever the simplified model happens to output. What to reuse: packages/dataviz for the arrival-time chart; no existing surface fits a deep-space trajectory tool, so the sim itself would be new.
mechanism: two-dial trajectory calculator: solar-cell heat tolerance and gravity-assist choice against a 25-year, 200 AU deadline
text: send a probe sun-diving to 200 AU using hot solar panels and thrusters. adjust panel heat-tolerance and pick a jupiter assist to beat a 25-year deadline. without the assist, you need cells twice as tough as today's best.

paperTitle: The Triadic Stress Index in Financial Markets
name: diag3
plan: The paper takes an index invented to flag stress in soil microbiome networks and points it, unaltered, at financial markets, testing it across five markets and twenty years including real crises. Its strongest result is a per-node decomposition: diag(A^3), the diagonal of the cubed correlation-network adjacency matrix, names which single asset is carrying a market's concentration with no parameter to tune, and does this far better than the next-best published alternative (0.97-0.99 accuracy versus 0.33-0.84), while its alarms are far cleaner than the industry-standard Absorption Ratio (about 4% false alarms versus roughly 59%). The toy: load a real historical correlation snapshot (the 2008 banking crisis, the 2020 crash, an ordinary calm month as a control), rendered as a network of assets sized by raw correlation. The visitor picks the node they think is most stressed — pure eyeballing, no formula — then the page runs diag(A^3) live, reveals the real answer, and shows what the Absorption Ratio would have flagged instead, scoring the guess against both. Turn one ships exactly that single-round guess-then-reveal on one fixed historical snapshot. What's hard: the honest framing — this is a coincident stress gauge the paper explicitly finds has zero lead time, not a forecasting or trading tool, and the copy has to say so plainly rather than let a 'crisis index' read as investment advice. What to reuse: nothing existing renders a weighted correlation network, so this builds its own small graph view; a shared scores table can hold a running 'beat the formula' tally across snapshots, which only gets interesting once a crowd has played enough rounds to see whether human intuition tracks diag(A^3) or the noisier baselines.
mechanism: guess-the-stressed-asset game on a real correlation network, scored against a live diag(A^3) computation
text: load a network snapshot from a real crisis. pick which asset you think is most stressed just by looking, then the formula scores your guess. it reads the moment perfectly—but it never predicts.

paperTitle: On the Assouad dimension of Weierstrass function graphs
name: assouad
plan: Weierstrass functions are the classic example of a curve that is continuous everywhere and smooth nowhere; their graphs are fractal, and how fractal is measured by dimension. This paper addresses the Assouad dimension, which — unlike the more familiar Hausdorff dimension, an average over the whole curve — measures the worst possible patch: whatever window, at whatever zoom level, looks the most complicated. Several prior indications had suggested this worst-case dimension might simply equal the maximum possible value, 2, for these graphs. The paper proves it can't: it derives a quantitative upper bound strictly below 2 for a broad family of these functions, including the related Takagi functions, settling the question in the negative for parameters where it had been conjectured to hold. Turn one: sliders for the two Weierstrass parameters (a, b) render the graph on canvas; the visitor drags a zoom box anywhere on the curve, and the page box-counts inside that window at a few scales to estimate a local dimension, shown live beside the window. The game is explicit: hunt for the window with the highest local estimate you can find, and watch it never break the paper's bound, however hard you zoom or wherever you search. What's hard: box-counting a fractal curve at finite scale is noisy, and honesty means showing the estimate with its scale-dependence visible — a small range, not a fake-precise single number — and restricting parameters to the class the theorem actually covers. What to reuse: the geometry/math wing's single-file conventions and canvas-plot patterns from its other extremal-geometry pages; a shared scores table for a 'highest local estimate found' table per (a,b) pair, checkable by anyone re-running the same zoom.
mechanism: zoom-and-box-count hunt for the most fractal patch of a Weierstrass curve, capped below dimension 2
text: zoom into a Weierstrass fractal curve, drag your window to the spikiest patches you can spot, and watch box-counting estimate how fractal that region is. the theorem caps the worst possible spikiness below dimension 2—hunt for the edge.

paperTitle: Impact of Higher-Order Interactions on Collective Motion
name: vicsek
plan: The Vicsek model is the standard toy for how birds, fish or bacteria snap into collective motion: each agent nudges its heading toward its neighbours' average, and as noise increases the flock's order falls off smoothly. This paper adds three-body ('triadic') alignment terms and finds the transition's character changes qualitatively: pure triadic alignment makes order collapse discontinuously, with hysteresis — the flock stays ordered at a noise level where it would already have broken up on the way up — and a distinct free-energy landscape and Binder-cumulant signature confirm it's a real jump rather than a numerical artifact. It also needs a higher density to sustain order at all. The mechanic: two dials, noise and triadic fraction (0 = pure pairwise, 1 = pure triadic), drive a small on-canvas agent simulation with a live order-parameter readout. Turn one ships the ramp: sweep noise up from zero while the order parameter plots live, then sweep back down over the same range — at high triadic fraction the down-sweep visibly overshoots the up-sweep, a hysteresis loop the visitor causes by turning a dial, not a canned animation. What's hard: getting a legible discontinuous jump out of a small, fast, client-side particle count without it reading as simulation noise; the paper's clean signature came from careful finite-size analysis a browser toy can only gesture at, so the page should present the jump as illustrating the mechanism rather than claiming to reproduce the paper's exact numbers. What to reuse: packages/dataviz for the order-parameter and hysteresis-loop charts; no existing surface runs a flocking simulation, so the agent loop itself is new, though it sits in the same category of small force-model sims as the O'Neill pack's other physics toys.
mechanism: two-dial flocking sim: pairwise vs triadic alignment, noise swept up and down to trigger hysteresis
text: watch a flock snap into alignment as noise drops, then sweep the noise back up—at high triadic fractions, the order doesn't restore until noise falls much lower. a hysteresis loop you trigger by turning dials.

paperTitle: A Fourier-analytic Uniqueness Theorem for Lattice-point Enumerators
name: shape-twins
text: draw a shape and try to match another by its lattice-point fingerprint. as you scale up, their curves must diverge eventually — the proof guarantees it — but nothing says how long you can fake them being the same first
plan:
The paper proves a rigidity result: if two bounded measurable shapes (boundary of measure zero) produce the same lattice-point enumerator L_P(t) = |tP ∩ Z^d| for every real t > 0 and every integer translate of the shape, they are the same shape almost everywhere. The proof is Fourier-analytic — a periodic point-counting function whose coefficients recover the shape's own transform — and it subsumes older uniqueness results for polytopes and symmetric bodies with one unified argument. The fact that makes it a toy: this is genuine rigidity, not approximation — agree everywhere on this count and you ARE the same shape.

Mechanic: the visitor draws a shape on a pixel-grid canvas; the site scales it by integer t = 1, 2, 3… and plots the growing sequence of lattice points caught inside, live, as a fingerprint curve. The challenge: draw a second, visibly different shape and try to match that fingerprint for as many values of t as possible before the sequences diverge — they must diverge eventually if the shapes differ on any positive-measure set, which the theorem guarantees, but nothing says how long you can fake it first.

Turn one: a single-shape canvas plus the live L_P(t) sequence for t = 1..12, no matching game yet — watching the fingerprint update as you draw is already the hook.

Hard part: the real theorem needs the enumerator across every integer translate, not just the shape sitting at the origin, and quietly dropping that changes what's actually proven — turn two adds a coarse translate grid rather than skipping it, and the page says plainly that translates are the theorem's teeth.

Reuse: the math wing's single-file explainer and canvas-grid conventions; scores for a "longest fake-twin run" leaderboard, since a claimed record is a (shape A, shape B, t) triple anyone can recompute instantly.
mechanism: draw a shape and try to match another shape's lattice-point count sequence for as long as possible

paperTitle: Learning to Synchronize in Minimum Time
name: sync-race
text: load N oscillators at random phases with limited power. race greedy control against a learned strategy to sync them all. the learned approach cuts sync time by 10%, and you watch both strategies race to full synchrony
plan:
The paper settles the minimum-time feedback law for pushing a population of identical Kuramoto oscillators into sync under a hard instantaneous power budget. Greedy control — push each oscillator to maximize the instantaneous growth of the order parameter r — is exactly optimal for two oscillators and provably suboptimal for more, confirmed against dynamic programming at N=3 and N=4. The paper explains why geometrically: the greedy closed loop is a reparametrized gradient flow that locks r onto a single fixed path (a Möbius orbit under first-harmonic forcing), independent of the power budget. A learned three-harmonic policy beats greedy by 10-14% at N=10-100, and reading the policy back out gives a clean two-constant control law, u_i proportional to -sin(phi_i) + a2*sin(2phi_i) + a3*sin(3phi_i), that recovers 84-99% of the advantage and holds unchanged from N=3 to N=1000.

Mechanic: the visitor sets N phases at random and a power budget, then races two controllers to full synchrony — greedy against the two-constant law — watching two order-parameter traces climb toward r=1 and the clock stop when each hits it. Turn one ships exactly that minus the race: a Kuramoto sim with an N slider, greedy control only, and a big number for time-to-sync; the second controller and the head-to-head race is turn two, once the reference law is wired in.

Hard part: making greedy's failure legible without dynamic programming. The fix is visual, not numeric — plot the order-parameter r(t) as a path in the complex plane and show that greedy's path is the same curve regardless of power, while the tunable law visibly bends the path shorter.

Reuse: g's canvas-simulation pattern for the oscillator physics; scores for a synchronization-time leaderboard per (N, budget) — a claimed record is a seed plus a control law, both free to re-simulate.
mechanism: tune a control law and race it against greedy Kuramoto synchronization

paperTitle: How many labels can a biological oscillator carry? A quality-factor screen for proposed information carriers
name: carrier-screen
text: tune frequency and timescale on an oscillator and watch a physics bound judge if it works in real brains. the famous 30GHz cortical field proposal fails instantly — noise drowns the signal completely. try finding one that doesn't
plan:
The paper answers a question that usually stays a debate: how many distinguishable labels can a biological oscillator actually carry? The bound is simple and substrate-independent — M ≤ Q = 2πντ, the oscillator's own quality factor, frequency times coherence time times 2π — derived purely from the physics of linewidth and coherence, taking no position on mechanism or on quantum effects in biology. Applied to a recently proposed 30GHz intracolumnar microwave field in cortex, Q comes out to 0.19: the linewidth is five times wider than the carrier itself, and a metabolic-power bound the paper also derives is exceeded by five to nine orders of magnitude. Screening eleven proposed carriers against this and five further criteria (including a two-sided requirement that a label be both readable and rewritable), only the slow, well-known neural rhythms survive.

Mechanic: two sliders, frequency ν and coherence time τ, feeding a live Q = 2πντ readout and a red/green checklist of the paper's criteria. The visitor's task is to find a (ν, τ) pair that survives every check while staying inside the literature-plausible range for a named, real proposal — starting with the paper's own microwave-field case, so the first thing anyone sees is the exact 0.19 failure recomputed live in front of them.

Turn one: that single case, hard-wired — sliders locked to the paper's own numbers, showing the failure, no free exploration yet. Free tuning across the other ten catalogued carriers is turn two.

Hard part: not letting visitors invent a carrier and have the site imply it's real biology — only the eleven named proposals get sliders; anything else stays clearly hypothetical.

Reuse: human's exhibit framing and copy conventions, for building a skepticism piece as the thing it critiques.
mechanism: tune frequency and coherence time and watch a quality-factor bound judge your information carrier

paperTitle: Non-Existence of EFX Chore Allocations for Monotone Cost Functions with Binary Marginals
name: impossible-chores
text: drag 53 indivisible chores between 18 agents and try to split them fairly. watch envy-free checks fail after each move — the catch is this exact setup has no fair solution at all, proven in code. see how close you can get
plan:
The paper closes an open case in fair division: with indivisible chores and monotone cost functions with binary marginals — each new chore either does or doesn't add a fixed unit of cost to what an agent already holds — does an envy-free-up-to-any-item (EFX) allocation always exist? For goods, yes, for every monotone binary-marginal function. For chores, the paper answers no, with two explicit counterexamples built on the same 18-agent, 53-chore construction (a "word gadget"), one for binary XOS costs and one for binary supermodular costs — no complete EFX split of that instance exists for either, and both results are machine-checked in Lean 4.

Mechanic: the visitor sees the real 18×53 cost grid (each cell a binary flag: does this chore cost this agent, given what they already hold) and drags chores between agents, with the site checking envy live after every move and reporting the fewest violating pairs achieved so far — a search with genuine near-misses, even though the true answer is always impossible. Turn one: render the fixed grid and a working drag-and-drop assignment with instant envy-checking against one of the two cost profiles (XOS) — no scoring or persistence yet, just try it and watch it fail.

Hard part: the impossibility is a property of this specific 18×53 gadget, not of chores in general, so shrinking the board to something screen-friendlier would misrepresent what the paper actually proved — it has to ship at full size, meaning a pannable or zoomable grid rather than a redesign.

Reuse: the math wing's drag-and-grid conventions; scores for a "closest attempt" leaderboard on fewest violating pairs, verifiable by anyone re-checking the same public cost grid.
mechanism: drag chores between agents trying to build an envy-free split that a proof says can't exist

paperTitle: Chooser-Picker Degree Games for Regular Graphs
name: edgeclaim
text: offered two edges each turn, you pick one. opponent takes the other. you hunt for an undefended vertex; they keep every vertex alive in their own edges. cubic graphs: they always win. find a way to beat them
plan:
The paper studies the Chooser-Picker game on the edges of a d-regular graph: each turn Picker offers two unclaimed edges, Chooser takes one, the other reverts to Picker. Chooser wants to build a subgraph with high maximum degree; Picker wants every vertex to keep a guaranteed minimum degree in Picker's own claimed edges. Beck's monograph lists beating the classical floor(d/4) defense bound as the first of his seven 'most humiliating' problems in combinatorial game theory, open for both this game and Maker-Breaker. This paper breaks it: Picker can always secure floor(d/3), and for cubic graphs (d=3) Picker can guarantee every vertex keeps degree at least 1 no matter how Chooser plays.

The mechanic is the game itself, playable: a board shows a regular graph's edges as unclaimed lines; on your turn as Chooser you're offered two, you click one, the other is auto-claimed by Picker. A live per-vertex degree counter on each side shows the state. Turn one ships the simplest proven case: a small cubic graph (d=3), human as Chooser against a bot playing Picker's degree-at-least-1 strategy, and a scoreboard for whether Chooser found any vertex Picker failed to defend (they shouldn't). The hard part is implementing Picker's actual strategy rather than a plausible-looking heuristic — it needs to come from the paper's construction, not intuition, or the 'Picker always wins' claim becomes false the first time a clever human beats it. Later turns raise d and let humans play Picker against each other, racing toward floor(d/3).

Reuse: games/ for the DO room and matchmaking, workers/scores for a Picker-defense-rate leaderboard across d.
mechanism: two-player edge-claiming game on a regular graph, one offering pairs, one choosing

paperTitle: A 5/4 bound for graphic $s$-$t$ path TSP on subcubic graphs
name: spanwalk
text: click vertices to draw a path from start to finish visiting everyone. edges can repeat. the paper proves the shortest such walk cannot beat a 5/4 coefficient on its length—and proves that coefficient is mathematically tight
plan:
The graphic s-t path TSP: given two marked vertices in a graph, find the shortest walk from s to t that visits every vertex, revisiting edges if needed. This paper proves that on any simple 2-connected graph with maximum degree 3 (subcubic), such a walk of length at most floor((5n+n2)/4)-1 always exists — where n is the vertex count and n2 the number of degree-2 vertices — including the hardest case where removing both s and t disconnects the graph. The 5/4 coefficient is tight; it cannot be improved, and for cubic graphs the bound is simply floor(5n/4)-1, the first such bound proved directly rather than derived from the general tour reduction.

The mechanic: a small subcubic graph is drawn on screen with s and t marked. The visitor clicks a sequence of vertices to build a walk (edges may repeat), a running length counter updates live, and the walk must touch every vertex to complete. On completion the length is compared against the paper's guaranteed bound for that graph, and against the actual shortest walk (computed server-side or by brute force for small n). Turn one ships one hand-picked graph, the click-to-walk mechanic, and the live comparison — no generator yet.

The hard part is generating subcubic graphs where hitting the bound is genuinely non-obvious; a random graph is usually too easy. Later turns should let players submit graphs, or crowd-search for hard instances, since every claimed walk is instantly checkable — nobody can fake a length. Reuse: math/ for the explainer conventions and layout, workers/scores for a per-graph best-length table.
mechanism: draw a shortest s-to-t walk visiting every vertex, scored against the paper's bound

paperTitle: Jamming transition in an active exclusion process
name: flowjam
text: particles on a ring: set density and how fast they flip direction. dense crowds should jam—but activity keeps them flowing. mark where you think the phase boundary sits at each switching rate, everyone builds the diagram together
plan:
A one-dimensional ring of sites holds hardcore particles (each site empty or occupied, no two particles share a site) with a self-propulsion direction that flips at a fixed switching rate. At infinite switching rate the model reduces to a known passive system with a jamming transition: below a critical density the particles flow, above it they clog into a low-mobility jammed phase. This paper's result is that activity fights jamming — the critical density needed to jam the system decreases as the switching rate drops, and below a threshold switching rate the ring never jams at all, staying fluid at any density. Mean mobility and the hole-cluster size distribution are the two measured quantities that show it.

The mechanic: a ring of particles rendered as a circular strip, two sliders — density and switching rate — and a run button. The simulation steps forward, particles hop and flip direction at the chosen rate, and a live mobility gauge and a hole-cluster-size histogram update as it runs. Turn one ships the ring, both sliders, the step simulation, and the mobility gauge only — enough to see jam versus flow by eye and by number, without the histogram.

The hard part is choosing a switching-rate range where the effect is visible in a ring small enough to render smoothly; too coarse and every setting looks the same. Once the single-player sim works, a crowd layer can have visitors mark where they think the phase boundary sits at their chosen switching rate and compare it against everyone else's marks, building a shared phase diagram nobody hand-typed. No existing surface reuses this cleanly; it would want packages/dataviz for the histogram and stand alone otherwise.
mechanism: set particle density and self-propulsion switching rate on a ring, watch traffic jam or flow

paperTitle: The Game of Marginal Utilities
name: cutline
text: split your budget across shared projects. more money in means lower payoffs for everyone. at equilibrium, richer players' picks always contain poorer players'—a perfect nesting that balances every incentive
plan:
m players each split a fixed budget across n shared projects. Project i pays player j a return of a_i * x_i^j / (b_i + sum of everyone's x_i) — a fixed reward divided among everyone who invested there, so pouring more into a popular project dilutes your own and everyone else's return from it. The paper proves this game has a unique Nash equilibrium, and the shape of that equilibrium is the surprising part: sort projects by a_i/b_i, and each player invests in exactly an initial segment of that sorted list — never a scattered subset — and richer players' segments strictly contain poorer players' segments, so the whole population's investments nest like Russian dolls, with a single equimarginal condition pinning down where every player's segment ends.

The mechanic: a row of projects sorted left to right by a_i/b_i, sliders or drag-bars for a live player's allocation across them, and a couple of bot opponents with fixed budgets whose allocations are visible as stacked bars on the same projects, updating your own return in real time as you drag. Turn one ships one human against two or three fixed-budget bots on five or six projects, sliders, and a live payoff number — no 'reveal equilibrium' overlay yet.

The hard part is making the nesting visible without a wall of numbers: the win is a visual where you can see your own segment sitting inside or around an opponent's, and watch it snap into place as everyone converges. A later turn adds the equilibrium overlay so players can check their guess against the closed-form solution, and a live multiplayer room where real allocations feed each other's congestion term instead of bots.

Reuse: games/ for the DO room once it's multiplayer, packages/dataviz for the stacked-segment chart.
mechanism: allocate a resource budget across shared projects against live opponents, congestion included

paperTitle: To EFX OR to MMS, That is the Question
name: envywall
text: drag eight items into three baskets. each person wants either envy-free or maximin-share. this paper proves no split makes everyone green. the browser checks all 6561 ways live—you can see the wall
plan:
Two classic fairness guarantees for dividing indivisible items among agents: envy-free up to any item (EFX) and maximin share (MMS). Both can fail to exist on their own. This paper asks about the looser combination — every agent gets EFX or MMS, agent by agent, their choice not fixed in advance — and expects flexibility to restore existence, since allowing either certificate per agent is strictly easier than requiring one uniformly. It doesn't: the paper constructs an explicit valuation instance with three agents and eight submodular goods where no allocation gives every agent EFX-or-MMS, strengthening prior EFX impossibility results. It also finds positive corners: with identical additive valuations, agents can even get EFX and MMS simultaneously.

The mechanic: the paper's actual eight-good, three-agent counterexample, loaded with its submodular valuations. The visitor drags items into three baskets and a live readout marks each agent green (satisfied, either way) or red (neither), for the current split. Since there are only 3^8 = 6561 ways to split eight items three ways, the browser can and should check all of them the moment you load the page, so the 'no solution exists' claim isn't asserted, it's exhaustively verified in front of you as you fail to beat it. Turn one ships exactly this: the fixed instance, drag-to-allocate, live per-agent status, and a counter of how many of the 6561 splits you or anyone has tried.

The hard part is making the valuations legible — submodular values over item sets need a compact display (a small table or an icon-weight per item) so 'why is agent 2 red' has a visible answer, not just a number. A second instance (the identical-additive case where a fully green split exists) makes a good second page, so the wall isn't the only mode. No existing surface fits; it would stand alone, reusing packages/dataviz for the per-agent status readout only.
mechanism: drag items to three players trying to satisfy fairness for each, hitting a proven wall

paperTitle: Convergent Detour Hijacking: Task-Preserving Resource Amplification in Skill-Based LLM Agents
name: detour-tax
plan: CDH is a two-stage prompt-only attack on LLM agents that use natural-language skill marketplaces: a skill's description gets it selected during tool-selection, then its instruction body reuses that same cover story to justify calling extra, unnecessary skills, before returning to finish the real task so nothing looks wrong. On DeepSeek-V4-Pro the coordinator skill got selected in 80% of tasks, and among those runs token spend rose 67% and wall-clock rose 92% while task completion stayed about the same — the attack is invisible in the one metric anyone checks. The toy hands you the attacker's job: given a task and a small roster of legitimate skills, you write one skill's description (what gets you picked) and its instructions (what it does once picked), trying to route the agent through as many extra skills as possible before it still finishes the task. A simulated agent — a small deterministic planner for turn one, not a live frontier model — reads your skill alongside the others, picks a plan, and the page shows its trajectory: which skills fired, in what order, and the two numbers that matter, tokens and time, next to whether the real task got done. Turn one ships this loop for a single fixed task and three legit skills. What's hard: making 'plausible detour' something a human can actually write in a text box and have a small local planner take seriously, without it degrading into keyword-stuffing — the description and body need to survive a semantic-relevance check, not just contain the right words. Reuse human/'s exhibit framing and its posture that the attacker's tools live on the page, not just an explanation of them; workers/scores for a fewest-tokens-per-successful-detour leaderboard. Ship as a defensive exhibit on a toy-scale planner, with the real defence named on the page — not as a working recipe against anyone's production agent.
mechanism: write a skill's description and instructions to get it picked by an agent, then route it through costly detours while the task still finishes
text: write a dummy skill to hijack an agent's routing: describe it to get picked, then snake the plan through unnecessary skills while the task still finishes. page shows token cost and wall time. top hijacks win

paperTitle: Robustness over efficiency in climate coalitions: a bistable model and a map of architectures
name: ignition-point
plan: The paper formalizes international climate cooperation as a coalition-formation game with two market channels — a membership premium that rewards joining and an outsider drain that punishes staying out — stabilized with robust-control tools against defection, renegotiation, and turnover. The headline result is that the system is bistable: a small remnant club and a near-universal coalition are two stable states separated by a critical mass, and once the big coalition has formed it withstands roughly twelve times the perturbation that would have stopped it from forming at all, while surviving membership-premium disorder up to about seven times its own value. Different treaty designs land in different places on a map of two robustness coordinates — ignition cost and collapse threshold — and the paper names names: a carbon-currency system (quantity-based rights, reissued and border-enforced) is self-igniting, a border adjustment is founding-dependent, an export rebate needs permanent political support, and designs with no outsider drain, like ETS linking, can't ignite a coalition at all even though they help once one exists. The toy: pick an architecture from that list, set your premium and drain, and try to push a starting population of countries over the critical mass into the big coalition — then hit it with a defection shock sized as a multiple of the ignition threshold and watch whether it holds or collapses back to the remnant club. Turn one ships one architecture, one shock slider, and the population trajectory. The hard part is making 'robust control' legible as a shock size rather than a proof — frame the twelve-times number as the actual game difficulty, not a footnote. No existing surface reuse; this is a self-contained population sim using packages/dataviz for the phase map.
mechanism: pick a treaty architecture and a shock size, and try to push a coalition past its critical mass without it collapsing back
text: push countries into a climate coalition and shock-test it. the big coalition is twelve times harder to break once formed than to build from nothing. pick your treaty design, set your shock size, watch it hold or collapse back to a remnant club

paperTitle: When should one stop the most exciting game? Sequential Inference for win-martingales
name: stopping-point
plan: A win-martingale is the running probability that the team currently ahead ends up winning — what a live scoreboard or an election forecast shows you in real time, given the outcome reveals at a fixed horizon. The paper asks exactly when a decision-maker watching that probability should stop and commit, under a running cost for continuing to watch and a terminal loss for being wrong, and gets a full free-boundary solution: a stopping boundary characterized by smooth-fit and C1 regularity and pinned down uniquely by a nonlinear integral equation — with one worked example where the optimal boundary has no limit as the horizon approaches, meaning the right moment to stop can keep changing right up to the buzzer. The toy simulates one path of a win-probability diffusion for a fictional game with a fixed final whistle. You watch the line jitter and click stop whenever you're ready to lock in a prediction of the winner; if you never click, the outcome reveals at the horizon anyway. After you stop, the page overlays the paper's computed optimal boundary on your path and shows your loss against the optimal loss for that exact path. Turn one ships a single game, one running-cost setting, and that after-action overlay. What's hard: choosing a running cost and terminal loss pair where stopping early is genuinely sometimes correct — get the numbers wrong and the optimal strategy degenerates to always-wait or always-stop-now, and the boundary is boring. Reuse the math/ wing's single-file explainer conventions and its citation-forward tone; workers/scores for a leaderboard of average regret against the optimal boundary across many played games, a real dataset about human stopping bias that nobody currently has.
mechanism: watch a live win-probability path and click stop to lock in a prediction before the reveal, scored against the computed optimal boundary
text: watch a live win-probability crawl like a game score or election forecast. click stop to lock in a prediction of who wins before it reveals. the page shows the math's optimal boundary and your regret against it. learn when to commit

paperTitle: Do LLMs Take Care of Their Own? Similarity Signals Can Induce Cooperation
name: mirror-match
plan: The paper puts LLM agents into repeated Prisoner's-Dilemma-style games and hands each one a similarity signal — a graded number claiming how alike its decision process is to its opponent's — then measures whether that number changes cooperation. It does, but unevenly: some models respond consistently across payoff structures and framings, others barely move, and — the detail worth building the toy around — models asked to judge another model's chain-of-thought reasoning by themselves tend to rate it as highly similar to their own, even when it isn't. The paper's own behavioral-game-theory model shows cooperation becomes an equilibrium once the similarity score crosses a threshold. The toy: you play a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma against a real small model, but instead of choosing cooperate or defect for a fixed opponent, your lever is the similarity score shown to it before each round — dial it honestly or lie. Watch its move and its running cooperation rate as you push the number up or down, and try to find the model's actual threshold by bisection rather than guessing. A second, quieter panel shows it its own last move's reasoning and asks it to rate similarity to a stranger's move, testing the self-identification finding live, on your session. Turn one: one model, five rounds, the similarity slider, and the cooperation-rate readout after each round. What's hard and worth naming: this needs live model calls, not a client-side stub, since the reasoning-based moves are the point — budget for a small hosted model and cap session length. Reuse games/'s room and turn-taking machinery and human/'s exhibit framing for the self-rating panel.
mechanism: play repeated prisoner's dilemma against a model while controlling the similarity score it's told about you
text: play prisoner's dilemma against a real model. your move is the similarity score you dial before each round: lie or tell the truth and watch its cooperation shift. models rate their own reasoning as more similar than it is

paperTitle: Maximally chaotic competition for attention in the cultural domain
name: chart-chaos
plan: The paper adds memory to the standard Lotka-Volterra model of items competing for attention — songs on a chart — using an exponential moving average of past popularity as feedback, and finds this produces a wide winnerless-chaos region: no song wins for long, ranks continually reshuffle, and the popularity distribution in a trailing top-k window is log-normal, collapsing to a power law when the feedback is fast relative to the charting period, matching real Billboard and Spotify statistics. The sharper finding: measuring the largest Lyapunov exponent across the chaotic region, real-world cultural data — music charts, Google Trends, Reddit, Wikipedia, movies, even paper citations — sits close to where that exponent is locally maximal, meaning these systems appear to run close to the most unpredictable setting available to them, not merely somewhere-chaotic. The toy: a simulated ten-item chart with two dials, memory span and feedback speed, updating live. Below the chart, a running estimate of the largest Lyapunov exponent, via a small perturbation-tracking scheme rather than the paper's full method, moves as you turn the dials, and a marked point later shows roughly where real-world fits land. Try to hand-tune the dials onto the peak rather than just into the chaotic region generally — that distinction is the whole point and the paper's whole surprise. Turn one ships the two dials, the live chart, and the live exponent readout, no marked real-world point yet. What's hard: computing a believable Lyapunov estimate cheaply and honestly in a browser tick loop, and being clear it's an estimate over a short simulated window, not the paper's asymptotic quantity. No existing surface reuse; a self-contained canvas sim using packages/dataviz for the exponent trace.
mechanism: tune memory and feedback speed for a simulated hit chart and read a live chaos meter, hunting for the point of maximum unpredictability
text: tune memory and feedback speed for a simulated music chart and read a live chaos meter. hunt for the peak where the chart is most unpredictable. spotify, billboard, reddit all run at this sweet spot: maximum possible disorder

paperTitle: Satellite Infrastructure Sharing: Orbit-Structured Stochastic Geometry Modeling and Connectivity Analysis in Heterogeneous Satellite Networks
name: shared-sky
plan: Real LEO mega-constellations increasingly overlap without coordination — different operators launching independently, sharing sky and interference whether they agree to or not. The paper models this properly: satellites and orbital shells as a spherical Cox point process, random orbital structure with satellites scattered along it, each satellite given a random communication range, combined into a spherical Cox-Boolean coverage model, and derives closed-form expressions for connection probability, expected number of connections, and downlink signal-to-interference ratio in this interference-limited multi-operator setting, validated against system-level simulation. The toy: a 3D globe where you add your own constellation — altitude, shell density, per-satellite range — into a sky that already holds other operators' constellations, starting with a few seeded ones, later crowd-contributed. Pick any point on Earth and the page computes, from the paper's closed forms, its connection probability and SIR given every constellation currently in the sky, live as more get added. The finding worth building around: adding operators raises coverage but the SIR does not move the way naive intuition expects, because the model is interference-limited — more satellites overhead helps you connect and hurts your signal quality at the same time, and the paper's formulas say exactly how much of each. Turn one: one constellation, one ground point, the two output numbers, no sharing yet. What's hard: implementing the Cox-Boolean closed forms correctly and fast enough to recompute on every globe interaction, and explaining orbit-structured stochastic geometry as 'how crowded is the sky, exactly, and where.' Reuse mega/'s 3D globe rendering; the sharing and persistence layer is future work, not turn one.
mechanism: add a satellite constellation to a shared sky and read live coverage and interference at any ground point, computed from the paper's closed forms
text: add your satellite constellation to a crowded sky. pick any spot on earth and read live coverage and signal quality from the paper's closed forms, as orbital shells stack overhead. more satellites help and hurt at once

paperTitle: Scalable Multi-Agent Maze Traversal with Local Communication
name: relay-maze
plan: The paper gives a distributed algorithm for many agents entering an unknown, possibly cyclic maze one at a time from a single start node, each seeing only its immediate neighbours, hunting for an undisclosed goal without collisions. Coordination is a leader-follower relay: exactly one agent explores at any instant, running a single-agent maze solver, while the rest queue and communicate only locally; leadership switches when useful. It's proven complete and its makespan is asymptotically as good, in the number of agents, as a strategy that could see the whole maze from the start — and simulations up to 625 agents show the average fuel spent per agent actually falls as you add more agents, beating agents who just each run the solver independently. The mechanic: visitor builds or picks a maze (cave network, cyclic pipe layout), drops agents in one at a time at the start, and watches the relay run — one agent lit up as the active explorer, the rest visibly queued behind it, leadership passing at junctions and dead ends. A live fuel counter shows the per-agent average dropping as the roster grows, which is the counterintuitive number worth proving to yourself. Turn one: a single fixed small maze, add agents one and two, and make the handoff itself legible — who's leading, why it switched — before generalizing to bigger mazes or agent counts. The hard part is exactly that legibility: the algorithm's whole point is agents that don't see the global map, so the UI has to show local-only knowledge without turning into unreadable spaghetti once agents queue up. Reuse games/'s Durable Object rooms to let a real group each drive one agent live instead of watching a bot swarm, and workers/scores for average-fuel-per-agent records across maze and agent-count combinations.
mechanism: n-agent maze exploration via leader-follower relay under strictly local communication
text: agents queue at a maze entrance, one explores at a time, handing off leadership at junctions and dead ends. watch the relay unfold and the queue light up. add more agents and the average fuel per explorer actually drops. the math seems backwards but it holds

paperTitle: The Shape of the Vertical Action Distribution Locates the Scatterers that Heat the Galactic Disc
name: midplane
plan: The paper works out, in closed form, what the vertical motion of disc stars should look like depending on where the objects that jostle them sit: p(Jz) proportional to exp[-(Jz/J0)^(2-b)], where b comes purely from how the scattering rate depends on action. Objects that fill the whole disc volume give b=1, a plain exponential tail; objects confined to a thin layer at the midplane, like giant molecular clouds, give b=1/2, a sharper cutoff, because a midplane scatterer only gets a shot at a star during its fast plane-crossing, not while it lingers near its slow turning points. Fit to 7589 real red-clump stars, b comes out at 0.51 — squarely the thin-layer answer — and the fit's amplitude converts to an effective scatterer mass around two million solar masses, matching real molecular-cloud catalogues. The mechanic: visitor is a detective with one dial, from 'thin midplane layer' to 'fills the whole disc,' that continuously sets b. Dialing it runs a toy population of stars getting kicked — fast, glancing kicks if scatterers are confined to a strip at the midplane; steady kicks throughout if they fill the column — and a live histogram of resulting vertical action builds up and visibly changes shape, cutoff sharpening as the dial moves toward 'thin layer.' Turn one ships just that: the dial, the kicking sim, and the live histogram, no real data yet. The hard part is making the mechanism visible, not just the output curve — the plane band where kicks land has to be drawn so the geometry, not a magic exponent, is doing the explaining. A later turn loads the real stellar sample and asks the visitor to fit b themselves, reproducing the paper's finding by hand. Reuse packages/dataviz for the histogram and curve overlay, and workers/scores for a closest-guess leaderboard once real data ships.
mechanism: dial where hidden scatterers live and watch the resulting vertical-action histogram change shape
text: dial where hidden scatterers sit—thin layer or spread everywhere—and watch the pattern of stellar motion shift and reshape. thin layers leave a sharper mark. see the geometry, then fit the real sample yourself to find where the kicks come from

paperTitle: Spectral phase transitions in Gaussian multi-index models
name: spectral-outlier
plan: The paper is about recovering a hidden low-dimensional direction from high-dimensional data where you only see nonlinear, noisy projections onto it — call it 'how many samples per dimension before a signal becomes findable.' Earlier work pinned an exact threshold, alpha_c, for when this is possible at all. This paper shows a much simpler method reaches that same threshold: build a matrix from the data, weighted by any fixed preprocessing of the labels, and look at its top eigenvalue. Below alpha_c it sits inside the bulk of noise eigenvalues; above alpha_c, a genuine outlier detaches, and its eigenvector recovers the hidden direction — and the paper shows the best possible choice of preprocessing is exactly the one an unrelated, more complicated method had already guessed. The mechanic: visitor drags a slider setting samples-per-dimension, generates fresh random data with a hidden direction baked in, and watches the live eigenvalue spectrum: a cloud of noise, plus one point that's either buried in the cloud or clearly detached from it. The reveal is watching that point cross from 'inside the pack' to 'its own thing' as the slider crosses the theoretical line. Turn one: fixed small dimension, one preprocessing choice, the slider, and an instant spectrum redraw on resample — the detachment itself is the whole demo. The hard part is making 'detached' visually unambiguous rather than a fuzzy judgment call, and keeping the eigendecomposition fast enough client-side for instant redraws. Crowd version: before revealing the true threshold, visitors mark where they think it is; aggregate everyone's guesses into a histogram against the actual constant, wisdom-of-crowd against a fixed number. Reuse packages/dataviz for both the spectrum and guess histogram, workers/scores for tightest-average-guess standings.
mechanism: slide the sample-to-dimension ratio and watch an eigenvalue detach from the noise bulk at the theoretical threshold
text: slide samples-per-dimension and watch one point split away from the noise cloud. below the threshold it stays buried in the pack; above it, stands alone. the simple method reaches the theoretical limit. mark where you think the line is, stack your guess against the crowd

paperTitle: Metastable soliton necklaces confined by the boundary of a flattop region
name: necklace
plan: In a two-component medium with competing cubic and quintic nonlinearities, the paper finds ring-shaped necklaces of solitons that hold together for a long but finite stretch — about a hundred diffraction lengths, even with noise added — not because the solitons attract, but because two effects fight to a draw: solitons repel each other within one component, while a flattop region's boundary in the other component pens the ring in. The maximum number of solitons a necklace can hold before it breaks apart is set by just two dials: how big each soliton is, and how wide the flattop region is. The mechanic: visitor sets soliton size and flattop width, seeds a ring of N solitons, and runs the beam forward in diffraction-length time, watching the ring either hold its shape for a long stretch or come apart. Push N up at fixed dial settings until the necklace stops holding — that ceiling is the paper's actual finding, not an aesthetic choice. Turn one ships a single fixed necklace, say six solitons, at one set of dial values, animating it holding together, with no dial control yet — proving the simulation itself looks like beads on a ring, not mush, before any interactivity is added. The hard part is exactly that: this is a real coupled nonlinear-Schrodinger-type system, and a faithful split-step solver has to run at interactive framerates in-browser on a coarse grid without losing the beaded look that makes the phenomenon legible. Crowd: a record table of the most solitons held metastably past a fixed threshold at a given size/width pair, checkable because anyone can replay the same seed and parameters, not just claim the number. Reuse existing in-browser WASM/shader simulation patterns from the generative-family sites, and workers/scores for the record table.
mechanism: tune soliton size and flattop width and watch a ring of solitons hold together or break apart
text: set soliton size and flattop width, seed a ring of bright beads, watch them hold or break. there's a maximum—push the count too high and the necklace falls apart. two dials set the ceiling for how many beads hold stable before it snaps

paperTitle: The Average Singular Value of a Real Square Gaussian Random Matrix Strictly Increases with Dimension
name: spectral-climb
text: pick an N, sample random matrices, watch the average singular value climb. each step up is guaranteed at least 1/(1000*N^2) — monotonic growth, not asymptotic
plan: The paper settles a Bandeira-Kennedy-Singer conjecture: for an N-by-N real Gaussian random matrix, the average singular value (scaled by N^-3/2) increases strictly with N, climbing toward the Marchenko-Pastur limit 8/(3*pi), and it proves the step-to-step gain is always bigger than 1/(1000*N^2) — a real quantitative floor, not just monotonicity in the limit. The toy hands the visitor that climb. Pick N with a slider, hit sample, and a client-side Gaussian matrix is drawn and its singular values averaged; the running mean lands as a dot at that N, with the 8/(3*pi) line drawn as a ceiling it approaches but the paper says never touches. Turn one ships that: slider, sample button, scatter of dots climbing toward the asymptote, with the first five N shown against the paper's exact closed forms so the visitor can check the site's arithmetic against the paper's own numbers before trusting anything further out. The hard part, named plainly: the theorem is about the expectation, and a single sampled matrix jitters around it by more than the guaranteed 1/(1000*N^2) gap — so a visitor clicking sample twice can watch the mean go the 'wrong' way and think the theorem is false. The fix is to show the running average with a shrinking confidence band and let the visitor keep sampling until the band is narrower than the guaranteed step, which turns the objection into the actual content of the page: rare law of large numbers made tangible, not hidden. What to reuse: packages/dataviz's charts.js for the scatter and band; the visitor's own repo via com.minomobi.lab.score to save the largest N at which they personally verified strict increase, higherIsBetter true.
mechanism: sample random matrices at chosen N and watch the averaged singular value climb monotonically toward a fixed limit

paperTitle: Topology-Preserving Meshing of Implicit Scalar Fields via Monotonicity Constraints
name: critical-mesh
text: drag bumps in an implicit field. a coarse mesh miscounts peaks and valleys; a mesh refined where needed catches them all while using far fewer triangles than brute-force refinement
plan: The paper attacks a specific failure mode in scientific visualization: when a scalar field is given implicitly (evaluable at any point, not sampled on a grid) and you triangulate it to find its critical points — peaks, pits, saddles, the Morse-Smale complex — a coarse or careless mesh can miss a critical point entirely or invent one that was never there. Its fix is an insight small enough to demo: if every edge of the mesh is monotonic along the field (the field never goes up then down along that edge), the resulting flat mesh is topologically honest, so refine only where an edge violates monotonicity. The toy puts the visitor in charge of a small implicit field — a handful of draggable Gaussian bumps and pits summed together — rendered live as a coarse uniform mesh next to the same field meshed by the paper's monotonicity-refinement rule. A critical-point counter sits on each: the coarse mesh's count visibly lies (a saddle merges into nothing, a bump splits into two) while the refined mesh's count holds steady as the visitor drags bumps around, using far fewer triangles than brute-force fine refinement would need. Turn one ships exactly that pair of meshes plus the counters and drag handles — no game yet, just the honest comparison, which is the whole point before anything else is added. The hard part, named: the paper's own abstract says the method is correct 'in our experiments,' not proven, so the page must not claim guaranteed correctness — frame it as a much better bet, not a proof, and let a visitor who drags hard enough occasionally catch it out, which is itself instructive. What to reuse: nothing existing quite fits; this is a new client-side canvas piece, a small monotonic-refinement routine written from the paper's rule, and com.minomobi.lab.score for triangle-count golf on a fixed challenge field, fewer triangles for a correct count being better.
mechanism: drag bumps in an implicit 2D field and compare a coarse mesh's wrong critical-point count against an adaptively refined mesh's correct one

paperTitle: Going in Circles: Collaborative Multi-Robot Treasure Hunting
name: circle-treasures
text: place treasures on a circle, draw a route. the paper solves the easy case first — one robot, treasures known — giving you an optimal to race against
