plan: The setup: n robots start together at the center of a disk, k treasures are hidden somewhere on the unit circle around them, robots move anywhere in the plane at speed at most 1, and the instant one robot finds a treasure every robot knows. The goal is the total time for every robot to have personally visited every treasure. The paper's real move is solving the easy version first — one robot, full advance knowledge of where every treasure sits on the circle — as a routing problem, and using that exact solution to bound the hard, blind, multi-robot version. That routing problem is the honest turn-one toy: place k treasure markers anywhere on a circle, and the visitor draws a route from the center that they believe visits all of them fastest, with a live timer totaling travel distance at speed 1. A solver button reveals the paper's optimal route and its length, so the visitor's route is scored against a real bound, not a guess at one. Only after that ships does it grow into the actual n-player game: each visitor in a shared room is a blind robot, treasures are hidden from everyone, and finding one broadcasts its location to the rest of the room instantly — so the group's time depends on how well strangers avoid duplicating each other's search, which is exactly the paper's problem and cannot be tested by one person alone. The hard part: making 'instant sharing' feel like a real coordination decision rather than the game solving itself — robots need enough independent choice (which direction, when to backtrack) that duplicated effort is a visible, embarrassing possibility, not something the interface prevents. What to reuse: games/'s Durable Object room pattern for the shared blind-search mode once turn one's solved routing puzzle exists; com.minomobi.lab.score for the single-robot best route length.
mechanism: route a robot around unknown treasures on a circle against an optimal bound, then coordinate blind robots in a shared room where discoveries are shared instantly

paperTitle: Enhancing the power of a quantum heat engine via control of the system-reservoir coupling
name: power-stroke
text: tune a quantum Otto engine's stroke timing and reservoir coupling. as you move the coupling dial, power rises while efficiency stays pinned — the paper's new lever beats stroke-timing alone
plan: A quantum Otto engine runs a working substance through hot and cold strokes against two reservoirs, and the standard way to get more power out of one is to change how long each stroke runs. This paper demonstrates, on real ultracold atoms, a second lever nobody had controlled directly before: the reservoir's own temperature changes the microscopic collision rate at which it exchanges heat, which makes the heating and cooling strokes relax at different, asymmetric rates — and tuning that asymmetry lets you extract more power from the cycle without giving up any efficiency, which stroke-timing alone cannot do. The toy is an engine room with two dials instead of one: stroke-time allocation, the obvious lever, and reservoir coupling, the paper's new one. Two gauges read power output and efficiency as the visitor adjusts either dial, run against a simple Otto-cycle simulation. Turn one ships the dials, the gauges, and a fixed-efficiency contour line on the power-vs-coupling plot, so the visitor can literally watch power rise while staying pinned to one efficiency value by moving only the second dial — the specific, checkable claim the paper makes. The hard part: making the asymmetric relaxation legible without hiding it inside a black-box formula; the honest move is to show the two strokes as separate little relaxation curves with different visible rates, so the coupling dial's effect on power is traceable back to a difference the visitor can actually see. What to reuse: packages/dataviz for the dual gauges and the power/efficiency contour plot; com.minomobi.lab.score for the highest power found at a target efficiency, higherIsBetter true.
mechanism: tune stroke timing and reservoir coupling on a simulated quantum Otto engine to raise power while efficiency stays pinned

paperTitle: Degree Game for Special Regular Graphs
name: degree-duel
plan: The Maker-Breaker degree game: two players alternately claim previously-unclaimed edges of a d-regular graph. Maker wants to maximize the top degree in their own claimed subgraph; Breaker wants to cap everyone's degree. A classic pairing strategy lets Breaker hold every vertex to at most floor(d/4) on any d-regular graph — a bound Beck called the first of positional game theory's seven most humiliating open problems, because nobody could push it further for general graphs. This paper does push it, for specific families: on the hypercube Q_d, Breaker can guarantee floor(d/3), and on the smallest case, Q_3 (the cube: 8 vertices, 12 edges, 3-regular), Breaker can force degree exactly 1 at every vertex, no exceptions. The mechanic: two players alternately click unclaimed edges of Q_3, shown as a cube diagram. One is Maker, one is Breaker; live per-vertex degree counts for each player's claimed edges. Turn one ships pass-and-play on Q_3 only, with a scoreboard showing whether Breaker actually held the 1-per-vertex guarantee. The hard part, and the whole point, is a real Breaker bot implementing the actual pairing strategy so a visitor can try to beat the bound and fail — a scorekeeper without an adversary is not the game, the same lesson as Eleven Hats' proper-colouring opponent. Later turns extend to bigger hypercubes, grids, and tori where the paper's bound is proven but untested by human play. Reuse: `games/`'s Durable Object rooms for matchmaking and a leaderboard tracking best degree achieved per graph family as d grows, which is a genuinely open question the paper doesn't answer for most families.
mechanism: alternating edge-claiming Maker-Breaker game on regular graphs, played against a pairing-strategy bot
text: claim cube edges, one turn each. maker wants high degree, breaker uses a pairing strategy to cap it at 1 per vertex

paperTitle: Estimating Community Boundaries in Geometric Random Graphs
name: seamfinder
plan: Take the unit square and split it with a vertical line at x=p into two communities. Scatter N points uniformly across it. Connect two points if they're close enough — but 'close enough' depends on whether they're in the same community (radius R_N) or different ones (radius R_N'). The result is a geometric stochastic block model: a dot-and-edge graph with a hidden seam. Given only that graph and the dot positions, the paper asks whether p can be recovered at all, and proves a sharp answer: consistent estimation is possible exactly when R_N and R_N' scale against N in certain ways, impossible otherwise, with an explicit estimator that converges to the true p whenever it's possible. The mechanic: the visitor sees the scattered, connected dots (p hidden) and drags a vertical line across the square to guess the seam by eye, scored on distance to the true value once revealed. Turn one ships exactly that — generate, guess, reveal, score — with N and the two radii fixed at values inside the solvable regime, no auth, no server. The hard part is the paper's other half: a mode where the radii are set outside the consistency conditions, so the same interface visibly stops being guessable rather than just getting harder — noise the eye can't beat and neither can the paper's estimator. Showing that boundary between 'estimable' and 'not' concretely, rather than as a footnote, is the actual point of building this instead of a generic dot-scatter demo. A later turn overlays the paper's own estimator's guess next to the visitor's, converging as N grows. Crowd feature: a running average of human guess error against the threshold, which nobody currently has for real people rather than the paper's asymptotics.
mechanism: drag a line to guess a hidden community boundary from a scattered, partially-connected point set
text: find the hidden vertical line in scattered dots where edges form at different distances per community. guess by eye, then see the true boundary revealed. the paper shows a phase transition: certain settings make the boundary unrecoverable

paperTitle: Ideal heat engine cycles at maximal efficiency -- the ideal gas and beyond
name: linear-medium
plan: A heat engine's working medium — the ideal gas, say — is fully described by a Helmholtz potential, a function of temperature and volume. The paper asks: starting from a general potential that's polynomial in both, which medium gives the highest efficiency for a given cycle (Stirling, Otto, or Brayton)? The answer is universal across all three cycles: the maximum is always achieved by media that are linear in temperature. That family includes the ideal gas, but also classical harmonic oscillators and phenomenological rubber-band models — three physically unrelated substances sharing one algebraic property and, because of it, the same efficiency ceiling. The mechanic: the visitor designs a working medium by setting the coefficients of a small polynomial (constant, linear, quadratic, cubic terms in temperature), picks a cycle, and the site actually runs that cycle on that medium and reports its efficiency against the linear-medium ceiling for the chosen cycle. The game is tuning the nonlinear coefficients to approach the ceiling as closely as possible, knowing from the paper that crossing it is impossible. Turn one ships the coefficient sliders, a cycle picker, and a live efficiency-versus-ceiling readout — no auth, no server. The hard part is real: deriving closed-form efficiency expressions for all three cycles from a general polynomial potential, not hardcoding the ideal-gas answer and faking the rest, since the derivation is the actual content of the paper. Reuse: `tide/`, the thermodynamics wing of the O'Neill cylinder pack, where 'design the habitat engine's working gas' is a natural framing; a leaderboard for closest approach to the ceiling with a genuinely nonlinear medium, checkable by recomputation the same way the Erdős toy's records are.
mechanism: tune a working medium's polynomial coefficients and run a heat-engine cycle against an efficiency ceiling
text: design a working medium for a heat engine by tuning polynomial terms in temperature. run your chosen cycle and see your efficiency vs a universal ceiling the paper derives. linear media always reach that ceiling

paperTitle: TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures
name: grid-slack
plan: TANGCO takes on a hard infrastructure problem: give every node in a network a slice of a fixed capacity budget, and when a node's load exceeds its capacity it fails and dumps its load onto its surviving neighbors — which can cascade through the whole system. Nobody knows the optimal way to spend a capacity budget across nodes, because whether the network survives is a non-differentiable fail-or-survive outcome, so the paper trains a graph neural network policy instead and tests it against four hand-designed heuristics on 450 synthetic graphs plus five real networks (power, road, air, internet). It beats the best heuristic almost everywhere, with robustness gains from 1.6% to 246% depending on the network. The toy hands visitors the same allocation problem on one small graph: drag a fixed total budget onto nodes, trigger a load shock at one node, and watch it propagate — anything over capacity fails and splits its load across its surviving neighbors, and the cascade either stalls or eats the network. Turn one ships one graph, one reproducible shock, a capacity slider per node, and a survival count compared live against three of the paper's own heuristics. What's hard: the cascade rule has to be the paper's actual local load-redistribution, not an invented one, and the shock needs a fixed seed so allocations are genuinely comparable across visitors rather than lucky or unlucky. Reuse: workers/scores for a leaderboard keyed by graph-plus-shock, so a submitted allocation is a checkable number, not a vibe.
mechanism: drag a fixed capacity budget onto network nodes and watch a load shock cascade or die out
text: drag a capacity budget across network nodes, shock one point, and watch the cascade die or propagate. the best policies beat hand-tuned heuristics by up to 246%

paperTitle: Beyond persuasion: Mobile electoral interfaces in polarized societies
name: swing-mass
plan: The paper builds a minimal model of polarized elections where two committed blocs almost never convert each other directly — instead, a third group of mobile voters gets allocated between the blocs by a Fermi-like probabilistic rule with a tunable rejection asymmetry. The result: how much an election swings in response to a shock is proportional to the size of that mobile group, not to how hard anyone tries to persuade the committed blocs. Push the dials in either direction and the model predicts a whole continuum of regimes, from frozen polarization to a highly responsive electorate. The toy puts the visitor in charge of the two dials — mobile fraction size, and rejection asymmetry — over a population split into three visible groups: bloc A, bloc B, and the mobile middle. Turn one ships the two dials, a shock button, and a before/after readout of the electoral split, with a second panel that tries to persuade committed voters directly and shows it doing almost nothing by comparison. What's hard: making the counterintuitive point land without sliding into implying anything about real elections or parties — labels stay neutral (Bloc A / Bloc B), the page states plainly that this is an abstract dynamical model, not a forecasting tool, and the susceptibility-scales-with-mobile-size claim has to be visibly demonstrated by the shock, not just asserted. The crowd fit: since the paper predicts a continuum of regimes, visitors submitting mobile-fraction and asymmetry pairs and their resulting susceptibility builds a shared map of the regime space nobody has drawn yet. Reuse: no existing surface fits directly; this ships standalone with packages/dataviz for the population and susceptibility visuals.
mechanism: set the mobile-voter fraction and rejection asymmetry, shock the population, and watch the electorate swing
text: set how many voters can swing and how much they resist, then shock the population. watch which dial moves the numbers—the swing tracks the mobile fraction size, not how hard you push the committed

paperTitle: Shared environmental risk selects asymmetric inheritance of a protective reserve
name: reserve-split
plan: The paper models a cell dividing a protective reserve between two daughters every generation, under a fixed partition policy: how much of the reserve goes to one daughter versus the other. Long-run fitness is set by the top Lyapunov exponent of the resulting random operator product across many generations. When the environment's shocks are mostly private to each lineage, even splitting wins; but once environmental innovation is sufficiently shared between the daughters, a separated, asymmetric split near a partition of roughly 0.2 becomes fitter instead — and the switch happens as a finite jump between the two strategies, not a smooth slide from one to the other. The toy puts the visitor in the mother cell's seat: one slider sets the partition (how unevenly the reserve is split), a second sets how much of each generation's environmental shock is shared versus private, and a run-generations button plays out many rounds and reports a growth-rate estimate for that pair of settings, tracked with a marker showing which partition currently wins. Turn one ships exactly that — two sliders, a run button, and the growth-rate readout — with the marker visibly jumping from even-split to the roughly-0.2 branch once shared risk crosses its threshold, rather than crawling there. What's hard: a live top-Lyapunov-exponent estimate has to come from an honest Monte Carlo average over many simulated generations, not a closed-form shortcut, and the framing needs to read as biology — a store of some protective resource split between daughter cells each round — rather than abstract linear algebra. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the growth-rate curve; no existing surface's simulation machinery fits a single-lineage generational sim like this one.
mechanism: split a protective reserve between two daughter lineages across generations and watch which split wins
text: you're a cell splitting a protective reserve between daughters every generation. tune the split ratio and how much environmental risk they share, run generations, and watch which strategy wins—even split loses once risk gets shared

paperTitle: The sensitivity of TESS to transiting planets in TOIs with close-in stellar companions
name: hidden-transit
plan: TESS's transit surveys assume single stars, but many host stars turn out to have a close-in companion invisible to TESS's own resolution — caught only by dedicated speckle interferometry. This paper compares 2052 TOIs confirmed single by speckle imaging against 188 TOIs in unresolved binaries, corrects each transit's signal-to-noise for dilution by the unseen companion, and builds sensitivity grids showing how detectability depends on planet radius, orbital period, host spectral type, and binarity. The sharpest finding: sensitivity is especially bad for a planet transiting the secondary star of an unresolved pair, and it gets worse the bigger the brightness gap between the two stars — a bias against small planets the catalog alone doesn't show you. The toy is a guessing game built on the paper's own released grids: visitors get a planet (radius, period), a star with a hidden companion at some magnitude difference, and a choice of which star it transits, and guess whether TESS would have flagged it before the sensitivity grid reveals the real call. Turn one ships that loop — pick a case, guess detected or missed, reveal the true call plus where it falls on the sensitivity grid — with a running accuracy score for the session. What's hard: this only works honestly if it pulls the paper's actual published sensitivity grids rather than inventing a plausible-looking detection curve; if the grids aren't retrievable in time, the page has to say so and fall back to a labeled approximation rather than presenting a guess as the paper's result. Reuse: workers/scores for a running-accuracy leaderboard, since the paper's most interesting number is how badly human intuition underrates the secondary-star bias, and that's a crowd statistic worth collecting.
mechanism: guess whether TESS would catch a planet hidden behind a close stellar companion, then check the real sensitivity grid
text: guess whether a planet detector would spot a world hiding behind its host star's close companion, then check the real sensitivity grid. secondary-star systems trip up intuition way harder than anyone expects

paperTitle: Power in Liquid Democracy: A Network Centrality Approach
name: proxy-power
plan: Liquid democracy lets you delegate your vote to someone else, who can re-delegate it again, and you can reclaim it any time — this paper asks who actually holds power in a network built that way. It proposes measuring it with Random Walk Decay centrality, a random-walk-based measure that discounts influence the further it travels through a delegation chain, argues for its advantages over alternatives like PageRank in this setting, derives an axiomatic characterization, and proposes ways to pick a representative slate of influential participants from the result. The toy is a small delegation network visitors build by hand: drag an arrow from yourself to whoever you delegate to, or keep your own vote, with chains running several hops deep, and watch two power measures update live side by side — a naive count of how many votes ultimately route through you, and a decayed random-walk measure in the paper's spirit. The two disagree exactly where delegation chains create hidden hubs, and that gap is the point. Turn one ships a fixed cast of eight to twelve participants, drag-to-redelegate, and the two live bar charts, plus one scripted scenario where everyone routes through a single popular node so the divergence is visible on load. What's hard: the abstract names the measure but not its closed form, so the toy implements a clearly labeled, defensible approximation — a decayed random walk over the delegation graph — and says plainly it's inspired by the paper's approach rather than a reproduction of its exact axioms. The real prize is a version built on real accounts, where the delegation network and the power ranking are made of visitors' actual choices rather than a toy cast. Reuse: auth.mino.mobi for identity once that version ships.
mechanism: redirect delegation arrows in a liquid-democracy network and watch two power rankings diverge
text: drag arrows to build a delegation network—delegate your vote to someone, they delegate to someone else—and watch two power measures diverge. naive vote-counting misses the hidden hubs that sophisticated centrality finds

paperTitle: The transversal achievement game on a square grid
name: transversal
plan: On an n×n board two players alternately claim empty cells; the first to own a full transversal (n cells, no two sharing a row or column) wins. The paper gives an independent proof that player one wins for every n≥4, and sharpens it to a bound nobody had: the strategy forces the win by ply 2n+3, on player one's own (n+2)-th move, with the strategy fully determined by a fixed rule on the current board so it can be coded directly rather than searched for. Small cases (n=4,5,6) are exhaustively verified against every legal defense, and the theorem is machine-checked in Lean. The mechanic: you play second against the site's implementation of that rule, on boards from n=4 up. You cannot win. The point isn't difficulty, it's watching the forced win land exactly on schedule — a live ply counter ticking toward 2n+3 makes the bound tangible instead of asserted. Turn one ships n=4 and n=5 single-player against the rule-following bot, board rendered as a grid with claimed cells colored per player and a highlight on which row/column a transversal would still need. The hard part: implementing the actual rule from the paper faithfully rather than a generic minimax bot, since the whole point is that this specific rule is what forces the 2n+3 bound — a bot that wins by brute search proves nothing. Reuse `games/`'s room and rendering conventions even for the single-player version (it's the same board-claiming primitive as their party games), and `workers/scores` for fastest-loss and largest-n-attempted tracking once a two-player queue exists.
mechanism: alternating-claim board game against an explicit, provably forced winning strategy
text: claim cells on a grid to form a transversal. the bot plays with a rule that forces a win by move n+2 — every game. you can't beat it. the whole point is watching the forced strategy tick down to checkmate exactly on schedule

paperTitle: Representation in Peer Selection: A Liquid Democracy Perspective
name: delegate
plan: Peer selection: a group must pick a fixed-size committee from among themselves. The paper restricts this to what it calls liquid profiles — each voter names exactly one trusted peer, and automatically approves everyone that peer approves, chaining transitively, mirroring delegation in liquid democracy. Under this one-delegate restriction, the paper shows proportionality guarantees that are normally hard to get from approval ballots become attainable, and it studies which committee-selection rules actually deliver them. The mechanic: visitors are the peer pool. Each names one other visitor they trust (from whoever is currently registered); the site computes each person's induced approval set by following the trust chain, then runs a committee-selection rule live and shows who got seated and why — highlighting which voters are represented through a chain of delegation rather than a direct vote. Turn one ships with a fixed small synthetic pool (a handful of named seats, pre-loaded trust graph) so the mechanic is checkable before any real identity system is wired in: draw the delegation graph, click a rule, watch the committee assemble and the approval-chain animate outward from each seat. The hard part: making a proportionality violation visible rather than asserted — probably a companion metric that flags a voter whose delegate's delegate's pick got seated only because of an unrelated third voter, so the trust-chain payoff is legible on the page, not just in a caption. Reuse the shared OAuth worker once real pools are wired up, so trust edges are between actual Bluesky identities, and `civ`/`polis`'s graph-rendering conventions for the delegation diagram.
mechanism: single-delegate transitive trust graph feeding a live committee-selection rule
text: name one person you trust. everyone they trust gets added to your approval set, chaining down. the site runs a committee-selection rule and shows you who's seated — and whether they got there through your vote or through their chain. trust shapes representation

paperTitle: Three trees suffice for a constant stretch in minor-free graphs
name: threetrees
plan: A tree cover of a graph is a small set of spanning trees such that every pair of vertices has its graph distance approximated, within a constant factor (the stretch), by at least one tree in the set. The paper shows any graph excluding a fixed minor H — a huge class that includes every planar graph — has a tree cover using just 3 trees with constant stretch, and proves this is tight: a toroidal grid needs at least 3, matching a recent lower bound exactly. The toy: hand the visitor a graph-building canvas restricted to a chosen forbidden minor (start with planar, since it's the easiest to draw without breaking the rule) and three tree-color pens. They lay down a graph, then try to cover it with 3 trees — drag edges into tree A, B, or C — while a live stretch meter reports the worst distance distortion across every vertex pair given the current coloring. Turn one ships a fixed small planar graph (12–16 vertices) with the three-pen assignment tool and the stretch meter; winning is getting the meter as close to the paper's constant as your coloring allows. What's hard: computing stretch live for every pair is the expensive part, and explaining a real-valued distortion bound to someone who has never heard the word without turning the page into a lecture — the meter has to carry that alone. The submission-worthy version is a visitor-built toroidal-grid-like graph that needs all 3 trees, since the paper names that exact shape as the extremal case. Reuse `math`/geometry's single-file explainer conventions and its stretch/metric visualizers, and `workers/scores` for best (lowest) stretch achieved per graph shape.
mechanism: manual 3-tree edge-coloring of a graph against a live worst-case stretch meter
text: color edges of a shape three ways, each forming a spanning tree connecting all vertices. a meter shows the distance stretch: how much longer paths get using one tree instead of the full graph. three colors always work for planar graphs. beat the paper's bound

paperTitle: Stochastic Spatial Metapopulation Modelling of HPAI Control and Poultry Restocking on Jolly Island
name: jolly
plan: A synthetic outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza on a fictional archipelago of farms (three production types: broiler, organic duck, other), simulated with a stochastic spatial SEIR model that includes local, environmental, movement, and distance-dependent spread, plus culling and restocking policy. The paper's numbers are concrete and a little brutal: preventive culling cuts cumulative burden from 16,362.7 to 13,631.9 infectious-farm-days (16.7%); confining farms earlier substantially shrinks the epidemic; and restocking timing is the real trade-off — restocking on 15 March met the rebound-probability threshold (0.20) under no tested policy, while 24 May was the first date any policy cleared it, and capacity-based restocking (versus flat-fraction) cut rebound probability from 0.780 to 0.533. You are the control authority: set a culling policy (reactive vs preventive), a confinement date, and a restocking date and fraction, run the outbreak on the island map, and watch two gauges — cumulative infectious-farm-days and rebound probability — respond, usually in opposite directions. Turn one ships the map, the three sliders, one run button, and both gauges reading out against the paper's own baseline numbers so a visitor's first run has something to compare against. What's hard: culling and confining too aggressively is cheap in the sim but devastating economically in reality, and the page has to hold that tension rather than reward the visitor for zeroing the epidemic — a farms-depopulated counter alongside the two gauges keeps the cost honest. Reuse `polis`/`civ`'s spatial agent-simulation machinery and stochastic-run scaffolding, and `packages/dataviz` for the gauge charts; crowd angle is a shared table of submitted policy triples ranked on the burden/rebound trade-off, the same pattern as a Pareto-frontier leaderboard.
mechanism: policy sliders (culling, confinement, restocking) driving a stochastic spatial outbreak sim against two competing gauges
text: an island's farms face avian flu. set your policy: culling (reactive or preventive), confinement date, restocking date. watch two gauges: infectious-farm-days and rebound probability. they pull opposite ways. see where the real trade-off lies

paperTitle: Capillary self-folding chains
name: capillary-fold
plan:
The paper builds physical chains of floating monomers where each segment's curved shape locally pushes the liquid surface up or down — an effective capillary charge, positive or negative. The counterintuitive physics: unlike electric charges, same-sign capillary charges attract and opposite signs repel, so the sequence of charges along a chain determines how it folds. Short chains obey nearest-neighbor rules and settle into one predictable shape — straight, zigzag, or a closed loop. Longer chains develop long-range interactions between non-adjacent segments, and the number of distinct stable folded shapes for a given charge sequence grows exponentially with chain length, mapped numerically in the paper and confirmed experimentally by shaking real chains until they hop between configurations.

The mechanic: the visitor assigns a +/- charge to each link of a chain, a toggle strip rather than a slider since this is discrete, like a genome. The site relaxes the chain under a same-attracts energy model and renders the fold. Turn one: chains of 4-6 links, one deterministic fold each, so a visitor can check the site against a hand-worked prediction before trusting it on longer chains. The hard part, for a later turn: past roughly ten links the fold stops being unique — the same sequence has several stable outcomes — and the site needs a shake action that injects noise, re-relaxes, and shows the visitor whether they landed on a genuinely new configuration or the one they already had.

Reuse: the WebGPU one-canvas-each shelf at `g/` for staging; `workers/scores` for a record table of most-metastable-sequence-found per chain length, since a claimed record is just a sequence anyone can re-relax and check.
mechanism: toggle a +/- capillary-charge sequence along a floating chain and watch it relax into a folded shape
text: toggle a +/- charge sequence along a floating chain and watch it fold. same charges attract, opposite ones repel — inverted electrostatics — so your sequence determines the shape. longer chains can settle into multiple different stable folds from the same sequence

paperTitle: Agent Behavioral Contracts II: Certifying Compositional Reliability Without Assuming Independence
name: correlated-fail
plan:
The paper tests an assumption every 'wire two AI agents together for redundancy' pitch quietly relies on: that when one agent in a pipeline fails, the odds another independently built agent also fails are unrelated to the first failure. Across 18,000 scored missions with a two-agent handoff, two instances of the same model co-fail on 90% of the missions where either fails at all — nowhere near independent. Swapping in a different model for one stage cuts that correlation in every one of six tested contrasts; swapping only the vendor while keeping the same underlying model does not move it at all, a result the authors pre-registered and report as a genuine null.

The mechanic: the visitor builds a small pipeline — pick a model for each of two or three stages from a short menu tagged by underlying model and by vendor — and the site shows two numbers side by side: the reliability you'd naively compute by multiplying each stage's solo success rate, and the real, correlation-corrected number, using the paper's measured co-failure statistics for same-model and different-model pairs. Turn one: a two-stage pipeline, four model choices, the two numbers and nothing else — no chart, no history, just the gap between what you assumed and what the data says. The hard part: making the same-vendor-different-model case land, since it's the surprising null and the naive intuition, 'at least it's a different company', is exactly what the paper shows doesn't help.

Reuse: `human/`'s exhibit framing for turning a paper's finding into something you poke at rather than read; `workers/scores` if a later turn adds a shared table of which pipeline configurations people have tried and how badly the naive estimate lied for each.
mechanism: assign models to pipeline stages and compare the naive reliability estimate against a correlation-corrected one
text: pick models for each stage of a pipeline and compare your naive reliability estimate against the measured number. two copies of the same model fail together on 90% of missions where either fails at all — nowhere near independent. swapping to a different model cuts that correlation sharply

paperTitle: Slow and Steady: Preventing MEV with Verifiable Delays
name: mev-delay
plan:
MEV, maximal extractable value, is the profit a block creator can take by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions the instant it spots an arbitrage or liquidation opportunity sitting in the mempool. This paper's defense doesn't hide transactions or add a committee — it forces every transaction through a verifiable delay before it can be included, long enough that a block creator cannot see an opportunity and react to it inside the same window without breaking the chain's liveness guarantee. The paper shows this holds against both Byzantine actors and purely rational ones, states the limits of the defense honestly, and reports that against real historical MEV data the mechanism would have blocked most of the extraction that actually happened.

The mechanic: the visitor is a searcher watching a live feed of price-moving events. With the delay at zero they can snipe nearly every opportunity by reacting the instant it appears — the paper's baseline problem, made playable. Dragging the delay up forces every reaction to queue behind a fixed wait, and the visitor watches their own capture rate collapse toward the rate a non-reacting participant would get by chance, the same collapse the paper argues is structural rather than a tuning accident. Turn one: single-player, one delay slider, one live feed, one running capture-rate number — no wallets, no chain, no real markets touched.

The hard part: making the delay read as a rule of the game rather than a lag switch. The visitor isn't slowed down, they're blind to anything that happened inside the delay window, and that distinction is the actual mechanism the paper is arguing for. A later turn can turn it into a multiplayer race using `games/`-style Durable Object rooms, where the point is that past a certain delay nobody can consistently win.

Reuse: `games/` DO rooms for the eventual multiplayer race; `workers/scores` for a capture-rate leaderboard measured at a fixed, published delay setting.
mechanism: drag a transaction-submission delay slider and watch your MEV capture rate collapse toward chance
text: you're a searcher hunting arbitrage in the mempool. drag a slider to delay your transactions and watch your capture rate collapse toward random chance. it's not lag slowing you down — you're blinded to opportunities happening inside the delay window, so you can't react to them

paperTitle: A Radon-Transform Perspective on Exoplanet Transits
name: shadow-twins
plan: The paper reframes what a transit light curve actually measures: during ingress and egress, the rate of change of brightness is a Radon-transform sample of the planet's silhouette, taken along the direction set by the local stellar limb. A single transit gives at most two such projection angles, so it constrains the silhouette's Fourier transform along only two radial slices — leaving, provably, a large null space of silhouettes that would produce an indistinguishable curve. The mechanic: the visitor draws a planetary silhouette on a disc (oblate, ringed, lumpy, whatever) and the site renders the resulting light curve and its ingress/egress derivative as two projection lines through Fourier space. Turn one ships that alone — draw, transit, see the curve and the two slices that curve actually pins down. The second layer, which can be a later turn, is the punch: given a target curve, search for a visibly different silhouette that reproduces it within noise, using only those two constraints, and lay the two shapes side by side. That search is the hard part — it's a constrained optimization over shape space, not a closed form, and needs to be fast enough to feel interactive; a coarse Fourier-slice matcher with a handful of free coefficients should do it without pretending to be a real inversion. What to reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the curve and Fourier-slice charts; no auth needed for turn one. The crowd payoff is a gallery of the most convincing twin pairs — shapes that look nothing alike but share a curve — submitted and voted on, which is exactly the paper's non-uniqueness result made into a hunt rather than a proof.
mechanism: draw a planet silhouette, see which two Fourier slices its transit curve actually constrains, then hunt for a visually different silhouette matching the same curve
text: draw any planet — lumpy, ringed, off-center, whatever. watch its transit curve shift and dip. then hunt for another planet that looks nothing like it but has the exact same curve. multiple silhouettes, one light signature

paperTitle: Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals
name: invariant-drill
plan: The paper builds INVARIANTEVAL, 28 real Ethereum exploits each paired with a human-authored program invariant that would have blocked it, and PONDEREPLAY, a replay harness that re-executes historical transactions to check an invariant's correctness. Replaying 108,637 historical transactions, the hand-written invariants block every one of the 28 attacks. The toy turns that into a drill: the visitor is shown a simplified before/after account-and-balance state from one historical exploit — a flash-loan drain, a reentrancy, whatever the first shipped case is — and builds an invariant from a menu of primitive predicates (balance deltas, ordering of calls, caller identity) rather than free-text code, since correctness of a hand-typed expression can't be checked client-side. The site then replays the real transaction sequence against the assembled invariant and reports pass/fail, plus whether it would also have blocked a batch of legitimate transactions (a false-positive check), because an invariant that stops everything is not a win. Turn one: one exploit, the predicate menu, and the replay-and-score against that single case — no leaderboard yet. What's hard: compressing 28 real EVM traces into legible, honest before/after states without a full EVM in the browser; this needs curated, simplified traces sourced faithfully from the paper's benchmark, not invented ones, and that curation is the real first-turn bottleneck, not the UI. What to reuse: `games/`-style puzzle framing and `workers/scores` for a leaderboard scored on exploits blocked minus false positives across the full 28, which is a genuine crowd-improves-it design since a broader invariant found by one visitor benefits everyone who plays after.
mechanism: assemble a program invariant from predicate pieces and replay a real historical exploit transaction against it to see if it would have been blocked
text: see a real ethereum exploit: a reentrancy, a flash-loan drain. build a safety rule from simple predicates — balance thresholds, call order, who's allowed to call. replay the attack. does your rule block it without breaking everything else

paperTitle: Local and quasilocal conservation laws of three-state IRF cellular automata and their quantum deformations
name: charge-race
plan: The paper studies two reversible three-state cellular automata (the species-preserving and species-flipping rules of Klobas and Prosen) and proves that within an explicit family of conserved quantities, the only nonzero propagation speeds are exactly plus or minus the square root of 3/23 — about 0.361, which matches a value the same authors had previously only estimated numerically. That's the toy's whole premise: an irrational speed limit, proven rather than fitted, sitting inside a grid you can watch tick. The mechanic: the visitor runs the automaton on a strip, drops a single tagged charge into an otherwise uniform background, and watches its front spread. A reference line moves across the grid at exactly sqrt(3/23) cells per step; the visitor's job is to see whether the charge's front keeps pace, falls behind, or — if they try to build an initial condition that seems to cheat — fails to beat it, because the paper's claim is that nothing in this conserved sector goes faster. Turn one ships one rule (species-preserving, the simpler of the two), the grid, and the race line; the quantum-deformed version and the second rule are later turns. The hard part, named honestly: the CA's actual transition table isn't in this abstract, it's defined in the cited 2022 paper, so the build must source that rule precisely rather than approximate it — get the rule wrong and the race line is decorating a different automaton. What to reuse: a plain canvas grid, no auth, no backend; `packages/dataviz` for the displacement-over-time plot that turns 'watch the race' into 'here's the measured slope converging on 0.361'.
mechanism: run a three-state cellular automaton, race a tagged charge's front against a reference line moving at the proven speed limit sqrt(3/23)
text: drop a charge into a cellular automaton. watch its front spread across the grid. race it against a reference line at exactly √(3/23) cells per step. nothing in this system accelerates past that speed — the paper proves it

paperTitle: Aging in a spin glass with a logarithmic potential
name: still-there
plan: The paper puts a random walker on a 2D lattice shaped by a discrete Gaussian free field: at each site the walker waits an exponentially distributed time whose mean grows with the field value there, then hops to a random neighbor. Below a critical temperature, the walker 'ages' — check its position at some time t, check again at time 2t, and there's a positive probability it's still near where it was, a probability governed asymptotically by the Generalized Arcsine Law with a parameter that depends on temperature. The mechanism driving it is concrete: the walker gets trapped for stretches that grow with the age of the system, in a landscape shaped by the field's near-extreme regions. The toy: the visitor sets a temperature, watches one walker cross a colored field (color = trap depth), picks a checkpoint time t, and bets whether the walker will still be nearby at 2t. Turn one ships a single run at a fixed small grid with the bet-and-reveal loop — no aggregation yet. What's hard, and should be named on the page: honestly sampling a discrete Gaussian free field in a browser at a grid size small enough to animate is a real numerical task, and the arcsine match will only be illustrative, not the paper's asymptotic result — say so rather than implying the small grid proves the theorem. The crowd payoff is the real point: pool every visitor's bet outcomes by temperature and trace out an empirical curve against the Generalized Arcsine Law's prediction, which is a distributed Monte-Carlo experiment on a genuinely slow phenomenon that one visitor alone can't resolve. Reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the field heatmap and the aggregate curve; no auth needed.
mechanism: watch a random walker cross a rugged potential landscape, bet whether it's still near its old position after the wait doubles, and pool results into the temperature-dependent arcsine curve
text: watch a random walker cross a rugged landscape. pick a time, bet whether it's still in the same region when time doubles. your bet plus everyone else's traces a curve: below critical temperature, walkers get trapped and freeze

paperTitle: Covering the ternary cube by binary subcubes
name: subcube
text: click subcubes on a 3×3 grid to cover every cell. each one picks two rows and two columns, lighting up the four cells at their intersection. you need at least ⌈(3/2)^n⌉ of them, but can you reach that floor?
plan: f(n) is the minimum number of subcubes of Z_3^n needed to cover it, where a subcube here is strict: every one of the n coordinates is restricted to 2 of its 3 possible values at once, not left free like an ordinary subcube. A counting argument gives f(n) ≥ (3/2)^n; the paper proves f(n) ≤ 2(3/2)^n − 1, answering a problem of Imre Leader, and shows f(n)/(3/2)^n is nondecreasing and converges to a constant C₃ pinned between 1.62227 and 2 — a genuinely open window. The mechanic: render Z_3^2 as a literal 3×3 grid, nine cells. A subcube is a choice of 2 of the 3 rows and 2 of the 3 columns; clicking one lights up the 4 cells at their intersection. The visitor clicks subcubes to cover every cell, and a live counter tracks how far above the ⌈(3/2)^n⌉ floor they land — beating your own count, or the site's, is the whole game. Turn one: ship exactly the 3×3 board (and ideally the 3×3×3 cube, 27 cells, still drawable) with click-to-place subcubes, a covered/uncovered readout, and the running lower bound displayed alongside. The hard part, named honestly: the interesting constant C₃ lives in the asymptotic regime, and n beyond 3 stops being renderable as a literal grid — a second-turn problem, not this one's. Reuse: math.mino.mobi's extremal-geometry family-resemblance framing for the writeup; workers/scores for a 'fewest subcubes at n' leaderboard, which is cheat-proof the same way the Erdős-rectangle toy is — any claimed cover is a list of subcubes anyone can recheck in milliseconds.
mechanism: cover a Z_3^n grid with all-coordinates-restricted-to-2-values blocks and race the (3/2)^n floor

paperTitle: The Gromov-Hausdorff Distance Between Consecutive Spheres
name: spheregap
text: match points from a circle to a sphere by dragging them. score yourself on the worst-case distance mismatch in your pairs. 60 degrees is the absolute minimum — a hidden triangle in the circle makes sure you never beat it
plan: The paper pins down the exact Gromov-Hausdorff distance between consecutive round spheres: d_GH(S^n, S^{n+1}) = ζ_n/2, where ζ_n = arccos(-1/(n+1)) is the angle between any two vertices of a regular simplex with n+2 vertices inscribed in S^n. For n=1 that simplex is an equilateral triangle in a circle, its vertex angle is 120°, so d_GH(S^1,S^2) = 60° exactly. This resolves a conjecture that was open for every n≥4, and a second result shows that as the dimension gap between two spheres grows slower than the spheres themselves, their Gromov-Hausdorff distance converges to exactly π/4 — spheres of different dimension never get more alike than that, however far out you go. The mechanic: the visitor builds a correspondence — drags points on a small sphere onto points of a bigger one, pair by pair — and the site scores the worst-case distance mismatch across every pair of matched points (the distortion). You cannot push distortion below ζ_n/2 no matter how you match, and after a few failed tries the site reveals why: the optimal matching runs through the vertices of that inscribed simplex. Turn one, scoped to n=1 only: circle-to-sphere, an explicit triangle-in-circle diagram, three draggable point-pairs, and a live distortion readout racing toward 60° and never beating it. The hard part, named: n≥2 needs an actual 3D-or-higher sphere renderer and the correspondence stops being three obvious points, so extending past n=1 is deliberately not turn one's job. Reuse: math.mino.mobi's geometry-pack shell and existing circle/sphere rendering; static, no backend, no auth.
mechanism: drag a point-matching between two spheres and get scored on the worst-case distance mismatch

paperTitle: Confinement transitions in half-space constrained Riesz gases
name: wallgas
text: tune the repulsion strength and wall pull on a 1D gas of particles. sometimes you can pull forever and the bulk cloud refuses to collapse. other times there's a critical strength where it snaps entirely onto the wall
plan: A Riesz gas is a cloud of like-charged particles repelling each other with a power-law force 1/r^s, held near a hard wall by an attractive pull. The paper proves a dichotomy in the interaction range s (dimension d): for the weakly long-ranged regime s ∈ (d−2, d) — which covers ordinary Coulomb repulsion — the equilibrium gas can never be pulled entirely onto the wall, however hard you pull; a bulk cloud always survives. For the strongly long-ranged regime s ∈ (d−3, d−2], there's a real confinement transition: past a critical wall strength, the whole equilibrium measure collapses onto the wall. The mechanic: two sliders, interaction exponent s and wall pull strength, over a 1D line of particles pinned to a half-line; the site numerically minimizes pairwise-repulsion-plus-wall-energy for a few dozen particles (gradient descent is fast enough to feel live) and plots the resulting density against distance from the wall. Turn one ships exactly that: two sliders, a live density profile, and a readout of whether the profile has collapsed to a spike at the wall or not. The payoff is dragging wall strength to its limit with s in the never-confines regime and watching the bulk refuse to vanish, then dropping s past d−2 and watching the same slider finish the job. The hard part, named plainly: the theorem is about a continuum equilibrium measure, not a 60-particle simulation, so the page has to say the jagged histogram stands in for a limit and that any 'critical strength' shown is read off the visible transition, not computed from the paper's formula. Reuse: g.mino.mobi's one-file canvas-sim shelf and no-build convention; packages/dataviz for the profile chart.
mechanism: push a charged 1D gas toward a wall and watch whether it can ever fully collapse onto it

paperTitle: A linear upper bound on the number of moves required for independent set reconfiguration with two sliding tokens
name: token-slide
plan: Two tokens sit on nonadjacent vertices of a graph. A move slides one token along an edge to a new vertex, and the two tokens must stay nonadjacent after every move -- this is the token-sliding version of independent-set reconfiguration. The open question, from Briański, Felsner, Hodor and Micek's 2021 paper on interval graphs, was how many moves a reconfiguration ever needs. This paper answers it for a graph on n vertices: if a target pair is reachable from a starting pair at all, it is always reachable within 4n moves -- a genuinely small, linear bound on a problem that could in principle need far more. The mechanic: click a token, click an adjacent empty vertex to slide it there; illegal moves (landing adjacent to the other token) simply aren't offered. The visitor is shown a start pair and a target pair on a small graph and slides tokens across until both land where they should, with a running move counter and the 4n ceiling shown as a par line to beat. Turn one ships one preset graph (12-20 vertices, force-directed layout), the click-to-slide interaction, a target-reached win state, and a feasibility check so an impossible target says so instead of leaving the visitor stuck forever. What's hard: 4n is only an upper bound, not the true optimum, so "par" isn't "best possible" -- the real optimum needs a server-side breadth-first search over the whole token-configuration space, tractable only for small graphs, and the site should be clear about which number it's showing. Reuse: `math`'s single-page explainer conventions for the write-up, `workers/scores` for a per-puzzle leaderboard (fewer moves wins), and later, crowd-submitted graphs ranked by how close players get to 4n.
mechanism: slide two tokens across a graph, one edge at a time while they stay nonadjacent, to reach a target pair
text: slide two tokens on a graph to reach a target pair. always possible in just 4n moves — a linear bound when the problem looked exponential

paperTitle: Adversarial Robustness in Smishing Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Adversarial Fragility in Classical vs. Transformer-Based Detection Systems
name: leet-drill
plan: Five smishing-message classifiers, tested against real attacks: three classical models (Random Forest, XGBoost, a CNN+BiLSTM) and two multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa), scored by how much accuracy attacks strip away (a Robustness Degradation Ratio). The finding: classical models collapse under character obfuscation and structural perturbation, losing up to 98.8% of their accuracy, while transformers hold up far better, losing at most 35.1% -- but transformers' own weak spot is specifically structural perturbation, and clean-text accuracy is no guide at all (XLM-RoBERTa scores higher clean than mBERT but degrades more under attack). Mechanic: the visitor edits a scam text message in a live box; two gauges, one modeling the classical detectors and one the transformer, score it as spam or not in real time. The goal is to keep the message readable as an obvious scam to a human while sneaking it past a gauge, using the paper's own attack families: swap characters, code-switch a word into another script, or reorder the sentence's structure. Turn one ships only the classical gauge -- cheap, deterministic, shippable as JSON weights, no model runtime needed -- with a fixed target message and a live score. A later turn adds the transformer gauge as a small distilled model running client-side, honestly labeled as a downscaled reproduction rather than the paper's own model. What's hard: the whole point is that transformers fail specifically at structural perturbation, so the gauges need per-attack-type feedback, not one blended score, or that finding disappears into a single number. This is a defensive-security exhibit, not a working recipe against any real filter, and the page should say so plainly. Reuse: `human`'s arcade-of-user-error framing and copy conventions, `workers/scores` for a fewest-edits-to-fool-both leaderboard.
mechanism: obfuscate a scam text message by hand and watch two live detector gauges try to catch it
text: edit a spam text — swap letters, rewrite a word in another alphabet, reorder the sentence — and watch two detectors score it live. classical models collapse; transformers mostly hang on

paperTitle: Altered Cosmic Organics as Venus' Ultraviolet Absorbers
name: venus-recipe
plan: Venus's clouds absorb UV light and nobody has known what does it since the 1970s. This paper proposes an answer: mixtures of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH ring molecules) and iron-bearing compounds, matched against real Mars Express/OMEGA reflectance spectra from UV to near-infrared, at all three of Venus's known cloud zones -- and the composition changes with altitude in a way that reads as cometary dust falling and reacting: 5-10 ring PAHs with ferric chloride at the reddish cloud tops, 3-4 ring PAHs with acid ferric sulfate in the decomposed aerosol layer below, 5-10 ring PAHs with ferric hydroxy sulfates in the sub-cloud atmosphere. Mechanic: three target curve silhouettes, one per zone; the visitor sets two sliders -- PAH ring-count skew, iron-compound family -- and a synthetic reflectance curve redraws live, chasing the target, with a fit score for how close the overlay gets. Turn one ships a single zone (cloud tops), the two sliders, and the live curve, built from simplified per-ring-count absorption bands rather than digitized real optical data, flagged plainly as such -- the actual OMEGA spectra aren't recoverable from an abstract. What's hard: staying honest about that approximation while still teaching the real shape of the result, which is that the composition has to shift zone to zone, not that any single fit is scientifically exact. A harder second turn adds the other two zones and scores a fit across all three at once, since a single-zone match alone doesn't show the paper's actual claim. Reuse: the `g` gallery's one-simulation-per-canvas convention, `workers/scores` for a tightest-triple-match leaderboard -- a crowd hunting a small composition space for the best simultaneous fit across three curves is a real, checkable search.
mechanism: mix PAH ring-count and iron-compound sliders to match Venus's UV/visible spectrum at three cloud altitudes
text: tune ring molecules and iron compounds to match venus' ultraviolet spectrum. the composition shifts with altitude as molecules fall through the cloud layers

paperTitle: Dynamic Trajectory Analysis of Meteoroids Showing Minimal Deceleration
name: no-brakes
plan: Most meteors slow down as they burn through the atmosphere, and the standard method for reading a fireball's trajectory -- alpha (ballistic coefficient) and beta (mass-loss parameter) -- depends on that deceleration. A real fraction of recorded fireballs barely decelerate at all, and the standard method can't place them. This paper builds a workaround using ablation coefficients borrowed from meteorite falls with known outcomes, runs it across ten years of the Global Fireball Observatory dataset, and finds these minimally-decelerating objects are about a third of everything recorded, occupying a distinct region of alpha-beta space that was previously inaccessible, mostly small bodies, some identifiable as iron by their emission spectra. Mechanic: the visitor gets a velocity-vs-time trace for a fireball and two sliders, alpha and beta, driving a real single-body drag-and-ablation model; they tune the sliders until the simulated curve overlays the given trace, and the fit lands as a point on the alpha-beta plane next to the paper's reported regions, naming what kind of object was just characterized. Turn one ships one preset trace, clearly of the minimally-decelerating kind, the two sliders, the live curve, and the scatter plot it lands on -- using a physically honest synthetic trace rather than real GFO data, flagged as such. What's hard: the paper reports a distinct region, not a hard boundary, so the toy should draw a fuzzy cloud, not a dividing line -- inventing precision the paper doesn't claim is the failure mode here. Reuse: `workers/scores` for a fewest-tries leaderboard per trace; a later turn could let visitors submit their own recorded meteor light curves, since fireball networks are already citizen-fed, growing a shared alpha-beta map instead of just fitting presets.
mechanism: tune a meteor's ballistic coefficient and mass-loss parameter to fit its light curve, then see where it lands in classification space
text: tune a meteor's ballistic coefficient and mass-loss rate to match its light curve, then read what it was. a third of fireballs barely decelerate — the method now handles them

paperTitle: One Empty Locker and Two Inspections: An Exact Optimal Team Strategy
name: pointer-lockers
text: n players find their own numbered object among n lockers, opening at most two. open your number first; if it's wrong, open whatever you saw inside. you win together exactly when every permutation cycle is length one or two — and you reach this with zero secret negotiation, just that rule
plan: N-1 players each need to find their own labeled object inside one of N lockers (one locker is empty). Nobody sees inside a locker until they open it; each player may open at most two, and the second may depend on what the first showed. They can agree on a strategy beforehand but get zero information about each other once play starts. The paper proves the best possible probability that every single player succeeds is I_N/N! — exactly the fraction of all permutations that are involutions (permutations built only from fixed points and swaps) — and gives the strategy that reaches it: label the empty locker with a fictitious number N, then everyone opens the locker matching their own number first, and if it is wrong, opens whatever locker the number inside pointed to. The clean way to see why: draw an arrow from each locker to the locker its contents points to. Everyone wins together exactly when every arrow-cycle in that picture has length one or two, nothing longer. Turn one: deal a random permutation across N lockers (N pickable, the three-door case doubles as the 'Return of Monty Hall' variant), render it as those arrows, let the visitor step one player at a time through the two-inspection rule, and colour each cycle as a win or a loss as soon as it resolves. Run it a thousand times silently and the win rate should converge on I_N/N! — watching that number converge live is the payoff. The hard part is making 'the strategy needs no real negotiation, just labeling' land as satisfying rather than anticlimactic; lean on the cycle-diagram reveal, not a lobby. Reuse: the geometry pack's single-file explainer scaffold (erdos/, guthkatz/) and workers/scores for a per-N attempt tally.
mechanism: follow-the-pointer two-inspection team search across N lockers, winning together iff the dealt permutation is an involution

paperTitle: The Erdos-Mullin Five-Edge Intersection Problem
name: five-edge-race
text: build the sparsest graph keeping five edges under any vertex relabeling. the paper's finding: the minimum is 2n−2 edges for large n. the adversary shuffles labels hunting for maximum edge-loss, so a graph that survives a thousand shuffles is still unrefuted, not proven
plan: For a graph G on n vertices and a permutation π of its vertices, count the edges G shares with its own relabeled copy πG. Mullin found a construction using 2n-2 edges that forces at least five shared edges under every possible relabeling; Erdős asked whether fewer edges could ever do that for large n. This paper answers no: f(n,5), the minimum edge count that guarantees five survivors under any shuffle, is exactly 2n-2 once n is large enough — a hard floor, and Mullin's construction already sits on it. The mechanic: the visitor builds a graph on a fixed vertex set by clicking edges, aiming to guarantee five overlapping edges under any relabeling while using as few edges as possible. A shuffle button applies permutations — random ones at first, then an increasingly targeted search — and reports the worst overlap found so far, i.e. the visitor's current lower bound on their own graph's guarantee. The visible par is 2n-2 edges; beating it should be impossible past small n, and the site should say so rather than let a lucky graph sit unchallenged. Turn one: a small fixed n (8-12), free edge editing, a shuffle button running exhaustive or heavily-sampled permutation search at that size, and a live edge-count-versus-2n-2 readout. The hard part, named plainly: the adversary is a search, not a proof, so a graph that survives a thousand shuffles at 2n-3 edges is unrefuted, not verified — the leaderboard needs 'best remaining challenger' language, not 'record'. Reuse: the geometry pack's explainer scaffold and result-table conventions (erdos/), workers/scores for the challenge table.
mechanism: build the sparsest graph that keeps five edges in common under any vertex relabeling, tested by adversarial shuffles

paperTitle: Noise-Induced Localized Patterns in Excitable Media: Amplitude versus Persistence
name: patch-budget
text: nudge two noise knobs — amplitude and how long noise stays correlated — to create a localized patch in an excitable medium. loud uncorrelated noise and quiet persistent noise reach the same outcome through wildly different paths, a tradeoff unified by one number: the integrated noise budget
plan: In a spatially extended excitable medium (the FitzHugh-Nagumo model — the standard toy equation for a nerve-like patch of tissue that either sits quiet or fires and recovers), random forcing can nucleate a transient localized patch of firing. The paper's finding is that two very different kinds of noise get you there: loud, uncorrelated (white) noise above some amplitude, or quieter noise that stays correlated in time long enough to accumulate — persistence substituting for volume. Both routes are unified by one number, the integrated noise strength, and a separate parameter — how fast the medium's inhibitor responds — decides whether the resulting excitation stays a localized patch or spreads through the whole system. The mechanic: two sliders, amplitude and persistence (correlation time), drive noise into a 1D strip of the medium; the visitor watches for one of three outcomes — quiet, a travelling alternating state, or a localized patch — and the goal is to find pairs of very different-looking (amplitude, persistence) settings that land on the same outcome, making the tradeoff tangible instead of asserted. Turn one ships that strip, the two sliders, a run button, and an outcome readout. The hard part: the classifier for 'localized patch' versus 'spreading' versus 'quiescent' has to be automatic (a threshold on how much of the strip is active over time), because a running tally of cheapest reliable patch-inducing noise budgets depends on it, and the finite-difference FitzHugh-Nagumo integrator has to run smoothly in-browser at interactive rates. Reuse: canvas grid-simulation conventions from g/'s shelf of one-canvas sims, and packages/dataviz for a live amplitude-versus-persistence phase map, filled in as runs accumulate.
mechanism: two noise knobs, amplitude and persistence, driving an excitable-medium strip toward a localized firing patch

paperTitle: PIPES: Securing Agent Perception with Provenance and Priors
name: pipes-perception
text: edit an attacker-controlled response in an agent's trace, trying to sneak a false claim past a provenance screen that tags where content came from. the paper cut attack success from 84.7% to 2.3% with one defense — you're testing if you can still find gaps in it
plan: Tool-using agents trust whatever a tool response tells them, but a response rarely says who produced which part of it or what authority that part actually carries. The paper shows this gap is exploitable: attacker-controlled content inside a tool response can make a claim that exceeds its own source's authority — 'the payment succeeded', 'the user is an admin' — and the agent acts on it because nothing marks the claim as out of scope. Their defense, PIPES, tags response content with where it came from and what it is allowed to assert, and screens each unit against that; across their benchmarks it cuts attack success from 84.7% down to 2.3% while barely touching legitimate task performance. The toy puts the visitor on the attacker's side of that number. A fixed multi-step agent trace is shown — a shopping assistant, several tool calls, one of them attacker-reachable — and the visitor edits the text of that one attacker-controlled response, trying to smuggle a claim past a provenance screen and get the agent to take an action it should not. The screen is real, just small: rule-based checks of source tags against claim content, not a full model. A shared tally shows the community's live attack success rate against the current screen — the paper's own metric, running as an open contest instead of a fixed benchmark number. Turn one: one scenario, one editable response, a pass or fail verdict, and that running percentage. The hard part is keeping the screen simple enough to build in one sitting while still being a real obstacle, not a strawman — and framing this plainly as a defense-testing exhibit against a toy-scale trace, not a working recipe against anyone's deployed agent.
mechanism: edit an attacker-controlled tool response to sneak an out-of-scope claim past a provenance screen

paperTitle: Rainbow percolation
name: rainbow-line
plan: The paper studies a random graph on points scattered along a line, where each point also carries a random height t in (0,1) drawn independently. Two points at distance d connect with probability min(1, beta/d)^2, but scaled by the taller of the two heights: (t or s) times |x-y| has to stay under beta. High points reach further. The paper proves a genuine phase transition in beta: below it every cluster stays finite, above it an infinite cluster appears, and it pins the threshold to the interval [1,31] rigorously while a numerical appendix puts the real value near 2 — a rare case where the proof and the simulation are honest about how far apart they are. It also shows a stripped-down version, where every point is pinned to the integers instead of scattered continuously, never percolates at all, collapsing straight from total fragmentation to a trivial one-cluster state with no phase transition in between, despite infinitely many edges still crossing every site. The toy: a horizontal line fills with points, each drawn as a dot whose height is its color-coded mark (rainbow: red=low, violet=high). A single beta slider draws the connections live and colors each cluster. Turn one ships the line, the slider, and a running count of the largest cluster's span so a visitor can watch it snap from scattered dust to one dominant band around beta=2, well inside the proven [1,31] bracket. The hard part is making the discrete-skeleton non-transition legible as a genuine contrast rather than a footnote — a toggle that pins points to a grid and shows the same slider producing no gradual growth, only a jump, is the honest way to do it. Reuse: the games/kit for the slider and canvas primitives, workers/scores for a crowd-refined estimate of beta_c collected across visitor runs at different point counts, tightening the published bound with cheap simulation the way the appendix already did once.
mechanism: slider-driven percolation on a marked point line, watching cluster size cross a threshold
text: adjust a slider and watch colored points cluster. they all stay separate until one threshold value, where they snap into one giant connected band

paperTitle: Stay or Stray - A Dynamical Systems Viewpoint of Popularity Bias
name: stay-or-stray
plan: Recommender systems and their users co-evolve: the model updates from what gets clicked, and what gets shown shapes what gets clicked, feeding back on two different clocks. The paper models this coupling as a two-time-scale stochastic process and finds it settles into one of two kinds of equilibrium: a popularity-bias trap, where a majority taste crowds out every niche permanently, or a symmetric one, where every taste class keeps getting shown. Which one you land in depends on the balance between how fast the model adapts and how much engagement niche content still gets before it's buried — and the paper derives the actual conditions that separate the two basins, then checks them against real production logs from a music platform. The toy: the visitor runs a small population of taste classes (five or six bars, one popular, the rest niche) feeding a toy recommender whose exposure updates each round from the previous round's clicks. Two dials: how aggressively the model chases engagement, and how much a niche class's fans still click when shown. Run the clock forward and watch the bars either flatten to one survivor or settle into a stable split — the same run replayed with the dials nudged crosses the paper's boundary and lands somewhere else. Turn one ships the bars, the two dials, and a step button that advances one round at a time so the collapse (or the stalemate) is watched happening, not just declared. The hard part is keeping five bars legible as they diverge, and choosing dial ranges wide enough to actually cross the boundary within a short run. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the bar chart and any phase-plane overlay, civ/'s round-stepping pattern for the simulation loop, and workers/scores for a crowd-found boundary map — submitted dial pairs labeled 'stayed mixed' or 'went popular', assembled into the same kind of boundary the paper derives analytically.
mechanism: two-dial recommender feedback loop, stepping rounds to watch a taste population either flatten or hold a split
text: adjust how fast a recommender adapts and how much niche tastes get clicks, then step through rounds and watch if five taste groups hold a split or collapse to one winner

paperTitle: Optimizing Wavefront-Deformation Sensor Placement for Active Radio-Telescope Surfaces
name: mirror-census
plan: AtLAST is a proposed 50-meter radio dish that needs its surface held accurate to about 20 millionths of a meter under gravity, wind, and thermal flex — far tighter than a passive structure can hold on its own, so the plan is active correction driven by a sparse grid of sensors reading the deformation live. You can't sensor every point on a 50-meter dish, so the paper's real contribution is picking where the few sensors go: it derives the dish's realistic deformation shapes from finite-element load cases, extracts their dominant patterns (a small basis that captures most of how the surface actually flexes), then greedily chooses sensor positions that let those patterns be reconstructed from partial readings, checked by leaving each sensor out in turn. Their result: 50 well-chosen sensors reconstruct every tested load case to under 2.7 microns worst-case residual. The toy: a visitor sees the dish from above as a grid, is given a fixed number of sensor tokens (fewer than 50, to keep it a real placement problem), and drops them anywhere on the surface. The site replays a set of precomputed deformation patterns (baked offline from the same style of load cases, not run live) against the chosen positions and reports the reconstruction error, directly comparable to the paper's 2.7-micron figure. Turn one ships the grid, a placement of exactly 12 tokens, and the error readout against one preloaded gravity-sag pattern — no basis math client-side, just precomputed patterns and a linear reconstruction check. The hard part is that the honest version of this needs real POD-basis data to score against, not an invented approximation, so the first turn should ship with a small number of genuinely representative patterns even if it means the token count stays low until more are added. Reuse: packages/dataviz for the grid and error readout, workers/scores for a placement leaderboard at a fixed sensor count, directly chasing the paper's own record.
mechanism: drag sensor tokens onto a dish grid and score the resulting surface-reconstruction error against precomputed deformation patterns
text: place sensors on a radio dish to score reconstruction error from precomputed flexes. fewer sensors than the paper used, same score: how close can you get?

paperTitle: Necessary and sufficient conditions of a class of bipartite graphs with local antimagic chromatic number 2 - an algebraic approach
name: vertex-sums
plan: Local antimagic labeling assigns the numbers 1..|E| to a graph's edges, one each; every vertex then carries the sum of its incident edges as its induced label, and adjacent vertices must never carry the same sum. The fewest distinct sums achievable for a graph is its local antimagic chromatic number, and two is the theoretical floor for anything with an edge. This paper gives an algebraic necessary-and-sufficient condition for exactly which bipartite graphs built from three hub vertices of higher degree, joined by paths, with every other vertex degree 2, can actually reach that floor of two. The toy hands the visitor one of these three-hub graphs -- three big dots, joined by paths whose lengths you can lengthen or shorten -- and lets you drag the numbers 1..|E| onto the edges. Every vertex shows its running sum live; any edge whose two endpoints share a sum lights up red. Turn one: generate a small three-hub graph, render draggable number tokens on its edges, compute and display vertex sums and a conflict count, and let assignments be swapped by dragging one label onto another. The hard part is honesty: before someone grinds against a graph, the site needs to check the paper's algebraic condition and say whether two sums are even reachable for that particular hub-and-path shape, so a loss reads as information rather than a deadend. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions for the framing and workers/scores for a fewest-swaps or fastest-to-two leaderboard per graph shape.
mechanism: drag numbers 1..|E| onto a three-hub graph's edges to force every vertex sum into one of just two values
text: drag edge numbers onto a three-hub graph so every vertex sum is one of two values. the paper proves which shapes allow it, which don't—and the site tells you upfront if it's possible for yours

paperTitle: Cyclic permutations of large subsets with polynomial values in multiplicative subgroups of finite fields
name: residue-circle
plan: Fix a prime p, an integer k with p congruent to 1 mod k, and a polynomial f. The paper proves that once a subset A of the field mod p passes an explicit size threshold c(p,k,f), its elements can always be arranged in a cycle so that f applied to every pair of neighbours lands in the subgroup of k-th power residues mod p -- and it bounds how small that threshold can be. The toy turns this into a seating puzzle: you are dealt a small set of residues mod a small prime (p=13 or so) and must drag them into a ring so that every adjacent pair's f-value is a perfect square, cube, or whichever power k is in play that round. Edges between correctly paired neighbours glow green; the rest stay grey, and the win condition is a fully green ring -- a genuine Hamiltonian cycle in the constraint graph the paper is proving is dense enough to have one. Turn one: fix p=13, k=2, f(t)=t, deal a random subset, render it as draggable tokens on a circle, and compute and colour the adjacency check live with no solver assist. The hard part is fairness: the paper's guarantee only kicks in above the threshold c(p,k,f), so a set below it may have no valid ring at all, and the site must show that number next to the set size rather than let a legitimate loss read as a skill failure. Reuse the math wing's explainer conventions for the framing, and workers/scores for a leaderboard on smallest solved set relative to the guaranteed threshold -- racing the bound, not just the puzzle.
mechanism: arrange a set of residues around a circle so every adjacent pair's polynomial value is a k-th power mod p
text: drag residues into a ring where neighbors satisfy a polynomial rule—all perfect squares, say, or all k-th powers. the paper proves once your set is large enough, a valid ring always exists

paperTitle: Universal entropic occupation statistics in disordered bosonic resonators
name: mode-split
