plan: Programmable microcavities behave as grand-canonical photon gases, and this paper shows their occupation statistics follow a universal entropic staircase -- for the two-mode case under uniform disorder, the exact conditional law for how photons split between the two modes is the Gauss-Kuzmin distribution, the same curve that governs the long-run frequency of digits in the continued-fraction expansion of a random real number. Two unrelated instruments, one distribution. The toy is two panels converging on the same curve. One: type in a real number (pi, sqrt2, a random seed) and watch its continued-fraction partial quotients accumulate into a histogram against a fixed Gauss-Kuzmin reference curve, visibly settling in as more digits are computed. Two: a small two-mode occupation simulator with sliders for temperature and disorder, sampling repeatedly and building the same kind of histogram. Turn one ships only the continued-fraction side, since it needs no physics simulation, just arithmetic: an input box, a running histogram bar chart against the reference curve, and a shared running tally so every visitor's numbers feed one crowd-scale histogram, since seeing the curve firm up only really lands once thousands of digits have piled in rather than one person's hundred. The physics panel is a second turn. The hard part is scope honesty: the exact Gauss-Kuzmin match is proven for two modes specifically, not the general N-mode staircase, and the page must say so rather than imply the whole family reduces to number theory. Reuse packages/dataviz for the histogram bars; no auth, no build, entirely client-side except the shared tally counter.
mechanism: watch a real number's continued-fraction digit histogram and a two-mode photon-occupation histogram converge on the same Gauss-Kuzmin curve
text: type numbers and watch their continued-fraction digits converge into a histogram shaped like gauss-kuzmin. that same curve governs how photons split across two modes in microcavities—number theory and physics, one distribution

paperTitle: On the Gap of Finite Posets
name: rankgap
text: elements in a partial order can't always be compared. a sampler places each on a line by expected rank in random orderings. the widest gap between ranks matters most. here's the surprise: a fence—two parallel chains—extended one rung at a time beats any denser structure
plan:
The paper defines gap(P): line up the expected rank of every element under a uniformly random linear extension, add the two endpoints 0 and n+1, and take the largest jump between consecutive values. It proves gap(P) ≤ 2w(P)−1, closing a chain of results (Brightwell–Trotter, Biró–Trotter, Aires–Kahn) that kept re-deriving weaker forms of the same bound tying that jump to width — the size of the poset's largest antichain. Then it shows the bound is nearly tight in the worst way: for every L there is a width-two poset with gap at least L, and a family P_r where the gap grows like (3/2)^r even though every subset's induced order carries almost no information (entropy under 3|X| bits). Width caps the jump, but only barely.

The mechanic: draw a poset by adding elements and dragging cover edges (no cycles, transitively reduced). The engine estimates every element's expected rank by sampling linear extensions and plots them on a 0..n+1 number line; the largest jump is highlighted against the live bound 2w(P)−1. Turn one ships a fixed width-two 'fence' poset with a button that extends it one rung at a time, so the visitor watches the gap climb past any width-3 poset's ceiling while width itself stays at two — the paper's central surprise, made visible instead of asserted.

What's hard: the sampler. Picking a uniformly random available minimal element at each step does not sample linear extensions uniformly and would quietly render a wrong gap; it needs a real mixing chain — start from one extension, do random adjacent transpositions, keep only moves that stay valid. Because gap is a sampled quantity rather than an exact arithmetic one, any later leaderboard of 'smallest poset achieving gap L at width w' can't be cheat-proof by simple recomputation the way an exact count would be, and needs a shared seed or small-n exact enumeration instead.

Reuse: the `math` wing's explainer conventions for the write-up; `scores` for that leaderboard once the verification story is settled.
mechanism: build a Hasse diagram and watch a Monte-Carlo sampler expose how far apart two elements land in a random linear extension

paperTitle: Fixed forests in the minimum spanning tree and cubic volume growth
name: minspan
plan: The paper studies the minimum spanning tree of the complete graph K_n with i.i.d. uniform edge weights, and proves two concrete things: the expected number of copies of any fixed small tree F inside the MST, scaled by n^|edges(F)|, converges to a computable constant Ψ(F) — closed forms Ψ(star S_k) ~ ζ(2)^k = (π²/6)^k and Ψ(path P_k) ~ k²/12 — and the ball of radius r around a random point in the MST has expected size asymptotic to r³/36. The tree has no coordinates and lives on a fully random complete graph, yet counting outward from any point grows like a ball in ordinary 3-space. Turn one: build the MST of a random complete graph (n≈500-1000, Kruskal on iid weights), let the visitor click a vertex and drag a radius slider r, and watch the ball light up node-by-node while a running count is plotted against the r³/36 curve. The hard part is making 'cubic growth with no underlying geometry' read as strange before it reads as confirmed — the tree has no embedding, so the match to r³/36 has to feel like a coincidence the visitor is watching resolve, not a stat printed on the page. Second layer: overlay counts of small stars and paths (S_3, S_4, P_3, P_4) against their closed-form Ψ, so the browser's finite-n empirical count visibly races toward the n→∞ limit. Reuse the math wing's page shell and the extremal-geometry family framing already used for erdos/hadwiger-style exhibits; a crowd leaderboard for 'closest empirical ball-growth exponent to 3,' since no single browser session reaches large enough n to pin the constant down alone — pooling sessions is a real improvement, not decoration.
mechanism: grow a random minimum spanning tree and race its empirical ball-growth curve against the proven r³/36 asymptotic
text: drag a radius slider around any node in a random tree; the ball fills in the exact density pattern of a solid sphere in 3d space. the tree has no embedding, no coordinates, no geometry — just randomness — yet the growth is cubic

paperTitle: Spectral gap of the normalized distance Laplacian
name: distlap
plan: Take a connected graph, build the matrix of all pairwise shortest-path distances, normalize it into a Laplacian, and take its smallest positive eigenvalue — the spectral gap, a measure of how well-connected the graph is. A 2025 conjecture guessed this gap is always at least 2/3. This paper proves a stronger, exact bound: gap ≥ 2/3 + 4/(3·t_max), where t_max is the largest 'transmission' in the graph (the biggest total distance from one vertex to every other vertex) — and equality holds if and only if the graph is a complete bipartite graph K_{m,m}. The bound names its own tight case. The toy: a graph builder — place vertices, click pairs to connect them, must stay connected — with the spectral gap computed live and shown against a floor line at 2/3. The visitor's job is to push the gap down toward the floor and discover by trial that they can only actually touch it by building K_{m,m}: two balanced groups, every cross-edge present, nothing within a group. Turn one: a fixed small vertex count (6-10), free-form edge editing, eigenvalues computed client-side (trivial-sized dense matrices), the gap number and its distance from the floor displayed live, with a 'closest ever' record kept per visitor. The hard part is explaining transmission and the distance Laplacian without a linear-algebra detour — lean on the moving floor line rather than the definitions: let the visitor watch the floor shift as t_max changes before naming either term. Reuse the math wing's shell and its existing extremal-geometry exhibit framing (borsuk, heilbronn); a leaderboard for lowest gap achieved at a given vertex count is a real extremal-graph-theory record, and it's cheat-proof because anyone can recompute the eigenvalue from a submitted adjacency list.
mechanism: build a connected graph and push its distance-Laplacian spectral gap toward the proven 2/3 floor, hit only by complete bipartite graphs
text: build a connected graph by placing vertices and edges, watch a live number track the graph. it has a proven floor at 2/3 reachable only by the complete bipartite graph — two groups, all edges between them, none within

paperTitle: CatPAL: Task-Aware Learning for Categorical Palette Recommendation
name: chroma
plan: CatPAL's finding is uncomfortable for anyone shipping one default categorical palette: task and palette choice jointly determine perceptual accuracy on scatterplots, so there is no single best color set — the best palette for 'spot the outlier' measurably differs from the best palette for 'count the clusters.' The paper backs this with forced-choice data across 39 colors and 39 shapes over seven scatterplot tasks, fit with Bradley-Terry ranking models, plus a redundant-gain metric for what pairing color with shape actually buys over either channel alone. The toy puts the visitor in the exact seat the paper's participants sat in. Show one scatterplot rendered twice, once per palette, with a task instruction above it ('which group has more points,' 'find the odd one out'), and ask which rendering answered it faster — a real, timed vote. Every vote becomes one data point in a live, publicly visible Bradley-Terry ranking, refit per task, so the site's own leaderboard can converge toward the paper's ranking or diverge from it, in public, as votes accumulate. Turn one: hand-pick a single task ('count the categories') and eight strong palettes from the paper, generate one underlying point cloud per round, render it twice with two of the eight palettes assigned at random, log the click, and show a live-updating ranked list beneath the game — no auth, votes are anonymous and cheap to cast. The hard part is holding task difficulty constant between the two renderings in a round: a harder point cloud biases the vote regardless of palette, so the underlying data must be fixed per round with only the color/shape encoding swapped between the pair. Reuses the crowd forced-choice judging pattern reef already runs for creature ratings; a Bradley-Terry fit is cheap client-side arithmetic once enough vote pairs accumulate.
mechanism: timed forced-choice votes between two palette renderings of the same scatterplot task, feeding a live public Bradley-Terry ranking
text: vote which color palette helped you solve a scatterplot task fastest — spot the outlier, count the clusters, find the odd group out. watch a live leaderboard build itself as the crowd decides which colors win which tasks

paperTitle: Squaring the circle: embedding $S^1$ in $\ell_1$
name: half-circle
plan: The paper works out exactly which subsets of a circle can be laid flat isometrically in ℓ1's taxicab metric. Two clean facts: if a closed subset X's overlap with its own antipodal reflection X* has positive arc-length measure, X cannot embed at all — which forces a hard ceiling of exactly half the circle's total length (measure π out of 2π), since anything bigger must overlap its own antipode. Conversely, any closed set whose intersection with every half-circle has measure zero does embed. The toy hands the visitor a circle and a paint tool: click or drag to mark arcs as 'kept,' and a live meter tracks two numbers — the measure claimed, and whether the kept set currently overlaps its own antipodal reflection (the disqualifying condition). The goal is to build the largest kept set possible without triggering the antipodal-overlap flag, racing toward but never past the π ceiling. Turn one ships this loop on a static circle: paint arcs, watch the antipodal-overlap check run live (highlight the offending overlap in red when it fires), and show current measure against the π line. The hard part is being honest about the gap between the two conditions in the paper — antipodal overlap is what rules a set out, disjoint-from-every-half-circle is what lets one in, and they are not exact opposites, so the toy should show both checks separately rather than implying one predicate settles everything. Reuse the math hub's (math.mino.mobi) single-file explainer conventions, and workers/scores for a record table of 'largest verified kept measure,' recomputable instantly by anyone since both checks are cheap arithmetic.
mechanism: select arcs of a circle while a live check tells you whether the set can still embed in ℓ1
text: paint arcs on a circle and race toward a hard ceiling: exactly half its length. the catch is your set can't overlap its own reflection

paperTitle: Online Interval Selection on a Simple Chain
name: no-takebacks
plan: The result: on a 'simple chain' of intervals (each overlaps only its immediate neighbours) presented online in random order, a deterministic algorithm allowed to revoke earlier picks achieves competitive ratio 2(1-1/√e) ≈ 0.786 against the offline optimum — worse than plain greedy with no revoking at all, which gets (1-1/e²) ≈ 0.864. Against an adversarial arrival order, any deterministic revoking algorithm is capped at 0.75. The extra power to take back a choice makes the guaranteed outcome worse, which is the whole reason to build this. The toy deals a stream of intervals along a line one at a time, in random order; for each, the visitor can accept it, skip it, or revoke a previously accepted interval to swap in the new one, always keeping the accepted set pairwise non-overlapping. At the end the visitor sees their total against two things: the true offline optimum for that exact stream, computable after the fact, and a simple no-revoke greedy bot fed the identical stream. Turn one ships one round: sequential single-interval prompts, an accept/skip/revoke choice each time, and an end-of-round reveal showing the visitor's score, the greedy bot's score, and the optimum, so the 'revoking made you worse' effect is visible on your own round rather than asserted. The hard part is making a single random-order stream feel legitimately random rather than rigged, and communicating the effect without leaning on the algebra — a reveal screen that replays the same stream against the no-revoke bot side by side is what should carry it. Reuse games/'s round structure and Durable Object machinery, and workers/scores for a running average of human competitive ratio across every round played, which is itself a live, improving estimate of how real people compare to the two proven bounds.
mechanism: accept, skip, or revoke intervals from a live random-order stream, chasing the offline optimum
text: intervals arrive one by one. accept, skip, or revoke to maximize your score. the catch: mathematically, the power to revoke makes your worst case worse

paperTitle: Relative Ehrhart theory I: relative Ehrhart eventual polynomials
name: container-count
plan: Classical Ehrhart theory counts lattice points inside the t-th dilate of a polytope P, and that count is eventually a polynomial in t. This paper replaces the lattice point with an arbitrary geometric object Q and counts valid translations of Q into tP instead, showing the counting function is still eventually quasi-polynomial, with a leading term of exactly vol(P)·t^d, independent of what Q actually is (only its dimension and that it fits matter). Swap the token for a different shape and the growth rate stays locked to the container's volume; only the lower-order wobble changes. The toy: pick a container polygon P (square, L-shape, a couple more presets) and a token shape Q (a point, then a short segment, then a small tromino), and step an integer t upward. At each t, the toy places Q by translation only — no rotation, no scaling — everywhere it validly fits inside tP, and plots the running count on a graph alongside a reference line at vol(P)·t^d. Turn one ships one fixed P, a toggle between 'point' and 'short segment' for Q, t stepping from 1 to about 12, and the live count plus graph, enough to see the counts hug the same slope regardless of which Q is selected. The hard part is keeping 'valid translation of Q into tP' cheap and visually legible at small t without it reading as an empty grid exercise — the payoff is entirely in watching two different-shaped tokens converge to the same line, so the graph, not the polygon fill, is the thing to get right. Reuse the math hub's single-file explainer conventions and the erdos entry's instantly-recomputable record-table pattern, extended here to a search for container/token pairs with the most visible early wobble.
mechanism: swap the token shape being packed into a growing polygon and watch the count graph's slope stay locked to the container
text: pack tokens into a growing polygon. swap between point, segment, and tromino—the growth rate stays locked to the same slope regardless

paperTitle: Two-point Approximate Shortest Path Queries among Convex Polygonal Obstacles in the Plane
name: slackbound
plan:
The paper gives a preprocessing scheme for a plane scattered with h disjoint convex polygonal obstacles (n vertices total): after preprocessing, any two query points get a path with (1+ε) multiplicative stretch over the true shortest route, plus a small additive slack bounded by 13 times the longest obstacle diagonal. Choosing ε trades preprocessing and query cost against how tight that guarantee is.

Mechanic: the visitor places convex obstacles on a canvas, drops a start and end point, and drags an ε slider. Two paths draw at once — the true shortest path, computed exactly via a visibility graph, and a guaranteed-quality approximate one — with the realized stretch ratio shown beside the paper's promised bound, so the visitor sees how much slack the guarantee actually leaves for a given layout.

Turn one: ship a handful of draggable convex polygons, an exact shortest path via visibility graph (well understood, easy to implement), and a stand-in approximate path — a coarser visibility graph, not the paper's actual data structure — that still honestly respects a chosen ε, with the page stating plainly that this is a simplified realization of the guarantee, not the paper's construction.

Hard part: the paper's real preprocessing structure is intricate and not a short build. The honest move is a simpler algorithm that still empirically satisfies the same stretch bound on the test layouts, labelled as an approximation of the approximation.

Reuse: the `math` wing's geometry hub for hosting; `scores` for an adversarial leaderboard — visitors submit obstacle layouts and an ε that push the realized stretch closest to the theoretical bound, ranked, and checkable by anyone recomputing both paths on the submitted layout.
mechanism: place convex obstacles and an epsilon budget, then compare the exact shortest path against the guaranteed-quality approximate one
text: place convex obstacles and set an epsilon value, then draw the true shortest path and a guaranteed approximation side by side. watch the approximation's actual stretch compare to the promised bound

paperTitle: Reassessing the Feasibility of PPG-Based Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Level Estimation
name: clarkegap
plan:
The paper re-evaluates five published PPG-based blood-glucose estimators under three progressively stricter train/test splits: random window-level, participant-aware, and leave-some-participants-out. Under naive random splitting the models look competitive; under the stricter splits nearly all collapse to near-zero or negative R², indistinguishable from predicting the mean. The sharper finding: across every model and every split — including that mean-only baseline — over 90% of predictions still land in the clinically acceptable zone of the Clarke Error Grid. The clinical metric never notices the collapse the statistical one shows plainly.

Mechanic: the visitor gets a synthetic dataset built with the same structural flaw as the real one (correlated windows within a fake participant, not the paper's actual data or models) and one toy baseline. Before running each of the three split protocols, they guess whether the numbers will look good. Then two readouts update side by side: R² and Clarke A+B percentage. The gap between the guess and the R² collapse is the exhibit.

Turn one: ship the three preset split buttons (random window, participant-aware, leave-some-participants-out) recomputing both metrics live on a small in-browser synthetic dataset, plus the pre-guess prompt.

Hard part: building synthetic data that honestly reproduces the leakage mechanism without implying it reproduces the paper's real dataset or scores — the page has to say plainly this is an illustration of the general phenomenon, not a replication.

Reuse: `human`'s exhibit framing, where the visitor is the specimen — an aggregate 'how many guessed wrong' counter across visits is this site's own version of the paper's finding, the same pattern `human/` already runs on other cognitive traps.
mechanism: pick a train/test split protocol on correlated data and watch a clinical-looking accuracy metric hide a statistical collapse
text: guess whether your model works, then switch between three data-split protocols. watch R² and clinical accuracy update: one collapses, one doesn't. same model, same synthetic data, opposite stories

paperTitle: Floor, Ceiling, and the Fusion Gap: How Much of Crowd Reading Attention Can Machines Predict?
name: the-other-half
plan: The paper scores a real benchmark against real bounds: predicting which sentences a crowd of unpaid, uninstructed readers highlighted in 120 web documents, each reader blind to the others. The floor is naive lead truncation; the ceiling is a split-half oracle, half the crowd predicting the other half. The gap between them is +0.2028 average precision, and frontier LLMs reach only 35-53% of it zero-shot; a five-model fusion plus a position prior reaches 60%, and a distilled 8B student keeps 90% of that edge. The toy strips this to its actual mechanic: show a visitor one short article and ask them to highlight not what they find important, but what they think a separate group of readers already highlighted — a prediction about other people's attention, not their own. Score the overlap against that document's real captured highlights, and place the visitor's score on a bar between the lead-sentence floor and the split-half ceiling, so the abstract 'gap' becomes a place your click landed. Turn one ships with a single preloaded document carrying the paper's own floor and ceiling baked in as static reference points, plus a sentence-toggle UI and a plain average-precision overlap score computed client-side. The hard part is compressing an AP-style metric into one legible readout without turning it into a stats page. What makes it worth a crowd rather than a quiz: once enough visitors highlight the same document, the site can recompute a live split-half oracle from its own users, regenerating the paper's headline result from a crowd nobody paid, same as the paper's own crowd. Reuse human/'s pattern of showing the live visitor split beside the published number, and workers/scores to store highlight submissions keyed by document id.
mechanism: predict which sentences a separate crowd already highlighted, scored against a live split-half oracle
text: read an article and guess which sentences other readers highlighted. watch your score land on a bar between a basic guess and a perfect oracle. once enough people play, the site builds a live oracle from all of you—your crowd becomes the measurement

paperTitle: A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search
name: shell-game
plan: A target hops between two sites according to a hidden Markov chain. Each round you pay to search one site, and even a correct search can miss — the target is really there with probability that isn't 1. Ross conjectured the optimal policy is always a threshold rule: search site 1 whenever your posterior belief that the target is there crosses one fixed number. Earlier work proved this across part of the parameter space; this paper closes the remaining case (det M > 0), so the threshold rule now holds for every two-site transition matrix in the classical range. The toy is a hider-and-seeker built on that exact math: each round the visitor picks a site to search, pays a cost, and gets a hit or miss, with misses possible even on a correct guess. A belief-o-meter tracks the single number the paper cares about — the Bayesian posterior that the target sits at site 1 — updating after every round. Turn one ships a fixed 2x2 transition matrix and fixed miss probabilities, two clickable sites, the belief-o-meter, and after a run of rounds, an overlay showing the optimal threshold computed live from that matrix against the visitor's actual search sequence: did you cross it early, late, or right on time? The hard part is real, not cosmetic — the threshold has to come from actually solving the Bellman recursion for the given matrix and costs client-side, especially once sliders let visitors change the transition matrix and watch the threshold move. No existing surface matches this shape closely; workers/scores could hold a 'total search cost vs. optimal policy's cost' leaderboard once the base game is proven fun.
mechanism: search one of two sites per round for a hidden Markov target, tracked against a live-computed optimal threshold
text: each round pick one of two sites to search, pay a cost, and maybe miss—even a correct guess fails sometimes. a belief meter shows your hunch of where the target hides. after several rounds, see if you switched at the exact moment the math says you should

paperTitle: A Proof of the Imbalance Conjecture
name: imbalance-mirror
plan: For an edge uv of a graph, its imbalance is |deg(u) - deg(v)|. Take every edge's imbalance and collect them into a multiset. Kozerenko and Skochko conjectured that whenever every edge has positive imbalance (no edge joins two same-degree vertices), that multiset is always 'graphic' — meaning some graph exists whose degree sequence matches it exactly. This paper proves it, via a bound on truncated imbalance sums that forces every Erdos-Gallai inequality to hold. It's surprising because being graphic is a strict, checkable condition, and there's no visible reason a graph's own imbalances should satisfy it for every graph — yet they always do. The toy turns this into a two-step, never-a-dead-end puzzle. Step one: the visitor draws a graph by clicking vertices and edges, under the one constraint the theorem needs (no equal-degree edge). Step two: the site computes that graph's imbalance multiset and hands it back as a target degree sequence, challenging the visitor to build any graph — a different one — realizing exactly that sequence. Because the theorem guarantees a solution exists, the puzzle can never be unsolvable, an inversion of the usual realizability puzzle where you don't know going in if you're chasing a ghost. Turn one ships the click-to-build graph editor with a live degree and imbalance readout, and the 'mirror' action that locks in the target sequence and switches to build mode with running Erdos-Gallai feasibility feedback. The hard part is making 'graphic sequence' land without a definitions wall — a tiny worked example inline, not a paragraph. Reuse math.mino.mobi's canvas-explainer scaffold and workers/scores for a fewest-vertices record per generated target.
mechanism: reconstruct a graph whose degree sequence matches the edge-imbalance multiset of one you drew
text: draw a graph by clicking vertices and edges. the site computes a target sequence from your graph and challenges you to build any other graph that matches it exactly. the proof guarantees a solution always exists—never an impossible puzzle, only the work of finding how

paperTitle: Longest convex chains with i.i.d. points
name: convex-trace
plan: Scatter n random points inside a triangle. Starting at one vertex A and ending at another vertex B, what's the longest chain of points you can string together that always turns the same way — a convex chain, tracing out part of a convex shape? This paper shows the answer grows like c*n^(1/3) to leading order, for any bounded sampling density, and pins the constant c down with an explicit variational formula whose maximizer (if unique) even describes the limiting curve shape the longest chain follows. The contrast is the hook: sample n points in a square instead and ask for the longest monotone chain (just increasing in both coordinates, no convexity needed) — that grows like c'*n^(1/2), a distinctly faster rate, and the paper connects its formula for c back to the older result for c'. The toy hands the visitor the actual search: n points scattered in a triangle, click dots in order starting from corner A, and the interface live-rejects any click that would break the convex-turn rule, so the constraint is felt by hand rather than read as a definition. The running counter is the chain's length. Turn one ships one fixed triangle, a scatter of roughly 40-60 points, click-to-build with live convexity rejection, and the length counter — no algorithm comparison or n-slider yet. A later turn adds an n-slider showing the theoretical n^(1/3) growth curve against the visitor's best-found chains, and a scores.mino.mobi record per (triangle seed, n) so results stay checkable by recomputation. The hard part is turning convexity rejection into an obvious, immediate visual reason rather than a confusing refusal. Reuse math.mino.mobi's geometry-pack scaffold.
mechanism: click through scattered points to build the longest chain that turns one way from corner to corner
text: click dots from corner to corner, always curving left or right but never switching. build the longest chain you can. the surprise: these chains grow slower than ones following weaker rules would, even though always-turn-one-way seems like the hardest constraint of all

paperTitle: Exact Periodicity, Surjectivity, and a Haar Limit Law for a Restarting Josephus Process
name: josephus
plan:
The paper studies a restarting Josephus process: people stand in a line, not a circle, and you eliminate every m-th one counting from the left — but after each elimination, counting restarts from whichever survivor is now leftmost, instead of continuing around. Write q = m-1 and F_n(q) for the eventual survivor's starting position; it obeys a simple reversal recursion. Three results, in increasing order of surprise: F_n's exact period in q is lcm(1,...,n), nothing short of it; every position 1..n is hit by some q, so no seat is unreachable; and, striking, if q is drawn uniformly at random modulo that period, the survivor's normalized position (F_n(q)-1)/(n-1) converges to a specific symmetric distribution on [0,1] that the authors prove is not any symmetric beta curve — without giving its actual shape.

The mechanic: a line of n dots, a step-size dial, and a run button that counts off with restart-at-leftmost, eliminating one dot per beat until one survivor remains, highlighted. Turn one ships exactly that — pick n (up to ~30), pick or randomize q, watch the elimination animate, read off F_n(q). The hard part is the limit-law claim: don't invent a formula the paper doesn't supply. The honest second layer is a running histogram of normalized survivor positions across repeated random-q runs, which visibly refuses to look like a bell curve — the paper's actual content is ruling shapes out, not nailing one down, and the toy should say that outright. Reuse the math hub's single-file explainer convention (erdos/, markov/); BigInt handles lcm(1..n) and the recursion cheaply. No backend needed for turn one; pooling every visitor's runs into one shared histogram is the natural next step.
mechanism: counts off and eliminates people in a line with restart-at-leftmost, driven by a chosen step size
text: you line up n people and count off to eliminate every m-th, restarting from the leftmost survivor. repeat for random m. the survivors end up scattered in a distribution the math proves is not any bell curve

paperTitle: Width distributions for rectangular boxes
name: silhouette
plan:
The paper gives a closed-form answer to a physical question: spin a rectangular box (edges a1, a2, a3) to a uniformly random orientation and measure its width in one fixed direction — w = sum ai|ui|. The cumulative distribution is elementary and exact; the density is smooth everywhere except at values equal to the edge lengths, the face diagonals, and the space diagonal, where it breaks in one of four classified ways (corner, square-root fold, superposition, terminal jump), each with a computed coefficient. Separately: the first three cumulants of the width distribution determine the box uniquely, among an explicitly characterized set of admissible triples.

The mechanic: sliders set a1, a2, a3; a spin button samples random directions on the sphere and drops each resulting width onto a number line, building a live histogram while the exact closed-form density draws over it as an overlay curve, with tick marks at the singular values so visitors can watch the histogram visibly kink exactly where the box's own diagonals say it should. Turn one ships the single interactive box: sliders, sampling, histogram, overlay, singularity marks — no server. The hard part is getting the piecewise formula exactly right, since it's a sum of positive-part terms, not a single clean expression, and any error there breaks the entire pitch, which is that the overlay is the real curve, not an approximation.

The crowd layer, once turn one is solid: a mystery box, only its width histogram shown, visitors submit guessed edge lengths, scored on accuracy — a genuine inverse problem, since three cumulants pin the box down uniquely. Reuse packages/dataviz for the chart and histogram, and workers/scores for the guess-the-box leaderboard once that mode exists.
mechanism: spins a box to random orientations and builds a live width histogram against the exact density
text: spin a box randomly and measure its width in one direction. repeat many times. the widths form a histogram with sharp corners at the edge and diagonal lengths — all predicted by one exact formula

paperTitle: Economical lattice coverings by determined segments
name: raylines
plan:
Alon (1991) asked how few points you need in an n x n integer grid so that the lines through pairs of them cover every grid point, and proved the answer is between order n^a and n^a log n for a = d(d-1)/(2d-1) in dimension d, leaving open whether the log factor is real. This paper closes the gap for both the line version and the stricter segment version — a point only counts as covered if it lies on the actual segment between two chosen points, not just on the extended line — and shows both are order n^a with no log factor. For the plane, a = 2/3.

The mechanic: an n x n grid of dots, click to add points to your covering set, and every closed segment between two chosen points draws itself and lights up every grid point it passes through, green for covered, red for not. Goal: cover the whole grid with as few points as possible. Turn one ships exactly this for the segment version (stricter but easier to reason about, since a covered point has to be visibly on a drawn segment, not on some line running off the edge of the board) — grid up to roughly 10x10, a point counter, and instant recomputation of coverage on every click.

The hard part is scale honesty: n^{2/3} scaling is an asymptotic statement, and a 10x10 board will not visibly demonstrate it — say so, and frame the toy as a search for small, checkable records rather than a demonstration of the theorem. The crowd layer is a leaderboard of fewest points used to cover each grid size, verifiable instantly by anyone re-running the click-to-coverage function, the same cheat-proof property as the Erdos leaderboard. Reuse the math hub's explainer conventions and workers/scores for the record table.
mechanism: click-to-place covering points on a grid, graded by instant segment-coverage feedback
text: click points on an n×n grid. segments between your chosen pairs must cover every grid point — green if covered, red if empty. beat the record for fewest points

paperTitle: On the largest Littlewood--Richardson coefficient
name: richardson
plan:
Littlewood-Richardson coefficients c^lambda_{mu,nu} count how a product of two Schur functions decomposes, and are famously expensive to reason about in general. This paper asks which partitions attain the largest possible c^lambda_{mu,nu} for a given size, and proves an unconditional structural fact about them: the maximizer always has mu contained in nu with the skew shape nu/mu a disjoint union of squares — turning an algebraic extremal question into a tiling question. It conjectures this is the only way to attain the maximum once the size n reaches 16, and confirms that numerically through n=45.

The unpacking that makes this a toy: a skew shape that's a disjoint union of squares is something you can literally see — a Young diagram with a checkerboard of solid blocks cut out. The mechanic is a partition builder: toggle cells in a grid to build mu and nu (mu contained in nu enforced by the UI), and the tool computes c^lambda_{mu,nu} live via the Littlewood-Richardson rule, showing it against the best value found so far for that size, plus a flag for whether nu/mu happens to decompose into squares. Turn one ships this for small n (roughly up to 10-12, where direct tableau-counting stays fast in-browser) — shape builder, live coefficient, running best-for-this-n.

The hard part is computational honesty: LR coefficients get expensive fast, and the paper's own n=45 check almost certainly used serious offline computation, not a browser loop — so frame the toy as searching the small-n frontier that's actually reachable, flagging any square-decomposition violation it happens to find, rather than promising to extend the paper's verified range. Reuse the math hub's explainer conventions and workers/scores for the per-n record table.
mechanism: builds skew Young-diagram shapes and reads off their Littlewood-Richardson coefficient live
text: build nested partition shapes by toggling cells. measure their score live. the shapes that beat the record always share one thing: the empty space between them is made of square blocks

paperTitle: Bounds on Odd and Odd-Even Induced Subgraphs
name: parity-cut
plan: The paper studies a deceptively simple demand: pick a target parity (odd or even) for every vertex of a graph, then find the largest subset S such that each chosen vertex's degree within S actually matches its target. Extending Zeng's odd-cut method to arbitrary parity prescriptions, it proves you can always find such a set with at least n/6 of the vertices — improving the previous 2n/21 bound — and for bipartite graphs a sharper 65/256·n bound via the F2-rank of the adjacency matrix. The toy hands the visitor a graph and a parity target per vertex (red wants odd, blue wants even) and lets them click vertices in and out of a working set. Every click recomputes each vertex's degree inside the current set live, so a vertex flashes green when it satisfies its parity and red when it doesn't — the whole point is that satisfying one vertex can break another, and the n/6 guarantee has to survive that interference. Turn one ships the graph, the parity badges, click-to-toggle, live pass/fail state, and a running best-size counter with the n/6 line marked. The hard part: this is NP-hard in general, so the game is honestly a search, not a solved puzzle — the site should never imply a unique discoverable optimum, only that the guarantee always holds and invite the visitor to beat it. Reuse the `math` pack's single-file explainer scaffold and accent styling (erdos/, heilbronn/ sibling conventions); a record table keyed by graph seed, storing best set size found via com.minomobi.lab.score with higherIsBetter true, turns a fixed puzzle into a chase — later turns can rotate in named graphs (Petersen, hypercubes) once the base mechanic is solid.
mechanism: toggling vertices into a set while a live parity check confirms admissibility
text: you assign each vertex odd or even, then click vertices in and out of your set trying to match each vertex's degree to its target parity. satisfying one breaks another, creating cascading conflicts. the surprise: you can always satisfy at least one sixth of them

paperTitle: The narrow escape problem in arbitrary dimension
name: trapdoor
plan: A Brownian particle wanders inside a closed room whose walls reflect it everywhere except for a few narrow holes; the narrow escape problem asks how long it takes to leave and where it exits. This paper extends the classical 2D/3D result to arbitrary dimension using a quasi-stationary-distribution approach, deriving the asymptotic expansion of the mean exit time and, the newer part, the full law of the exit position, both as the holes shrink to zero, checked against Monte Carlo. The toy: the visitor gets a domain — start with a disc, then a box — and a fixed hole budget, total boundary length they may open, and places holes by clicking the boundary. Hit run and hundreds of particles animate as reflecting random walks until they escape; a histogram of exit position and exit time accumulates live, overlaid against the paper's predicted curve, so the visitor watches simulation and theory converge rather than being told they agree. Turn one ships one hole, one domain, particles escaping, and the accumulating histogram against the theoretical line — no budget game yet. The hard part is honesty about scale: the paper's asymptotics are a hole-size-to-zero limit, so a browser sim with holes at any usable size is always an approximation, and the page has to say so rather than claim exact agreement. Once the base simulation is solid, the crowd layer is a hole-placement leaderboard: same domain, same total hole budget, ranked by measured mean exit time, checkable because anyone can rerun a submitted layout and get the same answer up to simulation noise. Reuse the `math` pack's canvas-explainer conventions for the domain renderer and `scores` for the ranked table, keyed by domain plus budget as the game slug.
mechanism: clicking escape holes onto a boundary and racing simulated particles against a theoretical exit-time curve
text: you place escape holes on a boundary and release particles that bounce randomly inside until they escape through a hole. watch where and when they exit—their positions and times accumulate in a histogram overlaid against the paper's theoretical prediction

paperTitle: Identification of generic polygonal domains by integral-geometric invariants
name: fingerprint
plan: Take a polygon, sample two random points inside it a huge number of times, and histogram the distances between them — that is the interpoint distance distribution, a one-curve fingerprint of the shape. This paper shows that for a generic polygon, that single curve (equivalently, the closely related Riesz energy function) pins down the polygon exactly, up to moving it around the plane — extending a classical result that only covered convex shapes to arbitrary polygonal domains, by tracking jumps in the curve's second and third derivatives at the polygon's own side lengths to recover every side length, their cyclic order, and every exterior angle. The toy hides a polygon and shows only its fingerprint curve; the visitor drags vertices of their own guess polygon on a canvas and watches their guess's curve redraw live, overlaid on the target curve, trying to make the two match. Turn one: a fixed small target (a quadrilateral), a draggable four-vertex guess, and the two curves rendered side by side updating on every drag — no scoring yet, just the felt experience that shape and curve move together and a good match really does mean the same polygon. The hard part is telegraphing why this is hard rather than mystical: point at a jump in the curve and label it as a side length so the invariant stops being an abstract graph and becomes readable. The crowd layer is a daily hidden polygon, procedurally generated from a shared seed, scored on time-to-match or vertex moves, via com.minomobi.lab.score with higherIsBetter false. Reuse the `math` pack's single-file scaffold and canvas conventions (erdos/, heilbronn/), and note that identification is only guaranteed for generic polygons — the paper's appendix has genuinely ambiguous symmetric edge cases, and the toy should not pretend otherwise.
mechanism: dragging a guess polygon's vertices until its live distance-histogram matches a hidden target's
text: you see a polygon's distance fingerprint—the histogram from sampling random pairs of points inside it—and rebuild the shape by dragging vertices until your curve matches the hidden one. every drag updates live. most polygons have unique fingerprints. most, but not all

paperTitle: Dynamic Traffic Allocation for Revenue Maximization on Creator Economy Platform
name: spotlight
plan: A platform decides, every day, whose feed gets the traffic: an established creator who converts clicks into ad revenue right now, or a rising one who converts traffic into followers who pay off later through word-of-mouth. This paper solves that continuous-time trade-off, and the optimal policy is stranger than always-feed-the-star: it is a most-valuable-creator-first rule that, under Bass diffusion dynamics, exhibits conditional reversal — temporarily starving the leader to prime a laggard's word-of-mouth — and it caps a successful creator's follower base at a ceiling instead of pouring in traffic forever, because past that ceiling the extra investment stops paying off. Naive heuristics, always-the-star or evenly-split fairness, lose up to 25% of achievable revenue against this policy. The toy: two creators, a daily traffic slider between them, a running revenue counter, and a follower-growth curve for each that responds to how much traffic it got and how many followers it already has. Turn one ships the two-creator simulation with the slider and the two live curves over a compressed year the visitor can scrub — no scoring yet, just the ability to feel a policy help or hurt. The hard part is the reversal: a naive player will always feed the leader, and the toy has to make it obvious after the fact that a rival's growth spurt paid off later — likely a replay comparing the player's cumulative revenue against the paper's optimal policy on the same random seed. The crowd layer: submit an allocation rule and rank it by revenue captured against a shared bank of generated creator populations, via `scores`. Honest risk: this is applied economics dressed as a toy, not a puzzle with one correct move, and the page should say plainly that the benchmark curve is the paper's optimum, not a claim any simple slider strategy reaches it exactly.
mechanism: sliding daily traffic between two creators and watching word-of-mouth growth reward or punish the split
text: you manage daily traffic allocation between two creators, watching followers accumulate from new traffic and existing word-of-mouth. after a year, compare your revenue to the paper's optimal strategy. the twist: sometimes feed the underdog instead of the star

paperTitle: Cubes in the Torus
name: torus-cover
plan:
Cubes in the Torus (2608.16883, math.CO) asks how many shifted copies of the p=2 block — a 2×2×...×2 cube — you need to cover every cell of the wraparound torus (Z/qZ)^n. The paper proves a genuinely surprising fact: for each modulus q there is a fixed constant Λ_q, always between 1 and 2, such that the true minimum count settles at (Λ_q + o(1))·(q/2)^n as the dimension n grows without bound. So no matter how many dimensions you add, covering never needs more than twice the naive volume-counting estimate, and never less than the estimate itself — a tight corridor around a quantity nobody had pinned down before this paper.

The mechanic: a q×q torus grid, edges wrapping both ways, and a 2×2 stamp placeable by translation only. Cover every cell with as few stamps as possible; overlaps are free, gaps are not. A live counter shows stamps-used divided by (q/2)², the ratio the paper bounds between 1 and 2, updating as you place each stamp. Turn one ships exactly that: pick q from a short list (3 through 8), stamp the grid by clicking, hit done when every cell is lit, see your ratio.

The hard part is the dimension: the theorem only bites as n grows, and a flat 2D grid never shows why. The natural next step is an n=3 mode — the same grid rendered as stacked layers, still stampable, still instantly checkable — which is where the exponent starts working against casual play.

Crowd angle: a per-q record table of the best ratio anyone has achieved, replayable and therefore uncheatable, converging toward the true Λ_q from above.

Reuse: the `math` (geometry) hub's single-file explainer conventions; `scores` for the per-q record table.
mechanism: click-to-place 2×2 stamp covering game on a wraparound torus grid, tracking the covering-count ratio
text: click a 2×2 stamp to cover every cell on a wraparound torus. the number you need stays between one and twice the naive volume estimate. always

paperTitle: Absence of critical scaling in the Schelling segregation model
name: staircase
plan:
Absence of critical scaling in the Schelling segregation model (2608.16557) re-runs the textbook Schelling story — agents on a grid relocate when too few neighbors share their type — at a scale nobody had: grids up to 320×320, over 12,500 runs, both the classic 8-neighbor Moore rule and extensions out to 168 neighbors. The finding upends the usual telling: there is no critical phase transition. Variance scales like plain statistical averaging (L^-2, not a critical exponent), the apparent critical tolerance doesn't drift correctly with grid size, and an exponent that looks real at small grids (α=0.81 at L=40-80) flips sign and collapses at L=320. With only 8 neighbors, the segregation measure is a staircase of 23 rational thresholds, not a smooth curve — discreteness, not criticality.

The mechanic: run the actual model — tolerance slider, live grid, segregation measure plotted against tolerance as it accumulates into a staircase, thresholds visible as flat steps and jumps rather than a smooth S-curve. Turn one ships this single-grid version with the staircase made visible: toggle a line showing where the 23 rational thresholds should land, and watch your own run's steps line up with them.

The real result needs a second dial the visitor becomes a scientist to use: run the same model at several grid sizes (40, 80, 160, 320) and check whether the segregation variance's apparent scaling survives — the honest version of the finite-size-scaling test the paper actually runs, shown as a live log-log plot rather than a Binder cumulant nobody asked for.

What's hard: making 'this isn't a phase transition' land without asking visitors to know what one is — the staircase itself is the demonstration, not an argument bolted on.

Crowd: every run at every grid size adds a data point to a shared scaling dataset, which is literally how the paper got its statistical power — a thousand visitors replicate the 12,500-run study for real.

Reuse: `civ`-style canvas agent sim conventions, `packages/dataviz` for the log-log plots.
mechanism: tunable Schelling segregation simulator with a live finite-size-scaling plot across grid sizes
text: slide a tolerance dial to watch agents relocate and segregate. it builds in exactly 23 jumps at rational thresholds—not a smooth phase transition

paperTitle: Complete characterization of the sign of the wave speed in the symmetric Lotka-Volterra system under strong competition
name: frontrunner
plan:
Complete characterization of the sign of the wave speed in the symmetric Lotka-Volterra system under strong competition (2608.16845) settles a question about two species competing hard enough that neither can invade the other locally: whichever diffuses faster still wins, always, for every competition intensity above the threshold and every diffusion ratio d≠1. Cranking up how fiercely the species fight changes nothing about who wins — only the equal-diffusion case (d=1) is a genuine standoff, with front speed exactly zero. The paper calls it the 'Unity is not strength' theorem.

The mechanic: a 1D strip seeded half one color, half the other, running a simple reaction-diffusion simulation. Two dials — diffusion ratio (who moves faster) and competition intensity (how hard they fight) — and a run button that animates the interface between colors sliding one way or the other. Turn one is exactly this, with a predict-then-run flow: guess the winner before hitting run, then watch. The game the toy invites is adversarial: try to find a competition intensity strong enough to make the slower diffuser win anyway. The theorem says you can't, so every attempt is a live falsification try, and losing the attempt is the point.

What's hard: a finite-difference reaction-diffusion solver has to run smoothly client-side at interactive speed, and the front has to look decisive rather than noisy at the boundary — the visual clarity is the whole argument, since nobody's reading the sign of a wave-speed integral.

Crowd angle: log every (diffusion ratio, competition intensity) attempt and its outcome in a public table. If the theorem holds, the table should read 100% faster-diffuser-wins except along the d=1 line — a crowd-built audit of a theorem, recomputable and impossible to fake.

Reuse: `packages/dataviz` for the front-position-over-time trace; `scores` for the attempt log.
mechanism: two-species diffusion-front race with diffusion-ratio and competition-intensity dials
text: two species race for space. adjust their speed and fierceness—predict the winner before you run. the faster diffuser always wins. always. except when they're equal

paperTitle: Sample Complexity of Peer Prediction
name: honest-signal
plan:
Sample Complexity of Peer Prediction (2608.16838) asks the minimum question underneath every peer-grading, review, or crowd-rating scheme: how few paired reports does it take before you can reward honesty at all, without ever checking ground truth? The answer is exact and surprising. With three or fewer sampled report-pairs, the only reward function that never rewards vagueness or lying is trivially zero — no incentive is possible at all. At exactly four or five samples with binary reports, one specific formula (Determinant Mutual Information, DMI) is the unique nontrivial choice. At six samples, uniqueness breaks and other valid rewards appear.

The mechanic: pair visitors anonymously around a shared hidden signal (a die roll, a short ambiguous clip) that only they can see, and have both report what they saw. A running DMI-style score is computed from the accumulating history of report-pairs and shown live as a single number next to a sample-count readout. Turn one ships the single-player version against a scripted history of past bot reports: submit honest or dishonest reports and watch the reward stay flat at zero while sample count is three or fewer, then watch it snap into a real, exploitable-if-you-lie score once it crosses four to five — the exact transition the paper proves.

What's hard: 'no reward is possible' isn't something a page can argue, only demonstrate — the flat-zero score at low sample counts has to be visibly, boringly flat, not just labeled that way, or the point doesn't land.

Crowd: real peer pairing is the natural endpoint — visitors matched live around a rotating shared signal, so the DMI reward computed at scale is the genuine mechanism the paper describes, not a simulated stand-in.

Reuse: `games` room/matching machinery for live pairing; `scores` for the running reward ledger.
mechanism: paired anonymous signal-reporting game scored by a live mutual-information reward that sharpens with sample count
text: match with strangers around a hidden signal, report what you saw, and check your score. but here's the math: below four or five pairs, no reward for honesty exists. the score stays flat at zero

paperTitle: Anchoring for Truthfulness: The Random-Anchor Volume Mechanism for Multi-Facility Location
name: anchor-liars
plan: The paper is about placing k public facilities on a line when everyone who reports a location might lie to pull the facility toward themselves, and nobody is allowed to pay for honesty. It introduces the Random-Anchor Volume mechanism: pick one reported location at random as an anchor, then pick further facility sites with probability weighted by the gaps between reports. The paper's sharp fact is a boundary: this mechanism can't be gamed in expectation for one, two, or three facilities, and it always can be gamed once you ask for four or more. The toy is a multiplayer con: a room of players each type their true or fake position on a number line, the mechanism opens k facilities from the reports, and everyone's payoff is the distance to their nearest open facility. The room tries to find a lie for someone that improves their expected payoff. Turn one ships k=3: a line, draggable position markers, a 'run the mechanism' button that samples the anchor and gap-weighted picks many times, and a payoff readout per player, so a solo visitor can already poke at whether lying ever pays off before anyone else joins. The hard part is making 'strategyproof in expectation' legible without a proof — show the histogram of a hundred re-rolls per report, not a single draw, since a single draw always looks beatable by luck even when the mechanism is honest on average. Reuse the games surface for the multiplayer room and workers/scores for a running tally of confirmed successful lies at k=4, which should be common, against k=3, where none should ever confirm.
mechanism: n players report positions on a line, a randomized mechanism opens k facilities from the reports, players try to find a lie that improves their own expected distance
text: pick your spot on a line. tell the truth or lie. facilities open from everyone's reports. you win by being close. lying never helps at 3 facilities on average. lying always pays off at 4

paperTitle: Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Crossing Method
name: origin-hunt
plan: The paper answers a question about random walks: take n steps in d dimensions, draw the convex hull around the partial sums (the path's corners), and ask how often that hull contains the starting point. The result is that the answer does not depend on the shape of the step distribution at all, only on n and d, as long as steps are symmetric and exchangeable — coin flips, Gaussians, and heavy-tailed noise all give the identical probability, and there's a closed formula for it (reproving Wendel's theorem along the way). The toy hands the visitor a distribution picker (coin flip, uniform, Gaussian, a skewed one added as a deliberate trap) plus sliders for n and d, runs a batch of random walks client-side, and plots the fraction whose hull swallows the origin against the paper's closed-form number live on the same axis. Turn one ships d=2 with three preset distributions and the running histogram versus the formula line, so the coincidence is visible before anything else is built. The hard part is the trap: the invariance needs symmetry and exchangeability, so the skewed-distribution preset should visibly miss the formula, and the honest interaction is a crowd hunt for the exact boundary of the family — which small deformations of a symmetric distribution the hull still doesn't notice, and which ones break it immediately. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions and workers/scores for a record table of the closest a submitted distribution came to breaking the invariant without doing so, which anyone can re-run and check.
mechanism: pick a step distribution, dimension, and step count, run random walks client-side, and watch the origin-containment rate match (or fail to match) a single closed-form number
text: pick a distribution for your random walk steps. does the convex hull around the path trap the starting point? coin flips, gaussian noise, or any symmetric distribution gives the same answer. swap to a skewed one and it breaks

paperTitle: Drive, Pack, Fly: The Travelling Thief Problem with Drone
name: loot-and-fly
plan: The paper bolts a drone onto the travelling thief problem: a ground vehicle drives a route and steals items along the way, but every item it carries makes it heavier and slower for the rest of the trip, so grabbing loot has a real cost measured in time. A drone launched from the vehicle can fly out and grab outlying items without adding to the vehicle's load, at a rental cost charged by time. The paper's finding worth building around is that the rental price, not the fleet size, is what decides whether the drone strategy pays off — tune that one dial and profitability flips even though nothing about the map or the items changed. The toy puts the visitor in the seat: a map of item locations with values and weights, a route to draw for the ground vehicle, and a drone with a budget of flight time to assign to whichever items are worth detouring for. Every choice updates a live profit counter that subtracts both the time penalty from accumulated weight and the drone's rental clock. Turn one ships a single fixed small map (under fifteen items) where the visitor draws the ground route by clicking stops in order and toggles which items the drone grabs, with the profit number recalculating instantly — routing optimization comes later, this turn is just making the weight-slows-you-down and rental-costs-time tradeoff feel real. The hard part is tuning the rental-cost dial so both extremes are reachable by a human, since the paper's whole point is that this single number flips the optimal strategy. Reuse workers/scores for a leaderboard of best profit per fixed map and rental price, since a thousand people trying the same map is a real record of how good the tradeoff can be played, not just a demo of it.
mechanism: draw a ground route and assign drone pickups against a live profit counter that penalizes carried weight and drone rental time
text: map out a route to steal from. pick which items your drone grabs versus what you carry. weight slows you down. drone flight costs time. shift the rental price a bit—whole strategy flips

paperTitle: Steering the Flow: Inverting Face Recognition Models via Gradient-Guided Flow Matching
name: reverse-the-face
plan: The paper is a face-recognition attack: given white-box access to a deployed face classifier, an attacker can steer a generative flow model — starting from pure noise and using the classifier's own gradients as a compass — toward an image the classifier confidently calls a specific identity, without ever having a real photo of that person. Their method hits 92% attack accuracy on a standard benchmark, which is the number that makes this a live threat rather than a curiosity. The toy inverts the roles for the visitor: they get a small, consented set of synthetic faces (no real people, generated for this exhibit) and a tiny classifier trained on them, plus a fixed step budget of gradient-guided nudges to a starting noise image, and the goal is to steer it into something the classifier calls a chosen target identity while a human judge — other visitors, voting blind — decides whether the result looks like a face at all. Turn one ships the classifier and a single target identity with a visible confidence readout that updates as the visitor spends steps, no voting yet, just watching noise resolve into a face-shaped thing under gradient steering. The hard part is keeping this entirely client-side and small enough to build in WASM — the paper's own model is too large for a browser, so the exhibit is a toy-scale reproduction of the mechanism, not the paper's actual attack, and the page needs to say so plainly. Reuse the human wing's exhibit framing (rig the visitor's own eye against the classifier's), the idol wing's posture of building the thing it critiques, and the existing client-side WASM inference pattern from ocr and phylofiction.
mechanism: spend a fixed budget of gradient-guided steps steering a noise image toward a face a small classifier recognizes as a chosen target, scored on classifier confidence and human vote
text: start with noise. steer it toward a face the classifier recognizes using gradient nudges from the classifier's own math. pick a target identity, spend your step budget, watch confidence climb. this is the defense exhibit version—synthetic faces, not the real attack

paperTitle: Continual-learning rules shape representational drift
name: drift-lab
plan: The paper trains small networks on a sequence of tasks and tracks how their internal representations of the same fixed probe inputs change over time under different anti-forgetting rules. Its finding is a real trade-off, not a vague one: experience replay keeps old tasks working while representations keep drifting task after task (and drift concentrates in later layers, not early ones), while directly anchoring the old weights during learning nearly freezes drift — and freezing it also makes the network worse at picking up new tasks. Stability and drift-suppression are not the same axis, and pushing on one visibly costs the other. The toy trains a tiny image classifier in-browser across a short sequence of tasks while the visitor holds two dials: how much old data gets replayed, and how strongly old weights get anchored. A fixed set of probe images never used for training is re-embedded after every task, and the page plots how far each probe's representation has moved from its starting point, layer by layer, next to a live accuracy readout on the earliest task. Turn one ships two tasks (not the full sequence), one dial (replay amount only, anchoring fixed off), and the layer-by-layer drift plot after task two, so the stability-vs-drift picture is visible before the full dial set exists. The hard part is training fast enough in-browser to feel interactive — tiny models on tiny tasks (a handful of classes, small images), not a faithful reproduction of the paper's networks. Reuse the WASM/client-side inference pattern already shipped in ocr and phylofiction, and packages/dataviz for the layer-by-layer drift chart.
mechanism: set replay and weight-anchoring dials, train a tiny network across sequential tasks in-browser, and watch old-task accuracy and per-layer representational drift move against each other
text: set two dials: how much old training data replays, how strongly old weights stay anchored. train a tiny network across tasks in-browser. old-task accuracy and representational drift move opposite ways. lock down one, you lose grip on the other

paperTitle: Boundary Layers and Sharp Asymptotics for Maximum-Area Small Polygons
name: small-polygons
plan: A small polygon is one with diameter at most 1 — the question, decades old, is how much area you can enclose. Write A_n for the best area achievable with n vertices; this paper, building on a companion paper's characterization of the true maximizers, works out exactly how A_n approaches its limit: A_n = pi/4 - 5*pi^3/(48n^2) - q*pi^3/n^3 + O(n^-4), and near the polygon's one pendant corner the optimal shape's angles settle into an alternating, exponentially damped wiggle, decaying by a fixed ratio (-3+sqrt5)/2 at every step — a boundary layer with a golden-ratio-flavoured multiplier. The toy: drag n vertices of a polygon on a canvas, with a live diameter readout that turns red the moment you exceed 1, and a live area readout next to the theoretical A_n for whatever n you've picked. Turn one ships a fixed small n (six or seven vertices), free dragging under the diameter constraint, and the area-vs-A_n comparison — no optimizer yet, just trying to beat your own last attempt, the same personal-best pattern the pack's heilbronn page already uses. A later turn adds a zoom on the pendant corner to show the actual boundary-layer wiggle predicted by the recurrence, and an in-page annealer for larger n. The hard part: the paper only characterizes the asymptotic shape, not an explicit polygon for every n — turn one needs the Bingane-Mossinghoff construction (prior literature, not this paper) to have anything to render or compare against, and the page must be honest that matching a competition record, not proving anything, is the game. Reuse: the geometry pack's single-file scaffold, drag-and-score pattern, and personal-best localStorage from heilbronn.
mechanism: drag polygon vertices under a live diameter-one constraint and watch the area converge toward the paper's asymptotic bound
text: drag vertices under diameter-one constraint to maximize area. the optimal boundary's corner settles into a golden-ratio pattern—fully predicted by the math

paperTitle: Statistical Mechanics of a Quantum Harmonic Oscillator with Folded Gaussian Frequency
name: soft-mode
plan: Take a large population of independent quantum harmonic oscillators, but instead of giving them all the same frequency, draw each one's omega from a folded Gaussian: omega=|xi| with xi ~ N(mu, sigma^2), so frequencies pile up near zero whenever mu is small. The paper derives the exact thermodynamics of this ensemble and shows something that reads like a paradox: at mu=0, a single such oscillator's heat capacity and entropy both vanish linearly in temperature as T approaches 0, not exponentially the way a normal gapped oscillator does — which people have called a 'third-law violation' for disordered phonon systems. The paper's actual point is that it isn't a violation: it's a spectral property, a kink in the frequency distribution at omega=0 rather than a genuine energy gap, and for a full lattice of these oscillators the geometry's density-of-states factor (van Hove) turns that linear vanish into a T^d power law, where d is just the lattice's dimension. The toy: sliders for mu and sigma generate N oscillators, live-plot their pooled heat capacity C(T) on a log-log axis down to low T, and a readout measures the curve's slope. Turn one ships exactly that single-population case — dragging mu toward zero flattens the curve from a steep exponential-looking drop into a straight line, visibly, with no lattice yet. The hard part, and the honest second turn: extending from independent oscillators to an actual d-dimensional lattice needs the van Hove density-of-states factor, which is real math this ensemble alone doesn't give you, so turn one should not claim the T^d result until that's built. Reuse: packages/dataviz's stats.js and charts.js for the log-log plot and slope fit, and the math pack's single-file scaffold.
mechanism: tune the mean and spread of a disordered oscillator population's frequencies and watch the low-temperature heat-capacity curve bend from an exponential drop to a power-law line
text: spread quantum oscillator frequencies. watch the heat capacity curve transform from exponential to power law as you tune the disorder

paperTitle: The resonance graphs of coronoid systems and nanotubes
name: kekule
plan:
A hexagonal system is a patch of hexagons on the honeycomb lattice; a perfect matching (edges chosen so every vertex touches exactly one) is exactly a Kekule structure of the corresponding benzenoid molecule. Flip one hexagon whose six boundary edges alternate in and out of the matching and you get another matching -- that is the resonance graph's edge relation. For hexagonal systems with no holes this flip graph is always connected: any Kekule structure reaches any other. Cut holes in it (a 'coronoid' system) and it can fall apart into pieces no sequence of flips connects. This paper gives a graph-theoretic test -- a flow invariant computed across the cuts between each hole and the outer boundary -- for when two matchings sit in the same piece, and uses it to settle a published conjecture about nanotubes (hexagonal systems rolled into a cylinder) by constructing one whose flip graph is fully connected, against expectation.

The toy: an SVG honeycomb board with some hexagons removed as holes, one starting Kekule structure highlighted. Click a flippable hexagon (the tool detects and glows the ones whose boundary currently alternates) to flip it; try to reach a shown target structure. Turn one ships one small board where the target is reachable and a second where exhaustive check shows it isn't -- the site tells you which, and you find out by trying. The hard part is keeping 'which hexagons are flippable right now' instant as the matching changes, and picking boards small enough to enumerate every matching client-side while still surprising.

Reuse: the math wing's single-page explainer style (erdos/ and siblings) for framing; workers/scores for a public gallery -- visitors submit a hole layout, the site enumerates its matchings and reports the flip graph's component count, which anyone can re-verify by recomputing, so a claimed disconnected example can't be faked.
mechanism: click a flippable hexagon to swap the perfect matching around it, trying to reach a target matching through the flip graph
text: click flippable hexagons to rearrange the pattern, trying to reach a target. flat honeycomb boards let you reach any pattern with enough flips, but poke holes in the board and some patterns become impossible to reach

paperTitle: The Bethe-Hessian down to the Percolation Threshold
name: bethe
plan:
Take a stochastic block model -- a random graph built from planted communities -- where every vertex has the same expected degree d. The Bethe-Hessian is a specific symmetric matrix built from the graph's adjacency and degrees; its negative eigenvalues are supposed to reveal the planted communities without knowing them in advance. This paper proves the count of negative eigenvalues exactly equals the number of communities the model can in principle detect, for every d greater than 1 -- and shows d>1 is the best possible threshold, matching the classic point at which a sparse random graph even has a giant connected piece. Below that the graph is too shattered for any spectral method built this way to work, not just this one.

The toy: build a small stochastic block model live -- sliders for node count, community count k, and average degree d -- and watch two numbers race: the true k, and the live count of negative Bethe-Hessian eigenvalues, plotted as dots on a number line (red for negative). Below d=1 the red count sits at zero no matter how strong the planted signal; cross d=1 and it snaps toward k. Turn one ships the slider, the live eigenvalue plot computed client-side on a small matrix, and the two-number readout -- no leaderboard yet, just the crossing made visible.

What's hard: the Bethe-Hessian's exact matrix definition, including the regularization parameter tying it to the average degree, has to come from the paper's body rather than the abstract -- get it wrong and the crossing point won't land at d=1. Client-side eigendecomposition of even a modest matrix needs a real, if simple, symmetric eigensolver.

Reuse: packages/dataviz for the eigenvalue strip; workers/scores for a later record table -- sparsest (n, d) at which a submission still separates k communities, re-checkable by anyone since the graph and its eigenvalues are exact.
mechanism: tune a random graph's average degree and watch a live eigenvalue count try to match its planted community count
text: adjust sliders to build a random graph with planted communities and watch a race unfold: how many communities are actually there, versus how many a spectral detector finds via eigenvalues. there's a magic line—below d=1 the detector fails completely; above it, it suddenly works

paperTitle: On the Incompatibility of Weighted PROPX and Pareto Optimality for Indivisible Chores
name: chores
plan:
Splitting chores fairly usually means proportionality: everyone's burden should be at most their fair share of the total. PROPX relaxes that to 'after removing any single chore from your own pile, you're still within your fair share' -- weaker and more achievable, especially once agents carry different weights (different entitlements to burden). Pareto optimality means no other split makes someone better off without making someone else worse off. The paper shows these two reasonable-sounding requirements cannot both hold, with weights, even in the smallest case that could break them: two agents and four chores. Above that -- more chores relative to agents -- they are always compatible; two agents and four chores is exactly where compatibility fails first.

The toy hands a visitor the paper's own two-agent, four-chore instance (exact weights and per-chore costs pulled from the full paper text, not guessed) and a drag interface: put each chore in one of two piles. Two live badges, 'PROPX' and 'Pareto optimal', update on every drag. There are only sixteen possible splits; turn one lets you try them all and keeps a checklist of which you've tried, so the impossibility isn't asserted, it's exhausted -- every split fails at least one badge, and you watch it happen. The hard part is the Pareto check, which requires comparing a split's costs against every other split, not just the current one, and getting the paper's actual counterexample numbers right rather than rounder ones that don't reproduce the incompatibility.

Reuse: workers/scores for a gallery of visitor-submitted instances at larger agent counts -- every submission is a finite check (list all splits, test both properties), so a claimed new counterexample is instantly re-verifiable, the same cheat-proof property as the paper's own instance.
mechanism: assign four chores to two agents by hand, trying to build a split that is both fair and not improvable
text: drag four chores into two piles and chase two contradictory goals: fair allocation and efficiency. both badges light up... wait, no they don't. one always blinks red. try all sixteen splits and watch the incompatibility exhaust itself

paperTitle: Matched Outcomes, Divergent Gaze: How Foveated MLLMs Search Compared to Humans
name: fovea
plan:
Human eyes only see sharply where the fovea points; finding something in a scene means a series of jumps (saccades) to candidate spots, confirming or rejecting each. The paper drives three multimodal LLMs through the same jump-by-jump, blur-matched view as real humans doing goal-directed visual search, and finds a split result: on whether the target is there and on how few jumps it takes to reach it, the models match or beat humans -- near-ceiling detection, often landing on the target in one saccade, faster than people do. But the shape of the search doesn't look human: model scanpaths are low-entropy, big-jump, and eerily consistent with each other -- three different models agree with each other more than two different humans agree with each other. Same answer, same speed, different process.

The toy: a scene rendered blurred except inside a small circle that follows your clicks -- your fovea.
